# Jeremiah 6 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch1-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-ancient-paths · Jeremiah 6:1–30 · [D, multi] — the ancient paths and rest for the soul, refused; the shameless who cannot blush

**The reading.** Amid the gathering siege, God issues a tender invitation that the people reject: "**Stand by the roads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, 'We will not walk in it'**" (v.16). Their prophets and priests "**have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace**" (v.14); and their consciences are dead: "**Were they ashamed when they committed abomination? No, they were not at all ashamed; they did not know how to blush**" (v.15). Their ears "**cannot listen**… the word of the LORD is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it" (v.10); and the refining fails: "**in vain the refining goes on, for the wicked are not removed**" (v.29). The finding is **the offer of *rest for the soul* on the *ancient good way*, flatly *refused* ("we will not walk in it") — and a conscience so dead it "**did not know how to blush**"** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior offered its truest good — "**rest for your souls**" on the tested "ancient paths" — and *choosing against it* ("we will not walk in it"); and a *shamelessness* so complete that the capacity to *blush* (the body's involuntary confession of wrong) is gone, joined to a word-deafness that finds God's word "an object of scorn" and takes "no pleasure in it"** *(inferred: v.16 is one of Scripture's tenderest inner-being invitations — "**ask for the ANCIENT PATHS… the GOOD WAY… and find REST for your souls**": the finding is that the deepest rest of the interior is found on a *proven, well-worn way* (the "ancient paths" — the tested road of covenant faithfulness), and that this rest is *offered* not imposed — but the interior can *refuse its own rest*: "**but they said, We will not walk in it**"; the finding is that the self can knowingly turn from the very thing that would give it rest, preferring its own way to soul-rest (the tragedy of a freedom used against itself); and v.15 names the terminal corruption — "**they did not know how to BLUSH**": the finding is that shame is a *God-given interior alarm* (the flush that involuntarily confesses wrong), and its *loss* is a deep degradation — a conscience so seared it can do abomination and feel no heat in the face; the "blush" is the body's honesty, and its absence marks an interior that has lost even involuntary self-awareness of wrong (the shamelessness of Zeph 3:5); and the failed refining (v.29, "in vain the refining goes on") completes it — the ordinary furnace of discipline cannot purify a metal this corrupt, "the wicked are not removed": the finding is that a sufficiently hardened, shameless, rest-refusing interior becomes *unrefinable* by ordinary means)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *rest for the soul on the ancient good way, refused ("ask for the ancient paths… find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk in it")* (thread — a gem: the interior refusing its own truest rest, freedom used against itself, w/ 6:16, Matt 11:28-29, Isa 30:15); *the conscience that cannot blush ("they did not know how to blush" — shame as a God-given interior alarm, its loss a deep degradation)* (new — a gem: the flush of shame as the body's honesty, its absence marking a seared conscience, w/ 6:15, 8:12, Zeph 3:5, 1 Tim 4:2); *word-deafness and scorn ("the word of the LORD is an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it")* (thread — the interior that finds no delight in God's word, w/ 6:10, Ps 1:2 inverted); *the unrefinable interior ("in vain the refining goes on, for the wicked are not removed")* (new — a heart too corrupt for the ordinary furnace, w/ 6:29).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** rest for the soul on the ancient good way, refused; the conscience that cannot blush; word-deafness and scorn; the unrefinable interior. Chapter 6 closes batch 1 with the tender offer of *soul-rest* on the ancient paths, flatly refused — by a conscience so dead it can no longer blush.
- **Book-level note (Jeremiah batch 1, chs 1–6):** the opening movement joins the *prophet's interior* (known and consecrated before birth, his fear met by presence, his own heart breaking, 1; 4:19) with the *great indictment of the people's interior* — the *two evils* of forsaking the fountain for broken cisterns (2:13), the *self-deceiving* "I am innocent" (2:35), the *open door of return* on the sole condition of *acknowledging guilt* (3:12-13), the demand to *circumcise the heart* and evict its lodging thoughts (4:4,14), the *correction-proof hardness* and heart that will not fear (5:3,24), and the *refused rest* on the ancient paths with the conscience that *cannot blush* (6:15-16). Master-findings: **the fountain vs the broken cisterns**; **repentance is honest self-acknowledgement, not self-repair**; **the decisive renewal is of the heart (circumcised, washed, ploughed)**; and **the gravest state is the self-hardened, shameless, rest-refusing interior.**
- **Threads carried forward:** the fountain/cisterns (→ 17:13); the deceitful heart (→ 17:9); circumcised/new heart (→ 31:33, the new covenant); the weeping prophet (→ 8:18, 9:1); return / seek with the whole heart (→ 29:13).

# Jeremiah 7 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch2-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-temple-trust · Jeremiah 7:1–34 · [D, multi] — false religious security; the sanctuary as talisman divorced from the heart

**The reading.** At the temple gate Jeremiah exposes a lethal complacency: "**Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD'**" (v.4). The people commit theft, murder, adultery, and idolatry, "**and then come and stand before me in this house… and say, 'We are delivered!'—only to go on doing all these abominations**" (vv.9–10). Behind it lies the core failure: "**they did not obey or incline their ear, but walked in their own counsels and the stubbornness of their evil hearts, and went backward and not forward**" (v.24). The finding is **a *false religious security* — trusting the *sanctuary itself* as a guarantee of safety ("the temple of the LORD") while the heart and conduct are corrupt — a religion that functions as a *talisman* rather than a relationship** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior using its *religion as insurance*: the temple treated as a magic guarantee ("we are delivered!") that permits continued evil — a *decoupling* of worship from obedience, so that the sacred building becomes a cover for a stubborn, un-turned heart; God's counter is that he never wanted the ritual apparatus but the *obeying heart* ("obey my voice… but they walked in the stubbornness of their evil hearts")** *(inferred: the repeated "**the temple of the LORD**" (v.4) names a specific inner-being corruption — treating a *holy thing* (the temple, and by extension any religious possession, office, or ritual) as a *charm* that secures one regardless of how one lives; the finding is that the interior can wield its religion as *insurance against consequences* — "we are delivered!" (v.10) said by people mid-sin, using the sanctuary to underwrite continued evil; this is worship *decoupled from the heart and life* (the exact inverse of what God asks: "obey my voice", v.23); and the deep diagnosis is v.24 — they "walked in the **stubbornness of their evil hearts**, and went **backward and not forward**": the finding is that beneath the false trust is a heart that *will not turn* — the religion is loud precisely because the interior is un-changed, using the temple's holiness to avoid the heart's surrender; and the chilling phrase about child-sacrifice, "which I did not command, **nor did it come into my mind**" (v.31), shows how far a religion untethered from the true God's heart can wander into the horrific while still calling itself worship)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *religion as talisman ("do not trust in these deceptive words: the temple of the LORD" — the sanctuary treated as a charm that secures regardless of the heart)* (thread — a gem: a holy thing wielded as insurance against consequences, worship decoupled from obedience, w/ 7:4-11, Mic 3:11, Matt 3:9, 1 Sam 4:3-11); *"we are delivered!" said mid-sin (using the sacred to underwrite continued evil)* (new — a gem: the interior invoking its religion to permit its sin, w/ 7:9-10); *the un-turned heart beneath the loud religion ("the stubbornness of their evil hearts… backward and not forward")* (thread — a gem: religion loud because the interior is unchanged, w/ 7:24, 7:26); *God wants the obeying heart, not the ritual apparatus ("obey my voice… I will be your God")* (thread — w/ 7:22-23, 1 Sam 15:22, Hos 6:6).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** religion as talisman; "we are delivered!" said mid-sin; the un-turned heart beneath the loud religion; God wants the obeying heart. Chapter 7's temple sermon exposes the deepest false security — trusting the *holy building* as a charm while the heart stays stubborn and the life stays corrupt.
- **Threads:** false religious security (w/ Mic 3:11, Matt 3:9); worship decoupled from the heart (← Isa 1:11-15, 29:13; → Jer 6:20); the un-turned heart (→ 8:5).

# Jeremiah 8 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch2-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-refuse-return-balm · Jeremiah 8:1–22 · [D, multi] — the refusal to return; no "what have I done?"; the balm-in-Gilead lament

**The reading.** God marvels at an un-natural persistence in sin: "**When men fall, do they not rise again? If one turns away, does he not return? Why then has this people turned away in perpetual backsliding? They hold fast to deceit; they refuse to return**" (vv.4–5). The absence of self-examination is exact: "**no man relents of his evil, saying, 'What have I done?' Everyone turns to his own course, like a horse plunging headlong into battle**" (v.6). Even migratory birds "**know their times… but my people know not the rules of the LORD**" (v.7). The chapter closes in the prophet's grief and a famous lament: "**My joy is gone; grief is upon me; my heart is sick within me**" (v.18); "**Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?**" (v.22). The finding is **a heart in *perpetual backsliding* that "*refuses to return*", marked by the absence of the single question "**What have I done?**" — and the prophet's anguished cry over an un-healed wound ("is there no balm in Gilead?")** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior's *un-natural fixity in the wrong direction* — the normal human motion is to fall and rise, to stray and return, but this heart has broken the natural rhythm and "refuses to return"; and the precise diagnostic is the *missing self-question* — "no man… saying, 'What have I done?'": the failure of the interior to ever *stop and interrogate itself*, plunging on "like a horse into battle" without reflection** *(inferred: vv.4–6 make a subtle inner-being observation — falling and returning is the *natural* rhythm ("when men fall, do they not rise?"), so a *perpetual* non-return is *un-natural*, a breaking of the ordinary human capacity to course-correct; the finding is that sin becomes deadly when it *disables the return reflex* — "they refuse to return" is not a single act but a *settled fixity*; and the mechanism is named in the missing question — "**no man… saying, What have I done?**" (v.6): the finding is that the hinge of all repentance is the interior's willingness to *stop and ask itself the reflective question* — "what have I done?" — and its absence ("everyone turns to his own course, like a horse plunging headlong") is the mark of an un-examined life racing on without a backward glance; the bird-analogy (v.7) sharpens it — even instinct-driven creatures "know their times", but the human, gifted with reflection, "knows not" — a self *below* the migratory stork in following its true rhythm; and the prophet's lament (vv.18–22) supplies the other side — the *griever* who feels the sickness the people will not feel, crying "is there no balm?" — a healing available (Gilead was famed for balm) yet un-applied because the patient "refuses to return")*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the disabled return-reflex ("they refuse to return… perpetual backsliding" — the natural rhythm of fall-and-return broken into a settled fixity)* (thread — a gem: sin deadly when it disables the capacity to course-correct, w/ 8:4-5, 5:3, Prov 24:16); *the missing self-question ("no man… saying, What have I done?" — the un-examined life racing on without reflection)* (new — a gem: the hinge of repentance is the reflective self-interrogation, and its absence is the mark of the plunging heart, w/ 8:6, Ps 4:4, Lam 3:40, 2 Cor 13:5); *below the instinct of the stork ("even the stork knows her times… but my people know not" — the reflective creature failing to follow its true rhythm)* (new — the self beneath the migratory bird, w/ 8:7, Isa 1:3); *the un-healed wound and the available balm ("is there no balm in Gilead?… why is the health not restored?")* (thread — a gem: healing available yet un-applied because the patient refuses to return, w/ 8:22, contrast 30:17).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the disabled return-reflex; the missing self-question; below the instinct of the stork; the un-healed wound and the available balm. Chapter 8 diagnoses the deadliest failure — a heart that "refuses to return" and never asks "what have I done?" — and grieves over a healing that stands available yet un-applied.
- **Threads:** refusing to return (← 5:3; → 8:6, contrast 3:12-13); self-examination "what have I done?" (w/ Lam 3:40, Hag 1:5); the balm / healing (→ 30:17, 33:6); the weeping prophet (→ 9:1).

# Jeremiah 9 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch2-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-boast-knowing-God · Jeremiah 9:1–26 · [D, multi] — the one legitimate boast: knowing God; the weeping prophet; refusing to know God

**The reading.** The chapter opens in the prophet's tears: "**Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!**" (v.1). Society has dissolved into deceit — "**they bend their tongue like a bow… they do not know me**" (v.3); "**they refuse to know me**" (v.6). Then the chapter's summit, which relocates all human glory: "**Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me, that I am the LORD who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness in the earth. For in these things I delight**" (vv.23–24). And the closing diagnosis: all are "**uncircumcised in heart**" (v.26). The finding is **the *one legitimate boast* — not wisdom, might, or riches, but *knowing God* — set against a people who "**refuse to know**" him, and framed by the *prophet's weeping*** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior's *ground of worth and glory* relocated: the three great human securities (intellect, power, wealth) are *disqualified* as objects of boasting, and the *only* worthy boast is *knowing God* — a *relational* knowing of his character (steadfast love, justice, righteousness) — so that the self's true riches are not what it *has or achieves* but *whom it knows*; and this is set against a people who *actively "refuse to know"* God, whose hearts are "uncircumcised"** *(inferred: vv.23–24 are one of Scripture's clearest statements about where the interior may rightly find its glory — the finding is that the three things the self most naturally *boasts in* — "wisdom… might… riches" (the achievements and possessions that seem to constitute worth) — are all *disqualified*; not because they are worthless but because they are the *wrong ground* of the self's confidence; and the *one* legitimate boast is "**that he understands and KNOWS me**" (v.24): the finding is that the interior's true glory is *relational, not proprietary* — it lies not in what one has attained but in *whom one knows*, and specifically in knowing God's *character* ("steadfast love, justice, righteousness… in these I delight"); to *know God* — and to know that these are the things he *delights* in — is the only boast that will hold, because it rests the self on an inexhaustible Other rather than on its own perishable achievements; and this is sharpened by contrast — the people "**refuse to know me**" (v.6), "uncircumcised in heart" (v.26): the finding is that the very knowing which is the one worthy boast is what the corrupt interior *declines* — it would rather boast in its wisdom/might/riches than *know God*; and framing it all is the prophet's *weeping* (v.1) — the one who does know God grieving over those who refuse to)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the one legitimate boast — knowing God ("let not the wise/mighty/rich boast… but let him who boasts boast that he knows me")* (thread — a gem: the interior's true glory relocated from what it achieves to whom it knows, resting on an inexhaustible Other, w/ 9:23-24, 1 Cor 1:31, Phil 3:8, Ps 20:7); *knowing God as relational, not proprietary (knowing his character — steadfast love, justice, righteousness — in which he delights)* (new — a gem: worth in relationship, not possession, w/ 9:24, John 17:3); *refusing to know God ("they refuse to know me… uncircumcised in heart" — the very knowing that is the one worthy boast, declined)* (thread — a gem: the corrupt interior would rather boast in its achievements than know God, w/ 9:6, 4:22, Hos 4:6); *the weeping prophet ("oh that my head were waters… that I might weep" — the one who knows God grieving over those who refuse to)* (thread — a gem: the cost of knowing God amid those who refuse, w/ 9:1, 8:18, 13:17, Luke 19:41).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the one legitimate boast — knowing God; knowing God as relational not proprietary; refusing to know God; the weeping prophet. Chapter 9 relocates all human glory — not wisdom, might, or riches, but *knowing God* — against a people who "refuse to know" him, framed by the prophet's tears.
- **Threads:** boasting only in knowing God (w/ 1 Cor 1:31, Phil 3:8); refusing to know God (← 4:22; w/ Hos 4:6); the weeping prophet (← 8:18; → 13:17); uncircumcised heart (← 4:4; → 31:33).

# Jeremiah 10 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch2-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-idols-vs-living-God · Jeremiah 10:1–25 · [D, multi] — dead carried idols vs the living God; God as portion; the way of man not in himself

**The reading.** Jeremiah mocks the idols and exalts the living God: idols "**are like scarecrows in a cucumber field, and they cannot speak; they have to be carried, for they cannot walk. Do not be afraid of them, for they cannot do evil, neither is it in them to do good**" (v.5). By contrast: "**There is none like you, O LORD… the LORD is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King**" (vv.6,10); idols are "**worthless, a work of delusion**" (v.15), while "**the LORD is the portion of Jacob… the LORD of hosts is his name**" (v.16). Then the prophet's submission and a profound confession of human limitation: "**Truly this is an affliction, and I must bear it**" (v.19); "**I know, O LORD, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps. Correct me, O LORD, but in justice; not in your anger**" (vv.23–24). The finding is **dead idols (that "*must be carried*" and can do neither harm nor good) set against the *living God* who is the soul's "*portion*" — and the humbling confession that "**the way of man is not in himself**", closing in a plea for *measured correction*** *(stated)*. The operation is **the contrast of two objects of trust by their *capacity*: the idol is *inert* — carried, speechless, powerless for evil or good — a dead thing the self must prop up; the LORD is *living* — the active, true God who is the interior's *"portion"* (its allotted inheritance and treasure); and flowing from this, the interior's *honest self-limitation* — "the way of man is not in himself… not in man to direct his steps" — the confession that the self *cannot navigate its own life*, met not with despair but with a prayer to be *corrected in justice, not anger*** *(inferred: the idol-satire (v.5) makes an inner-being point by contrast — the idol "**must be carried**… **cannot do evil, neither… good**": the finding is that a false god is a *burden the worshipper sustains* (the god you carry, as Isa 46), utterly *inert*, while the LORD is "the **living** God" (v.10) who is himself the worshipper's "**portion**" (v.16, cheleq — one's allotted share, treasure, inheritance): the finding is that the interior's ultimate good is not a possession it holds but a living Person who is its *portion* — the difference between a dead thing you carry and a living God who carries and satisfies you; and then vv.23–24 turn inward with rare humility — "**the way of man is NOT IN HIMSELF, that it is not in man who walks to DIRECT HIS STEPS**": the finding is a fundamental confession of *creaturely limitation* — the self does not have within itself the resource to *direct its own life*, to know or secure its own way (the negation of autonomy); and this confession does not collapse into despair but into *dependence and submission* — "**correct me, O LORD, but in justice, not in your anger**" (v.24): the finding is that the self that admits it cannot direct itself *asks to be directed and corrected* by God, and even asks for the correction to be *measured* ("in justice… not… bring me to nothing") — a trust that welcomes discipline while pleading it be proportionate; the idol-worshipper carries a dead god and cannot direct his steps; the true worshipper is carried by the living God and submits his steps to be corrected)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the dead idol carried vs the living God who is one's portion (idols "must be carried… cannot do good or evil" vs "the living God… the portion of Jacob")* (thread — a gem: the god you prop up vs the living Person who is your treasure, w/ 10:5,10,16, Isa 46:1-4, Ps 73:26, 16:5); *"the way of man is not in himself" (the creaturely confession that the self cannot direct its own steps — the negation of autonomy)* (new — a gem: the interior's honest self-limitation, w/ 10:23, Prov 16:9, 20:24, Ps 37:23); *dependence welcoming correction ("correct me, O LORD, but in justice, not in your anger" — the self that cannot self-direct asks to be directed, pleading measured discipline)* (new — a gem: submission that welcomes proportionate correction, not despair, w/ 10:24, Ps 6:1, 38:1); *bearing affliction submissively ("this is an affliction, and I must bear it")* (thread — w/ 10:19, Lam 3:27-28).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the dead idol carried vs the living God who is one's portion; "the way of man is not in himself"; dependence welcoming correction; bearing affliction submissively. Chapter 10 sets the inert idol (a burden the self props up) against the living God who is the soul's *portion*, and confesses that the self cannot direct its own steps — asking instead to be corrected in measure.
- **Book-level note (Jeremiah batch 2, chs 7–10):** the movement exposes *false securities of the interior* and names the true good. Its findings: *religion as talisman* — the temple trusted as a charm while the heart stays stubborn (7); the *disabled return-reflex* and the missing self-question "what have I done?", with the balm that stands available yet un-applied (8); the *one legitimate boast* — knowing God rather than boasting in wisdom, might, or riches (9); and the *dead idol vs the living God who is one's portion*, closing in the confession that "the way of man is not in himself" (10). Master-findings: **worship divorced from the heart is a charm, not a relationship**; **repentance hinges on the self-question "what have I done?"**; **the interior's one true boast is knowing God**; and **the self cannot direct its own steps — it is made to be carried and corrected by the living God.**
- **Threads carried forward:** the deceitful heart (→ 17:9); knowing God (← 9:24); the fountain/portion (← 2:13; Ps 16:5); the weeping prophet (→ 13:17, 14:17); measured correction (→ 30:11).

# Jeremiah 11 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch3-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-covenant-lamb · Jeremiah 11:1–23 · [D, multi] — the innocent lamb unaware; committing the cause to the heart-testing God

**The reading.** After the covenant-lawsuit — Judah "**walked in the stubbornness of his evil heart**" (v.8) — the chapter turns personal: Jeremiah's own townsmen at Anathoth plot to kill him. Here begins the first of his *confessions*: "**But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. I did not know it was against me they devised schemes**" (v.19). His response is not revenge but *entrustment*: "**O LORD of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you have I committed my cause**" (v.20). The finding is **the wronged *innocent* — "a gentle lamb", unaware of the plot against him — *committing his cause* to "the God who tests the heart and the mind" rather than avenging himself** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior betrayed and endangered *handing over* its case to God: rather than plotting back or despairing, Jeremiah *commits* ("rolls onto", galah) his cause to the one "**who tests the heart and the mind**" — trusting that the God who *reads the interior* will judge rightly — so vindication is relinquished to God, not seized by the self** *(inferred: v.19's "**gentle lamb led to the slaughter**" images an interior *innocent and unsuspecting* — Jeremiah "did not know" the schemes, the vulnerability of the guileless among the treacherous; and his response (v.20) is the confessions' recurring inner-being posture — "**to you have I committed my cause**": the finding is that the betrayed interior's mature move is *entrustment* — to *hand over* the matter of one's vindication to God rather than to manage it oneself (revenge, self-defence, bitterness); and the ground of the entrustment is precisely that God "**tests the heart and the mind**" (v.20, boneh libbot ukelayot — examines the innermost self): the finding is that trusting God with one's cause rests on trusting that he *sees the interior truly* — both the plotter's hidden malice and the victim's real innocence — so justice can be safely left to the one who reads hearts; the "let me see your vengeance" is raw and un-sanitised (the confessions do not pretend to serenity), yet it is *committed to God*, not enacted by the self)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the innocent unaware ("like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter… I did not know" — the guileless vulnerable among the treacherous)* (thread — a gem: the unsuspecting integrity of the innocent, w/ 11:19, Isa 53:7, Ps 44:22); *committing the cause to God ("to you have I committed my cause" — the betrayed interior handing over its vindication rather than avenging itself)* (thread — a gem: entrustment instead of self-managed revenge, w/ 11:20, 20:12, Rom 12:19, 1 Pet 2:23); *trusting the God who tests the heart ("who tests the heart and the mind" — justice safely left to the one who reads the interior)* (thread — a gem: entrustment grounded in God's true sight of the heart, w/ 11:20, 17:10, Ps 7:9); *the raw un-sanitised plea ("let me see your vengeance" — committed to God, not enacted by the self)* (new — the confessions' honest, un-serene prayer, w/ 11:20, 20:12).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the innocent unaware; committing the cause to God; trusting the God who tests the heart; the raw un-sanitised plea. Chapter 11 opens Jeremiah's confessions — the betrayed prophet, "a gentle lamb", *entrusting* his cause to the God who reads the interior rather than avenging himself.
- **Threads:** the confessions (→ 12:1, 15:10, 17:14, 20:7); committing one's cause / not avenging (→ 20:12; w/ Rom 12:19, 1 Pet 2:23); God tests the heart (→ 17:10; w/ Ps 7:9).

# Jeremiah 12 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch3-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-why-wicked-prosper · Jeremiah 12:1–17 · [D, multi] — the complaint of the prospering wicked; the toughening answer; God's own grief

**The reading.** The second confession opens with the ancient wound: "**Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why do all who are treacherous thrive?**" (v.1). Jeremiah notes the hypocrites' interior: "**you are near in their mouth and far from their heart**" (v.2). God's answer is not consolation but a *summons to be toughened*: "**If you have raced with men on foot, and they have wearied you, how will you compete with horses? And if in a safe land you are so trusting, what will you do in the thicket of the Jordan?**" (v.5). And God discloses his *own* grief: "**I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my heritage; I have given the beloved of my soul into the hands of her enemies**" (v.7). The finding is **the honest complaint "**why does the way of the wicked prosper?**" — met not by an explanation but by a *call to grow stronger* ("how will you compete with horses?") — and God's own *grieved* heart over the judgment he must bring** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior *permitted to argue* with God ("I would plead my case", opening with "righteous are you" — the complaint framed *inside* faith), and *answered* not with the resolution it wanted but with a *challenge to endure harder things* — the racing-with-horses answer that treats the present distress as *training* for worse to come; and the disclosure that God himself is *grieved*, giving up "the beloved of my soul", so the sufferer is not alone in his anguish** *(inferred: v.1's complaint is a model of *faithful protest* — Jeremiah does not conclude against God ("**RIGHTEOUS are you, O LORD**") yet insists on pleading his case: the finding is that the interior may bring its hardest question ("why do the wicked prosper?") *to* God, honestly, without it being unbelief — the complaint is lodged *within* the relationship, not against it; and God's answer (v.5) is startling and instructive — instead of *explaining* the prosperity of the wicked, he *raises the stakes*: "if footmen have wearied you, how will you race horses?" — the finding is that God sometimes answers the interior's "why?" not with an explanation but with a *summons to greater strength*, treating the present trial as *preparation* for harder ones (the answer reframes the complaint as a training-question: are you being toughened or worn down?); and v.7 opens an unexpected window — "**the beloved of my soul**" given to her enemies: the finding is that the God who must judge is himself *grieved* by it, so the prophet's anguish over his people is *shared* by God — the sufferer complains to a God who is *also* suffering the loss)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *faithful protest ("righteous are you… yet I would plead my case: why does the way of the wicked prosper?" — the hardest question lodged inside faith, not against it)* (thread — a gem: honest complaint that does not conclude against God, w/ 12:1, Hab 1:2-4, Ps 73:1-3, Job 21); *near in the mouth, far from the heart (the hypocrite's interior — God on the lips, absent from the heart)* (thread — w/ 12:2, Isa 29:13, Matt 15:8); *the toughening answer ("how will you compete with horses?" — the "why?" met not with explanation but a summons to greater strength, the trial as training)* (new — a gem: God reframing the complaint as a training-question, w/ 12:5, Heb 12:1-11); *God's own grief ("the beloved of my soul given to her enemies" — the judging God himself grieved; the sufferer's anguish shared by God)* (new — a gem: the interior complains to a God who also suffers the loss, w/ 12:7, Hos 11:8, Luke 19:41).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** faithful protest; near in the mouth far from the heart; the toughening answer; God's own grief. Chapter 12 (confession 2) lets the prophet lodge the hardest question inside his faith — "why do the wicked prosper?" — and is answered not with explanation but a summons to be toughened, by a God who is himself grieved.
- **Threads:** faithful protest / "why?" (← Hab 1; w/ Ps 73, Job 21); the toughening answer (w/ Heb 12); God's grief (→ Hos 11:8; ← Isa 63:9).

# Jeremiah 13 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch3-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-loincloth-cling · Jeremiah 13:1–27 · [D, multi] — made to cling to God; pride spoiling; the leopard's spots

**The reading.** Jeremiah wears a linen loincloth (worn against the skin), hides it by the Euphrates, and finds it later "**spoiled… good for nothing**" (v.7). The meaning: "**As the loincloth clings to the waist of a man, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me, declares the LORD, that they might be for me a people, a name, a praise, and a glory, but they would not listen**" (v.11); "**even so will I spoil the pride of Judah**" (v.9). The prophet grieves: "**if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride**" (v.17). And the diagnosis of habituated evil: "**Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil**" (v.23). The finding is **the intimacy God *intended* — a people "made to *cling* to him" like a garment worn close, for his "praise and glory" — *refused* through *pride*; and the sobering law that a self *accustomed to evil* can no more do good than a leopard change its spots** *(stated)*. The operation is **the disclosure of God's *design for the interior* — to be worn *close against him*, clinging like an intimate garment, existing "for his glory" — and the tragedy of that intimacy *spoiled by pride*; and the exposure of *habituation* — evil practised long enough becomes *second nature*, so ingrained the self *cannot reform itself* ("accustomed to do evil")** *(inferred: the loincloth-image (v.11) is a startling picture of *intended intimacy* — "**as the loincloth CLINGS to the waist… so I made [them] CLING TO ME**": the finding is that God designed the interior to be worn *close against himself*, in the most intimate proximity, "**for a people, a name, a praise, and a glory**" — the self's very purpose is nearness to God and being his adornment; and the ruin of this is *pride* ("I will spoil the **pride**", v.9) — the swollen self will not be worn close, and so, like the buried loincloth, rots "good for nothing" (the intimacy refused leaves the self useless to its purpose); and v.23 names the deeper bind — "**can the leopard change his spots? then also you can do good who are ACCUSTOMED to do evil**": the finding is that evil *habituated* becomes *constitutional* — practised so long it is now the self's "spots", as unchangeable by mere effort as skin-colour; the finding is not that change is impossible absolutely (God can give a new heart) but that *self*-reform is impossible for a will grooved by long habit — the accustomed evildoer cannot lift himself out; the prophet's response is *secret weeping* over their pride (v.17) — grief, not contempt, over an interior that has made itself unable to return)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *made to cling to God (the interior designed to be worn close against him, for his praise and glory)* (new — a gem: the self's purpose is intimate nearness to God, clinging like a garment, w/ 13:11, Deut 10:20, Ps 63:8); *intimacy spoiled by pride ("I will spoil the pride… but they would not listen" — the swollen self refusing to be worn close, rotting useless)* (thread — a gem: pride ruining the intended intimacy, w/ 13:9,15,17); *habituated evil as second nature ("can the leopard change his spots? then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil" — evil practised long enough becomes constitutional, beyond self-reform)* (new — a gem: the accustomed will cannot lift itself out, w/ 13:23, Rom 7:18, Ezek 36:26); *secret weeping over pride ("my soul will weep in secret for your pride" — grief, not contempt, over the self made unable to return)* (thread — w/ 13:17, 9:1, Luke 19:41).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** made to cling to God; intimacy spoiled by pride; habituated evil as second nature; secret weeping over pride. Chapter 13 discloses the interior's designed *intimacy* — worn close against God like a garment — ruined by pride, and the bind of *habituated evil* that a self cannot reform on its own.
- **Threads:** clinging to God / intended intimacy (w/ Deut 10:20, Ps 63:8); pride (← 13:9; → 48:29); habituated evil / the need of a new heart (→ 17:9, 31:33; w/ Ezek 36:26); the weeping prophet (← 9:1; → 14:17).

# Jeremiah 14 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch3-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-drought-hope · Jeremiah 14:1–22 · [D, multi] — hope set on God amid deserved judgment; "do not leave us"; the prophet's tears

**The reading.** In a devastating drought, the people pray a remarkable prayer — *owning* their guilt yet *appealing* to God's own name: "**Though our iniquities testify against us, act, O LORD, for your name's sake; for our backslidings are many; we have sinned against you. O you hope of Israel, its saviour in time of trouble, why should you be like a stranger in the land?… Yet you, O LORD, are in the midst of us, and we are called by your name; do not leave us**" (vv.7–9). The prophet weeps: "**let my eyes run down with tears night and day… for the virgin daughter of my people is shattered**" (v.17). The chapter closes with hope pinned on God alone: "**Are there any among the false gods of the nations that can bring rain?… Are you not he, O LORD our God? We set our hope on you, for you do all these things**" (v.22). The finding is **a prayer that *acknowledges deserved judgment yet appeals to God's name and presence* ("do not leave us"), setting its *whole hope on God alone* ("we set our hope on you")** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior praying from *within* its guilt — not denying the judgment is deserved ("our iniquities testify against us… we have sinned") but appealing *past its own worthiness* to *God's character and presence* ("for your name's sake"; "you are in the midst of us; do not leave us") — and locating its *entire hope* in God as the only one who can give what is needed (rain, salvation)** *(inferred: the prayer's structure is instructive — it *fully concedes* the guilt ("our backslidings are many; we have sinned", v.7) yet does not therefore despair; instead it *pivots to God's own name*: "act **for your name's sake**" (v.7): the finding is that a heart praying from acknowledged guilt can still appeal — not on its own merit (there is none) but on *God's* stake in his people ("we are called by your name", v.9); and the plea "**do not leave us**" (v.9) names the interior's deepest fear (God as "a stranger… a traveler who turns aside for a night", v.8 — present but detached) and asks for the opposite — *committed presence*; and the closing "**we set our hope on you**" (v.22) locates hope by *elimination* — the idols cannot bring rain, only the LORD can, so the interior's hope is fixed on the sole One able to give: the finding is that hope, at its truest, is *not optimism about outcomes* but a *settled reliance on the only One who can act* — pinned to God's character and ability precisely when one's own case is hopeless)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *praying from within acknowledged guilt ("our iniquities testify against us… yet act, O LORD, for your name's sake" — conceding the judgment is deserved yet appealing past one's worthiness to God's name)* (thread — a gem: the guilty heart appealing on God's stake, not its own merit, w/ 14:7, Dan 9:18-19, Ps 25:11, 79:9); *"do not leave us" — the fear of God as a detached stranger answered by asking for committed presence* (new — a gem: the interior's deepest fear (God present but detached) met by the plea for real nearness, w/ 14:8-9, Exod 33:15); *hope set on God alone by elimination ("are there any among the idols that can bring rain?… we set our hope on you" — hope fixed on the only One able to act)* (thread — a gem: hope as settled reliance on the sole One who can give, not optimism about outcomes, w/ 14:22, 17:13, Ps 130:5-7); *the prophet's ceaseless tears ("let my eyes run down with tears night and day")* (thread — w/ 14:17, 9:1, 13:17).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** praying from within acknowledged guilt; "do not leave us"; hope set on God alone by elimination; the prophet's ceaseless tears. Chapter 14 models the prayer of a guilty people who do not deny the judgment but appeal to God's *name and presence*, pinning their whole hope on the only One who can act.
- **Threads:** praying from guilt on God's name (w/ Dan 9:18-19, Ps 79:9); committed presence (w/ Exod 33:15); hope on God alone (→ 17:13; w/ Ps 130); the weeping prophet (← 9:1, 13:17).

# Jeremiah 15 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch3-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-woe-is-me-return · Jeremiah 15:1–21 · [D, multi] — eating God's words as delight; the isolation of the calling; the raw complaint; the prophet called to return

**The reading.** The third confession is the rawest yet. Jeremiah laments his very existence: "**Woe is me, my mother, that you bore me, a man of strife and contention to the whole land!**" (v.10). He recalls the joy of God's word: "**Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart, for I am called by your name, O LORD**" (v.16). He names the cost — isolation: "**I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation**" (v.17). Then he accuses God directly: "**Why is my pain unceasing, my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?**" (v.18). God's answer is stunning — the prophet himself is called to *repent*: "**If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me. If you utter what is precious, and not what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth**" (v.19); and re-commissioned, "**I am with you to save you**" (v.20). The finding is **the word of God *eaten as joy and heart-delight*, the *isolation* it costs, a *raw accusation* (God as a "deceitful brook"), and God's answer calling the *prophet himself to return*** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior of the suffering servant of the word laid bare — its *nourishment* ("I ate your words… the delight of my heart"), its *loneliness* ("I sat alone"), and its *breaking-point* where it accuses God of failing it ("like waters that fail") — met not by rebuke but by a *call to the complainer himself to repent* of his worthless words and return, with the promise of renewed presence** *(inferred: three inner-being movements. First, "**I ate them, and your words became… the delight of my heart**" (v.16): the finding is that God's word can be the interior's deepest *nourishment and joy* — internalised ("ate"), it becomes *gladness*, not duty (the same as Ps 119); the word feeds the self. Second, the *cost* — "**I sat ALONE, because your hand was upon me**" (v.17): the finding is that a genuine calling can *isolate* — the hand of God that fills one with his concern also sets one apart from ordinary fellowship ("did not sit with revelers"); the joy of the word and the loneliness of the vocation coexist. Third, and most striking, the *complaint and its answer* — Jeremiah accuses God of being "**a deceitful brook, waters that fail**" (v.18, the bitterest thing a thirsty man can say — the stream you counted on has dried up), and God's reply is not "how dare you" but "**IF YOU RETURN, I will restore you**" (v.19): the finding is that even the *prophet* — the faithful sufferer — needs to *repent*, to sort "the precious from the worthless" in his own words, and that God's restoration is offered to him on the same terms as to everyone (return); the confession is honest enough to show the man of God himself faltering into bitter accusation, and grace enough to show God calling him back rather than casting him off — "I am with you to save you" (v.20))*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *God's word eaten as joy and heart-delight ("I ate them, and your words became the delight of my heart" — the word as the interior's nourishment and gladness, not duty)* (thread — a gem: the word internalised becomes joy, w/ 15:16, Ps 119:103, Ezek 3:3, Job 23:12); *the isolation of the calling ("I sat alone, because your hand was upon me" — the vocation that sets one apart from ordinary fellowship)* (new — a gem: joy of the word and loneliness of the calling coexisting, w/ 15:17, Ps 102:7); *the raw accusation against God ("will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?" — the faithful sufferer's bitter complaint)* (thread — a gem: the honest breaking-point where even the man of God accuses him, w/ 15:18, 20:7, Job 6:15-20); *the prophet himself called to return ("if you return, I will restore you… utter what is precious, not worthless" — grace calling the complainer to repent, not casting him off)* (new — a gem: even the faithful sufferer needs to return, restored on the same terms, w/ 15:19, Rev 2:5).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** God's word eaten as joy and heart-delight; the isolation of the calling; the raw accusation against God; the prophet himself called to return. Chapter 15 (confession 3) lays bare the servant of the word — its nourishment, its loneliness, its bitter breaking-point — and God's answer calling the *prophet himself* to repent and be restored.
- **Threads:** the word as delight (w/ Ps 119:103, Ezek 3:3); the raw complaint (→ 20:7; w/ Job 6:15); the sufferer called to return (w/ Rev 2:5); "I am with you" (← 1:8, 19; 15:20).

# Jeremiah 16 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch3-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-no-wife-refuge · Jeremiah 16:1–21 · [D, multi] — the costly sign-bearing life; God as strength, stronghold, refuge

**The reading.** Jeremiah's *life itself* is made a sign of the coming desolation: he is forbidden to marry and have children (v.2), forbidden to enter "**the house of mourning**" to grieve the dead (v.5), forbidden to enter "**the house of feasting**" to celebrate (v.8) — every ordinary human comfort withheld as a living parable. Behind the people's coming exile is the old failure: "**every one of you follows his stubborn, evil will, refusing to listen to me**" (v.12). Yet the chapter closes in the prophet's confession of trust: "**O LORD, my strength and my stronghold, my refuge in the day of trouble, to you shall the nations come… and say: 'Our fathers have inherited nothing but lies… Can man make for himself gods? Such are not gods!'**" (vv.19–20). The finding is **a *vocation so costly it renounces marriage, mourning, and feasting* — the prophet's whole life bent into a sign — held together by a confession of *God as "strength, stronghold, refuge"*** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior asked to *forgo ordinary human goods* (family, shared grief, shared joy) for the sake of the calling — its personal life *emptied* to become a message — and *sustained* not by those forgone comforts but by *God himself* as its "strength, stronghold, and refuge"** *(inferred: the threefold renunciation (vv.2,5,8) is extraordinary — no wife, no attendance at funerals, no attendance at feasts: the finding is that a calling can demand the *surrender of ordinary human comforts* — even the basic solidarities of shared grief and shared joy — so that the prophet's very *loneliness and abstention* preach (his empty life embodies the coming end of "the voice of mirth and the voice of the bridegroom", v.9); the interior here bears a cost that goes beyond words into the shape of a whole life; and the sustaining counterweight is the confession of vv.19–20 — "**O LORD, MY STRENGTH and my STRONGHOLD, my REFUGE in the day of trouble**": the finding is that the self stripped of ordinary supports finds its support *in God directly* — when family, fellowship, and celebration are withheld, God himself becomes the strength, the fortress, the shelter (the same triple refuge as Ps 18:2); the renunciation is bearable only because the One for whom it is made is *himself* the refuge that the renounced things could only have partially given; and the contrast is drawn — the nations will confess their inherited "lies" and self-made "gods" that "are not gods" (v.20), while the prophet's refuge is the living God — so the costly emptying is not loss into a void but exchange of lesser comforts for the ultimate one)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the costly sign-bearing life (marriage, mourning, and feasting renounced — the whole life bent into a message)* (new — a gem: a calling that demands the surrender of ordinary human comforts, the empty life itself preaching, w/ 16:2-9, Ezek 24:16-18, 1 Cor 7:29-31); *the self sustained by God when ordinary supports are withheld ("my strength and my stronghold, my refuge in the day of trouble")* (thread — a gem: God himself the support when family/fellowship/joy are stripped away, w/ 16:19, Ps 18:2, 46:1); *the exchange of lesser comforts for the ultimate refuge (the renounced goods given only partially what God gives fully)* (new — the emptying as exchange, not void, w/ 16:19-20); *self-made gods that are not gods ("can man make for himself gods? such are not gods")* (thread — w/ 16:20, 10:5, Isa 44:9-20).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the costly sign-bearing life; the self sustained by God when ordinary supports are withheld; the exchange of lesser comforts for the ultimate refuge; self-made gods that are not gods. Chapter 16 shows a vocation so costly it empties the prophet's ordinary life into a sign — sustained only by God as "strength, stronghold, refuge".
- **Threads:** the costly calling (← 15:17; w/ Ezek 24:16-18); God as refuge/stronghold (→ 17:17; w/ Ps 18:2, 46:1); idols not gods (← 10:5; w/ Isa 44).

# Jeremiah 17 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch3-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-heart-deceitful-trust · Jeremiah 17:1–27 · [D, multi] — the two trusts; the deceitful heart searched by God; heal me

**The reading.** The chapter opens with sin *engraved on the interior*: "**The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron; with a point of diamond it is engraved on the tablet of their heart**" (v.1). Then the two ways, defined by *what the heart trusts*: "**Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the LORD. He is like a shrub in the desert… in an uninhabited salt land**" (vv.5–6); "**Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD… He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes… is not anxious in the year of drought**" (vv.7–8). Then the great diagnosis: "**The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it? 'I the LORD search the heart and test the mind'**" (vv.9–10). And the prophet's plea: "**Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed**" (v.14). The finding is **two interiors distinguished by their *trust* — the man trusting *flesh* (a desert shrub) and the man trusting *the LORD* (a water-rooted tree) — and the *deceitful, unsearchable heart* that only *God* can read and heal** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior's stability shown to depend entirely on the *object of its trust*: trust in "flesh" (man, self, the created) leaves it a *stunted shrub in salt land* — exposed, fruitless, unwatered; trust in "the LORD" makes it a *tree by the stream* — rooted, *unafraid in heat*, *un-anxious in drought*, fruitful regardless of conditions; and beneath the choice lies the *deceitful heart* — so twisted it deceives even *itself* ("who can understand it?"), knowable only to the God who "searches the heart", and healable only by him** *(inferred: vv.5–8 draw the definitive contrast of the interior by its *trust-object* — the finding is that the self's *stability, fruitfulness, and freedom from fear* are functions of *what it trusts*: the one who "makes flesh his strength" (v.5, trusting the human, the created, the self) is a "shrub in the desert" — *stunted and exposed*, in "a salt land" where nothing grows; the one who "trusts in the LORD" is "a tree planted by water" whose *roots reach the stream*, so that "**when heat comes**" and "**in the year of drought**" it does *not fear* and is *not anxious* but *still bears fruit* (vv.7–8): the finding is that trust in God produces an interior *un-shaken by adverse circumstances* — the tree's roots reach past the surface weather to a constant source, so heat and drought (the trials that wither the shrub) cannot touch its life; and vv.9–10 supply the reason such trust cannot be self-generated — "**the heart is deceitful above all things… who can understand it?**": the finding is that the heart is *not transparent even to itself* — it deceives its own owner, so twisted and sick that no self-examination can fully know it ("who can understand it?"), and *only God* "searches the heart" (v.10) and can *heal* it (v.14, "heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed"); so the two trusts and the deceitful heart belong together — the self cannot be trusted (deceitful), therefore the self must not be the object of trust (cursed shrub), therefore trust must rest on the LORD (blessed tree), and the deceitful heart itself must be searched and healed by God, not by its own inspection)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the two trusts — flesh vs the LORD ("cursed is the man who trusts in man… blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD" — the interior's stability a function of its trust-object)* (thread — a gem: what the self trusts determines whether it is a stunted shrub or a water-rooted tree, w/ 17:5-8, Ps 1, Prov 3:5); *trust in God as freedom from fear in adversity (the tree "does not fear when heat comes… not anxious in the year of drought" — roots past the surface weather to a constant source)* (new — a gem: the God-trusting interior un-shaken by the trials that wither the self-truster, w/ 17:8, Ps 46, Isa 26:3); *the deceitful, self-opaque heart ("the heart is deceitful above all things… who can understand it?" — the heart that deceives even its own owner)* (thread — a gem: the interior not transparent to itself, beyond self-examination, w/ 17:9, Ps 19:12, Jer 2:35); *only God searches and heals the heart ("I the LORD search the heart… heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed" — the heart knowable and curable only by God)* (thread — a gem: the deceitful heart must be searched and healed by God, not by its own inspection, w/ 17:10,14, Ps 139:23-24, Ezek 36:26).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the two trusts — flesh vs the LORD; trust in God as freedom from fear in adversity; the deceitful, self-opaque heart; only God searches and heals the heart. Chapter 17 is batch 3's summit — the interior is a stunted shrub or a water-rooted tree depending on *what it trusts*, and its deceitful, self-opaque heart can be known and healed only by God.
- **Book-level note (Jeremiah batch 3, chs 11–17):** the movement joins the *prophet's confessions* — the betrayed lamb committing his cause (11), the "why do the wicked prosper?" met by the toughening answer (12), the raw "deceitful brook" complaint answered by a call to the prophet's own return (15), the sign-bearing life sustained by God as refuge (16) — with the great *diagnoses of the heart*: made to *cling* to God but spoiled by pride and *habituated evil* (13); praying *from within guilt* on God's name (14); and the summit — the *two trusts* (shrub vs tree) and the *deceitful heart* that only God can search and heal (17). Master-findings: **the interior is designed to cling to God**; **its stability is a function of what it trusts (flesh withers, God-trust bears fruit through drought)**; **the heart is deceitful even to itself and healable only by God**; and **even the faithful sufferer is called to return.**
- **Threads carried forward:** the deceitful heart / new heart (→ 31:33); the fountain of living water (← 2:13; 17:13); committing one's cause (→ 20:12); trust (Ps 1; Isa 26:3); the confessions (→ 20:7-18).

# Jeremiah 18 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch4-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-potter-clay · Jeremiah 18:1–23 · [D, multi] — the reworkable clay; God's dealing conditional on turning; the defiant self-will

**The reading.** At the potter's house Jeremiah watches: "**the vessel he was making of clay was spoiled in the potter's hand, and he reworked it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter**" (v.4). The lesson: "**like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel**" (v.6) — and God's dealing is *responsive*: "**if that nation… turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster… if it does evil… I will relent of the good**" (vv.7–10). So the summons: "**Return, every one from his evil way**" (v.11). But the people answer with flat defiance: "**That is in vain! We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart**" (v.12). The finding is **the interior as *clay in the potter's hand* — *reworkable* when spoiled, its future *conditional on turning* — met by a *defiant self-will* that says "we will follow our own plans"** *(stated)*. The operation is **the disclosure that the self is *malleable in God's hands* — spoiled clay *reworked*, not discarded — and that God's dealings are *not fixed fate but responsive* to the interior's *turning* ("if it turns… I will relent"); against which stands the *hardened autonomy* that refuses the potter's hand — "we will follow our own plans… the stubbornness of his evil heart"** *(inferred: the potter-image (vv.4,6) makes two inner-being points. First, the self is *clay* — pliable, *re-formable*: the "spoiled" vessel is not thrown away but "**reworked into another vessel**" — the finding is that the interior, marred, remains *workable* in God's hands, capable of being made again (grace as re-formation, not scrapping); second, and crucially, vv.7–10 attach a *conditionality* — God's declared intentions (to pluck up or to build) are *responsive to the interior's response*: "if that nation **turns**… I will relent" — the finding is that the future is not sealed fate but genuinely *hinges on the heart's turning*, so repentance is never futile (God stands ready to "relent"); against this open, hopeful picture stands v.12's chilling refusal — "**That is in vain! We will follow OUR OWN PLANS**": the finding is that the defiant self *rejects the potter's hand altogether* — it will not be clay, insisting on its "own plans" and "the stubbornness of its evil heart"; the tragedy is not that God will not rework them but that they *will not be reworked* — the clay that hardens itself against the wheel; the imprecatory close (vv.19-23) shows even the prophet's interior strained to the point of praying against his plotters — the confessions do not sanitise his anguish)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the self as reworkable clay (the spoiled vessel "reworked into another" — the interior marred yet re-formable in God's hands)* (thread — a gem: grace as re-formation, not scrapping, w/ 18:4,6, Isa 64:8, Rom 9:20-21); *God's dealings conditional on turning ("if that nation turns… I will relent" — the future hinging on the heart's response, so repentance is never futile)* (new — a gem: not sealed fate but responsive to turning, w/ 18:7-10, Jonah 3:10, Ezek 18:21-23); *the defiant self that will not be clay ("we will follow our own plans… the stubbornness of his evil heart" — the interior refusing the potter's hand)* (thread — a gem: hardened autonomy rejecting re-formation, w/ 18:12, 2:25, 7:24); *the strained imprecatory heart (the prophet's anguish praying against his plotters)* (thread — the confessions' un-sanitised rawness, w/ 18:19-23, 20:12).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the self as reworkable clay; God's dealings conditional on turning; the defiant self that will not be clay; the strained imprecatory heart. Chapter 18 offers the hopeful picture — the interior is *reworkable* clay and its future *hinges on turning* — against the defiant "we will follow our own plans".
- **Threads:** potter/clay (← Isa 29:16, 45:9, 64:8; → 19:11); conditional relenting (w/ Jonah 3:10, Ezek 18); defiant self-will (← 2:25, 7:24); the confessions (← 15:18; → 20:7).

# Jeremiah 19 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch4-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-broken-flask · Jeremiah 19:1–15 · [D, multi] — the fired flask broken past mending; the point of no return; the stiffened neck

**The reading.** Where chapter 18 showed soft clay *reworked*, chapter 19 shows a *fired* vessel *shattered*. Jeremiah takes "**a potter's earthenware flask**" (v.1) to the Valley of Slaughter, and after pronouncing judgment, "**you shall break the flask… and shall say, 'So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel, so that it can never be mended'**" (vv.10–11). The cause is the same hardening: "**they have stiffened their neck, refusing to hear my words**" (v.15). The finding is **the *fired flask broken irreparably* ("so that it can never be mended") — the dark counterpart to the reworkable clay — marking a *point past re-forming*, reached by a *stiffened neck* that "refused to hear"** *(stated)*. The operation is **the sober disclosure that the interior which *will not be reworked* (18:12) eventually passes from *soft clay* to *fired pottery* — from the state where it can be re-formed to the state where it can only be *broken*; the difference is *time and hardening*: the neck "stiffened" long enough becomes a vessel set hard, and set hard, it "can never be mended"** *(inferred: the two potter-signs are deliberately paired and must be read together. Chapter 18's clay is *soft, on the wheel* — spoiled but *reworkable* ("reworked into another vessel"); chapter 19's flask is *fired, finished* — and when it fails, it can only be *smashed* ("**can never be mended**", v.11): the finding is that there is a *movement* in the hardening interior from the *malleable* to the *set* — a heart that repeatedly refuses the potter's hand does not stay soft forever but *fires hard*, passing a threshold past which re-formation is no longer possible; the "stiffened neck, refusing to hear" (v.15) is the process that fires the clay; the finding is a solemn warning about the *urgency* of turning — the same self is, at one stage, re-formable clay (grace's invitation, 18) and at a later stage, a brittle vessel fit only for breaking (judgment's finality, 19) — and the transition is made by *persistent refusal to hear*; the interior does not remain indefinitely open; hardening, prolonged, becomes irreversible)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the fired flask broken past mending ("so will I break this people… that it can never be mended" — the interior passed from reworkable clay to set pottery fit only for breaking)* (thread — a gem: the movement from malleable to irreparable, the dark counterpart to ch.18, w/ 19:11, Prov 29:1, Heb 6:4-6); *hardening as a threshold-crossing process ("they have stiffened their neck, refusing to hear" — the persistent refusal that fires the clay hard)* (new — a gem: prolonged refusal moving the self past re-formation, w/ 19:15, 7:26, Zech 7:11-12); *the urgency of turning while still soft (the two potter-signs paired — grace's invitation before the clay fires)* (new — the solemn warning about time, w/ 18:4/19:11, 2 Cor 6:2).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the fired flask broken past mending; hardening as a threshold-crossing process; the urgency of turning while still soft. Chapter 19 is the dark counterpart to chapter 18 — the interior that will not be *reworked* as soft clay eventually *fires hard* into a flask that "can never be mended".
- **Threads:** the reworkable clay vs the fired flask (← 18:4; 19:11); the stiffened neck / hardening (← 7:26, 17:23; w/ Prov 29:1); the point of no return (w/ Heb 6:4-6).
