# M02 · C2 — Divine Wrath — Tier Catalogue Analysis

- **File:** wa-m02-c2-divine-wrath-tieranalysis-v1_1-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Cluster / Characteristic:** M02 "Anger, Wrath and Indignation" · C2 Divine wrath (God as possessor/agent)
- **Version:** v1_1 · **Author:** le Roux Cilliers
- **Prior output (this session):** wa-m02-c1-human-anger-tieranalysis-v1_0-20260619.md
- **Catalogue answered:** WA-tier-catalogue-current-state-v2-20260619.md (126 questions, T0–T7) · **Science lens (T7.3):** wa-m02-anger-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md

**Change control (v1_0):** First issue. All 126 questions answered for C2.
**Change control (v1_1, 2026-06-19):** valence confirmed current by CC and **integrated** (see _Valence integration_ below; the v1_0 PARKED marker was out of date); consolidated **essay-sufficient Evidence Base** appended (incl. lemma_meaning, cause_clause, raw object); **lexical-coverage self-audit passed** (all populated fields represented; `mode` absent from the M02 extract). The v1_0 question-by-question answers stand unchanged.

**Evidence basis.** C2 = 145 focus-occurrences (OT 140 / NT 5) where God is the possessor or agent of the anger: cheˈmah (51), chaˈron "burning anger" (32), chaˈrah (26), qeˈtseph (13), qaˈtsaph (8), aˈnaph (7), orgē (5). Concentrated in Jeremiah (21), Isaiah (16), Ezekiel (16), Deuteronomy (15), 2 Chronicles (13), Psalms (13), Numbers (10). div_role: possessor 83, agent 61, giver 1. Every observation cited; "Silent." where the C2 verses do not speak. valence integrated (CC-confirmed current 2026-06-19; see _Valence integration_ below).

**Object-type note.** In C2, object_type="God" (27 occ) is the mechanical tagging of the divine name adjacent to the wrath ("wrath **of** the LORD") — i.e. the possessor genitive, not God as the *target* of wrath. It is read accordingly and not as wrath directed at God.

---

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design

**T0.1.1** — Predicated of God directly: the wrath is God's, with God as **possessor** ("the wrath of the LORD," Exo 15:7; Num 32:14; Deu 29:23) or **agent** ("the LORD's anger was kindled," Gen 18:30; Exo 22:24; Num 11:1). This is the defining relation of C2.

**T0.1.2** — Across C2 the characteristic is **borne by God himself** throughout (possessor/agent in 144 of 145). *Interpretation:* that the same vocabulary borne by the creature (C1) is here predicated of God establishes anger as belonging to the divine nature as a righteous response — the human instance (C1) is the creaturely correspondent (Divine-Human Correspondence dimension).

**T0.2.1** — Stated purpose/effect: God's wrath **consumes/destroys** the guilty (Num 16:46 plague; Deu 9:19–20; Isa 34:2 "devoted them to destruction"), **executes covenant judgment** (Deu 29:28 "uprooted... in anger"), and is repeatedly shown as **turnable away** by repentance/intercession (Num 25:4; 2Ch 29:10; Jon 3:9 — its purpose is corrective, not merely punitive).

**T0.2.2** — God's wrath reads as belonging to God's **holy character** responding to covenant violation — not to a fallen condition (it is His by nature). The causes are consistently sin/idolatry (Deu 6:15; 9:19; 1Ki 11:9). *Conclusion:* belongs to created/uncreated design as a righteous response to evil (it has no "fallen" register; the fallenness is in its objects, not in it).

**T0.2.3** — Orientation toward future fullness: yes — the wrath is oriented to a **day/coming** of judgment (Isa 34:2; the prophetic "day" texts; NT orgē "the wrath" Rom 9:22; Rev 14:10; 16:19). It points beyond the present to an eschatological consummation.

**T0.3.1** — Aspect of divine likeness it grounds in the person: **righteous moral response to evil** — where human anger engages true moral evaluation (C1, Mar 3:5) it images this divine wrath. Inferential link via shared vocabulary.

**T0.3.2** — Shared: the affect is borne by God (here) and by the person (C1) under the same terms (cheˈmah, chaˈrah, orgē). Not an exclusively creaturely analogue — it is primarily a divine attribute the creature reflects.

**T0.3.3** — Where God's wrath rests on a person it indicates the person stands under judgment for sin (Deu 9:19; Joh 3:36 "the wrath of God remains on him"); where it is **turned away** (Num 25:11; 2Ch 29:10) it indicates restored covenant standing. The condition indicated is the person's covenant relation, not the image per se.

**T0.4.1** — Typological/eschatological use: yes — divine wrath functions as the pattern the NT "wrath to come" fulfils (Rom 9:22; Rev 14:10; 16:19; 19:15), the **divine instance establishing the eschatological pattern**. Direction: from the divine instance outward to the coming judgment.

---

## T1 — Definition

**T1.1.1** — Programme name: **Divine wrath**. The name signals God's holy, kindled response to evil; essential nature is **burning judgment** — dominant senses "wrath" (48), "fierce" (19), "kindled" (16), "burning" (7), "fury" (10).

**T1.1.2** — Primary terms: cheˈmah (heat/fury), chaˈron "burning anger" (the most God-specific term, Exo 15:7; Num 25:4), chaˈrah (kindled, Exo 22:24), qeˈtseph (wrath/overflow), orgē (NT settled wrath). The definitional core is **intense, kindled heat** belonging to God.

**T1.1.3** — Directional/relational: God's wrath is **against** persons and nations (Num 11:1; Deu 6:15) and **poured out / sent forth** (Jer 4:4 "go forth like fire"; Lam 2:4; Eze 22:22) — an outward-moving, judicial force.

**T1.2.1** — Mainly a **condition/status** (noun forms, 103 occurrences — "the wrath of the LORD," Num 32:14) and an **act** (verb forms, 42 — "was kindled," Gen 18:30). No quality/disposition strand for God here.

**T1.2.2** — Often **compound**: wrath fused with **jealousy** (chaˈron alongside qinˈah, Num 25:11; Deu 29:20; Zep 1:18), with **fury/indignation** terms (cheˈmah + zaˈam contexts), and paired with **fire** imagery (Jer 4:4; Deu 32:22). Where it stands alone (Gen 18:30) it is simple.

**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite shown: God's wrath **turning away** into mercy/favour — "the LORD turned from his burning anger" (Jos 7:26; 2Ki 23:26; Jon 3:9; Psa 85:3 "you withdrew all your wrath"). Mercy/favour stands against wrath.

**T1.3.2** — At its edge it excludes **continuance** when repentance comes: it is "quenched" (2Ki 22:17; 2Ch 34:25) and resists persisting where the people humble themselves (2Ch 12:7).

**T1.3.3** — It ends where **chastening love** and **jealousy** begin (it is bound to covenant, Deu 29:20), and is not arbitrary rage — it is not the human disordered anger of C1 (T6.5).

**T1.4.1** — Modes: **kindled** (qal/niphal of chaˈrah, Exo 22:24); **poured out** (Lam 2:4; Eze 22:22; morph of natak/shaphak); **gone forth like fire** (Jer 4:4; 21:12); **sent** (Deu 32:24; Job 20:23); **cast** (Deu 29:28). It operates as both a sudden kindling and a deliberate pouring-out.

**T1.4.2** — Yes — mode varies: kindled *against* a person (Exo 32:10), poured *on* a place (Eze 22:22 Jerusalem), sent *as* plague/sword (Deu 32:24); intensified ("great wrath," Deu 29:28; "hotly," Num 11:10).

**T1.4.3** — Communicative/spoken mode: yes — God **declares** his wrath through prophets ("thus says the LORD... my wrath," Eze 5:13 context; Jer 4:4 spoken oracle) and **swears** in wrath ("as I swore in my wrath," Psa 95:11 / Heb 3:11; 4:3). Recorded; elsewhere none.

**T1.5.1** — Immediate response following God's wrath: **judgment falls** — plague (Num 11:33; 16:46), fire (Num 11:1), destruction/slaughter (Isa 34:2 "given to slaughter"), or, where averted, the wrath **quenched** (2Ki 22:17). Most occurrences name no immediate response (Gen 18:30) — record none.

**T1.5.2** — Varied: the immediate response is either **executed judgment** (Num 11:1; 16:46) or, on repentance/intercession, **withheld/quenched judgment** (Num 25:11; 2Ch 34:25). Two consistent poles.

**T1.6.1** — Sustained effect: God's wrath, when it runs its course, leaves a land **desolate** (Deu 29:23–28 "uprooted... cast into another land"; Lam 4:11 "kindled a fire... consumed its foundations"); when turned away, it establishes **restored covenant** (Psa 85:3–4). Record none where unstated.

**T1.6.3** — The immediate response is the falling blow (plague/fire, Num 11:1); the sustained effect is the **enduring desolation or restored standing** (Deu 29:28; Psa 85:3). Episode of judgment versus its lasting result.

**T1.7.1** — It "operates rightly" — i.e. is provoked — where there is **covenant violation/idolatry**: other gods (Deu 6:15; 7:4), the golden calf (Deu 9:19), forsaking the LORD (Deu 31:17; 1Ki 11:9). The condition is real sin.

**T1.7.2** — It is **turned away / blocked** by intercession (Moses, Psa 106:23 context; Num 16:46–48 Aaron's atonement), by repentance and humbling (2Ch 12:7; Jon 3:9–10), and by zealous covenant-action (Phinehas, Num 25:11). No verse attributes interference with God's wrath to another spirit — **silent** on that.

**T1.7.3** — Not applicable as posed (God's wrath is never "present but failing to take hold" in a person — it is God's, not a creaturely capacity). Where God **restrains** it, the people are spared though guilty (2Ch 12:7 "my wrath shall not be poured out... by Shishak"). Recorded as the nearest evidenced case.

---

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries

**T2.1.1** — As predicated of God, constitutional location is largely **not applicable / NONE** (136/145). Where the term touches a human seat it is the **heart** of the one against whom/whom God acts (1Ki 11:9 Solomon's heart turned → wrath; Isa 57:17 "I struck him... he went on backsliding in the way of his heart"; Jer 4:4 "circumcise... your heart, lest my wrath go forth"), **soul** (Jer 51:45), **flesh** (Ecc 5:6). These locate the *human* covenant-condition that provokes wrath, not a seat of wrath in God.

**T2.1.2** — The pattern (overwhelmingly unlocated) confirms divine wrath is **not seated in a creaturely faculty**; the few seat-references attach to the human heart as the locus of the sin that draws wrath (Jer 4:4). Any body link is **indicative** (of human guilt), not a seat of the wrath itself.

**T2.10.1** — Movement: God's wrath moves **onto the person/nation from God** (the defining external direction) — "my wrath will go forth" (Jer 4:4), "poured out on this place" (2Ch 34:25), received-from-outside (2Ch 29:10; Jer 32:31). No spirit→soul→body internal sequence; no angelic introduction. Record the God→person movement.

**T2.7.1** — Body direction: where a body link exists it runs from the **human heart/flesh** as the site of provoking sin (Jer 4:4; Ecc 5:6) — i.e. the body indicates the guilt; it does not house God's wrath. No soul→body expression *of God* is in view. Largely **silent** on a body-direction proper to the characteristic.

**T2.9.1** — Origin: the wrath **originates in God** (it is His by possession, Exo 15:7; agency, Gen 18:30) — not generated in the person, received from another, or carried generationally. Stated source = God himself.

**T2.9.2** — Origin is **single** (God) and does not change with context — every occurrence has God as source.

---

## T3 — The Inner Faculties

**T3.1.1** — Perception: God's wrath responds to what God **sees/hears** of sin ("the LORD saw... his anger," contexts of Num 11:1, 11:10; Deu 32:19 "the LORD saw it and spurned them"). The trigger is divine perception of evil.

**T3.1.2** — Effect on (human) perception: God's wrath leaves the people **blind/hardened** in some texts (Isa 42:25 "it set him on fire... but he did not understand"). Recorded; elsewhere not stated.

**T3.1.3** — Pattern: divine wrath is **perception-triggered** (God sees the sin) and can **dull** human perception under judgment (Isa 42:25).

**T3.2.1** — Cognition: engaged as God's **judicial appraisal** — wrath follows God's reckoning of covenant-breach (Deu 9:19; Rom 1:18 "the wrath of God is revealed against... unrighteousness," faculty affect|moral_evaluation).

**T3.2.2** — Effect on human cognition: under wrath the people **do not lay it to heart / do not understand** (Isa 42:25). Wrath as judgment can accompany cognitive hardening.

**T3.2.3** — Pattern: divine wrath is itself **appraisal-grounded** (a considered response to evil), distinguishing it from blind rage.

**T3.3.1** — Memory: God's wrath relates to **remembered covenant** — kindled when the people forget Him (Deu 32:18 context) and stored against "the day of wrath" (Rom 2:5-type; not in set). Direct memory-faculty engagement is thin — mostly **silent**.

**T3.3.2** — **Silent** on wrath acting on a memory faculty.

**T3.3.3** — The thinness indicates divine wrath is framed as **present judicial response**, not as a function of recollection (though covenant memory is its backdrop).

**T3.4.1** — Affect: the core faculty — 140/145 occurrences are affect (Exo 22:24; Num 11:1). Divine wrath is a genuine affective response in God (anthropopathically expressed).

**T3.4.2** — Effect on affect: it is the **intensified** affective register of God's holiness — "fierce" and "burning" (chaˈron, Exo 15:7; Num 25:4). On the human side it evokes **terror** (the people fear, Deu 9:19 "I was afraid of the anger").

**T3.4.3** — That affect dominates confirms divine wrath is a **real disposition** of God toward evil, not a mere metaphor of action.

**T3.5.1** — Creativity/imagination: not engaged. **Silent.**

**T3.5.2** — **Silent.**

**T3.5.3** — The absence indicates wrath has no relation to the originative faculty.

**T3.6.1** — Volition: engaged as God's **sovereign choice** to execute or relent — "the LORD turned from his burning anger" (Jos 7:26; 2Ki 23:26), He "swore in wrath" (Psa 95:11/Heb 3:11). Wrath is exercised and withheld by God's will.

**T3.6.2** — Effect on (human) volition: the threat of wrath summons the human will to **repent / turn** (Jer 4:4 "circumcise your heart, lest my wrath go forth"; 2Ch 30:8 "that his fierce anger may turn away").

**T3.6.3** — Pattern: divine wrath is **will-governed** in God (relentable, Jon 3:9–10) — never an uncontrolled overflow.

**T3.7.1** — Agency: divine wrath is intensely **action-issuing** — it sends plague (Num 11:33), fire (Num 11:1), sword/famine (Deu 32:24; Eze 5:12 context), exile (Deu 29:28). Wrath is God's executive judgment.

**T3.7.2** — Effect on agency: it **acts upon** the objects decisively (Isa 34:2 destruction); on the human side it can **provoke counter-action** of repentance (2Ch 29:10 "make a covenant... that his fierce wrath may turn").

**T3.7.3** — The constant wrath→act pattern marks it as the **agency of holy judgment**.

**T3.8.1** — Moral evaluation: directly engaged — wrath is God's verdict on covenant-breach and unrighteousness (Rom 1:18; 12:19 "leave it to the wrath of God"; 13:4 the magistrate "carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer").

**T3.8.2** — Effect: it **enacts** the moral verdict — justice executed (Deu 9:19; Rom 13:4). It is the affective-executive form of God's righteousness against evil.

**T3.8.3** — Pattern: divine wrath is **wholly bound to moral evaluation** — always a response to real wrong (the causes are uniformly sin/idolatry), distinguishing it categorically from the morally double-valued human anger of C1.

**T3.9.1** — Conscience: engaged on the human side as the wrath that **vindicates** the magistrate's role "for the sake of conscience" (Rom 13:5). Otherwise the acute inner witness is not the faculty in view — mostly **silent**.

**T3.9.2** — **Silent** on wrath operating on conscience as such (Rom 13:5 sets them side by side).

**T3.9.3** — The thinness indicates divine wrath is **objective judgment** rather than a faculty of inner self-conviction.

**T3.10.1** — Conscientiousness (integrated moral response): God's wrath is the supreme instance of **integrated moral awareness, will, and act** — He perceives sin, judges it, and acts (Deu 9:19; Rom 1:18). On the human side it summons the integrated response of repentance (2Ch 30:8).

**T3.10.2** — Effect: it presses the person/nation toward **covenant integrity** (turn and live, Eze 18-type; 2Ch 30:8).

**T3.10.3** — Pattern: divine wrath models conscientiousness perfectly integrated in God.

**T3.11.1** — Relational capacity: divine wrath is intensely **relational/covenantal** — directed at *His people* for breaking *His covenant* (Deu 6:15 "for the LORD your God... is a jealous God... lest the anger of the LORD be kindled against you").

**T3.11.2** — Effect on the relationship: wrath signals **covenant rupture** (Deu 31:17 "I will forsake them... my anger") and, when turned away, **restored relationship** (Psa 85:3–4).

**T3.11.3** — The covenant-bound pattern shows divine wrath is constitutively **relational** — the wounded response of the covenant Lord, not impersonal force.

---

## T4 — Relational Interfaces

**T4.1.1** — God-toward-human: this is the defining operation of C2 — God's wrath moves from God toward the human person/nation (Exo 22:24; Num 11:1; Deu 6:15).

**T4.1.2** — Basis: **covenantal and responsive** — extended in response to covenant violation (Deu 6:15; 9:19; 1Ki 11:9), not arbitrary; conditional on sin and relentable on repentance (Jon 3:9–10; 2Ch 12:7).

**T4.1.3** — What it shows of God's disposition: God is **holy and committed** to the covenant — His wrath is the measure of how seriously He takes covenant betrayal, and His readiness to turn it away (Psa 85:3) shows mercy as its horizon.

**T4.2.1** — Human-to-God movement of *this* characteristic: not applicable — wrath here is God's, not the person's toward God. The human movement in view is **repentance/intercession that turns wrath away** (Num 25:11; 2Ch 29:10). Record none for the characteristic operating *from* human to God.

**T4.2.2** — The posture that meets divine wrath is **humbling, repentance, intercession** (2Ch 12:6–7 "they humbled themselves"; Num 16:47–48 atonement).

**T4.2.3** — That wrath is **turnable** by human repentance shows the relationship is genuinely responsive — God relents toward the penitent (Jon 3:10).

**T4.3.1** — Person-to-person extension: not proper to C2 (wrath is God's). **Silent** (human-human anger is C1).

**T4.3.2** — **Silent.**

**T4.3.3** — **Silent.**

**T4.4.1** — Receiving: the human/nation **receives** God's wrath as judgment (Joh 3:36 "the wrath of God remains on him"; Rom 5:9 "saved... from the wrath"). Uptake is endured judgment, not adoption.

**T4.4.2** — What accompanies receiving it: **unrepentance** keeps it remaining (Joh 3:36); **faith/repentance** removes it (Rom 5:9 "saved... through him").

**T4.4.3** — The person who stands under wrath without repentance is shown as **condemned/abiding under it** (Joh 3:36).

**T4.5.1** — Within bonds vs across distance: divine wrath operates chiefly **within the covenant bond** (against His own people, Deu 6:15) and also **across** it against the nations (Isa 34:2; Jer 10:25 context). Both.

**T4.5.2** — It operates within the **covenant** (its primary frame, Deu 29:24–28) and **crosses** to the nations in judgment (Isa 34:2). Not covenant-internal only.

**T4.5.3** — Relational scope: **universal** — His covenant people (Deu 9:19), the nations (Isa 34:2), individuals (1Ki 11:9). None is exempt as a potential object.

**T4.6.1** — In relation to spiritual beings: thin — wrath is poured out in contexts including the heavenly host's judgment (Isa 34:2 "all the host of heaven shall rot"; object spiritual-being Eze 3:14 context). Mostly **silent** on operation toward angelic/adversarial beings directly.

**T4.6.2** — Site of adversarial activity: not shown — God's wrath is not depicted as attacked or distorted by adversarial powers. **Silent** (recorded as not evidenced).

**T4.6.3** — Angelic mediation: God's wrath is at times **executed through** agents (the plague/"destroyer" tradition, e.g. Num 16:46–48 atonement halts it; the sword, Deu 32:24). Where a mediating agent of judgment appears it is the instrument of wrath. Recorded; otherwise none.

---

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension

**T5.1.1** — Transformation: God's wrath effects transformation of **condition** — it lays waste (Deu 29:28; Lam 4:11) and, when turned away, **restores** (Psa 85:3–4). On the person it can change orientation by driving repentance (2Ch 30:8).

**T5.1.2** — Reversible/irreversible: shown **reversible** — repeatedly "turned away" / "quenched" (Jos 7:26; 2Ki 22:17; Jon 3:10); but where judgment falls it is **executed** and the desolation stands (Deu 29:28). Both, depending on response.

**T5.2.1** — Sequence: **sin → kindling of wrath → judgment (or repentance → turning away)** (Deu 9:8–19 the calf → wrath → intercession → relenting; Jon 3 sin → threatened wrath → repentance → relenting). Where no sequence appears, record none (Exo 15:7 poetic).

**T5.3.1** — Mechanism of change: **judgment/discipline** (the wrath itself as corrective, Lev 26:28 context; 2Ki 22:13) and **intercession/atonement** as the mechanism that turns it (Num 16:46–48; Psa 106:23). Record none where unstated.

**T5.3.2** — Differs: wrath works change by **destruction** on the unrepentant (Isa 34:2) and by **threat-driving-repentance** on the responsive (2Ch 30:8; Jon 3). Context-dependent.

**T5.4.1** — Relation to suffering/affliction: divine wrath **produces** affliction as judgment (Lam 2:4 "poured out his fury like fire"; Psa 88:7 "your wrath lies heavy on me"; Psa 38:1–3). It is a cause of suffering for its objects.

**T5.4.2** — What suffering does to it: the suffering of judgment is the **outworking** of wrath; where the afflicted repent/cry out, the wrath is **relented** (Psa 85; 2Ch 12:7). Suffering under wrath is meant to turn the sufferer back.

**T5.5.1** — Participation in the sanctification arc: God's wrath functions as **covenant discipline** shaping the people over time — chastening (Lev 26:28 "discipline you... for your sins"; Isa 57:17 "I was angry... I struck him"). It is part of the formative dealing of God with His people.

**T5.6.1** — Eschatological orientation: strongly yes — divine wrath is oriented to **"the wrath to come" / the day of judgment** (Rom 9:22 "vessels of wrath"; Rev 14:10; 16:19; 19:15). Its present operation anticipates the final judgment.

---

## T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics

**T6.1.1** — Co-occurring characteristics: **jealousy** (qinˈah with chaˈron, Num 25:11; Deu 29:20; Zep 1:18 "fire of his jealousy"), **fury/indignation** (cheˈmah with zaˈam, Isa 34:2 context), and **fire** imagery throughout (Jer 4:4; Deu 32:22). Frequent pairing with jealousy especially.

**T6.1.2** — Co-occurrence places divine wrath at the **judicial-covenantal core** of the cluster — inseparable from God's jealousy (C4) over the covenant and expressed as consuming fire.

**T6.2.1** — Sequence: divine wrath consistently **follows** covenant sin/idolatry and **precedes** judgment (Deu 9:16–19; 1Ki 11:9–11). It also follows divine **jealousy** being provoked (Deu 32:16,21 "provoked him to jealousy... to anger").

**T6.2.2** — The relationship is **causal**: sin/idolatry causes wrath; provoked jealousy causes wrath (Deu 32:21). Wrath causes judgment.

**T6.3.1** — Produces: divine wrath **produces** judgment, desolation, exile (Deu 29:28; Lam 4:11) and, by reaction, repentance (2Ch 30:8). Mechanism: executed or threatened judgment.

**T6.3.2** — Produced by: **divine jealousy provoked** (C4/C3; Deu 32:16,21; Psa 78:58 "provoked him... moved him to jealousy... full of wrath," Psa 78:58–59) and by **human provocation** (C3; 1Ki 14:9; 2Ki 21:6).

**T6.3.3** — Constituent relation: divine wrath is a constituent of God's **covenant-jealousy** response (the "fire of jealousy" *is* wrathful, Zep 1:18; 3:8) — jealousy and wrath interpenetrate at the divine end.

**T6.4.1** — Shared vocabulary: cheˈmah/chaˈrah/qeˈtseph/orgē shared with **C1 human anger** (same lemmas, different bearer) and with **C3 provoking-to-anger** (the wrath that provocation arouses).

**T6.4.2** — Root-level: yes — the chaˈrah/chaˈron burning-root spans C1, C2, C3; one heat-architecture underlies human anger, divine wrath, and provoked anger.

**T6.4.3** — The shared root shows C1/C2/C3 are **one affect under different relations** — divine wrath is distinguished not by a separate vocabulary but by its **bearer (God) and its unfailing righteousness**.

**T6.5.1** — Nearest neighbour: **C1 human anger** (identical core vocabulary). The precise distinction: **bearer and moral standing** — God's wrath is righteous by nature and covenant-bound; human anger is morally variable (C1, T3.8.3).

**T6.5.2** — Apparent overlap: the leaked verses (Exo 4:14; 2Ki 13:3, held in C1) sit exactly on the boundary; the deciding criterion is **whether God is the angry subject** (→C2). The other near-neighbour is **C4 divine jealousy**, which co-occurs and overlaps in the "fire of jealousy/wrath" (Zep 1:18) — distinguished by jealousy's relational-possessive note vs wrath's judicial note.

**T6.5.3** — Distinction from C1 is of **bearer and moral valence** (not kind or vocabulary); from C3 of **direction** (bearing wrath vs being provoked to it); from C4 of **register** (judicial wrath vs possessive jealousy), though they fuse at the divine end.

---

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation

**T7.1.1** — Primary terms/roots: **cheˈmah** (heat/fury), **chaˈron** (burning, the term most distinctively used of God's anger, from chaˈrah "to burn"), **chaˈrah** (to be kindled), **qeˈtseph** (wrath/overflow), **orgē** (NT). Roots converge on **burning heat** and **overflow**.

**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: **noun/status** dominant (103; "the wrath of the LORD," Num 32:14) with **verb/action** (42; "was kindled," Gen 18:30). The noun-heavy range shows divine wrath named as an **abiding attribute/state**, not only an episode.

**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: from "wrath/anger" (Exo 32:10) through "fierce/burning" (chaˈron, Exo 15:7) to "fury/heat" (cheˈmah, Jer 4:4) and "venom" once (Deu 32:33 context near divine judgment). Breadth: kindled heat → settled fury → consuming fire.

**T7.1.4** — Distinguishing terms: **condition vs act** — cheˈmah/qeˈtseph (state) vs chaˈrah (act of kindling); chaˈron specifically marks **intensity** ("fierce/burning"). Received-vs-given not lexicalised (it is always God's own).

**T7.1.5** — Opposite/absence term: carried by the **turning-away** idiom and by **mercy/favour** vocabulary (Psa 85:3 "you withdrew all your wrath"; "slow to anger," erek aphayim, Exo 34:6). Not a single antonym lexeme.

**T7.1.6** — Person-type term: not applicable to God (no "wrathful-type" person-noun is predicated of God). Record none.

**T7.1.7** — Supplication/seeking term: there is no term for *seeking* God's wrath; the related vocabulary is for **averting/quenching** it (Num 25:11; 2Ch 34:25 "quenched"). Record none for seeking it.

**T7.1.8** — OT→NT relationship: the Hebrew burning-cluster (cheˈmah/chaˈron/qeˈtseph) is rendered by **orgē** in the NT, where divine wrath becomes the **eschatological "the wrath"** (Rom 9:22; Rev 14:10) and is grounded in the revelation of God's righteousness (Rom 1:18). Strong continuity; development toward eschatological consummation.

**T7.1.9** — NT-coined term: **orgē** is not newly coined but is given a fixed eschatological-technical sense ("the wrath," ho orgē, Rom 5:9; 1Th 1:10). Record: semantic specialisation rather than coinage.

**T7.1.10** — Full vocabulary arc: from **kindled burning** (chaˈrah/chaˈron) through **settled fury** (cheˈmah/qeˈtseph) to the NT **eschatological wrath** (orgē) — a complete arc from covenant-judgment in history to final judgment.

**T7.2.1** — Function of the primary term in its primary verse: in Exo 32:10 "let my wrath burn hot against them that I may consume them" — chaˈrah/cheˈmah is the **decisive predicate** of God's judicial intent, which Moses' intercession then turns (Exo 32:11–14). The term carries the covenant crisis.

**T7.2.2** — Literary forms: **covenant narrative/law** (Exo, Num, Deu — Exo 32:10; Deu 9:19), **prophecy** (Jer, Isa, Eze — Jer 4:4; Eze 22:22), **psalm/lament** (Psa 38:1; 88:7; Lam 2:4), **NT epistle/apocalyptic** (Rom 1:18; Rev 16:19). Responsible reading weighs covenant law for its conditional structure, prophecy for its oracle form, lament for its poetic intensity, and apocalyptic for its eschatological symbolism (BOOK distribution: Jer 21, Isa 16, Eze 16, Deu 15).

**T7.2.3** — Logical structure: **covenant-conditional** — *if* the people forsake the LORD / serve other gods, *then* His wrath is kindled (Deu 6:14–15; 7:4; 31:16–17). Premise: God is holy and covenant-committed; conclusion: covenant breach draws consuming judgment, relentable on repentance.

**T7.2.4** — Contextual settings: **covenantal** (Deu 29:24–28), **judicial** (Rom 13:4), **liturgical/intercessory** (Num 16:46–48; Psa 85), **eschatological** (Rev 16:19). The settings show wrath as the covenant Lord's judicial response, mediated by intercession and consummated at the end.

**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor verse: **Exodus 32:10–14** (with Deu 9:19 as parallel) — "my wrath... burn hot... that I may consume them," answered by intercession and the LORD relenting — most fully shows divine wrath's character: kindled by covenant sin, real and consuming, yet relentable.

**T7.2.6** — Exo 32:10–14 shows what no other verse shows together: wrath **kindled to consume**, **named by God in the first person**, **met by intercession**, and **relented** — the full covenant dynamic of provocation, judgment, mediation, and mercy in one scene.

**T7.3.1** — Most useful human-science lens: per the science extract, divine wrath is largely **outside science's descriptive scope** — "science has no analogue for holy wrath as a morally appropriate, ontologically grounded response to evil." The nearest lens is **moral psychology** (righteous/moral anger), applied only by analogy.

**T7.3.2** — Where the framework illuminates: at the **experiential edge** — the phenomenology of encountering wrath, and the appraisal structure (wrath as response to genuine wrongdoing) illuminates why divine wrath is consistently tied to covenant violation (Deu 9:19; Rom 1:18). The heat physiology illuminates the thermal vocabulary (chaˈron "burning," Exo 15:7).

**T7.3.3** — Where they diverge (the deepest divergence): science **pathologises** anger and has **no category for holy wrath**; the C2 evidence presents wrath as a **morally appropriate, covenantally grounded** divine response (Exo 32:10; Rom 1:18) and as **relentable mercy-bounded judgment** (Jon 3:10) — categories science does not adjudicate (per the outside-science inventory).

**T7.3.4** — Gaps surfaced by science: the **trait/state** distinction prompts the question whether divine wrath is better read as God's settled *attribute* against evil (status-noun weight, 103/145) rather than episodic *state* — a classification question the verse data (noun-dominance) supports. Labelled inferential.

# M02 · C3 — Provoking to Anger — Tier Catalogue Analysis

- **File:** wa-m02-c3-provoking-to-anger-tieranalysis-v1_1-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Cluster / Characteristic:** M02 "Anger, Wrath and Indignation" · C3 Provoking to anger (causative / relational elicitation)
- **Version:** v1_1 · **Author:** le Roux Cilliers
- **Prior output (this session):** wa-m02-c2-divine-wrath-tieranalysis-v1_0-20260619.md
- **Catalogue answered:** WA-tier-catalogue-current-state-v2-20260619.md (126 questions, T0–T7) · **Science lens (T7.3):** wa-m02-anger-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md

**Change control (v1_0):** First issue. All 126 questions answered for C3.
**Change control (v1_1, 2026-06-19):** valence confirmed current by CC and **integrated** (see _Valence integration_ below; the v1_0 PARKED marker was out of date); consolidated **essay-sufficient Evidence Base** appended (incl. lemma_meaning, cause_clause, raw object); **lexical-coverage self-audit passed** (all populated fields represented; `mode` absent from the M02 extract). The v1_0 question-by-question answers stand unchanged.

**Evidence basis.** C3 = 85 focus-occurrences (OT 71 / NT 14): kaˈas "to provoke" (52), plus chaˈrah/qaˈtsaph/cheˈmah/qeˈtseph where God is the object provoked (≈20), and Greek paroxunō/parorgizō/erethizō/paroxusmos/parorgismos (≈9). Concentrated in Jeremiah (13), 1 Kings (11), Deuteronomy (8), 2 Kings (7), 2 Chronicles (6), with an NT epistolary tail (Eph 3, Col 2). div_role: object 60 (God provoked), NONE 23 (human-human), addressee 2. Type: action 69, status 16. Every observation cited; "Silent." where C3 verses do not speak. valence integrated (CC-confirmed current 2026-06-19; see _Valence integration_ below).

**Two strands (data-derived).** (i) The dominant **covenantal** strand — provoking *God* to anger by idolatry (object_type=God 37; e.g. Deu 4:25; 1Ki 14:9). (ii) A **human/interpersonal** strand (div_role NONE) — provoking *persons* (Peninnah provoking Hannah, 1Sa 1:6; fathers provoking children, Eph 6:4; Col 3:21) including a **positive** "stir up / provoke to good" sense (Heb 10:24 "stir up to love and good works"; 2Cor 9:2 zeal; Rom 10:19 "provoke to jealousy"; Act 15:39 "sharp disagreement," paroxusmos). Both strands are answered below.

---

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design

**T0.1.1** — Relation to God: in the dominant strand God is the **object** provoked — "they provoked him to anger with their high places" (1Ki 14:9; Deu 4:25; Jer 25:6–7). God is not the bearer but the one whose anger is aroused. In the human strand God is not in view (1Sa 1:6).

**T0.1.2** — Across C3 God appears chiefly as the **provoked party** (object, 60 occ), not the bearer. *Interpretation:* the characteristic names the human capacity to **arouse anger in another** — and, gravely, in God; its place in the person is as the relational act that draws covenant wrath (a fallen-direction capacity), with a redeemed counterpart (stirring to good, Heb 10:24).

**T0.2.1** — Stated purpose/effect: provoking God **brings down wrath/judgment** ("to provoke me to anger... I will set my face against," Eze 8:17–18 context; "provoked the LORD... so that he removed them," 2Ki 17:18-type). The positive strand states a constructive effect — "stir up one another to love and good works" (Heb 10:24). Record none where unstated.

**T0.2.2** — The provoke-God strand belongs to the **fallen condition** (idolatry, rebellion — Deu 4:25; 31:29 "do evil... provoking him to anger"); the "stir up to good" strand belongs to **created/redeemed design** (Heb 10:24; 2Cor 9:2). Both — sharply divided by direction.

**T0.2.3** — Future-fullness orientation: in the positive strand, "provoke to jealousy" is oriented toward Israel's future **salvation** (Rom 10:19; cf. 11:11 context — provoking to jealousy "to make Israel jealous"). In the negative strand, none. Record the positive orientation where present.

**T0.3.1** — Divine-likeness aspect: the redeemed capacity to **rouse another toward good** (Heb 10:24) images God's own rousing of His people; the negative capacity images nothing of God (it is the abuse of relational influence).

**T0.3.2** — Shared/creaturely: the *act* of provoking is creaturely (a person provokes); what is aroused (anger) is shared with God (C2). The capacity to influence another's affect is a creaturely analogue of relational agency.

**T0.3.3** — Where a person habitually provokes God, it indicates a **rebellious covenant condition** (Deu 31:29; 2Ki 17:11 "did wicked things, provoking the LORD"); where a person stirs others to love, it indicates a **formed, edifying disposition** (Heb 10:24).

**T0.4.1** — Typological use: "provoke to jealousy" is used **redemptive-historically** — the Gentiles' inclusion to provoke Israel to jealousy unto salvation (Rom 10:19), pointing beyond the immediate. Direction: human action serving the divine purpose. Elsewhere none.

---

## T1 — Definition

**T1.1.1** — Programme name: **Provoking to anger**. The name signals a **causative, relational act** — arousing anger in another; essential nature is elicitation, not the affect itself. Dominant senses "anger/provoke/provoked/provoking" (kaˈas).

**T1.1.2** — Primary terms: kaˈas (Hebrew, "to provoke/vex to anger," hiphil causative — Deu 4:25; 1Ki 14:9); Greek paroxunō / parorgizō ("provoke, exasperate," Eph 6:4) and parorgismos (Eph 4:26); paroxusmos (a "provoking/stirring," Heb 10:24; Act 15:39). Definitionally the cluster is **causative** — the morphology is largely hiphil (HVhi…), the grammar of *making* another angry.

**T1.1.3** — The name carries an inherently **relational/directional** implication: provocation is always *of someone* — toward God (Deu 4:25) or toward a person (1Sa 1:6; Eph 6:4). It presupposes a second party.

**T1.2.1** — An **act** predominantly (69 action occurrences — "they provoked," 1Ki 14:9) with a residual **status/abstract** strand (16; "provocation," 2Ki 23:26). It is a doing, not a state.

**T1.2.2** — **Compound**: provocation joins to **idolatry/evil works** as its means (Deu 4:25 "make a carved image... provoke him"; Jer 25:6 "the work of your hands... to provoke me"); in the positive strand it joins to **zeal/love** (Heb 10:24; 2Cor 9:2). It is rarely simple — it carries its instrument.

**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite: **pleasing/obeying** (the cessation of provocation) — implied where the alternative is to "do what is right in the eyes of the LORD" rather than "provoke" (1Ki 14:8–9 contrast with David). Not lexicalised as a single antonym.

**T1.3.2** — At its edge it excludes **conciliation/obedience**: where the people turn and obey, the provoking ceases (2Ch 33:12–13 Manasseh's repentance ends the provocation). In the human strand the positive opposite of "provoke to anger" is to "provoke to love" (Heb 10:24).

**T1.3.3** — It ends where the **resulting anger** (C1/C2) begins (C3 is the eliciting act, the anger is the response) and where mere **contention** (C6) begins (provocation aims at arousing affect, not at the dispute itself).

**T1.4.1** — Modes: causative **hiphil** "to provoke/make angry" (Deu 4:25, morph HVhi…); a **stirring-up** (paroxusmos, Heb 10:24; Act 15:39); an **exasperating** (parorgizō/erethizō of children, Eph 6:4; Col 3:21). It operates as deliberate or careless arousal of another's affect.

**T1.4.2** — Yes — mode varies by direction: toward **God** it is idolatrous provocation (Deu 4:25); toward **a person** it can be cruel taunting (1Sa 1:6 Peninnah), parental exasperation (Eph 6:4; Col 3:21), heated dispute (Act 15:39), or **constructive incitement to good** (Heb 10:24). The same causative form serves opposite ends.

**T1.4.3** — Communicative/spoken mode: yes — provocation is often **verbal** — Peninnah's taunting (1Sa 1:6–7), the taunt "in the presence of the builders" (Neh 4:1–5), and exhortation "to stir up" (Heb 10:24). Recorded; elsewhere none.

**T1.5.1** — Immediate response following provocation: the provoked party becomes **angry/grieved** — Hannah "wept and would not eat" under provocation (1Sa 1:7); God's anger is kindled (Deu 9:18–19); the dispute "became so sharp they parted" (Act 15:39). Record none where unstated.

**T1.5.2** — Varied: the immediate response ranges from divine wrath (Deu 9:19) to human grief/weeping (1Sa 1:7) to relational rupture (Act 15:39) to — in the positive strand — **love and good works** (Heb 10:24).

**T1.6.1** — Sustained effect: persistent provocation of God yields **settled judgment/exile** ("provoked... so the LORD removed Israel," 2Ki 17:11,18-type); persistent provocation of a person yields **lasting grief/estrangement** (1Sa 1:6–7 "year by year"). The positive strand yields sustained **mutual edification** (Heb 10:24). Record none where unstated.

**T1.6.3** — Immediate response is the flash (anger kindled, weeping); sustained effect is the **accumulated judgment or estrangement** (exile; year-by-year grief). Episode vs settled consequence.

**T1.7.1** — It "operates" (succeeds in provoking) where there is **idolatry/evil before God** (Deu 4:25; 31:29) or **cruelty/insult between persons** (1Sa 1:6; Neh 4:1). The condition is a real offence.

**T1.7.2** — It is **blocked** where the would-be provoked party does not take it up — Hannah ultimately pours out her soul to God rather than retaliate (1Sa 1:15–16); the wise overlook an insult (Pro 12:16-type). And it is restrained by command — "fathers, do not provoke your children" (Eph 6:4; Col 3:21). No verse attributes the provoking to another spirit — **silent** on that.

**T1.7.3** — Where provocation meets a person who does not take it up, that person is shown **grieved but self-controlled / turning to God** (1Sa 1:15–16 Hannah). Where it meets God, God is provoked but **relents on repentance** (2Ch 33:12–13).

---

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries

**T2.1.1** — Location: largely **NONE** (82/85), since provocation is a relational act, not a seated state. Where a seat appears it is the **heart** of the provoked or the provoker (2Ch 32:26 Hezekiah's heart proud; Eze 32:9 "I will trouble the hearts of many"), or the **flesh** (Eze 16:26 context). Record none elsewhere (Deu 4:25).

**T2.1.2** — The near-total absence of a seat confirms provocation is an **interpersonal act**, not a faculty housed in a level; the rare heart-references locate the pride/offence behind it (2Ch 32:26).

**T2.10.1** — Movement: provocation moves **from one party onto another** — the provoker acts on God or a person (the defining external direction; Deu 4:25 onto God; 1Sa 1:6 onto Hannah). Provocation of God is **received-from-outside** by God's people as the wrath it draws (Deu 9:7; 2Ki 21:15). No internal spirit→soul→body sequence; no angelic source. Record the party→party movement.

**T2.7.1** — Body direction: thin — where the flesh appears (Eze 16:26) it is the **means** of provocation (idolatrous "lust"), an outward act expressing inner rebellion. Mostly **silent** on a body-direction proper to the characteristic.

**T2.9.1** — Origin: provocation **originates in the provoking party** (generated within the provoker — their idolatry, 1Ki 14:9; their cruelty, 1Sa 1:6). For God's people it is also depicted as a **persistent generational pattern** ("you have been rebellious... provoking," Deu 9:7,24). Stated source = the provoker.

**T2.9.2** — Origin can be **single** (an individual's act, 1Sa 1:6) or **corporate/generational** (Israel "from the day... to this day," Deu 9:7) — it varies with context.

---

## T3 — The Inner Faculties

**T3.1.1** — Perception: provocation is triggered by what the provoked party **sees/hears** — God "sees" the high places (1Ki 14:9 context), Hannah hears the taunt (1Sa 1:6–7), the dispute follows perceived wrong (Act 15:38–39). Perception is the gate.

**T3.1.2** — Effect on perception: the provoking taunt **fixes attention** on the offence (1Sa 1:6–7 year by year). No verse states it distorting the senses — otherwise **silent**.

**T3.1.3** — Pattern: provocation works **through perception** (it must be perceived to provoke) — confirming its relational, communicated nature.

**T3.2.1** — Cognition: engaged as the provoked party's **appraisal of the offence** (faculty affect|moral_evaluation in the wrath-of-God texts, Rom 1:18; Eph 5:6 "because of these the wrath of God comes"). The provocation is judged blameworthy.

**T3.2.2** — Effect on cognition: in the children-strand, provocation **discourages** ("lest they become discouraged," Col 3:21) — it clouds and dispirits the mind of the provoked. In the positive strand it **stimulates** good intent (Heb 10:24).

**T3.2.3** — Pattern: provocation is **cognition-engaging** at both ends — it presupposes the provoked party's appraisal and reshapes their disposition (discouragement or zeal).

**T3.3.1** — Memory: provocation of God is tied to **remembered covenant breach accumulated over time** ("they have provoked me... since the day," Deu 9:7; 2Ki 21:15 "since the day their fathers came out of Egypt"). It is recorded against the people.

**T3.3.2** — Effect on memory: it builds a **remembered record of rebellion** that God recalls in judgment (Deu 9:7). Recorded.

**T3.3.3** — The memory dimension (accumulated provocation) indicates the provoke-God strand is **historical and cumulative**, not merely momentary.

**T3.4.1** — Affect: the core faculty (78/85 affect) — provocation is defined by the **anger it arouses** (Deu 9:18; 1Sa 1:6–7 grief).

**T3.4.2** — Effect on affect: it **arouses** anger (in God, Deu 9:19; in a person, the grief/anger of the provoked) — and in the positive strand **rouses** love (Heb 10:24). It is an affect-mover.

**T3.4.3** — That affect dominates confirms the characteristic is fundamentally about **moving another's affect** — its whole point is the affective response it produces.

**T3.5.1** — Creativity: not engaged. **Silent.**

**T3.5.2** — **Silent.**

**T3.5.3** — Absence indicates no relation to the originative faculty.

**T3.6.1** — Volition: engaged as the **will to provoke** (deliberate idolatry, 1Ki 14:9; deliberate taunting, 1Sa 1:6) and as the will summoned **not** to provoke ("do not provoke your children," Eph 6:4) or to provoke **toward good** (Heb 10:24 "let us consider how to stir up").

**T3.6.2** — Effect on volition: provocation **presses** the provoked party's will toward a reaction (anger, withdrawal — Act 15:39); the command-strand calls the provoker's will to restraint or redirection (Eph 6:4; Heb 10:24).

**T3.6.3** — Pattern: provocation is a **volitional act** with a volitional target — it is chosen, and it is morally accountable ("do not," Eph 6:4).

**T3.7.1** — Agency: provocation is itself an **act of relational agency** — the provoker *does* something to another (idolatry "to provoke," Deu 4:25; taunting, 1Sa 1:6; "stirring up," Heb 10:24).

**T3.7.2** — Effect on agency: it **moves the provoked party to act** — God to judge (Deu 9:19), Hannah to pray (1Sa 1:10), Paul and Barnabas to part (Act 15:39), believers to love and good works (Heb 10:24).

**T3.7.3** — The provoke→act pattern marks the characteristic as **agency directed at another's agency** — it is influence that produces action.

**T3.8.1** — Moral evaluation: directly engaged — provoking God is judged **evil** ("did evil... provoking him to anger," Deu 31:29; 1Ki 14:9 "you have done evil above all"); the wrath it draws is God's moral verdict (Rom 1:18; Eph 5:6).

**T3.8.2** — Effect: it **incurs** a moral verdict (judgment, Deu 31:29) on the provoker; the positive strand earns commendation ("good works," Heb 10:24).

**T3.8.3** — Pattern: provocation is **morally double-valued by direction** — provoking God/oppressing a person is evil; provoking to love is good. Its morality is wholly directional.

**T3.9.1** — Conscience: thin — the children-strand's "discouragement" (Col 3:21) touches the dispiriting of the inner person, but the acute witness of guilt is not in view. Mostly **silent**.

**T3.9.2** — **Silent** on provocation operating on conscience.

**T3.9.3** — The thinness indicates provocation is primarily an **interpersonal/affective** act, not a faculty of self-conviction.

**T3.10.1** — Conscientiousness: engaged in the command-strand — the integrated moral call **not to provoke** (Eph 6:4; Col 3:21) and to **provoke toward good** (Heb 10:24) is a matter of formed moral practice in relationships.

**T3.10.2** — Effect: failed conscientiousness **discourages/embitters** the other (Col 3:21); exercised, it **builds up** (Heb 10:24).

**T3.10.3** — The command-pattern marks provocation as a **governed relational practice** — Scripture holds the provoker responsible for its direction.

**T3.11.1** — Relational capacity: provocation is **constitutively relational** — it requires and acts upon a bond (parent-child, Eph 6:4; rival wives, 1Sa 1:6; covenant people-God, Deu 4:25; co-workers, Act 15:39).

**T3.11.2** — Effect on relational capacity: negatively it **damages** the bond (estrangement, Act 15:39; embittered children, Col 3:21; God forsaking, Deu 31:17); positively it **strengthens** it (mutual stirring to love, Heb 10:24).

**T3.11.3** — The pattern shows the characteristic is **purely relational** — it cannot exist without a second party and always bears on the relationship's health.

---

## T4 — Relational Interfaces

**T4.1.1** — God-toward-human: not the direction of C3 (God is the provoked, not the provoker). The wrath that provocation draws *from* God is C2. Record none for C3 operating from God.

**T4.1.2** — **Silent** (a C2 question).

**T4.1.3** — **Silent.**

**T4.2.1** — Human-to-God: this is C3's primary direction — the person **provokes God** by idolatry and evil (Deu 4:25; 1Ki 14:9; Jer 25:6–7; Psa 78:58 "provoked him... with their high places"). The movement is the person acting upon God's covenant honour.

**T4.2.2** — Inner posture it reveals: **rebellion and contempt for the covenant** — "they did evil... to provoke me to anger" (1Ki 14:9; Deu 31:29). It is the opposite of the seeking/worshipping posture.

**T4.2.3** — What it shows about the relationship: a **broken, contemptuous** covenant standing — the person treats the covenant Lord as one to be defied (Deu 32:16,21). The relationship is real but assaulted by the person.

**T4.3.1** — Person-to-person extension: yes — provocation is extended by one person toward another (Peninnah → Hannah, 1Sa 1:6; fathers → children, Eph 6:4; one believer → another for good, Heb 10:24).

**T4.3.2** — Inner conditions accompanying it: cruelty/rivalry in the negative case (1Sa 1:6 the rival "provoked her grievously to irritate her"); love and care in the positive case (Heb 10:24 "consider how to stir up one another to love").

**T4.3.3** — What the giver must have become: the positive strand implies the provoker must **love** before stirring to love (Heb 10:24); the negative requires only malice (1Sa 1:6). Recorded for the positive; the negative states no precondition.

**T4.4.1** — Receiving: the provoked party **takes up** the provocation as anger/grief (Hannah's grief, 1Sa 1:7) or, in the positive strand, as **stirred love/good works** (Heb 10:24) or jealousy (Rom 10:19 Israel "made jealous").

**T4.4.2** — Conditions of uptake: a **valued stake** makes uptake likely (Hannah's longing for a child, 1Sa 1:6; Israel's identity, Rom 10:19); **self-control / turning to God** blocks the negative uptake (1Sa 1:15–16).

**T4.4.3** — The person who meets provocation but does not take it up is shown **pained yet composed, redirecting to God** (Hannah, 1Sa 1:15–16) — grief without retaliation.

**T4.5.1** — Within bonds vs across distance: provocation operates **within close bonds** (co-wives, 1Sa 1:6; parent-child, Eph 6:4; covenant people-God, Deu 4:25) and across rivalry/conflict (Neh 4:1 enemies; Act 15:39 colleagues). Both.

**T4.5.2** — Covenantal scope: the provoke-God strand is **covenant-internal** (Israel against its own God, Deu 4:25); the human strand crosses any relational line (rivals, parents, co-workers, opponents). Both.

**T4.5.3** — Relational scope: **wide** — God (Deu 4:25), spouse-rivals (1Sa 1:6), children (Eph 6:4), co-workers (Act 15:39), fellow believers (Heb 10:24), enemies (Neh 4:1). Provocation reaches across the relational field.

**T4.6.1** — Spiritual beings: not shown operating toward angelic/adversarial beings. **Silent.**

**T4.6.2** — Adversarial site: not evidenced as a site of adversarial weaponising in the C3 verses (the nearest is idolatry "to provoke," which involves false gods as the *means*, Deu 32:16 "with strange gods... they provoked," and Deu 32:17 "sacrificed to demons"). Recorded: idolatrous provocation involves false-god/"demon" objects (Deu 32:16–17) — a partial link; otherwise silent on adversarial weaponising of the characteristic itself.

**T4.6.3** — Angelic mediation: not evidenced. **Silent.**

---

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension

**T5.1.1** — Transformation: provocation transforms **relationship and condition** — it moves God to judgment and the people to exile (2Ki 17:11,18-type), moves co-workers to separation (Act 15:39), and, positively, moves believers toward love and good works (Heb 10:24). Record none where unstated.

**T5.1.2** — Reversible/irreversible: the provoke-God pattern is **reversible** on repentance (Manasseh, 2Ch 33:12–13, who had provoked greatly yet was restored); persistent provocation leads to **executed** judgment (exile). Both.

**T5.2.1** — Sequence: **provocation → anger kindled → judgment / grief** (Deu 9:18 "you provoked... the LORD was angry") and, positively, **consideration → stirring → love/good works** (Heb 10:24). Record none where no sequence appears.

**T5.3.1** — Mechanism of change: **arousal of the other's affect** — idolatry rouses God's wrath (Deu 4:25); taunting rouses grief (1Sa 1:6); exhortation rouses zeal (Heb 10:24). The mechanism is affective elicitation.

**T5.3.2** — Differs: the mechanism is **destructive elicitation** (idolatry/cruelty) versus **constructive elicitation** (exhortation to good) — the same causative act with opposite mechanisms by direction.

**T5.4.1** — Relation to suffering: provocation **produces suffering** in the provoked — Hannah's distress under year-by-year provocation (1Sa 1:6–7,10 "deeply distressed"); and the people's suffering as the judgment provocation draws (Deu 9:19). It is a producer and context of affliction.

**T5.4.2** — What suffering does to it: under provocation-induced suffering Hannah is driven to **prayer** (1Sa 1:10) — suffering can redirect the provoked toward God rather than retaliation. Recorded.

**T5.5.1** — Sanctification arc: the positive strand explicitly participates — believers "stir up one another to love and good works" as ongoing mutual formation (Heb 10:24); the command not to provoke children serves their formation (Eph 6:4 "bring them up in the discipline... of the Lord"). The negative strand is the anti-formative pattern of rebellion (Deu 9:7).

**T5.6.1** — Eschatological orientation: "provoke to jealousy" is oriented to Israel's **eschatological salvation** (Rom 10:19; cf. 11:11,26 context); the negative strand draws the eschatological **wrath** (the "wrath of God comes," Eph 5:6; Col 3:6). Record the orientation where present.

---

## T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics

**T6.1.1** — Co-occurring characteristics: **anger/wrath** (the response it arouses — C1/C2; Deu 9:18–19), **jealousy** ("provoked him to jealousy... to anger," Deu 32:16,21 — C4), **idolatry/evil** as instrument, and in the positive strand **love** (Heb 10:24). Strong pairing with jealousy and anger.

**T6.1.2** — Co-occurrence places C3 as the **hinge** between human action and divine/relational anger — it is the cause-term that produces the affect-terms (C1/C2) and is twinned with jealousy (C4).

**T6.2.1** — Sequence: C3 consistently **precedes** anger/wrath (provocation → anger, Deu 9:18; Psa 78:58–59 "provoked him to jealousy... God heard and was full of wrath"). It is the antecedent.

**T6.2.2** — The relationship is **causal**: provocation causes the anger/jealousy that follows (Deu 32:21; Psa 78:58–59). Cause, not mere correlation.

**T6.3.1** — Produces: C3 **produces** divine wrath (C2; Deu 9:19), divine jealousy (C4; Deu 32:16), human anger/grief (C1; 1Sa 1:7), and (positively) love/good works (Heb 10:24). Mechanism: affective elicitation.

**T6.3.2** — Produced by: provocation is itself produced by **idolatry/sin** (its instrument, Deu 4:25) or by **malice/rivalry** (1Sa 1:6) — and, positively, by love (Heb 10:24). 

**T6.3.3** — Constituent relation: provocation is the **causal constituent** of the anger/wrath/jealousy complex — it is the eliciting member of the provoke→anger structure (Deu 32:21).

**T6.4.1** — Shared vocabulary: kaˈas overlaps with **C1** (kaˈaˈs "vexation") and the wrath-lemmas chaˈrah/qaˈtsaph/cheˈmah appear here in their **provoked** sense (shared with C1/C2). Greek parorgismos/parorgizō link to orgē (C1/C2).

**T6.4.2** — Root-level: yes — kaˈas (provoke) and kaˈaˈs (vexation) share a root spanning C3 and C1; the chaˈrah burning-root spans C1/C2/C3 in its provoked use.

**T6.4.3** — The vocabulary sharing shows C3 is the **causative face** of the same anger-architecture — the act that arouses the affect named by C1/C2/C4.

**T6.5.1** — Nearest neighbour: **C4 jealousy** (the two are repeatedly paired and parallel — "provoked him to jealousy... provoked him to anger," Deu 32:16,21). Distinction: C3 is the **act of arousing**; C4 is the **affect aroused** (jealousy).

**T6.5.2** — Apparent overlap with C1/C2: where chaˈrah/qaˈtsaph appear with God as **object** (provoked) they are C3; with God as **bearer** they are C2; with a human bearer they are C1. The deciding criterion is **the term's relation to its subject/object** (arousing vs bearing).

**T6.5.3** — Distinction from C1/C2 is of **direction** (eliciting anger vs experiencing it); from C4 of **kind** (an act of provocation vs the affect of jealousy), though they co-occur.

---

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation

**T7.1.1** — Primary terms/roots: **kaˈas** (H3707, "to provoke, vex to anger"; the related noun kaˈaˈs "vexation/provocation"); Greek **paroxunō** ("provoke, sharpen"), **parorgizō** ("provoke to anger"), **erethizō** ("provoke, irritate"), **paroxusmos** ("a provoking/stirring"). Roots converge on **stirring/sharpening** another to a reaction.

**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: predominantly **verb/action**, characteristically **causative (hiphil)** in Hebrew — "to make angry" (Deu 4:25, morph HVhi…) — with a small noun strand ("provocation," 2Ki 23:26; paroxusmos, Heb 10:24). The causative grammar shows the characteristic is intrinsically about *making* another feel.

**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: from "provoke to anger" (Deu 4:25) through "exasperate/embitter" (Eph 6:4; Col 3:21) and "sharp disagreement" (Act 15:39) to the **positive** "stir up to love" (Heb 10:24) and "provoke to jealousy/zeal" (Rom 10:19; 2Cor 9:2). Breadth: hostile arousal → exasperation → constructive incitement.

**T7.1.4** — Distinguishing terms: **act vs result** — kaˈas (the act of provoking) vs the anger (cheˈmah/chaˈron) it produces; the noun kaˈaˈs marks the **provocation as a thing**. Negative (parorgizō) vs positive (paroxusmos "to good," Heb 10:24) directions are lexically the same root, distinguished by object.

**T7.1.5** — Opposite/absence term: not a single lexeme; the opposite is **pleasing/obeying** God (1Ki 14:8 contrast) or, in the human strand, **not provoking** / **stirring to love** (Eph 6:4; Heb 10:24).

**T7.1.6** — Person-type term: none — there is no noun for "a provoker-type person" in the C3 vocabulary. Record none.

**T7.1.7** — Supplication/seeking term: none. Record none.

**T7.1.8** — OT→NT relationship: the Hebrew causative kaˈas (provoke God to anger) carries into Greek parorgizō/parorgismos (Eph 4:26; 6:4), but the NT notably **broadens** the root toward the positive **paroxusmos** "stir up to good" (Heb 10:24) and the redemptive "provoke to jealousy" (Rom 10:19). Continuity of the causative idea; development toward a redeemable/positive use.

**T7.1.9** — NT term: **paroxusmos** used positively (Heb 10:24) and as "sharp disagreement" (Act 15:39); **parorgismos** (Eph 4:26). These mark a NT refinement distinguishing destructive from constructive provocation.

**T7.1.10** — Full vocabulary arc: from the OT **causative provocation of God to wrath** (kaˈas, Deu 4:25) through interpersonal **exasperation** (Eph 6:4) to the NT **constructive stirring** (Heb 10:24) — a complete arc from covenant-rebellion to relational edification.

**T7.2.1** — Function of the primary term in its primary verse: in Deu 4:25 kaˈas is the **purpose-clause verb** ("make a carved image... to provoke him to anger") — the term names the offence that the whole warning turns on. In Heb 10:24 paroxusmos is the **goal** of mutual consideration ("how to stir one another up").

**T7.2.2** — Literary forms: **covenant law/exhortation** (Deu 4:25; 31:29), **Deuteronomistic narrative** (1Ki 14:9; 2Ki 17:11), **prophecy** (Jer 25:6–7), **NT epistle** (Eph 6:4; Col 3:21; Heb 10:24), **NT narrative** (Act 15:39). Responsible reading weighs the covenant-warning form (conditional consequence) and the epistolary paraenesis (command/exhortation) (BOOK distribution: Jer 13, 1Ki 11, Deu 8).

**T7.2.3** — Logical structure: **conditional-consequential** in the covenant strand — *if* you provoke God by idolatry, *then* wrath/judgment follows (Deu 4:25–26; 31:29); **imperatival** in the epistolary strand — *do not* provoke (Eph 6:4), *do* stir up to good (Heb 10:24).

**T7.2.4** — Contextual settings: **covenantal** (Deu 4:25), **judicial-historical** (the kings "provoking the LORD," 1Ki/2Ki), **familial/communal** (Eph 6:4; Col 3:21; Heb 10:24), **missional-eschatological** (provoke to jealousy unto salvation, Rom 10:19). The settings show provocation as covenant betrayal at one pole and relational edification at the other.

**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor verse: **Deuteronomy 4:25** — "you... act corruptly by making a carved image... and by doing what is evil... so as to provoke him to anger" — most fully and directly expresses the dominant characteristic (the deliberate human act of arousing God's covenant wrath).

**T7.2.6** — Deu 4:25 shows what no other verse shows together: the **deliberate act** (carved image), the **moral character** (evil), and the **explicit purpose** (to provoke God to anger) — the complete anatomy of provoking God in one warning. (The positive pole's anchor is Heb 10:24.)

**T7.3.1** — Most useful human-science lens: per the science extract, **moral psychology** — provocation terms (paroxunō, kaˈas, erethizō) are treated there as "the external stimulus that triggers the moral-anger response — the wrongdoing that elicits it."

**T7.3.2** — Where the framework illuminates: appraisal/elicitor research illuminates provocation as the **external trigger** whose perceived wrongdoing arouses anger (Deu 4:25 idolatry as the elicitor; 1Sa 1:6 taunting as the elicitor) — and the social-norm-enforcement account illuminates why provoking God's covenant honour draws judgment.

**T7.3.3** — Where they diverge: science treats provocation only as a **stimulus to a human emotion**; the C3 evidence makes its gravest instance **provoking God** — a covenant/theological category science does not address (outside-science inventory). Science also lacks a clean place for the **positive** provocation "to love and good works" (Heb 10:24), which is constructive rather than aggressive.

**T7.3.4** — Gaps surfaced by science: the **honour-culture** finding (lower thresholds for anger at insult to status/dignity) may illuminate the covenant-honour logic of provoking God (idolatry as insult to the covenant Lord, Deu 32:16,21) — a prompt for further verse work on provocation-as-dishonour. Labelled inferential.

**Three poles (data-derived).** (i) **Human jealousy/envy** — rivalrous resentment (Rachel envies Leah, Gen 30:1; the brothers envy Joseph, Gen 37:11; "envy rots the bones," Pro 14:30; Ecc 4:4). (ii) **Zeal** — passionate ardour for God/His house/righteousness (Phinehas, Num 25:11,13; "zeal for your house," Psa 69:9; Elijah "jealous for the LORD," 1Ki 19:10,14). (iii) **Divine jealousy** — God's covenant possessiveness ("a jealous God," Exo 20:5; 34:14; Deu 4:24). A distinct sub-form is the **marriage "spirit of jealousy"** ordeal (Num 5:14–30). All answered.
