# M02 · C6 — Strife / Quarrel / Contention — Tier Catalogue Analysis

- **File:** wa-m02-c6-strife-quarrel-tieranalysis-v1_0-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Cluster / Characteristic:** M02 "Anger, Wrath and Indignation" · C6 Strife / quarrel / contention
- **Version:** v1_0 · **Author:** le Roux Cilliers
- **Prior output (this session):** wa-m02-c5-indignation-tieranalysis-v1_0-20260619.md
- **Catalogue answered:** WA-tier-catalogue-current-state-v2-20260619.md (126 questions, T0–T7) · **Science lens (T7.3):** wa-m02-anger-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md

**Change control (v1_0):** First issue. All 126 questions answered for C6. **valence used** (CC-confirmed current 2026-06-19).

**Evidence basis.** C6 = 83 focus-occurrences (OT 66 / NT 17): riv "strife/dispute/lawsuit/cause" (60), eris "quarrel" (9), antilogia "dispute" (4), matsˈtsah/meˈriˈvah/matsˈtsut "strife" (6), filoneikia/filoneikos "love of dispute" (2), logomachia "quarrel about words" (1), thumomacheō (1). Concentrated in Proverbs (14), Psalms (7), Isaiah (7), Jeremiah (6). Type: **status 80** (a noun — a thing/event, not an act). valence: neutral 41, sinful 33, forbidden 1.

**Inner-being relevance caveat (decisive — GR-PROG-007).** C6 is **faculty-NONE in 82 of 83 occurrences**: strife/quarrel is an external relational/forensic *event*, not an inner-being state. Retained in M02 by researcher decision (DEC-3); its occurrences split sharply by the term-level filter:
- **Inner-being-engaging (passes filter):** strife as the **fruit of an inner state** — "pressing anger produces strife" (Pro 30:33); strife and jealousy "of the flesh" (1Cor 3:3; cf. Gal 5:20); the **dispute over greatness** driven by pride (Luk 22:24, the one affect-tagged occurrence); the act of **committing one's cause to God** from the soul/heart (Jer 11:20; 20:12; Lam 3:58; Pro 22:23); the **divine covenant-lawsuit** engaging the people's heart (Hos 4:1; Mic 6:2).
- **Inner-being-peripheral (fails filter):** the **judicial-procedural** sense — "lawsuit/case/cause" as legal procedure (Exo 23:2–3,6; Deu 17:8; 19:17; 21:5; 25:1; 2Sa 15:2,4). These engage no inner-being characteristic and should be filtered out at VC classification.

Answers below cover the characteristic as constituted, flagging which strand each finding rests on. A consolidated Evidence Base follows.

---

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design

**T0.1.1** — Relation to God: God **has a controversy/indictment (rîb)** with His people and the nations — "the LORD has a controversy with the inhabitants of the land" (Hos 4:1); "the LORD has an indictment against his people" (Mic 6:2); "an indictment against the nations" (Jer 25:31) — div_role agent. God is also the one to whom a person **commits his cause** (Psa 35:23; Lam 3:58 "you have taken up my cause") and who **pleads the cause** of the oppressed (Pro 22:23; Psa 74:22). Most human-strife occurrences have no God-relation (Gen 13:7).

**T0.1.2** — Across C6, contention is **borne by God** as covenant-lawsuit (Hos 4:1; Mic 6:2) and by the **creature** as quarrel/strife (Gen 13:7; 1Cor 3:3). *Interpretation:* the divine instance is **judicial covenant-contention**; the creaturely instance ranges from righteous cause-pleading (1Sa 24:15) to sinful quarrelling (1Cor 3:3). The shared term riv links God's just controversy and human strife.

**T0.2.1** — Stated purpose/effect: human strife **divides and harms** — herdsmen's strife forces separation (Gen 13:7–9); "pressing anger produces strife" (Pro 30:33); strife of the flesh marks immaturity (1Cor 3:3). God's controversy **summons to judgment/repentance** (Mic 6:2). The committed cause **secures vindication** (Lam 3:58–59; 1Sa 24:15). Record none where unstated.

**T0.2.2** — valence confirms the split: **sinful 33 / forbidden 1** (the quarrel/strife pole — Pro 17:14; 1Cor 3:3; Tit 3:9) vs **neutral 41** (the judicial-cause and divine-lawsuit pole — Exo 23:2; Mic 6:2). Human quarrelsome strife belongs to the fallen condition; just cause-pleading and the divine lawsuit belong to the moral order of justice.

**T0.2.3** — Future-fullness orientation: the divine controversy is oriented to a **day of vindication/recompense** ("the day of vengeance, the year of recompense for the cause of Zion," Isa 34:8); the committed cause looks to future **vindication** (Lam 3:58–59). Record where present; the human-quarrel pole has none.

**T0.3.1** — Divine-likeness aspect: the aspect instantiated is **just contention for the right** — pleading the cause of the oppressed images God who "will plead their cause" (Pro 22:23); committing one's cause to the righteous Judge images trust in His justice (Jer 11:20). Sinful quarrelling images nothing of God.

**T0.3.2** — Shared/creaturely: just cause-contention is a **creaturely analogue** of God's righteous controversy; quarrelsome strife is a purely creaturely disorder. The rîb vocabulary is shared between God's lawsuit and human dispute.

**T0.3.3** — Where a person commits their cause to God it indicates **faith in the righteous Judge** (Jer 11:20); where a person is given to strife it indicates a **fleshly, immature condition** (1Cor 3:3 "you are still of the flesh... there is jealousy and strife among you").

**T0.4.1** — Typological use: the **covenant-lawsuit (rîb)** form is typological-covenantal — God's formal indictment summoning the mountains as witnesses (Mic 6:1–2) points to the covenant-court reality. Direction: divine instance establishing the pattern. Elsewhere narrative/wisdom, no typology.

---

## T1 — Definition

**T1.1.1** — Programme name: **Strife / quarrel / contention**. The name signals an **external relational/forensic conflict** — strife, quarrel, dispute, lawsuit — not an inner affect. Senses: strife 18, cause 16, dispute 9, case/lawsuit 9, quarrel(ing) 7, indictment 3.

**T1.1.2** — Primary terms: riv (Hebrew, "strife, dispute, legal case, controversy"; verb "to contend/plead a cause") — the dominant term, spanning quarrel and lawsuit; Greek eris ("quarrel, strife," a work of the flesh, Gal 5:20), antilogia ("dispute, hostility"), logomachia ("quarrel about words"). Definitionally a **contention between parties** — interpersonal or forensic.

**T1.1.3** — Directional/relational: contention is inherently **between two parties** — "a quarrel between" herdsmen (Gen 13:7), a "cause between a man and his neighbour" (Deu 25:1), God's controversy "with" His people (Hos 4:1). It is irreducibly two-party.

**T1.2.1** — Predominantly a **condition/status** (noun, 80 of 83) — strife/a dispute/a cause is a *thing* that exists between parties (Pro 17:14 "the beginning of strife"), not chiefly an act of the inner being. (The single affect/act occurrence is the prideful "dispute" of Luk 22:24.)

**T1.2.2** — **Compound** where it engages the inner being: strife joins **anger** ("pressing anger produces strife," Pro 30:33), **jealousy** ("jealousy and strife," 1Cor 3:3), **pride** (the dispute over greatness, Luk 22:24), and a cluster of **works of the flesh** (eris, Gal 5:20 context; Rom 1:29). As a bare legal term it is simple (Deu 17:8).

**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite: **peace / a quiet, unifying disposition** — "it is an honour for a man to keep aloof from strife" (Pro 20:3); slowness to anger that "quiets contention" (Pro 15:18). Peace stands against strife.

**T1.3.2** — At its edge it excludes **forbearance and unity**: the wise "keep aloof" (Pro 20:3); believers are charged to **avoid** quarrels (Tit 3:9; the Lord's servant "must not be quarrelsome," 2Ti 2:24). Strife resists peaceable forbearance.

**T1.3.3** — It ends where **anger/jealousy** (its inner cause, C1/C4) begins — strife is the *outward event* those affects produce (Pro 30:33; 1Cor 3:3) — and where mere **legal procedure** begins (the inner-being-peripheral "cause/lawsuit," Deu 17:8). It is contention itself, not the affect behind it.

**T1.4.1** — Modes: a **quarrel/strife** between parties (Gen 13:7); a **legal cause/lawsuit** (Exo 23:2–3; Deu 25:1); a **covenant-lawsuit** God brings (Mic 6:2); a **cause committed to God** for vindication (Jer 11:20; Lam 3:58); **fleshly quarrelling/dissension** in the church (1Cor 3:3; Tit 3:9). Multiple modes.

**T1.4.2** — Yes — mode varies sharply by context: **interpersonal** quarrel (Gen 13:7), **forensic** case (Deu 25:1), **divine** covenant-lawsuit (Hos 4:1; Mic 6:2), **prayerful** cause-committing (Jer 11:20), **ecclesial** dissension (1Cor 3:3). Same term, very different registers.

**T1.4.3** — Communicative/spoken mode: yes, intrinsically — contention is conducted in **speech** (pleadings; "quarrels about words," 1Ti 6:4; the dispute "arose among them," Luk 22:24); God's controversy is a **spoken indictment** (Mic 6:1–2). Recorded.

**T1.5.1** — Immediate response: strife issues in **separation** (Abram and Lot part, Gen 13:8–9); the dispute over greatness draws **Jesus' correction** (Luk 22:24–26); the committed cause draws **God's action to vindicate** (Lam 3:58–59). Record none where unstated.

**T1.5.2** — Varied: separation (Gen 13:8), rebuke (Luk 22:25), or divine vindication (Lam 3:58). No single immediate response.

**T1.6.1** — Sustained effect: strife, sustained, **escalates** ("the beginning of strife is like letting out water; so quit before the quarrel breaks out," Pro 17:14) and **divides** communities (1Cor 1:11; 3:3). God's controversy, sustained, brings **judgment** (Hos 4:1–3 the land mourns). The committed cause yields lasting **redemption** (Lam 3:58). Record none where unstated.

**T1.6.3** — Immediate response is the flash (separation/rebuke); sustained effect is the **escalation/division or vindication** (Pro 17:14; 1Cor 3:3; Lam 3:58). Episode vs settled result.

**T1.7.1** — It "operates" (rightly, valence neutral) as **just cause-pleading** — the oppressed whose cause God pleads (Pro 22:23; 23:11), the innocent committing their cause to God (Jer 11:20; 1Sa 24:15). The condition is a genuine claim of justice.

**T1.7.2** — It is **distorted** (valence sinful) as **quarrelsomeness of the flesh** — from jealousy (1Cor 3:3), pride (Luk 22:24), "pressing anger" (Pro 30:33), an "unhealthy craving for controversy" (1Ti 6:4); it is **forbidden** to the Lord's servant (2Ti 2:24; Tit 3:9). No verse attributes strife to another spirit — **silent** on that.

**T1.7.3** — Where strife is present in the fleshly form, the person is shown **immature and divisive** ("of the flesh... behaving only in a human way," 1Cor 3:3) or **proud** (Luk 22:24, contending for greatness against Christ's example).

---

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries

**T2.1.1** — Locations (only where the inner being is engaged): **soul** — "the LORD will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them" (Pro 22:23); "you have taken up my cause... you have redeemed my life" (Lam 3:58); "consider him who endured such hostility... lest you grow weary in your souls" (Heb 12:3, antilogia); **conscience|heart** — "O LORD... who test the heart and the mind... to you have I committed my cause" (Jer 11:20; 20:12); **flesh** — "he is entering into judgment with all flesh" (Jer 25:31). 77/83 locate no seat (Gen 13:7) — record none.

**T2.1.2** — The pattern: most strife occurrences locate **no seat** (an external event), confirming the faculty-NONE finding. Where a seat appears it is the **heart/soul** of one **committing a cause to God** (Jer 11:20; Lam 3:58) or **wearying under hostility** (Heb 12:3) — the inner being is engaged only at the cause-committing/endurance edge, not in strife as such. Any body link (Jer 25:31) is **indicative** of universal judgment.

**T2.10.1** — Movement: strife moves **between parties** (external; Gen 13:7); the divine controversy moves **from God onto** the people (Hos 4:1); the committed cause moves **from the person up to God** (Jer 11:20). Strife is also **received-from-outside** as assault on the innocent (Psa 74:22; 1Ti 6:4). No internal spirit→soul→body sequence; no angelic source. Record the party-to-party and person-to-God movements.

**T2.7.1** — Body direction: thin — "all flesh" comes under God's contention (Jer 25:31); souls "grow weary" under hostility (Heb 12:3). Where a link exists it runs **the contention bearing down on the person's soul/flesh** (Heb 12:3; Jer 25:31). No soul→body expression proper to the characteristic — mostly **silent**.

**T2.9.1** — Origin: strife **originates between parties from an inner cause** — **anger** (Pro 30:33), **jealousy/flesh** (1Cor 3:3), **pride** (Luk 22:24), **hatred** ("hatred stirs up strife," Pro 10:12). The divine controversy originates **in God's covenant claim** (Hos 4:1). Stated sources, where given, are inner affects (the flesh) or God's just claim.

**T2.9.2** — Origin is **multiple**: fleshly affects (Pro 10:12; 30:33; 1Cor 3:3), God's covenant claim (Hos 4:1), and a genuine injustice provoking a just cause (1Sa 25:39). It changes with context.

---

## T3 — The Inner Faculties

**T3.1.1** — Perception: strife is triggered by perceived **insult/wrong** — Nabal's insult provokes the cause David would have pursued (1Sa 25:39); the dispute over greatness follows the perception of rank (Luk 22:24). Perception is the gate where the inner being is engaged.

**T3.1.2** — Effect on perception: contention **fixes** parties on the grievance (1Cor 1:11–12 partisan alignment); no verse states it distorting the senses generally — otherwise **silent**.

**T3.1.3** — Pattern: where C6 engages the inner being it is **perception-triggered**; the procedural-legal occurrences engage perception only formally.

**T3.2.1** — Cognition: engaged in the **"quarrels about words/controversy" form** — "an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words" (1Ti 6:4); "foolish controversies... quarrels about the law" (Tit 3:9). Strife here is a **disorder of reasoning** (logomachia).

**T3.2.2** — Effect on cognition: such strife **degrades** thought into "envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions" (1Ti 6:4); committing one's cause to God **settles** the mind in trust (Jer 11:20).

**T3.2.3** — Pattern: the controversy-form **engages and corrupts cognition** (1Ti 6:4; Tit 3:9); the legal-procedural form engages cognition only as formal adjudication.

**T3.3.1** — Memory: thin — the divine controversy invokes **remembered covenant** ("no faithfulness... no knowledge of God," Hos 4:1). Direct memory-faculty engagement is limited — mostly **silent**.

**T3.3.2** — **Silent** on strife acting on a memory faculty.

**T3.3.3** — The thinness indicates strife is framed as a **present event**, covenant memory only the backdrop of the divine lawsuit.

**T3.4.1** — Affect: **almost never** the term's own faculty (NONE 82/83). The single affect-engaging occurrence is the **prideful dispute** over greatness (Luk 22:24). Otherwise strife engages affect only **as its cause** (anger/jealousy produce it, Pro 30:33; 1Cor 3:3), not as its own faculty.

**T3.4.2** — Effect on affect: strife **inflames** the affects it springs from (escalating, Pro 17:14) and wearies the soul (Heb 12:3).

**T3.4.3** — The near-total faculty-NONE pattern is the **defining finding**: strife is **not an inner affect** but an external event produced by inner affects — the basis of the GR-PROG-007 caveat.

**T3.5.1** — Creativity: not engaged. **Silent.**

**T3.5.2** — **Silent.**

**T3.5.3** — Absence indicates no relation to the originative faculty.

**T3.6.1** — Volition: engaged where the will is summoned **away** from strife — "keep aloof from strife" (Pro 20:3); "have nothing to do with foolish controversies; they breed quarrels" (2Ti 2:23–24) — and where one **chooses** to commit a cause to God rather than self-avenge (1Sa 24:15; Jer 11:20).

**T3.6.2** — Effect on volition: fleshly strife **captures** the will toward division (1Cor 3:3); the disciplined will **withdraws** (Pro 20:3) or **redirects** to God's justice (Jer 11:20).

**T3.6.3** — Pattern: strife engages the **will** chiefly as something to be *refused* (Pro 20:3; 2Ti 2:24) or *redirected* (commit the cause to God, Jer 11:20).

**T3.7.1** — Agency: strife is **enacted agency between parties** (the quarrel "between" herdsmen, Gen 13:7; the lawsuit pursued, Deu 25:1); committing a cause is the agency of **appeal to God** (Lam 3:58); God's controversy is His **judicial agency** (Mic 6:2).

**T3.7.2** — Effect on agency: strife **drives** separation (Gen 13:9), partisan division (1Cor 1:11), or — redirected — **rest in God's action** (1Sa 24:15; Pro 22:23).

**T3.7.3** — The pattern shows strife as **agency exercised between parties** — destructive when fleshly, just when it is God's controversy or a cause rightly committed to Him.

**T3.8.1** — Moral evaluation: engaged at both poles — fleshly strife is **condemned** (Gal 5:20 context; 1Cor 3:3; Tit 3:9); God's controversy **is** a moral indictment (Hos 4:1; Mic 6:2); a just cause is **morally vindicated** (1Sa 24:15). valence: sinful 33, forbidden 1, neutral 41.

**T3.8.2** — Effect: strife **expresses** a moral state — the fleshly verdict on the quarreller (1Cor 3:3) and God's verdict on the covenant-breaker (Mic 6:2).

**T3.8.3** — Pattern: contention is **morally split** — sinful when fleshly quarrelling, righteous/neutral when it is God's just controversy or the oppressed's cause (the valence sinful-33/neutral-41 split confirms this).

**T3.9.1** — Conscience: engaged where the one committing a cause appeals to God who **tests heart and mind** — "O LORD of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind... to you have I committed my cause" (Jer 11:20; 20:12). The conscience appeals to the searching God.

**T3.9.2** — Effect on conscience: committing the cause to the heart-testing God **rests** the conscience in His justice (Jer 11:20). Recorded; elsewhere not stated.

**T3.9.3** — The Jeremiah cases indicate the cause-committing form engages **conscience** (the heart known to God), though strife as such does not.

**T3.10.1** — Conscientiousness: engaged where the integrated moral person **refuses** strife and **commits** the cause to God (Pro 20:3; Jer 11:20; 2Ti 2:24).

**T3.10.2** — Effect: exercised conscientiousness **avoids** strife and entrusts justice to God (Pro 20:3; Jer 11:20); its failure yields **fleshly division** (1Cor 3:3).

**T3.10.3** — The pattern marks the *response to* strife (avoid it / commit the cause to God) as a **test-site of integrated character**, even though strife itself is not an inner faculty.

**T3.11.1** — Relational capacity: strife is **purely relational** — it exists only between parties (Gen 13:7; Deu 25:1; Hos 4:1) and is the **breakdown** of relational capacity (division, 1Cor 1:11; separation, Gen 13:9).

**T3.11.2** — Effect on relational capacity: strife **fractures** bonds (Abram/Lot separate, Gen 13:9; the church divides, 1Cor 3:3); committing one's cause to God **preserves** the relationship from vengeance (David spares Saul, 1Sa 24:12,15).

**T3.11.3** — The pattern shows C6 is **constitutively relational** (it cannot exist without two parties) and is chiefly the **rupture** of relationship — its inner-being relevance lies in the affects that drive it and the trust that refuses it.

---

## T4 — Relational Interfaces

**T4.1.1** — God-toward-human: yes — God **contends** with humans in covenant-lawsuit (Hos 4:1; 12:2; Mic 6:2; Jer 25:31) and **pleads the cause** of the oppressed (Pro 22:23; 23:11; Psa 74:22).

**T4.1.2** — Basis: **covenantal and responsive** — God's controversy is grounded in covenant unfaithfulness (Hos 4:1 "no faithfulness... no knowledge of God") and His cause-pleading in His commitment to justice for the weak (Pro 22:22–23). Conditional on the moral situation.

**T4.1.3** — What it shows of God's disposition: God is a **righteous Judge** who both **indicts** covenant-breakers (Mic 6:2) and **advocates** for the oppressed (Pro 22:23) — His contention reveals committed justice.

**T4.2.1** — Human-to-God: yes — the person **commits/pleads their cause to God** ("to you have I committed my cause," Jer 11:20; "plead my cause, O LORD," Psa 35:1,23; "you have pleaded the cause of my soul," Lam 3:58). The movement is the appeal of the wronged to the righteous Judge.

**T4.2.2** — Inner posture required: **trust in God's justice and surrender of self-vengeance** — "may the LORD judge between me and you" (1Sa 24:12,15). The posture is faith that lets God contend.

**T4.2.3** — What it shows: committing one's cause to God shows a relationship of **trust in His righteous judgment** (Jer 11:20; Lam 3:58) — the wronged person rests in God rather than self-avenging.

**T4.3.1** — Person-to-person extension: yes — strife/quarrel is "extended" between persons (Gen 13:7; the Corinthian quarrels, 1Cor 1:11; brother against brother, 1Cor 6:6 context). It operates as mutual contention.

**T4.3.2** — Inner conditions accompanying it: **anger, jealousy, pride, hatred** drive it (Pro 10:12; 30:33; 1Cor 3:3; Luk 22:24); an "unhealthy craving for controversy" (1Ti 6:4).

**T4.3.3** — What the giver must have/become: no virtue is required to start a quarrel; it requires a **fleshly** condition (1Cor 3:3). To rightly contend for a *just cause* one must have a genuine claim and entrust it to God (1Sa 24:15). Recorded.

**T4.4.1** — Receiving: the other party **receives** the strife as conflict (Gen 13:7) or the just/divine contention as **indictment** (Mic 6:2; Jer 25:31). Uptake is endured contention.

**T4.4.2** — Conditions of uptake: a **shared stake** (land, Gen 13:7; rank, Luk 22:24; doctrine, 1Ti 6:4) draws parties in; **covenant guilt** makes one the object of God's controversy (Hos 4:1).

**T4.4.3** — The person who meets contention and does not take up the quarrel is shown **keeping aloof / yielding** (Abram yields to Lot, Gen 13:8–9; the honourable man keeps aloof, Pro 20:3).

**T4.5.1** — Within bonds vs across distance: strife operates **within close bonds** (kinsmen, Gen 13:7–8; brothers in the church, 1Cor 1:11) and **across** them (the nations, Jer 25:31; legal cases between strangers, Deu 25:1). Both.

**T4.5.2** — Covenantal scope: God's controversy is **covenant-internal** (against Israel, Hos 4:1; Mic 6:2) and **crosses** to the nations (Jer 25:31). Human strife crosses any line. Both.

**T4.5.3** — Relational scope: **wide** — kinsmen (Gen 13:7), the church (1Cor 3:3), neighbours in court (Deu 25:1), the oppressed and their oppressors (Pro 22:23), God and His people (Mic 6:2), God and the nations (Jer 25:31). Contention reaches across the relational field.

**T4.6.1** — Spiritual beings: not shown operating toward angelic/adversarial beings (the nearest is "the rebellion of Korah," Jude 11, antilogia — human rebellion). **Silent** on a spiritual-being interface.

**T4.6.2** — Adversarial site: not evidenced as a site of adversarial weaponising. **Silent** (recorded as not evidenced).

**T4.6.3** — Angelic mediation: not evidenced. **Silent.**

---

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension

**T5.1.1** — Transformation: strife transforms **relationship and condition** — it forces separation (Gen 13:9), divides a church (1Cor 3:3); God's controversy transforms a people toward **judgment or repentance** (Mic 6:2–8); a committed cause transforms the wronged toward **vindication/redemption** (Lam 3:58). Record none where unstated.

**T5.1.2** — Reversible/irreversible: strife is **resolvable** — quit before it breaks out (Pro 17:14), keep aloof (Pro 20:3), make peace (Gen 13:8–9); once escalated it can become **entrenched** division (1Cor 1:11; 3:3). Both, depending on response.

**T5.2.1** — Sequence: **inner affect (anger/jealousy/pride) → strife → division/escalation** (Pro 30:33; 1Cor 3:3; Pro 17:14); **wrong suffered → cause committed to God → vindication** (1Sa 24:12–15; Lam 3:58); **covenant sin → God's controversy → judgment** (Hos 4:1–3). Record none where no sequence appears.

**T5.3.1** — Mechanism of change: **escalation** ("letting out water," Pro 17:14) for unchecked strife; **withdrawal/peacemaking** (Gen 13:8; Pro 20:3) and **entrusting to God** (Jer 11:20) for resolution; **judicial indictment** for God's controversy (Mic 6:2). Record none where unstated.

**T5.3.2** — Differs: strife is changed by **avoidance/peacemaking** (Pro 20:3), by **entrusting the cause to God** (1Sa 24:15), or, for the guilty, by **God's judgment** (Mic 6:2). Context-dependent.

**T5.4.1** — Relation to suffering: strife **produces suffering** (the oppressed whose cause must be pleaded, Pro 22:22–23; souls wearied by "hostility," Heb 12:3) and arises amid the suffering of **injustice** (1Sa 25:39; Lam 3:58).

**T5.4.2** — What suffering does to it: the suffering of injustice drives the wronged to **commit their cause to God** rather than retaliate (1Sa 24:12–15; Lam 3:58); enduring "hostility" without growing weary is set as the **formative** path (Heb 12:3, looking to Christ who endured antilogia). Suffering can turn contention Godward.

**T5.5.1** — Sanctification arc: the *response to* strife participates in sanctification — the believer is formed by **refusing quarrelsomeness** (2Ti 2:24; Tit 3:9), **keeping aloof** (Pro 20:3), and **enduring hostility** while looking to Christ (Heb 12:3). Fleshly strife is the **mark of immaturity** to be outgrown (1Cor 3:1–3).

**T5.6.1** — Eschatological orientation: the divine controversy is oriented to a **day of recompense** (Isa 34:8); the committed cause looks to **final vindication** (Lam 3:58–59). Record where present; the human-quarrel pole has none.

---

## T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics

**T6.1.1** — Co-occurring characteristics: **anger** ("pressing anger produces strife," Pro 30:33; "a hot-tempered man stirs up strife," Pro 15:18 — C1), **jealousy** ("jealousy and strife," 1Cor 3:3 — C4), **hatred** ("hatred stirs up strife," Pro 10:12 — M06), **pride** (the dispute over greatness, Luk 22:24 — M08). Strife co-occurs as the **product** of these affects.

**T6.1.2** — Co-occurrence places C6 as the **outward fruit** of the inner anger/jealousy/hatred/pride family — the relational event those characteristics generate, sitting at the boundary of the inner-being field.

**T6.2.1** — Sequence: strife consistently **follows** an inner affect — anger (Pro 30:33), jealousy (1Cor 3:3), hatred (Pro 10:12) — and **precedes** division/escalation (Pro 17:14; 1Cor 1:11). Downstream of the affects.

**T6.2.2** — The relationship is **causal**: the inner affects *produce* strife (Pro 30:33; Pro 10:12). Strife is the effect, not the cause.

**T6.3.1** — Produces: strife **produces** division, separation, escalation, and weariness of soul (Gen 13:9; 1Cor 3:3; Pro 17:14; Heb 12:3).

**T6.3.2** — Produced by: strife is **produced by** anger (C1; Pro 30:33), jealousy (C4; 1Cor 3:3), hatred (Pro 10:12), pride (Luk 22:24), and "fleshly" immaturity (1Cor 3:3). This is its defining structural feature — it is an **output** of the inner-being affects.

**T6.3.3** — Constituent relation: strife is **not a constituent of** an inner faculty (it is faculty-NONE); rather the inner affects are constituents of the situations that *generate* it. It is the relational **expression** of those affects, not an element of them.

**T6.4.1** — Shared vocabulary: riv is **distinct** from the anger-lemmas; it is **collocated** with anger/hatred terms (Pro 30:33; 10:12). NT eris/eritheia/logomachia are the strife terms, distinct from orgē/thumos.

**T6.4.2** — Root-level: the riv root generates strife/cause/contend within C6; it does **not** share a root with the burning-anger family — the link is causal/collocational, not etymological.

**T6.4.3** — The vocabulary picture shows C6 is a **distinct relational-forensic category** that the anger affects *produce* — explaining both why it sits in the anger cluster (as their fruit) and why it is lexically and faculty-distinct (it is an event, not an affect).

**T6.5.1** — Nearest neighbour: **C1 human anger** (its most frequent cause — Pro 30:33; 15:18). The precise distinction: anger is the **inner affect**; strife is the **outward relational event** that affect produces.

**T6.5.2** — Apparent overlap: where riv is rendered "angry/contention" near anger terms (Pro 15:18) the line can blur; the **precise boundary** is faculty — strife is faculty-NONE (an event between parties), anger is an affect within a person. The procedural "cause/lawsuit" sense is further still from the inner being and fails the GR-PROG-007 filter.

**T6.5.3** — The distinction from C1/C4 is one of **kind and constitutional status** — an external relational/forensic event (C6) vs an inner affect (C1 anger, C4 jealousy). Strife relates to the affects as their **product**, not as a peer affect.

---

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation

**T7.1.1** — Primary terms/roots: **riv** (H7379, "strife, dispute, legal cause, controversy"; verb "to contend, plead a cause") — root sense of **contending/conducting a case**; Greek **eris** ("quarrel, strife"), **eritheia** ("rivalry"), **antilogia** ("dispute, contradiction, hostility"), **logomachia** ("word-battle"). Roots converge on **two-party contention**, interpersonal or forensic.

**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: predominantly **noun/status** (80 of 83 — "strife/a cause," Pro 17:14) with a verbal "contend/plead" use (riv as verb, 1Sa 24:15) and one participial "love of dispute" (filoneikos). The noun-dominance shows the characteristic is a **state of contention between parties**, not an inner act.

**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: a single Hebrew term (riv) spans **interpersonal quarrel** (Gen 13:7), **legal lawsuit/case** (Deu 25:1), **covenant-lawsuit/indictment** (Mic 6:2), and **pleading/contending for a cause** (1Sa 24:15; Pro 22:23). The Greek adds **factional rivalry** (eritheia), **verbal quarrelling** (logomachia), and **hostility** (antilogia). Breadth: private quarrel → court case → covenant-court → just advocacy.

**T7.1.4** — Distinguishing terms: **the cause vs the quarrel** — riv as a just "cause" (Pro 22:23) vs sinful "strife" (Pro 17:14); **act vs status** — the verb "contend/plead" (1Sa 24:15) vs the noun "strife" (Pro 17:14). The Greek distinguishes **factional rivalry** (eritheia) from **verbal quarrel** (logomachia).

**T7.1.5** — Term for the opposite/absence: not a single lexeme; the opposite is **peace** and the wisdom of **keeping aloof** (Pro 20:3) and **not being quarrelsome** (2Ti 2:24, amachos "not contentious" — a near-antonym). Recorded.

**T7.1.6** — Person-type term: **filoneikos** ("contentious, dispute-loving," Luk 22:24 context) and the "contentious/quarrelsome man/wife" of Proverbs (Pro 21:19; 26:21) — a person-type for the habitually contentious. Recorded.

**T7.1.7** — Supplication/seeking term: the **cause-pleading** vocabulary functions as a "seeking justice from another" term — "plead my cause, O LORD" (Psa 35:1,23; 43:1); riv as appealing to God to contend for one. Recorded (a seeking-of-vindication term).

**T7.1.8** — OT→NT relationship: the Hebrew riv (covenant-controversy and just cause) gives way in the NT to **eris/eritheia/logomachia** as **vices of the flesh** to be put off (Gal 5:20; 1Cor 3:3; Tit 3:9), while righteous advocacy is carried by other vocabulary. Continuity of "contention"; development that **moralises** quarrelling as a fleshly vice and relocates righteous advocacy.

**T7.1.9** — NT term: **logomachia/logomacheō** ("word-battle," 1Ti 6:4; 2Ti 2:14) is a distinctively NT-era formation marking **doctrinal quarrelling**; **eritheia** ("selfish rivalry/factionalism") likewise. Their coinage marks a NT concern with **church-dividing strife**. Recorded.

**T7.1.10** — Full vocabulary arc: from the OT **riv** holding quarrel, lawsuit, covenant-controversy, and just advocacy in one root, to the NT splitting of **fleshly strife** (eris/eritheia/logomachia, to be put off) from righteous advocacy — an arc from a unified contention-term to a moralised division between sinful quarrelling and just contention.

**T7.2.1** — Function of the primary term in its primary verse: in Mic 6:2 riv ("indictment/controversy") is the **governing legal metaphor** of the oracle. In Pro 30:33 riv ("strife") is the **result clause** — "pressing anger produces strife" — naming the social fruit of the inner affect.

**T7.2.2** — Literary forms: **wisdom** (Pro 17:14; 20:3; 30:33), **narrative** (Gen 13:7; 1Sa 24–25), **law** (Exo 23:2–3; Deu 25:1), **prophetic covenant-lawsuit** (Hos 4:1; Mic 6:1–2), **lament** (Lam 3:58; Psa 35), **NT epistle** (1Cor 1:11; 3:3; 1Ti 6:4; Tit 3:9), **NT narrative** (Luk 22:24). Responsible reading distinguishes wisdom maxim, legal procedure, prophetic rîb form, and epistolary vice-list (BOOK distribution: Pro 14, Psa 7, Isa 7, Jer 6).

**T7.2.3** — Logical structure: **wisdom-consequential** — *if* anger/hatred presses, *then* strife results; *therefore* keep aloof (Pro 30:33; 20:3; 17:14); **covenant-forensic** — premise: covenant unfaithfulness; God's indictment; call to repentance (Mic 6:1–8); **vice-list** — strife among the works of the flesh to be put off (Gal 5:19–21; 1Cor 3:3).

**T7.2.4** — Contextual settings: **judicial** (Exo 23:2–3; Deu 25:1), **covenantal-forensic** (Hos 4:1; Mic 6:2), **communal/ecclesial** (1Cor 1:11; 3:3), **wisdom-instructional** (Pro 20:3), **lament/petition** (Psa 35; Lam 3:58). The settings show contention as legal procedure, covenant lawsuit, church division, wise avoidance, and prayer for vindication.

**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor verse: **Micah 6:2** ("the LORD has an indictment against his people, and he will contend with Israel") for the divine pole, and **1 Corinthians 3:3** ("there is jealousy and strife among you... are you not of the flesh?") for the human-fleshly pole. Together they most fully express C6.

**T7.2.6** — These anchors show what no single verse shows alone: Mic 6:2 that contention can be **God's righteous covenant-lawsuit**; 1Cor 3:3 that strife is the **fruit of the flesh** and a mark of immaturity — framing C6 as a relational event spanning divine justice and human carnality.

**T7.3.1** — Most useful human-science lens: per the science extract, **social and evolutionary psychology** — rivalry and strife sit under "Jealousy and rivalry" (social comparison; competition for scarce goods), with strife terms (riv, eris, matsˈtsah) explicitly there.

**T7.3.2** — Where the framework illuminates: social-comparison and resource-competition research illuminates strife as **competition for scarce goods/status** — herdsmen over land/water (Gen 13:7), the Corinthians over teacher-allegiance (1Cor 1:11–12), the disciples over rank (Luk 22:24). Scarcity/competition amplifying contention matches the evidence.

**T7.3.3** — Where they diverge: science treats strife as social conflict only; the C6 evidence makes its weightiest instance the **covenant-lawsuit of God** (Hos 4:1; Mic 6:2) and the **just cause committed to God** (Jer 11:20) — theological/forensic categories science does not address. Scripture also **moralises** strife as a work of the flesh to be put off (Gal 5:20; 1Cor 3:3).

**T7.3.4** — Gaps surfaced by science: the rivalry/competition lens prompts testing whether C6's occurrences are better classified by their **driving affect** (anger vs jealousy vs pride) — since the data shows strife is faculty-NONE and produced *by* those affects (Pro 30:33; 1Cor 3:3; Luk 22:24). This supports the GR-PROG-007 recommendation to filter C6 by the inner state each occurrence engages. Labelled inferential — convergent with the relevance caveat above.

## Closing notes
- **Questions answered:** all 126. Silence recorded where C6 verses do not speak (T3.5 creativity; parts of T3.3 memory; T4.6 spiritual beings/angelic).
- **Decisive feature:** C6 is faculty-NONE (82/83) — an external relational/forensic event, not an inner affect. Inner-being relevance lies only in (a) strife as the **fruit** of inner affects (Pro 30:33; 1Cor 3:3; Luk 22:24), (b) **committing one's cause to God** (Jer 11:20; Lam 3:58), and (c) God's **covenant-lawsuit** (Hos 4:1; Mic 6:2). The procedural legal-case occurrences (Exo 23:2–3; Deu 17:8) should be filtered out at VC classification per GR-PROG-007.
- **Provenance:** read-resolved fields supporting; valence (sinful 33 / neutral 41 / forbidden 1) used; T7.3 from the science extract.

# M02 · C7 — Bitterness — Tier Catalogue Analysis

- **File:** wa-m02-c7-bitterness-tieranalysis-v1_0-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Cluster / Characteristic:** M02 "Anger, Wrath and Indignation" · C7 Bitterness
- **Version:** v1_0 · **Author:** le Roux Cilliers
- **Prior output (this session):** wa-m02-c6-strife-quarrel-tieranalysis-v1_0-20260619.md
- **Catalogue answered:** WA-tier-catalogue-current-state-v2-20260619.md (126 questions, T0–T7) · **Science lens (T7.3):** wa-m02-anger-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md

**Change control (v1_0):** First issue. All 126 questions addressed for C7. **valence used** (CC-confirmed current 2026-06-19).

**Evidence basis — and an explicit thinness warning.** C7 = **only 4 focus-occurrences**, all the single Greek noun **pikria** ("bitterness"), all NT, all status-type, all faculty-NONE, all with no stated cause, origin, intensity, or constitutional seat: Act 8:23 ("in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity"), Rom 3:14 ("their mouth is full of curses and bitterness"), Eph 4:31 ("let all bitterness... be put away from you"), Heb 12:15 ("a root of bitterness springs up... causes trouble... defiles many"). valence: sinful 3, forbidden 1. **Because the evidence is this sparse, a large number of catalogue questions are honestly answered "Silent."** Where the four verses do speak, the finding is given and cited; nothing is inferred beyond them except where explicitly labelled. A consolidated Evidence Base follows.

**Note on scope.** This C7 focus set captures only the NT pikria occurrences seeded to M02. The wider Hebrew "bitterness" field (marah/mar — e.g. Naomi "call me Mara," Ruth 1:20; "bitterness of soul," 1Sa 1:10; Job 7:11; 10:1) lies **outside this focus set** and is flagged at T7.1.8 as a known gap for cross-checking.

---

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design

**T0.1.1** — Relation to God: none of the four verses predicates bitterness of God; God does not bear pikria. In Heb 12:15 the "root of bitterness" is set in explicit contrast to "the grace of God" that the community must not fail to obtain. So bitterness stands **opposed to grace**, never borne by God. Record: no divine-bearer relation.

**T0.1.2** — Across C7 bitterness is borne only by the **creature**, and always as a **disorder** (Act 8:23 Simon; Rom 3:14 the depraved mouth; Eph 4:31 the believer to put it off; Heb 12:15 the defiling root). *Interpretation:* bitterness is a wholly fallen-condition characteristic — it images nothing of God and has no righteous form in this set.

**T0.2.1** — Stated purpose/effect: bitterness **"causes trouble" and "defiles many"** (Heb 12:15); it fills the mouth with "curses" (Rom 3:14); it accompanies "the bond of iniquity" (Act 8:23). Its effect is corrupting and contaminating. Record none beyond these.

**T0.2.2** — valence (sinful 3, forbidden 1) confirms bitterness belongs **wholly to the fallen condition** — it is to be "put away" (Eph 4:31, the forbidden case) and is a mark of the unregenerate mouth (Rom 3:14) and of a heart "not right before God" (Act 8:21,23). No created/holy register appears.

**T0.2.3** — Orientation toward future fullness: none — bitterness is oriented only to **corruption** (defiling many, Heb 12:15), the opposite of the grace toward which the community presses. **Silent** on any positive future orientation.

**T0.3.1** — Divine-likeness aspect: none. Bitterness images nothing of God; it is the inner corrosion grace removes (Eph 4:31). **Silent** on a positive image-aspect.

**T0.3.2** — Shared/creaturely: a purely **creaturely disorder** — not a shared attribute. Record: not borne by God.

**T0.3.3** — Where bitterness is present it indicates a **heart not right before God** (Act 8:21,23 "your heart is not right... you are in the gall of bitterness") and a condition that **defiles** community (Heb 12:15). It marks corrupted inner standing.

**T0.4.1** — Typological/eschatological use: the **"root of bitterness"** of Heb 12:15 alludes to Deu 29:18 ("a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit" — covenant apostasy), giving bitterness a **covenant-warning** resonance. Direction: an OT covenant-warning applied to the NT community. Otherwise none.

---

## T1 — Definition

**T1.1.1** — Programme name: **Bitterness**. The name signals a **settled inner sourness/resentment** that corrupts speech and community. Sense: "bitterness" (pikria) in all four.

**T1.1.2** — Primary term: **pikria** (Greek, "bitterness") — from pikros ("sharp, bitter" to taste), used metaphorically for **resentful, harsh inner disposition** (Eph 4:31) and corrupt speech (Rom 3:14). The single term carries the whole characteristic in this set.

**T1.1.3** — Directional/relational: bitterness is implicitly **against** others — it issues in "curses" against people (Rom 3:14) and "defiles many" relationally (Heb 12:15); it is listed among relationship-destroying vices to put off (Eph 4:31 "bitterness... wrath... anger... clamor... slander"). Record the relational, corrupting direction.

**T1.2.1** — A **condition/status** (all four are status-type nouns) — bitterness is a settled state, not an act. "Gall of bitterness" (Act 8:23), "full of... bitterness" (Rom 3:14), "all bitterness" (Eph 4:31), "root of bitterness" (Heb 12:15) all name a state.

**T1.2.2** — **Compound** in three of four — bitterness is listed alongside partner vices: with **iniquity** (Act 8:23 "bond of iniquity"); with **cursing** (Rom 3:14); with **wrath, anger, clamor, slander, malice** (Eph 4:31, co-terms orgē/kakia/blasfēmia); and it "defiles" (miainō, Heb 12:15). It rarely stands alone — it clusters with anger and malice.

**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite: **the grace of God** and the kindness that replaces it — Heb 12:15 opposes the bitter root to "the grace of God"; Eph 4:32 opposes the bitterness of 4:31 to "be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving." Grace/kindness/forgiveness stands against bitterness.

**T1.3.2** — At its edge it excludes **kindness and forgiveness** — the remedy is to "put away... and be kind... forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you" (Eph 4:31–32). Bitterness resists forgiveness.

**T1.3.3** — It ends where **wrath/anger** (C1) shade into a *settled* resentment — bitterness is the **chronic, settled** form listed beside the more acute "wrath and anger" (Eph 4:31), distinguished as the sour residue rather than the hot flare.

**T1.4.1** — Modes: as **"gall of bitterness"** (a poisoning condition, Act 8:23); as **bitter speech** ("mouth full of... bitterness," Rom 3:14); as a **disposition to be put off** (Eph 4:31); as a **"root" that springs up** and spreads (Heb 12:15). The root-mode (latent then springing up and defiling) is the most developed.

**T1.4.2** — Yes — mode varies across the four: a present poisoning state (Act 8:23), corrupt speech (Rom 3:14), a vice to renounce (Eph 4:31), a latent-then-spreading root (Heb 12:15). Same noun, four facets.

**T1.4.3** — Communicative/spoken mode: yes — bitterness issues in **speech** ("their mouth is full of curses and bitterness," Rom 3:14). Recorded; the other three are dispositional.

**T1.5.1** — Immediate response: in Eph 4:31 the called-for response is to **"put it away"** (the one immediate_response value in the data); in Heb 12:15 the response to guard against is the trouble and defilement it causes. Otherwise **silent** on an immediate response.

**T1.5.2** — Not enough data to vary — only Eph 4:31 states a response (put it away). **Silent** elsewhere.

**T1.6.1** — Sustained effect: bitterness **"springs up... causes trouble... defiles many"** (Heb 12:15) — its sustained effect is **spreading contamination** of the community. This is the clearest effect in the set.

**T1.6.3** — The data does not distinguish an immediate flash from a sustained effect except in Heb 12:15, where the sustained effect is **communal defilement**. Otherwise **silent**.

**T1.7.1** — Conditions where it "takes hold": bitterness takes root in a **heart not right before God** (Act 8:21,23) and where the community **"fails to obtain the grace of God"** (Heb 12:15). The condition is a grace-deficient, unforgiving heart.

**T1.7.2** — It is **removed/blocked** by repentance (Act 8:22 "repent... pray that... the intent of your heart may be forgiven") and by putting it off in favour of kindness and forgiveness (Eph 4:31–32). No verse attributes bitterness to another spirit — **silent** on that.

**T1.7.3** — Where bitterness takes hold, the person is shown **bound in iniquity and unforgiven** until repentance (Act 8:23) and the community **defiled** (Heb 12:15). It is a corrupting, spreading condition.

---

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries

**T2.1.1** — Location: **NONE stated** in all four (location field empty). The nearest seat-language is the **heart** in the surrounding context — "your heart is not right before God" (Act 8:21) and "the intent of your heart" (Act 8:22) — placing bitterness near the **heart** by context, though the pikria term itself carries no seat. Record: term-intrinsic location NONE; context implies the heart (Act 8:21–22).

**T2.1.2** — The term carries **no constitutional seat** of its own (consistent with its faculty-NONE status). Any heart-link is **contextual/indicative** (Act 8:21–22), not lexicalised. No body link appears. **Silent** on a body relation.

**T2.10.1** — Movement: the only movement shown is the **"root... springs up"** of Heb 12:15 — bitterness rising from a latent root within the community/person and **spreading outward to defile many**. No spirit→soul→body sequence; no angelic introduction. Record the latent-root → springing-up → defiling-others movement.

**T2.7.1** — Body direction: **silent** — no body-direction is stated (location NONE throughout).

**T2.9.1** — Origin: stated origin **NONE** in the data; contextually, bitterness arises from a **heart not right before God** (Act 8:21) and from **failing to obtain grace** (Heb 12:15) — i.e. generated within a grace-deficient heart. The "root" image (Heb 12:15) implies an inner latent source. Record contextual origin; term-intrinsic origin NONE.

**T2.9.2** — With only contextual data, origin appears **single** (an inner, grace-deficient heart) — but the evidence is too thin to assert variation. **Largely silent.**

---

## T3 — The Inner Faculties

**T3.1.1** — Perception: **Silent** — no verse links bitterness to a perceptual trigger (the data gives no cause). (Contextually Simon's bitterness follows his seeing the apostles' power, Act 8:18–19, but the pikria verse itself states no perception.)

**T3.1.2** — **Silent.**

**T3.1.3** — **Silent** — too thin to establish a perception pattern.

**T3.2.1** — Cognition: engaged only indirectly via "the **intent** of your heart" that must be forgiven (Act 8:22) — bitterness is bound up with a corrupt intent/disposition. Otherwise **silent**.

**T3.2.2** — **Silent** on an effect on cognition.

**T3.2.3** — Too thin to establish a cognition pattern. **Largely silent.**

**T3.3.1** — Memory: **Silent** — no memory link is stated. (Resentment's conceptual tie to remembered injury is not lexicalised in these four verses.)

**T3.3.2** — **Silent.**

**T3.3.3** — **Silent.**

**T3.4.1** — Affect: bitterness is conceptually an **affective state** (a settled sour resentment), but the term is tagged **faculty-NONE** in all four — Scripture here treats pikria as a **named disposition/condition** rather than analysing it as a faculty-event. Record: affective in concept, faculty-NONE in the data.

**T3.4.2** — Effect on affect: it is grouped with **wrath and anger** as kindred affective vices to put off (Eph 4:31) — i.e. it belongs to and sours the angry-affective field. Recorded.

**T3.4.3** — The faculty-NONE tagging indicates bitterness is presented as a **settled condition to be renounced** (Eph 4:31), not dissected as an inner mechanism — consistent with its thin, vice-list treatment.

**T3.5.1** — Creativity: not engaged. **Silent.**

**T3.5.2** — **Silent.**

**T3.5.3** — **Silent.**

**T3.6.1** — Volition: engaged as the object of a **command of the will** — "let all bitterness... be put away from you" (Eph 4:31) and "see to it that no one fails... that no root of bitterness springs up" (Heb 12:15). The will is summoned to renounce and vigilantly prevent it.

**T3.6.2** — Effect on volition: bitterness is something the regenerate will must **actively remove** and **guard against** (Eph 4:31; Heb 12:15) — it opposes the will's pursuit of grace and kindness (Eph 4:32).

**T3.6.3** — Pattern: the clearest faculty-engagement in C7 is **volitional** — bitterness is chiefly addressed as a vice to be **chosen against** (Eph 4:31; Heb 12:15).

**T3.7.1** — Agency: bitterness is **agency-corrupting** — it fills the mouth with curses (Rom 3:14, an act of corrupt speech) and "causes trouble" (Heb 12:15). Its agency is destructive.

**T3.7.2** — Effect on agency: it **drives** cursing speech (Rom 3:14) and communal harm (Heb 12:15). Recorded.

**T3.7.3** — Pattern: where agency appears, bitterness **issues in harmful speech and trouble** (Rom 3:14; Heb 12:15).

**T3.8.1** — Moral evaluation: directly engaged — bitterness is uniformly **condemned** (valence sinful 3 / forbidden 1): a state needing forgiveness (Act 8:22–23), a mark of depravity (Rom 3:14, in Paul's catena on universal sin), a vice to put off (Eph 4:31), a defiling root to prevent (Heb 12:15).

**T3.8.2** — Effect: it **incurs and expresses** a negative moral verdict — "you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity" (Act 8:23); it defiles (Heb 12:15).

**T3.8.3** — Pattern: bitterness is **uniformly sinful** in this set — no righteous or neutral instance (unlike anger C1 or indignation C5). Its moral valence is singular.

**T3.9.1** — Conscience: engaged where Simon is called to **repent and seek forgiveness for the intent of his heart** (Act 8:22) — the bitterness is to be brought to a convicted, repentant conscience. Otherwise **silent**.

**T3.9.2** — Effect on conscience: it is a condition the awakened conscience must **repent of** (Act 8:22). Recorded; elsewhere not stated.

**T3.9.3** — The Act 8:22–23 case indicates bitterness engages conscience as **a thing to repent of**, though this is a single instance.

**T3.10.1** — Conscientiousness: engaged in the **community-vigilance** charge — "see to it that no one... that no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble" (Heb 12:15) — integrated moral watchfulness against it. And the put-off/put-on of Eph 4:31–32 is integrated moral practice.

**T3.10.2** — Effect: failed vigilance **lets bitterness defile many** (Heb 12:15); exercised, it **protects the community's grace** (Heb 12:15) and replaces bitterness with kindness (Eph 4:32).

**T3.10.3** — The pattern marks bitterness as a **target of integrated moral vigilance** — both personal (put it off) and communal (watch that no root springs up).

**T3.11.1** — Relational capacity: bitterness is **relationally corrosive** — it issues in curses against others (Rom 3:14) and **"defiles many"** (Heb 12:15); it is listed among the vices that destroy fellowship, opposed to being "kind... forgiving one another" (Eph 4:31–32).

**T3.11.2** — Effect on relational capacity: it **contaminates community** (Heb 12:15) and **poisons speech** (Rom 3:14); its removal **restores** kindness and forgiveness (Eph 4:32).

**T3.11.3** — The pattern shows bitterness, though thinly evidenced, is consistently **relationally destructive** — its whole evidenced effect is the corruption of speech and community.

---

## T4 — Relational Interfaces

**T4.1.1** — God-toward-human: not borne by God; the only God-relation is **opposition** — bitterness is contrary to "the grace of God" (Heb 12:15) and is the condition God must **forgive** (Act 8:22). **Silent** on God extending bitterness (He does not).

**T4.1.2** — **Silent** (God does not bear or extend bitterness).

**T4.1.3** — What it shows of God: only that God's **grace** is its opposite and remedy (Heb 12:15; Act 8:22 forgiveness). Recorded indirectly.

**T4.2.1** — Human-to-God: Simon's bitterness places him in "the bond of iniquity" before God, requiring **repentance and prayer to God** for forgiveness (Act 8:22–23). The movement is the bitter person needing to turn to God for cleansing.

**T4.2.2** — Inner posture required: **repentance** ("repent... and pray to the Lord," Act 8:22). The remedy posture.

**T4.2.3** — What it shows: bitterness shows a **heart not right before God** (Act 8:21) — a disordered God-relation needing repentance.

**T4.3.1** — Person-to-person extension: yes — bitterness is extended as **curses against others** (Rom 3:14) and **defilement of many** (Heb 12:15); it is a relationship-destroying vice (Eph 4:31).

**T4.3.2** — Inner conditions accompanying it: a **grace-deficient, unforgiving heart** (Heb 12:15; Eph 4:31–32 set against forgiveness). 

**T4.3.3** — What the giver becomes: one whose **mouth is full of cursing** (Rom 3:14) and who **defiles** others (Heb 12:15) — a source of communal corruption. Recorded.

**T4.4.1** — Receiving: others **receive** bitterness as its **defilement** ("defiles many," Heb 12:15) and its **curses** (Rom 3:14). Uptake is contamination.

**T4.4.2** — Conditions of uptake: **proximity in community** ("springs up... defiles many," Heb 12:15) — the community is contaminated by an unchecked bitter root.

**T4.4.3** — Those who receive it are **defiled** (Heb 12:15). The community is the victim.

**T4.5.1** — Within bonds vs across distance: operates **within the community** (defiling many, Heb 12:15; the church addressed, Eph 4:31) and as general human depravity (Rom 3:14). Chiefly within bonds.

**T4.5.2** — Covenantal scope: the Heb 12:15 warning is **community-internal** (the covenant community guarding against an apostate root, echoing Deu 29:18). Recorded.

**T4.5.3** — Relational scope: **community and speech** — those cursed (Rom 3:14), the "many" defiled (Heb 12:15), the church called to put it off (Eph 4:31). Narrower than the other characteristics, fitting its sparse data.

**T4.6.1** — Spiritual beings: not shown toward angelic/adversarial beings. **Silent.**

**T4.6.2** — Adversarial site: not evidenced. **Silent.**

**T4.6.3** — Angelic mediation: not evidenced. **Silent.**

---

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension

**T5.1.1** — Transformation: bitterness transforms a community toward **defilement** (Heb 12:15); its removal transforms the believer toward **kindness and forgiveness** (Eph 4:31–32). Record none beyond these.

**T5.1.2** — Reversible/irreversible: shown **reversible** by repentance (Act 8:22) and by putting off / putting on (Eph 4:31–32); if left, it **spreads** (Heb 12:15). Both, by response.

**T5.2.1** — Sequence: **failing to obtain grace → root of bitterness springs up → causes trouble → defiles many** (Heb 12:15) — the one clear developmental sequence. Also **bitterness/iniquity → repentance → forgiveness** (Act 8:22–23). Record none elsewhere.

**T5.3.1** — Mechanism of change: **repentance and prayer** (Act 8:22) and **deliberate put-off/put-on** replacing bitterness with kindness and forgiveness (Eph 4:31–32). The remedy mechanisms.

**T5.3.2** — Differs: removed by **repentance** (Act 8:22) or **renunciation-and-replacement** (Eph 4:31–32); prevented by **communal vigilance** (Heb 12:15). 

**T5.4.1** — Relation to suffering: **Silent** — the four verses do not tie bitterness to suffering/affliction (the broader Hebrew "bitterness of soul" field, which does, lies outside this set — see T7.1.8).

**T5.4.2** — **Silent.**

**T5.5.1** — Sanctification arc: bitterness is explicitly a **vice to put off** in the sanctification process (Eph 4:31, within the put-off/put-on of 4:22–32) and a **root to be vigilantly prevented** lest it defile the community's pursuit of holiness (Heb 12:14–15, "strive for... holiness... see to it that no root of bitterness"). It is firmly placed in the sanctification arc as something to be removed.

**T5.6.1** — Eschatological orientation: indirectly — the Heb 12:15 warning stands in a passage oriented to **not falling short / not being like Esau** (12:15–17) and to the coming unshakable kingdom (12:28). Bitterness threatens perseverance toward that end. Recorded indirectly; otherwise **silent**.

---

## T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics

**T6.1.1** — Co-occurring characteristics: **wrath and anger** (Eph 4:31 "bitterness and wrath and anger," co-terms orgē — C1), **malice/evil** (kakia, Eph 4:31), **slander/blasphemy** (blasfēmia, Eph 4:31), **cursing** (Rom 3:14), **iniquity** (Act 8:23), **defilement** (miainō, Heb 12:15 — links to the defilement cluster M10c). It clusters tightly with anger and malice.

**T6.1.2** — Co-occurrence places bitterness as the **settled, sour residue** within the anger family — listed first in Eph 4:31's progression "bitterness → wrath → anger → clamor → slander," it reads as the **root disposition** from which the louder forms grow.

**T6.2.1** — Sequence: in Eph 4:31 bitterness **heads** the vice-list (the settled state underlying wrath/anger/clamor); in Heb 12:15 it is a **root** that springs up first and then defiles. It reads as **prior/underlying** to the more acute angry expressions.

**T6.2.2** — The relationship is **source-like**: bitterness is presented as a **root/underlying disposition** (Heb 12:15; Eph 4:31 heading the list) from which louder anger and slander proceed. (Inferential from word-order and the root-image; labelled as such.)

**T6.3.1** — Produces: bitterness **produces** cursing (Rom 3:14), trouble, and defilement of many (Heb 12:15). 

**T6.3.2** — Produced by: contextually, by a **heart not right before God** (Act 8:21) and **failing to obtain grace** (Heb 12:15). The term itself states no producer (cause NONE).

**T6.3.3** — Constituent relation: bitterness reads as a **constituent root** of the anger/malice complex (Eph 4:31) — the settled resentment underlying its more active members. Inferential.

**T6.4.1** — Shared vocabulary: pikria is **distinct** from the orgē/thumos anger lemmas but is **listed with** them (Eph 4:31) — shared collocation, not shared root. It links lexically to the **defilement** field via miainō (Heb 12:15).

**T6.4.2** — Root-level: the pikr- root (pikria/pikros/pikrainō) is its own family ("bitter to taste" → metaphorical resentment); it does **not** share a root with the anger family — the link is collocational/conceptual.

**T6.4.3** — The vocabulary picture shows C7 is a **distinct, narrowly-attested disposition** (one term, four verses) that sits within the anger cluster by **collocation** (Eph 4:31) and by its shared corrupting effect, not by shared lexis.

**T6.5.1** — Nearest neighbour: **C1 human anger** (listed immediately beside it, Eph 4:31 "bitterness and wrath and anger"). The precise distinction: anger is the **acute flare**; bitterness is the **chronic, settled sourness** underlying it.

**T6.5.2** — Apparent overlap: bitterness and "wrath/anger" appear together (Eph 4:31); the **precise boundary** is duration/register — bitterness is the **settled resentful root**, wrath/anger the **active outbursts**. Bitterness also links to **defilement** (Heb 12:15), distinguishing its **contaminating** character.

**T6.5.3** — Distinction from C1 is one of **chronicity** (settled resentment vs acute anger); from the defilement field one of **emphasis** (resentful disposition vs ritual/moral staining), though Heb 12:15 joins them.

---

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation

**T7.1.1** — Primary term/root: **pikria** (G4088, "bitterness"), from **pikros** ("sharp, bitter"); cognate verb **pikrainō** ("to make bitter"). Root sense: **bitter to the taste**, extended metaphorically to **resentful, harsh inner disposition** and corrupt speech.

**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: **noun/status only** in this set (all 4) — bitterness named as a **state/condition** ("gall of bitterness," "root of bitterness"), never as a verb or quality-adjective here. The range is narrow: a settled noun-state.

**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: within four verses — a **poisoning condition** ("gall of bitterness," Act 8:23), **corrupt speech** ("full of... bitterness," Rom 3:14), a **vice to renounce** (Eph 4:31), a **spreading root** (Heb 12:15). All negative; breadth limited to facets of one resentful disposition.

**T7.1.4** — Distinguishing terms: none internal to the set (single term). The **"gall" (cholē)** and **"root" (rhiza)** and **"defile" (miainō)** are the accompanying images that distinguish the facets (poison / latent source / contamination). Recorded.

**T7.1.5** — Opposite/absence term: **the grace of God** (Heb 12:15) and **kindness/forgiveness** (Eph 4:32, chrēstos/forgiving) function as the structural opposites. Idiomatic, not a single antonym lexeme.

**T7.1.6** — Person-type term: none in this set (no "bitter-type person" noun; pikros as a person-descriptor — e.g. "do not be harsh/bitter to them," Col 3:19, pikrainō — lies just outside the focus set). Record none here; flag Col 3:19 as adjacent.

**T7.1.7** — Supplication/seeking term: none. Record none.

**T7.1.8** — OT→NT relationship and **scope gap**: this focus set is **NT-only (pikria)**. The **Hebrew bitterness field is absent from the set** — marah/mar ("bitter; bitterness of soul"): Naomi "call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly" (Ruth 1:20–21); Hannah "bitterness of soul" (1Sa 1:10); Job "I will speak in the bitterness of my soul" (Job 7:11; 10:1); "the bitter in soul" (Job 3:20); Hezekiah (Isa 38:15,17). That field includes **grief-laden, non-sinful** bitterness (bitterness of affliction), which the NT pikria set does **not** capture. **This is a known gap**: C7 as constituted reflects only the NT resentment-bitterness, not the OT affliction-bitterness. Flagged for researcher review and possible cross-cluster check with M03 (Grief). *(Inferential/flagged — not in the focus set.)*

**T7.1.9** — NT-coined term: pikria is not NT-coined (classical Greek), but its **metaphorical-ethical use** for resentful disposition (Eph 4:31) and the **"root of bitterness"** covenant-allusion (Heb 12:15, echoing Deu 29:18 LXX) are characteristic NT/LXX developments. Recorded.

**T7.1.10** — Full vocabulary arc: within this set, a **single noun** (pikria) presenting bitterness as a **uniformly sinful, settled, contaminating disposition** — poison (Act 8:23), corrupt speech (Rom 3:14), vice to renounce (Eph 4:31), defiling root (Heb 12:15). The fuller biblical arc (including OT affliction-bitterness) lies outside the set (T7.1.8).

**T7.2.1** — Function of the primary term in its primary verse: in Eph 4:31 pikria **heads the list** of vices to "put away," functioning as the **root resentment** from which the following (wrath, anger, clamor, slander) flow — the term governs the call to renounce relational sin. In Heb 12:15 it is the **subject of the warning** ("root of bitterness... defiles many").

**T7.2.2** — Literary forms: **NT narrative** (Act 8:23, Peter's rebuke of Simon), **epistolary catena/argument** (Rom 3:14, within Paul's OT-quotation chain on universal sin), **epistolary paraenesis** (Eph 4:31, the put-off/put-on exhortation), **epistolary warning** (Heb 12:15, the covenant-perseverance warning). Responsible reading weighs the rebuke, the OT-catena (Rom 3:14 quotes Psa 10:7), the ethical exhortation, and the covenant warning.

**T7.2.3** — Logical structure: **imperatival** (Eph 4:31 "put away"; Heb 12:15 "see to it... that no root"), **diagnostic** (Act 8:23 "you are in the gall of bitterness"), and **indictment-by-citation** (Rom 3:14, evidencing universal depravity). The structure is consistently **condemnatory/remedial**.

**T7.2.4** — Contextual settings: **disciplinary** (Act 8, confronting Simon), **doctrinal** (Rom 3, universal sin), **pastoral-ethical** (Eph 4, church relationships), **covenant-perseverance** (Heb 12, the community guarding holiness). The settings show bitterness as a sin to repent of, evidence of depravity, a relationship-vice, and a community threat.

**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor verse: **Hebrews 12:15** — "see to it... that no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled" — most fully expresses C7's character: bitterness as a **latent root** that **springs up, troubles, and defiles a community**, set against **the grace of God**. (Eph 4:31 is the key remedial anchor.)

**T7.2.6** — Heb 12:15 shows what no other verse in the set shows together: bitterness's **latency** (a root), its **active emergence** (springs up), its **harm** (causes trouble), its **contagion** (defiles many), and its **opposite** (the grace of God) — the fullest single picture available in this sparse set.

**T7.3.1** — Most useful human-science lens: per the science extract, **moral/social psychology of resentment and rumination** — bitterness as **chronic resentment**, the settled, ruminative residue of unresolved anger/grievance (distinguished from acute anger).

**T7.3.2** — Where the framework illuminates: rumination/resentment research illuminates bitterness as the **settled, festering** form (consistent with its noun-state, root-image treatment, Heb 12:15; Eph 4:31 heading the list) and its **contagion** in groups (defiling many, Heb 12:15) parallels findings on resentment spreading socially. The forgiveness literature illuminates the prescribed remedy (Eph 4:32 forgiveness).

**T7.3.3** — Where they diverge: the four verses present bitterness as **uniformly sinful and requiring repentance/forgiveness before God** (Act 8:22–23; Eph 4:32 "as God in Christ forgave you") — a moral-theological framing science does not supply. Science also recognises **legitimate, grief-borne bitterness** (closer to the OT affliction-field, T7.1.8) that this NT-only set excludes — a divergence created by the focus set's scope, not by the science.

**T7.3.4** — Gaps surfaced by science: the resentment/grief distinction prompts the **scope question** flagged at T7.1.8 — whether C7 should incorporate the OT "bitterness of soul" field (Ruth 1:20; 1Sa 1:10; Job 7:11), which the science would classify as grief-borne rather than resentment-borne bitterness. Labelled inferential — a concrete prompt for researcher review of C7's membership.

---

## Closing notes
- **Questions addressed:** all 126; a high proportion are honestly **"Silent"** owing to the 4-verse evidence base. Where the verses speak (volition — put it off, Eph 4:31; effect — defiles many, Heb 12:15; moral verdict — uniformly sinful; repentance — Act 8:22), findings are given and cited.
- **Key data feature:** one term (pikria), 4 NT verses, all status/faculty-NONE, valence sinful 3 / forbidden 1 — uniformly negative; reads as the settled "root" resentment underlying the louder anger family (Eph 4:31).
- **Flagged scope gap (T7.1.8 / T7.3.4):** the OT Hebrew "bitterness of soul" field (marah/mar — Ruth 1:20; 1Sa 1:10; Job 7:11) — including grief-borne, non-sinful bitterness — is **outside this focus set**. Recommend researcher review of whether C7 membership should extend to it (possible M03 cross-check).
- **Provenance:** the four verses and read-resolved context; valence CC-confirmed current and used; T7.3 from the science extract.
