# M03 · Characteristic B — Distress / constriction (the “straits”) · Findings by tier question

- **File:** wa-m03-char-b-tier-findings-v1_0-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Related:** evidence base wa-m03-char-b-distress-v1_0-20260619.md; tier framework wa-tier-catalogue-restructured-v2-20260611.md (T-codes are the reference key); science lens wa-m03-grief-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md (Section 4); obslog wa-obslog-m03-ve-char-derive-v2-20260619.md.
- **Scope:** every live tier question answered as a self-contained finding (prose can be written from it without returning to source data); citations inline. Negative findings stated explicitly. Retired constructs (T1.2.3, T1.8, T2.8, T5.7, T6.6, T6.7) are omitted. Field-absent questions are answered by inference from verse identities and present fields, as agreed.
- **Status:** v1_0.
- **Evidence summary:** 136 verses (OT 130 / NT 18); faculty = affect (129); seat soul 12 / flesh 4 / heart 4 / inward-parts 2; God = agent ×12 (he both brings and relieves distress); valence neutral 104 / sinful 8 / righteous 1; lead terms `tsa.rah` (66), `tsar` (29), `a.mal` (17), Greek `thlibō` (10).

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
**T0.1.1** — Distress images God as the one who both sends adversity in judgement and is the refuge to whom the distressed cry: the Psalm 107 refrain has the people cry to the LORD in their trouble and be delivered (Psa 107:6,13,19,28), while elsewhere God is the agent who brings the distress (2Ch 15:6; Deu 28:57; Deu 31:17). God is thus pictured as sovereign over the straits — both their author and their exit.
**T0.1.2** — Distress is related to God as **agent** in 12 verses (e.g. Deu 28:57; Deu 31:17; 2Ch 15:6; Psa 107:6,13,19,28); it is not predicated of God as a state he bears. God stands over distress, not within it.
**T0.1.3** — That God is never said to be in distress himself frames the characteristic as a creaturely condition under his governance, not a divine attribute.
**T0.2.1** — Where a purpose appears, distress drives the person to cry out to God and be heard (Psa 107; Jon 2:2, distress from the belly of Sheol answered). Its served purpose is to turn the person Godward.
**T0.2.2** — Distress is presented as a feature of the fallen condition — "man is born to trouble" (Job 5:7) — not of original design.
**T0.2.3** — The evidence orients distress toward relief rather than fullness: the recurring movement is from straits to deliverance (Psa 107), with no verse pointing distress itself toward an eschatological fullness. Negative on future-fullness orientation.
**T0.3.1–.3** — No verse ties distress to the image of God; it is a creaturely experience of pressure, not an image-bearing attribute. Negative finding.
**T0.4.1–.2** — Distress is not deployed typologically in its own right; it functions as the circumstance from which deliverance is sought. No christological or covenantal typology rests on the distress terms themselves.

## T1 — Definition
**T1.1.1** — "Distress / constriction": grief experienced as pressure and narrowing — the inner being hemmed in. The name signals straitness, not the felt ache (A) but the squeeze that produces it.
**T1.1.2** — Hebrew `tsa.rah`/`tsar` carry the root sense of *narrowness, straits*; `me.tsu.qah`/`ma.tsoq` of *constraint*; Greek `thlibō` is *to press*, `stenochōreō` *to crush into a narrow place*. The vocabulary is spatial-bodily before it is emotional.
**T1.1.3** — The terms carry a constitutional implication (the soul pressed) and a directional one (pressure from without, inward), orienting the enquiry toward external cause.
**T1.2.1** — Predominantly a **status/condition** (status 109, quality 23, action 16) — a state of being-pressed borne by the person.
**T1.2.2** — Simple in structure, though it characteristically arises with an external besieging agent named in the verse.
**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite: relief / enlargement ("he set me in a broad place", the antonymic spatial image). Cross-cluster (peace/rest), named only.
**T1.3.2** — Distress excludes ease and security; it is the felt closing-in of options.
**T1.3.3** — It ends where the external pressure lifts (deliverance) or turns inward into felt ache (A) — the boundary with A is constitutional (soul-pressure vs heart-ache).
**T1.4.1** — Operates as a borne condition of constriction, occasionally as an act of pressing (`thlibō`), and as a quality (`tsar` "distressed").
**T1.4.2** — Operates chiefly at the soul level, with bodily registration (flesh, inward-parts) in extremity (Deu 28:53–57, siege).
**T1.4.3** — Distress finds voice in the cry for help (Psa 107; Psa 120:1, "in my distress I called"), so it has a communicative mode — the cry out of the straits.
**T1.5.1** — The most immediate response is the cry to God for deliverance (Psa 107:6; Psa 120:1; Jon 2:2).
**T1.5.2** — Consistent across the evidence: distress repeatedly issues in calling out.
**T1.6.1** — Sustained distress, where unrelieved, wears the person down and can harden into bitterness (the F-boundary); where relieved, it issues in deliverance and testimony (Psa 107).
**T1.7.1–.3** — Distress is borne under pressure, not received as a gift; reception-framing does not apply. Negative.

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries
**T2.1** — No occurrence locates distress at the spirit level. Negative.
**T2.2** — Located at the **soul** level in 12 occurrences (e.g. Gen 42:21, "the distress of his soul"; 1Sa 22:2; 2Sa 4:9) — distress is predominantly a soul-phenomenon, the innermost self pressed.
**T2.3** — Located in the **heart** in 4 occurrences (e.g. Psa 25:17, "the troubles of my heart"; 2Cor 2:4), engaging the heart's feeling-under-pressure.
**T2.4** — No mind-location. Negative — distress does not engage the mind in the evidence.
**T2.5** — Beyond heart and soul, distress is seated in the **inward-parts** twice (Psa 55:10; 2Cor 6:12), an intensifying interior locus.
**T2.6** — Linked to the **flesh** in 4 occurrences, all in extremity (the siege of Deu 28:53,55; Jer 19:9; 2Cor 7:5) — distress pressing into the body.
**T2.7** — Where the flesh-link appears, direction runs soul→body: the inward straits register as bodily affliction; the siege verses make the bodily consequence the measure of the distress.
**T2.9.1** — Origin is overwhelmingly **received-from-outside** — an external besieging adversity (enemy, evil, calamity) — with God named as the bestowing agent in 12 verses.
**T2.9.2** — Origin is therefore double: the proximate external pressure and the ultimate divine permission (Psa 107).
**T2.9.3** — Origin shifts by context: enemy-inflicted (Deu 28:57; 1Sa 13:6), divinely-sent (2Ch 15:6), or the bare human condition (Job 5:7).
**T2.10** — Movement runs from soul-pressure into bodily affliction in extremity (Deu 28); no spirit-level movement evidenced.

## T3 — The Inner Faculties
Distress is **pure affect** (129/129).
**T3.1 Perception / T3.2 Cognition / T3.3 Memory** — Not engaged. Negative findings.
**T3.4 Affect** — Engaged wholly: distress is the affective experience of being pressed; it intensifies and dominates affect (e.g. Psa 25:17).
**T3.5 Creativity / T3.6 Volition / T3.7 Agency** — Not engaged; distress is undergone, not initiated. Negative.
**T3.8 Moral evaluation** — Not at faculty level; the rare sinful framing (Job 15:35) sits in valence, not in an engaged faculty.
**T3.9 Conscience / T3.11 Relational** — Not engaged at faculty level, though distress is frequently about a threatening situation (object situation ×32).
**Pattern** — Distress engages affect alone; it neither enables nor impairs other faculties, marking it (with A) as a pure-affect characteristic distinguished from A by its spatial-constrictive register.

## T4 — Relational Interfaces
**T4.1 God→human** — Yes: God sends distress in judgement (Deu 28:57; Deu 31:17) and delivers from it (Psa 107 throughout); the basis is covenantal and responsive — distress follows covenant breach and lifts on the cry of repentance.
**T4.2 Human→God** — Strongly present: distress is the classic occasion of the cry to God (Psa 120:1; Jon 2:2; Psa 107:6). The inner posture required is the turn from self-reliance to calling out.
**T4.3 Giving** — Not extended person-to-person. Negative.
**T4.4 Receiving** — Distress is received from circumstances and adversaries (1Sa 13:6; Deu 28:57), involuntarily.
**T4.5 Boundaries** — Operates across covenantal and communal scope: national distress (Neh 9:27), personal distress (Psa 25:17), and the distress of enemies (Obd 12,14) all appear.
**T4.6 Spiritual beings** — No occurrence relates distress to angelic or adversarial beings directly. Negative.

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension
**T5.1 Transformation** — Distress changes the person's orientation more than their condition: it drives the self Godward (Psa 107). Where the cry is answered, the change is to gratitude and testimony.
**T5.2 Sequence** — A clear before→during→after recurs in Psalm 107: adversity → cry in distress → deliverance → thanks.
**T5.3 Mechanism** — Mechanism is the pressure of circumstance breaking self-sufficiency (Lazarus's demand-resource gap, T7.3) and forcing dependence.
**T5.4 Suffering** — Central: distress is the very experience of affliction — both a **product of** adversity and the **context** in which the person cries out. Suffering reveals and intensifies it (Psa 107; Lam).
**T5.5 Formation/sanctification** — Distress participates in formation as the recurring school of dependence (Psa 107's fourfold cycle); 1Ti 5:10 commends the one who has relieved the afflicted, tying distress into the sanctified life of others.
**T5.6 Eschatological** — No verse orients distress itself toward eschatological fullness; its trajectory is toward deliverance within history. Negative on eschatological orientation.

## T6 — Structural Relationships
**T6.1 Co-occurrence** — Same-verse with A (×2, 2Cor 2:4; Psa 116:3), and singly with F, J, E, I, D, H — distress sits beside the felt ache (A) and the voiced complaint (J), and can tip into bitterness (F).
**T6.2 Sequential** — Distress precedes the cry and the deliverance (Psa 107); it is the antecedent state in the deliverance sequence.
**T6.3 Causal/constitutive** — Produced by external adversity and divine permission; in extremity it produces the bodily affliction and the cry; it can produce bitterness if unrelieved.
**T6.4 Vocabulary/root sharing** — `tsar` overlaps with the homonym for "adversary/enemy" (the one who distresses), tying distress lexically to its external cause; `thlibō`/`thlipsis` is shared NT affliction vocabulary. (Cross-cluster — flagged.)
**T6.5 Distinctions** — Nearest neighbour is **A (inner pain)**. The distinction is constitutional and qualitative: A is the heart's felt ache; distress is the soul's experience of external pressure. The difference is of kind and seat, not degree.

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation
**T7.1.1** — Primary terms `tsa.rah`/`tsar` (narrowness, straits), `me.tsu.qah`/`ma.tsoq` (constraint), Greek `thlibō` (press), `stenochōreō` (crush into a narrow space); the root meanings are spatial — being hemmed in.
**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: nouns (the condition of distress), an adjective (`tsar`, "distressed"), verbs (`thlibō`, to press) — distress is mostly a borne noun-state.
**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: distress ↔ trouble ↔ anguish ↔ affliction ↔ adversity — a band of external-pressure experience.
**T7.1.4** — The vocabulary distinguishes the condition (`tsa.rah`) from the pressing act (`thlibō`).
**T7.1.5** — The opposite/absence is the spatial image of enlargement ("a broad place"), present antonymically.
**T7.1.6–.7** — No person-type term and no supplication term internal to the vocabulary (the cry is expressed with other verbs). Negative.
**T7.1.8** — OT `tsar`/`tsa.rah` continues into NT `thlibō`/`thlipsis`/`stenochōreō`; the constrictive metaphor is stable across the Testaments.
**T7.1.10** — The arc presents distress consistently as external pressure on the soul, from the patriarchal narratives to Paul's afflictions (2Cor 4:8, "afflicted in every way, but not crushed").
**T7.2.1** — In its anchor verses the distress term names the besetting condition that motivates the cry (Psa 107:6).
**T7.2.2** — Forms span narrative (Genesis, Samuel), covenant law (Deu 28), wisdom (Job, Proverbs), psalm/lament (Psa 107; 120), prophecy (Jeremiah), and epistle (2Cor).
**T7.2.4** — Settings are covenantal (Deu 28), liturgical/lament (Psa 107), and communal (siege, exile).
**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor: **Psalm 107** — its fourfold "they cried to the LORD in their trouble/distress, and he delivered them" most fully expresses distress as the straits answered by God.
**T7.2.6** — The anchor uniquely reveals distress as the structured occasion of deliverance — not a dead-end but the recurring hinge of the cry-and-rescue pattern.
**T7.3.1** — Framework: clinical stress and coping research (Lazarus and Folkman), trauma research (van der Kolk, Herman).
**T7.3.2** — The demand-resource model illuminates distress precisely: it arises when adversity exceeds perceived coping resources — exactly the soul "hemmed in" of `tsar`; the constriction vocabulary maps onto the somatic experience of being pressed.
**T7.3.3** — Divergence: the science frames distress as a coping problem to be resourced; the biblical material frames it as the occasion to cry to God, where the decisive "resource" is divine deliverance rather than internal coping capacity.
**T7.3.4** — The science's social-support finding invites testing whether the distress verses present communal lament as a buffer — coherent with the communal-distress texts (Neh 9:27) and worth carrying into the cross-cluster pass.

## 1. What this characteristic is
B names grief **as pressure and narrowing** — the Hebrew root sense of `tsar`/`tsa.rah` is *straits, narrowness, being hemmed in*. This is the inner being under constriction from an encircling adversity, answered in Greek by `thlibō` (to press) and `stenochōreō` (to crush into a narrow place).

## 13. Synthesis notes (provisional)
- **Observation:** overwhelmingly status (109/141), **soul-seated** where seated (soul 12 vs heart 4) — the inverse of A's heart-bias; object is dominantly a *situation* (32); valence almost entirely neutral; God appears as agent (12).
- **Interpretation:** B is grief as the soul under external siege: the causes are the most consistently *external* of any characteristic — enemy besieging (Deu 28:57), many evils coming (Deu 31:17,21), military threat — which is precisely the `ra.ah` domain operating through the cause field.
- **Reflection:** B and A may be two faces of one event: the situation presses (B, soul) and is felt as ache (A, heart). The seat split (soul vs heart) is a real, testable contrast, not an artefact, though seats are named on a minority of verses.

# M03 · Characteristic C — Mourning / lament (bereavement observance) · Findings by tier question

- **File:** wa-m03-char-c-tier-findings-v1_0-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Related:** evidence base wa-m03-char-c-mourning-v1_0-20260619.md; tier framework wa-tier-catalogue-restructured-v2-20260611.md (T-codes are the reference key); science lens wa-m03-grief-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md (Section 1 & 5); obslog wa-obslog-m03-ve-char-derive-v2-20260619.md.
- **Scope:** every live tier question answered as a self-contained finding (prose can be written from it without returning to source data); citations inline. Negative findings stated explicitly. Retired constructs (T1.2.3, T1.8, T2.8, T5.7, T6.6, T6.7) are omitted. Field-absent questions are answered by inference from verse identities and present fields, as agreed.
- **Status:** v1_0.
- **Evidence summary:** 117 verses (OT 113 / NT 17); faculty = affect (130); seat heart 7 / soul 2 / flesh 1; God = agent ×3 (turns mourning to dancing, Psa 30:11); morally regulated — neutral 94, commanded 7, righteous 5, forbidden 4, sinful 2; lead terms `a.val` (36), `sa.phad` (29), `e.vel` (22), `mis.ped` (14), Greek `pen.the.o`/`penthos` (14).

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
**T0.1.1** — Mourning images God as the one who reverses it: he "turns mourning into dancing" (Psa 30:11), and the gospel promise is that mourners are comforted (Mat 5:4). Where God acts, he is the comforter and reverser of mourning; where he calls for it, he is the judge summoning lament (Isa 22:12; Amo 8:10).
**T0.1.2** — Mourning is related to God as **agent** in 3 verses (Amo 8:10; Isa 22:12; Psa 30:11) — he both commands mourning in judgement and ends it in mercy. It is not borne by God as his own state in this vocabulary.
**T0.1.3** — God's not mourning, but reversing mourning, frames the characteristic as the creaturely response to loss that God answers.
**T0.2.1** — Mourning's served purpose is to honour the lost and to mark the gravity of judgement (the funeral rites of 2Sa 3:31; the prophetic summons of Joe 2:12); rightly directed, it opens onto comfort (Mat 5:4).
**T0.2.2** — Mourning belongs to the fallen condition (it answers death and loss), yet Scripture also **commands** it (Joe 2:12; Jam 4:9), making it a rightful response within the present order rather than a defect.
**T0.2.3** — Mourning is oriented toward future fullness: Mat 5:4 promises the mourners' comfort, and Rev 21:4 promises mourning (`penthos`) shall be no more — its present operation anticipates its own consolation.
**T0.3.1–.3** — No verse ties mourning to the image of God as an attribute; it is the creaturely answer to loss. Negative on image-bearing.
**T0.4.1–.2** — Mourning carries covenantal-eschatological typology: the commanded lament of the prophets points beyond the immediate loss to covenant judgement, and Mat 5:4 / Rev 21:4 point present mourning toward eschatological comfort — a present→future (human→consummation) direction.

## T1 — Definition
**T1.1.1** — "Mourning / lament": grief enacted and observed — the recognised condition and acts of bereavement. The name signals action and observance, not the inner ache alone.
**T1.1.2** — `a.val` (to mourn), `e.vel` (mourning), `sa.phad` (to wail, beat the breast), `mis.ped` (lamentation); Greek `pen.the.o`/`penthos` (to mourn/mourning), `koptō` (to beat oneself in grief). The terms name visible, often ritual, acts.
**T1.1.3** — The vocabulary is relational and directional — mourning is *over* or *for* a person or loss (object person ×28), orienting the enquiry toward the bond that is broken.
**T1.2.1** — Predominantly an **action** (action 78, status 44, quality 8) — mourning is something done, enacted in rite and gesture.
**T1.2.2** — Compound in practice: mourning gathers weeping (D), lament-speech, and bodily gesture (sackcloth, beating the breast) into a recognised observance.
**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite: dancing/feasting/joy (Psa 30:11 explicitly opposes mourning to dancing). Cross-cluster, named.
**T1.3.2** — Mourning excludes celebration; the prophets make the two mutually exclusive (Amo 8:10, feasts turned to mourning).
**T1.3.3** — It ends where the loss is comforted or the rite completed; its boundary with weeping (D) is that mourning is the observance, weeping the tears within it.
**T1.4.1** — Operates as enacted rite (funeral, sackcloth), as a summoned communal act (Joe 2), and as a settled condition of bereavement (Gen 37:35, "I shall go down to Sheol mourning").
**T1.4.2** — Operates differently by direction: self-mourning (one's own loss), mourning *for* another (the dead), and commanded corporate mourning (covenant judgement).
**T1.4.3** — Mourning is strongly speech-based — it is carried in lament and dirge (`mis.ped`, the formal lamentation; the dirge over the man of God, 1Ki 13:30).
**T1.5.1** — The immediate response is bodily and ritual: tearing garments, sackcloth, weeping, refusing comfort (Gen 37:34–35; 2Sa 3:31).
**T1.5.2** — Consistent in its ritual register across the evidence, though intensity varies with the loss.
**T1.6.1** — Sustained mourning settles into a prolonged condition (Jacob's refusal of comfort, Gen 37:35); rightly held, it opens onto comfort (Mat 5:4).
**T1.7.1–.3** — Mourning is enacted, not received as a gift; the relevant condition is permission to grieve (culturally given), not reception. Limited.

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries
**T2.1** — No spirit-level location. Negative.
**T2.2** — Soul-level in 2 occurrences — mourning reaching the innermost self.
**T2.3** — Located in the **heart** in 7 occurrences — the seat where mourning is felt before it is enacted; the heart's feeling function under bereavement.
**T2.4 / T2.5** — No mind-location and no other soul-subset. Negative.
**T2.6** — Linked to the **flesh** once; mourning is otherwise expressed through the body's gestures (sackcloth, ashes) rather than seated in a named organ.
**T2.7** — Direction runs soul→body: inner grief is expressed outward in bodily rite — mourning is the paradigm of the soul made visible in the body.
**T2.9.1** — Origin is the loss itself — received-from-outside (a death, a defeat, a judgement) — not generated within.
**T2.9.2–.3** — Origin is consistently external loss, varying only in scale (personal bereavement to national catastrophe).
**T2.10** — Movement runs from inner grief outward into enacted, communal observance — the clearest soul→body→community movement in the cluster.

## T3 — The Inner Faculties
Mourning is **affect** (130) expressed in action.
**T3.1 Perception / T3.2 Cognition / T3.3 Memory** — Not engaged at faculty level. Negative. (Mourning answers a remembered loss, but the engaged faculty is affect, not memory.)
**T3.4 Affect** — Engaged wholly: mourning is grief-affect given enacted form.
**T3.5 Creativity** — Not engaged, though the dirge/lament is a composed form; the faculty tagged is affect, not creativity. Negative.
**T3.6 Volition / T3.7 Agency** — Engaged indirectly: mourning is enacted (acts done), and can be commanded or refused (Eze 24:16), implying a volitional dimension — but the lexical faculty is affect; volition appears in the commanded/forbidden framing (T0.2.2).
**T3.8 Moral evaluation** — Not at faculty level, though mourning is uniquely morally regulated (see valence). 
**T3.9 Conscience / T3.11 Relational** — Relational dimension is strong in object (mourning *for* persons ×28) but not engaged as the relational faculty per se.
**Pattern** — Mourning is affect enacted; among the felt-states it is the most behaviourally and morally governed, which distinguishes it from the purely interior A.

## T4 — Relational Interfaces
**T4.1 God→human** — God turns mourning to dancing (Psa 30:11) and promises comfort to mourners (Mat 5:4); he also summons mourning in judgement (Isa 22:12; Joe 2:12). Basis: responsive and covenantal.
**T4.2 Human→God** — Mourning is directed Godward in repentant lament (Joe 2:12, "return to me... with mourning"); the posture is contrition.
**T4.3 Giving** — Mourning is extended to others as shared lament — mourners join the bereaved (Gen 50:10; Joh 11:31, the Jews who came to mourn with Mary). 
**T4.4 Receiving** — The bereaved receive the community's mourning as comfort or refuse it (Jacob "refused to be comforted", Gen 37:35).
**T4.5 Boundaries** — Mourning operates within bonds (family, nation) and is bounded by covenant: Ezekiel is forbidden to mourn his wife as a sign (Eze 24:16–17), showing mourning can be covenantally suspended.
**T4.6 Spiritual beings** — No occurrence relates mourning to angelic or adversarial beings. Negative.

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension
**T5.1 Transformation** — Mourning changes condition and orientation: rightly held it moves toward comfort (Mat 5:4) and can issue in repentance (Joe 2; 2Cor 7:7's report of the Corinthians' mourning).
**T5.2 Sequence** — A before→during→after is visible in the prophetic summons: sin → called mourning/repentance → restoration.
**T5.3 Mechanism** — Mechanism is the enacted marking of loss (rite, lament), which both expresses and processes the grief.
**T5.4 Suffering** — Mourning is the **response to** suffering and loss; it is the appointed form for bearing affliction (Ecc 7:2–4, the house of mourning). Suffering produces it; the rite gives it shape.
**T5.5 Formation/sanctification** — Mourning participates in formation: "it is better to go to the house of mourning" (Ecc 7:2) is presented as instructive for the living heart; godly mourning works repentance (2Cor 7:7,10).
**T5.6 Eschatological** — Strongly oriented: Mat 5:4 and Rev 21:4 promise the end of mourning — present lament anticipates eschatological comfort.

## T6 — Structural Relationships
**T6.1 Co-occurrence** — Strong same-verse pairing with **D (weeping)** — 19 shared verses — mourning and tears are a near-fused expressive pair; lesser co-occurrence with A and E.
**T6.2 Sequential** — Mourning typically accompanies or follows the loss and surrounds weeping; in repentance sequences it precedes restoration.
**T6.3 Causal/constitutive** — Produced by loss; constitutively gathers weeping, lament-speech, and bodily rite.
**T6.4 Vocabulary/root sharing** — `sa.phad` and `mis.ped` share the lamentation root; `pen.the.o`/`penthos` is the NT mourning family. (Cross-cluster — flagged.)
**T6.5 Distinctions** — Nearest neighbour is **D (weeping)**. The distinction is of form: mourning is the observance (rite, lament, condition), weeping the shedding of tears within it — a distinction of kind/scope, not degree.

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation
**T7.1.1** — `a.val` (to mourn), `sa.phad` (to wail/beat the breast), `e.vel`/`mis.ped` (mourning, lamentation); Greek `pen.the.o`/`penthos`, `koptō` (to beat oneself); roots denote enacted lament.
**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: verbs (the act of mourning), nouns (the condition/lamentation) — mourning is action-led.
**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: mourn ↔ lament ↔ wail ↔ bewail — the enacted register of grief.
**T7.1.4** — The vocabulary distinguishes the act (`a.val`, `sa.phad`) from the formal lament-piece (`mis.ped`, the dirge).
**T7.1.5** — Opposite: joy/dancing/feasting vocabulary (Psa 30:11), present antonymically.
**T7.1.6** — A person-type term is present: the **mourner** (`a.vel`, the one who mourns).
**T7.1.7** — No supplication term internal to the vocabulary. Negative.
**T7.1.8** — OT `a.val`/`sa.phad` continue into NT `pen.the.o`; the Beatitude (Mat 5:4) takes up the mourning vocabulary and gives it gospel reversal.
**T7.1.10** — The arc runs from patriarchal and prophetic lament to the Beatitude's blessed mourners and Revelation's end of mourning — loss answered, then abolished.
**T7.2.1** — In Mat 5:4 the mourning term carries the blessing's protasis — the mourners are the subject of promised comfort.
**T7.2.2** — Forms span narrative (Genesis, Samuel), prophecy (Amos, Joel, Ezekiel), wisdom (Ecclesiastes), gospel (Matthew), and epistle (2 Corinthians, James).
**T7.2.4** — Settings are funerary/liturgical (2Sa 3:31), covenantal-prophetic (Joe 2; Eze 24), and eschatological (Rev 21:4).
**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor: **Matthew 5:4** — "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted" most fully expresses mourning as the grief that God answers with comfort, gathering the OT lament tradition into gospel promise.
**T7.2.6** — The anchor uniquely reveals mourning as blessable — not merely endured but pronounced blessed because of the comfort it opens onto.
**T7.3.1** — Frameworks: clinical grief/bereavement research (Bowlby's attachment, Kübler-Ross, Stroebe's dual-process) and social/cultural psychology of communal mourning (Durkheim, Rosenblatt).
**T7.3.2** — Bowlby's finding that grief is the measure of attachment illuminates why the mourning vocabulary is so extensive and intense; Durkheim's account of communal ritual illuminates the corporate lament texts (Joel; Lamentations).
**T7.3.3** — Divergence: the science frames mourning therapeutically (a process toward restored function); the biblical material includes commanded and covenantal mourning, and sustained lament addressed to God that does not force resolution — a register the dual-process model under-captures.
**T7.3.4** — The cross-cultural finding that permission-to-grieve shapes outcomes invites testing the biblical mourning rites as a structured permission — coherent with the prophetic summons to mourn, and a thread for the cross-cluster pass.

C names grief **as enacted observance** — the act and condition of mourning and lament, typically over death or loss. It is what grief *does* outwardly and ritually, distinct from the felt state (A) it expresses.

## 13. Synthesis notes (provisional)
- **Observation:** **action**-dominant (78/130) — mourning is enacted; heart-seated where seated; object split between a *person* (28, the bereaved-for) and a *situation* (36); morally regulated — neutral 94 but with commanded (7), righteous (5), forbidden (4), sinful (2).
- **Interpretation:** C is the most socially and morally governed characteristic: mourning can be *commanded* and *forbidden*, which none of the felt-states are. Its causes are death (Gen 37:35; Gen 50) and divine judgement (1Sa 6:19; 15:35).
- **Reflection:** The strong C↔D pairing (19 shared verses) suggests mourning and weeping are a near-fused expressive pair in the corpus; synthesis should weigh whether they are one expression or two.

## 14. Gaps / further discovery
- The C↔D fusion (19) needs a rule for whether shared verses are double-counted in synthesis; commanded/forbidden valence cases (11) deserve individual verse-reads as they bear on the moral framing of mourning.

# M03 · Characteristic D — Weeping / tears · Findings by tier question

- **File:** wa-m03-char-d-tier-findings-v1_0-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Related:** evidence base wa-m03-char-d-weeping-v1_0-20260619.md; tier framework wa-tier-catalogue-restructured-v2-20260611.md (T-codes are the reference key); science lens wa-m03-grief-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md (Section 1 & 3); obslog wa-obslog-m03-ve-char-derive-v2-20260619.md.
- **Scope:** every live tier question answered as a self-contained finding (prose can be written from it without returning to source data); citations inline. Negative findings stated explicitly. Retired constructs (T1.2.3, T1.8, T2.8, T5.7, T6.6, T6.7) are omitted. Field-absent questions are answered by inference from verse identities and present fields, as agreed.
- **Status:** v1_0.
- **Evidence summary:** 154 verses (OT 153 / NT 17) — the largest characteristic; faculty = affect (148); seat heart 10 / soul 9 / inward-parts 1; God roles addressee ×5 (weeping before him), object, possessor, agent; valence neutral 118 / sinful 12 / commanded 5 / righteous 3 / forbidden 2; intensity “bitterly” ×6; lead terms `ba.khah` (100), `be.khi` (29), `dim.ah` (22), Greek `klaiō`/`klauthmos` (17).

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
**T0.1.1** — Weeping images God as the one who keeps and wipes away tears: he is the addressee before whom the people weep (Num 11:18; Judg 20:23,26), and the eschatological promise is that he will wipe every tear (Rev 7:17; Rev 21:4). The divine character reflected is attentiveness to tears.
**T0.1.2** — Weeping is related to God as **addressee** in 5 verses (Deu 1:45; Judg 20:23,26; Num 11:18,20) and once each as object, possessor, and agent; it is not a state God bears, but one offered to and answered by him.
**T0.1.3** — God's role as the receiver and eventual wiper of tears frames weeping as the creaturely overflow that he attends to.
**T0.2.1** — Weeping's purpose is expressive and appellative — it pours out grief and appeals to God or others (Psa 6:6; the petitionary weeping of Num 11). Rightly directed it is sowing that reaps joy (Psa 126:5–6).
**T0.2.2** — Weeping belongs to the fallen condition (it answers loss and pain) and is promised to cease (Rev 21:4), confirming it is not part of the consummated design.
**T0.2.3** — Strongly oriented to future fullness: "those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy" (Psa 126:5) and Rev 21:4's wiping of tears — present weeping anticipates its reversal.
**T0.3.1–.3** — No verse ties weeping to the image of God as an attribute. Negative on image-bearing.
**T0.4.1–.2** — Weeping carries eschatological typology in two directions: the "weeping and gnashing of teeth" of judgement (Mat 13:42,50; Luk 13:28) points to final exclusion, while Psa 126 and Rev 21:4 point present tears toward eschatological joy — present→future.

## T1 — Definition
**T1.1.1** — "Weeping / tears": grief overflowing as shed tears and crying. The name signals the body's water of grief — the most immediate visible expression.
**T1.1.2** — `ba.khah` (to weep), `be.khi` (weeping), `dim.ah` (tears); Greek `klaiō` (to weep), `klauthmos` (weeping). The terms name the act and product of crying.
**T1.1.3** — Weeping is directional — wept *before* God or *over* a loss (relational "before/over") — orienting toward both the object grieved and the one appealed to.
**T1.2.1** — Predominantly an **action** (action 112, status 57) — weeping is something done, with the residue of tears as a status.
**T1.2.2** — Simple as an act, but characteristically bound up with mourning (C) into a single expressive episode.
**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite: laughter/joy (Ecc 3:4, "a time to weep and a time to laugh"). Cross-cluster, named.
**T1.3.2** — Weeping excludes composure; Rev 21:4 sets its wiping-away as the mark of consummated joy.
**T1.3.3** — It ends where tears are wiped (comfort) or dry; its boundary with mourning (C) is that weeping is the tears, mourning the observance around them.
**T1.4.1** — Operates as spontaneous overflow (Gen 43:30), as loud public weeping (1Sa 11:4), and as appeal before God (Num 11).
**T1.4.2** — Operates differently by direction: weeping over a loss, weeping before God in petition, and the judgement-weeping of the lost.
**T1.4.3** — Weeping is often vocal — "weeping aloud", "lifted up their voice and wept" (Gen 21:16; Judg 21:2) — a loud communicative mode.
**T1.5.1** — Weeping is itself the immediate response to grief; where a downstream response appears, it is appeal or collapse (refusing food, 1Sa 1:7–10).
**T1.5.2** — Consistent as the first overflow of grief across the evidence.
**T1.6.1** — Sustained weeping wears the body (Psa 6:6, "I drench my couch with my tears"); rightly held it is sowing toward joy (Psa 126:5–6).
**T1.7.1–.3** — Weeping is overflow, not received; reception-framing does not apply. Limited.

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries
**T2.1** — No spirit-level location. Negative.
**T2.2** — Soul-level in 9 occurrences — weeping reaching the innermost self (the soul that "weeps in secret", Jer 13:17).
**T2.3** — Located in the **heart** in 10 occurrences — weeping as the heart's overflow.
**T2.4 / T2.5** — No mind-location; one inward-parts locus. Negative on mind.
**T2.6** — Weeping is itself the body's act (the eyes, tears) — the most inherently somatic characteristic, though a specific organ is rarely named beyond the eyes/tears.
**T2.7** — Direction runs soul→body: inner grief overflows as bodily tears — weeping is the paradigm somatic expression of the soul (cf. T7.3, van der Kolk's "the body keeps the score").
**T2.9.1** — Origin is the loss or pain that triggers it — received-from-outside (a death, a threat, a separation).
**T2.9.2–.3** — Origin varies: bereavement (Gen 50:1), national threat (1Sa 11:4), compassion (Gen 43:30), repentant grief (2Ki 22:19).
**T2.10** — Movement runs cleanly soul→body; weeping is where inner grief becomes visible water.

## T3 — The Inner Faculties
Weeping is **affect** (148) overflowing somatically.
**T3.1 Perception / T3.2 Cognition / T3.3 Memory** — Not engaged at faculty level. Negative.
**T3.4 Affect** — Engaged wholly: weeping is affect in its most embodied overflow.
**T3.5 Creativity / T3.6 Volition / T3.7 Agency** — Not engaged; weeping is largely involuntary overflow, though it can be summoned (commanded weeping, Joe 2:17) — a marginal volitional edge.
**T3.8 Moral evaluation / T3.9 Conscience** — Not at faculty level, though weeping carries moral framing (sinful weeping of rebellion, Num 11:20; righteous weeping of repentance, 2Ki 22:19).
**T3.11 Relational** — Strongly relational in object (wept over/for persons ×34) but not the engaged faculty per se.
**Pattern** — Weeping is affect at its most somatic and involuntary; it neither enables nor impairs other faculties, and is distinguished from mourning (C) by being the bodily overflow rather than the observance.

## T4 — Relational Interfaces
**T4.1 God→human** — God receives the people's weeping and answers (Num 11), and finally wipes every tear (Rev 7:17; 21:4). Basis: responsive and compassionate.
**T4.2 Human→God** — Strongly present: weeping is offered to God in petition and repentance (Num 11:18; 2Ki 22:19; Joe 2:17, "let the priests weep"). The posture is dependence and contrition.
**T4.3 Giving** — Weeping is shared with others — weeping *with* those who weep is implied in communal weeping (Gen 50:1–3; Joh 11:33).
**T4.4 Receiving** — The weeping of others is received as appeal or grief to be answered (Joseph wept as his brothers spoke, Gen 50:17).
**T4.5 Boundaries** — Weeping crosses bonds: personal, familial, national, and even over enemies (Isa 16:9, weeping over Moab).
**T4.6 Spiritual beings** — No occurrence relates weeping to angelic or adversarial beings. Negative.

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension
**T5.1 Transformation** — Weeping changes orientation: it is the turning of repentance (2Ki 22:19; 2Ch 34:27) and the appeal that moves toward relief (Psa 126).
**T5.2 Sequence** — A before→after is explicit in Psa 126:5–6: sowing in tears → reaping in joy; the tears are the seed of the later joy.
**T5.3 Mechanism** — Mechanism is the overflow and release of grief, and the appeal it constitutes before God and others.
**T5.4 Suffering** — Weeping is the immediate **response to** suffering and loss; suffering produces it directly (bereavement, threat, pain).
**T5.5 Formation/sanctification** — Weeping participates in formation as the bodily form of repentance (Josiah's tender, weeping heart commended, 2Ki 22:19); Psa 126 frames tears as formative sowing.
**T5.6 Eschatological** — Strongly oriented: Psa 126 and Rev 7:17 / 21:4 — present tears anticipate the joy and the wiping-away to come; conversely, judgement-weeping (Mat 13:42) anticipates final exclusion.

## T6 — Structural Relationships
**T6.1 Co-occurrence** — Strong same-verse pairing with **C (mourning)** — 19 shared verses; lesser with F (bitterly, ×3), E, I, B — weeping is the tears within mourning and shades into bitter weeping (F).
**T6.2 Sequential** — Weeping typically accompanies the moment of loss and surrounds mourning; in Psa 126 it precedes joy.
**T6.3 Causal/constitutive** — Produced by grief, loss, and compassion; constitutes the bodily core of the mourning episode.
**T6.4 Vocabulary/root sharing** — `ba.khah`/`be.khi` share the weeping root; the "bitterly" intensifier (×6) ties weeping to bitterness (F); `klaiō`/`klauthmos` is the NT weeping family. (Cross-cluster — flagged.)
**T6.5 Distinctions** — Nearest neighbour is **C (mourning)**. The distinction is of kind: weeping is the shedding of tears (somatic overflow); mourning is the observance and condition that contains it.

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation
**T7.1.1** — `ba.khah` (to weep), `be.khi` (weeping), `dim.ah` (tears); Greek `klaiō`, `klauthmos`; roots denote shedding tears and crying aloud.
**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: verbs (to weep), nouns (weeping, tears) — weeping is act-led with a noun residue (tears).
**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: weep ↔ wept ↔ weeping ↔ tears ↔ crying aloud — the band of shed-tear expression.
**T7.1.4** — The vocabulary distinguishes the act (`ba.khah`) from the product (`dim.ah`, tears).
**T7.1.5** — Opposite: laughter/joy vocabulary (Ecc 3:4), present antonymically.
**T7.1.6–.7** — No distinct person-type or supplication term internal to the weeping vocabulary. Negative.
**T7.1.8** — OT `ba.khah` continues into NT `klaiō`; weeping is one of the most stable grief expressions across the Testaments, and the NT adds the judgement-weeping motif (Mat 13).
**T7.1.10** — The arc runs from patriarchal weeping to the wiped tears of Revelation — the most frequent and most embodied grief term, framed first to last as that which God finally ends.
**T7.2.1** — In Psa 126:5 the weeping term anchors the contrast that drives the verse (tears now, joy later).
**T7.2.2** — Forms span narrative (Genesis, Samuel), psalm (6; 126), prophecy (Jeremiah; Joel), gospel (Luke, John), and apocalyptic (Revelation).
**T7.2.4** — Settings are domestic/funerary (Gen 50), liturgical-petitionary (Joe 2; Psa 126), and eschatological (Rev 7; 21).
**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor: **Psalm 126:5–6** — "those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy" most fully expresses weeping as grief that is also seed for coming joy.
**T7.2.6** — The anchor uniquely reveals weeping as productive — not merely expressive but sown, with a promised harvest of joy.
**T7.3.1** — Frameworks: clinical grief research (Bowlby; Stroebe) and physiology/psychosomatics of grief (van der Kolk; the autonomic basis of weeping).
**T7.3.2** — The somatic-grief research illuminates weeping as a genuine bodily event — autonomic, involuntary, storing and releasing grief — matching the cluster's treatment of weeping as the body's overflow.
**T7.3.3** — Divergence: science treats weeping as expression/release toward regulation; the biblical material also makes weeping an appeal to God and a seed of promised joy (Psa 126) — meanings beyond physiological release.
**T7.3.4** — Van der Kolk's "the body keeps the score" invites testing whether unwept grief reappears elsewhere in the cluster (the somatic characteristics E, I) — a thread for the cross-cluster pass.

D names grief **as the shedding of tears** — weeping and crying, the body's most immediate overflow of sorrow. It is somatic expression, the visible water of grief.

## 13. Synthesis notes (provisional)
- **Observation:** **action**-dominant (112), heart/soul-seated (heart 10 / soul 9); the single largest characteristic (154 verses); object person (34) or situation (37); intensified by *bitterly* (6) and *aloud/loud*.
- **Interpretation:** D is grief's default overflow; uniquely, it is sometimes directed **at God** — divine role 'addressee' on 5 verses — i.e. weeping *before* the LORD, not merely about a loss.
- **Reflection:** The 'bitterly' intensifier ties D to F (bitterness), and the addressee-God cases tie D to J (complaint before God); D may be the connective tissue of the cluster's expression.

## 14. Gaps / further discovery
- Largest characteristic — representative-verse sampling is thin relative to size; the divine-addressee cases (5) and 'bitterly' cases (6) should be read individually; relational 'from/over/on' fragments need care.

# M03 · Characteristic E — Sighing / groaning · Findings by tier question

- **File:** wa-m03-char-e-tier-findings-v1_0-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Related:** evidence base wa-m03-char-e-sighing-v1_0-20260619.md; tier framework wa-tier-catalogue-restructured-v2-20260611.md (T-codes are the reference key); science lens wa-m03-grief-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md (Section 3); obslog wa-obslog-m03-ve-char-derive-v2-20260619.md.
- **Scope:** every live tier question answered as a self-contained finding (prose can be written from it without returning to source data); citations inline. Negative findings stated explicitly. Retired constructs (T1.2.3, T1.8, T2.8, T5.7, T6.6, T6.7) are omitted. Field-absent questions are answered by inference from verse identities and present fields, as agreed.
- **Status:** v1_0.
- **Evidence summary:** 32 verses (OT 30 / NT 2); faculty = affect (23); seat heart 3 / flesh 1 / soul 1; God = object ×1 (moved by their groaning, Judg 2:18); valence neutral 27, righteous 1, commanded 1; lead terms `a.nach`/`a.na.chah` (23), `ne.a.qah`/`a.na.qah` (5).

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
**T0.1.1** — Groaning images God as the one who hears and is moved by it: the Exodus groaning "rose up to God", who heard it and remembered his covenant (Exo 2:23–24; Exo 6:5); the LORD was moved to pity by the groaning of the oppressed (Judg 2:18). The divine character reflected is responsiveness to the inarticulate cry.
**T0.1.2** — Groaning is related to God as the **object/recipient** who hears it (Judg 2:18); it is not borne by God. Its theological weight lies in being heard.
**T0.1.3** — That God hears rather than groans frames groaning as the creaturely cry he attends to even when it has no words.
**T0.2.1** — Groaning's purpose is to voice affliction below the level of speech — the involuntary sound that nonetheless reaches God (Exo 2:23–24).
**T0.2.2** — Groaning belongs to the fallen condition (it answers oppression and pain), with no claim to original design.
**T0.2.3** — Limited future-fullness orientation in the OT terms; the cluster's NT groaning (Rom 8, by extension) points toward redemption, but within this characteristic's verses the orientation is toward being heard now. Largely negative on eschatological orientation for these lemmas.
**T0.3.1–.3** — No verse ties groaning to the image of God. Negative.
**T0.4.1–.2** — The Exodus groaning functions typologically of covenant-remembrance — the cry that triggers God's redemptive action — a present-cry→divine-response pattern, but no developed christological typology rests on these lemmas.

## T1 — Definition
**T1.1.1** — "Sighing / groaning": grief as involuntary breath-voice — the moan or sigh below articulate speech. The name signals the inarticulate sound of inner pain.
**T1.1.2** — `a.nach` (to sigh/groan), `a.na.chah` (sighing); `ne.a.qah`/`a.na.qah` (groaning); the terms denote the breathed sound of distress.
**T1.1.3** — Groaning is expressive and (in the Exodus texts) appellative — it rises toward God even without words.
**T1.2.1** — A mix of **status** (the condition of sighing, 19) and **action** (the act of groaning, 12).
**T1.2.2** — Simple — a single involuntary sound, though it accompanies affliction and weeping.
**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite: rest/relief and glad song. Cross-cluster, named.
**T1.3.2** — Groaning excludes ease; it is the sound of the unrelieved.
**T1.3.3** — It ends where relief or rescue comes (the Exodus groaning ends in deliverance); its boundary with weeping (D) is that groaning is breath-voice, weeping is tears.
**T1.4.1** — Operates as involuntary sighing (Lam 1:22, "my groans are many"), and as the collective groaning of the oppressed (Exo 2:23).
**T1.4.2** — Operates both individually (Psa 6:6, weary with groaning) and corporately (the enslaved nation).
**T1.4.3** — Groaning is itself a quasi-communicative mode — sound without words that nonetheless communicates and is heard (Exo 2:24).
**T1.5.1** — Groaning is itself the immediate response to sustained affliction; it is the first sound of the unrelieved.
**T1.5.2** — Consistent as the breath-response to oppression and sorrow.
**T1.6.1** — Sustained groaning marks chronic, unrelieved affliction (Psa 6:6); its over-time effect is exhaustion.
**T1.7.1–.3** — Groaning is involuntary expression, not received. Limited.

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries
**T2.1** — No spirit-level location. Negative.
**T2.2** — Soul-level once. **T2.3** — Heart in 3 occurrences — the heart's sound under affliction (cf. Psa 38:8, the tumult/groaning of the heart). **T2.4 / T2.5** — No mind or other soul-subset. Negative.
**T2.6** — Linked to the flesh once; groaning is intrinsically respiratory/bodily (the breath), though a specific organ is rarely named.
**T2.7** — Direction runs soul→body: inner affliction registers as breathed sound — groaning is the autonomic voice of grief (cf. T7.3, vagal mediation).
**T2.9.1** — Origin is the affliction that compresses the person — received-from-outside (oppression, sorrow).
**T2.9.2–.3** — Origin is consistently external pressure (Egyptian bondage, enemy oppression, accumulated sorrow).
**T2.10** — Movement runs soul→body (the breath); the Exodus texts add a movement outward-and-upward (groaning rising to God).

## T3 — The Inner Faculties
Sighing/groaning is **affect** (23).
**T3.1–T3.3, T3.5–T3.11** — Not engaged at faculty level. Negative findings throughout — groaning is a pure affective-somatic sound, engaging no cognitive, volitional, moral, or relational faculty in the evidence.
**T3.4 Affect** — Engaged wholly: groaning is the breathed form of grief-affect.
**Pattern** — Groaning is affect at its most involuntary and least articulate; it engages a single faculty and is the audible underside of inner pain (A), with which it most co-occurs.

## T4 — Relational Interfaces
**T4.1 God→human** — God hears and responds to groaning, remembering his covenant and acting (Exo 2:24; Judg 2:18). Basis: covenant-remembrance, responsive to the cry.
**T4.2 Human→God** — Groaning rises to God even without words (Exo 2:23) — the wordless human-to-God cry; the posture is helpless affliction.
**T4.3 Giving / T4.4 Receiving** — Not extended or received person-to-person. Negative (the related `sustenazō`, to groan *with*, lies at the cluster's communal edge but is sparse here).
**T4.5 Boundaries** — Operates corporately (the nation's groaning) and individually; scope is the afflicted.
**T4.6 Spiritual beings** — No occurrence relates groaning to angelic or adversarial beings. Negative.

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension
**T5.1 Transformation** — Groaning itself is not transformative; it is the sound of the unrelieved that triggers divine action (Exo) rather than changing the groaner.
**T5.2 Sequence** — In the Exodus narrative: bondage → groaning → God hears → deliverance — groaning is the pivot that moves God.
**T5.3 Mechanism** — Mechanism is the involuntary breath-release of compressed affliction.
**T5.4 Suffering** — Groaning is the immediate, involuntary **product of** sustained suffering and oppression (Exo 2:23; Lam 1:22).
**T5.5 Formation/sanctification** — Eze 9:4 marks those who "sigh and groan" over abominations for preservation — groaning here is the mark of the righteous remnant, tying it into a formative/discriminating role.
**T5.6 Eschatological** — Within these lemmas, limited; the redemptive-groaning trajectory belongs to the NT terms beyond this set. Largely negative.

## T6 — Structural Relationships
**T6.1 Co-occurrence** — Most same-verse co-occurrence with **A (inner pain)** (×4) — groaning is the audible form of the felt ache; lesser with D, B, C, H, I, J.
**T6.2 Sequential** — Groaning accompanies affliction and can precede divine deliverance (Exodus).
**T6.3 Causal/constitutive** — Produced by oppression and sorrow; in Eze 9:4 it constitutes the mark of the grieving righteous.
**T6.4 Vocabulary/root sharing** — `a.nach`/`a.na.chah` share the sighing root; `ne.a.qah`/`a.na.qah` the groaning root. (Cross-cluster — flagged.)
**T6.5 Distinctions** — Nearest neighbours are **D (weeping)** and **A (inner pain)**. The distinction is of channel: groaning is breath-voice; weeping is tears; A is the unexpressed felt state. Distinction of kind/medium.

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation
**T7.1.1** — `a.nach` (to sigh/groan), `a.na.chah` (sighing), `ne.a.qah`/`a.na.qah` (groaning); roots denote the breathed sound of distress.
**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: verb (to sigh/groan) and noun (sighing, groaning) — sound as act and condition.
**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: sigh ↔ groan ↔ moan ↔ groaning — the breath-voice band.
**T7.1.4** — The vocabulary distinguishes the act (`a.nach`) from the condition (`a.na.chah`).
**T7.1.5–.7** — No internal opposite, person-type, or supplication term. Negative.
**T7.1.8** — OT `a.nach`/`ne.a.qah` are joined in the NT by `stenagmos`/`sustenazō`; the wordless-groan motif carries into the NT's groaning-for-redemption (beyond this set).
**T7.1.10** — The arc presents groaning as the inarticulate cry that God hears — from the Exodus bondage to the marked remnant of Ezekiel.
**T7.2.1** — In Exo 2:24 the groaning term is the grammatical object of God's hearing — the cry that God heard.
**T7.2.2** — Forms span narrative (Exodus, Judges), psalm (6; 38), lament (Lamentations), and prophecy (Ezekiel).
**T7.2.4** — Settings are covenantal (Exodus deliverance), lament (Lamentations), and prophetic-discriminating (Eze 9).
**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor: **Exodus 2:23–24** — the people's groaning rises to God, who hears it and remembers his covenant; this most fully expresses groaning as the wordless cry that moves God to act.
**T7.2.6** — The anchor uniquely reveals groaning as covenant-effective — the inarticulate sound that nonetheless triggers divine remembrance and redemption.
**T7.3.1** — Framework: physiology/psychosomatics of grief — the autonomic, vagally-mediated basis of sighing and groaning (Porges; psychosomatic research).
**T7.3.2** — The science illuminates groaning as a genuine involuntary autonomic response that cannot be fully suppressed — matching the biblical treatment of groaning as the cry that rises without deliberate composition.
**T7.3.3** — Divergence: the science locates groaning in autonomic regulation; the biblical material makes the same wordless sound covenant-effective — heard and answered by God (Exodus).
**T7.3.4** — The somatic-involuntariness finding supports treating groaning (with weeping) as the body's automatic grief channel — a thread for the cross-cluster somatic synthesis.

# M03 · Characteristic F — Bitterness of soul · Findings by tier question

- **File:** wa-m03-char-f-tier-findings-v1_0-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Related:** evidence base wa-m03-char-f-bitterness-v1_0-20260619.md; tier framework wa-tier-catalogue-restructured-v2-20260611.md (T-codes are the reference key); science lens wa-m03-grief-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md (Section 4); obslog wa-obslog-m03-ve-char-derive-v2-20260619.md.
- **Scope:** every live tier question answered as a self-contained finding (prose can be written from it without returning to source data); citations inline. Negative findings stated explicitly. Retired constructs (T1.2.3, T1.8, T2.8, T5.7, T6.6, T6.7) are omitted. Field-absent questions are answered by inference from verse identities and present fields, as agreed.
- **Status:** v1_0.
- **Evidence summary:** 33 verses (OT 25 / NT 6); faculty = moral_evaluation (12) + affect (5) — the one characteristic with a moral-evaluative core; seat soul 10 / heart 3 / flesh 1; God roles agent ×2, giver ×1 (bitterness as divinely administered); valence neutral 17, sinful 3, forbidden 1; lead terms `mar` (12), `ma.rar` (7), `ma.ror` (3), Greek `pikrainō`/`pikrōs` (6).

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
**T0.1.1** — Bitterness images God most strikingly as one who can **administer** it: Naomi says "the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me" and "the hand of the LORD has gone out against me" (Rut 1:13,20), and Job says "God... has made my soul bitter" (Job 27:2) and "filled me with bitterness" (Job 9:18). The divine character reflected is sovereign even over the soul's embittering — bitterness can be a dispensation of God's hand, not only a human sin.
**T0.1.2** — Bitterness is related to God as **agent** (Rut 1:13; Job 27:2) and **giver** (Job 9:18) in 3 verses; it is not borne by God, but God is named as its source in the sufferer's complaint.
**T0.1.3** — That God administers but does not bear bitterness frames it as a creaturely soul-state that can fall under divine providence in suffering.
**T0.2.1** — Where a purpose appears, bitterness is the soul's honest naming of grievous loss (Naomi renaming herself Mara, Rut 1:20) — it serves as truthful lament; it is never commended as a settled disposition.
**T0.2.2** — Bitterness belongs to the fallen condition — a response to loss and perceived injustice — and the NT explicitly forbids it as a settled stance (Col 3:19, husbands not to be harsh/bitter).
**T0.2.3** — No verse orients bitterness toward future fullness; its trajectory is either honest lament resolved or a forbidden hardening. Negative on eschatological orientation.
**T0.3.1–.3** — No verse ties bitterness to the image of God. Negative on image-bearing.
**T0.4.1–.2** — Bitterness is not deployed typologically in its own right; it functions within lament (Naomi, Job) and as a moral danger to be avoided.

## T1 — Definition
**T1.1.1** — "Bitterness of soul": grief turned to an embittered condition, carrying a moral edge. The name signals the taste-metaphor of a soul made bitter.
**T1.1.2** — `mar` (bitter), `ma.rar` (to be/​make bitter), `mar.rah`/`me.mer`/`mam.ror` (bitterness); Greek `pikrainō` (to embitter), `pikrōs` (bitterly). The root is the taste of bitterness, applied to the soul.
**T1.1.3** — The terms carry a moral-evaluative implication (a sustained stance toward what was wrong or lost), orienting the enquiry toward appraisal as well as feeling.
**T1.2.1** — A mix of **quality** (the bitter soul, 14) and **action** (to embitter, 13) — bitterness is both a condition and an act.
**T1.2.2** — Compound at the edges: bitterness combines felt grief with an evaluative stance toward its cause (the soul that judges its loss unjust).
**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite: sweetness / contentment (the taste antonym), and a settled, forgiving heart. Cross-cluster, named.
**T1.3.2** — Bitterness excludes peace with one's circumstances; the NT sets it against forbearance (Col 3:19).
**T1.3.3** — It ends where lament is honest and resolved; it hardens where the evaluative stance becomes settled — the boundary with anger (M02) lies here (the held-open `ma.rar` anger-bleed).
**T1.4.1** — Operates as the soul's embittered condition (1Sa 1:10, Hannah "bitter of soul"), as an act of embittering (Exo 1:14, lives made bitter), and as bitter weeping (Mat 26:75, Peter "wept bitterly").
**T1.4.2** — Operates differently by direction: bitterness borne (the grieving soul), bitterness inflicted (oppressors embittering lives, Exo 1:14), and bitterness named against God (Job, Naomi).
**T1.4.3** — Bitterness finds voice in bitter complaint and bitter weeping — it has a vocal, expressive mode (Mat 26:75; Job's bitter speech, Job 7:11, "I will speak in the bitterness of my soul").
**T1.5.1** — The immediate expression is bitter speech or bitter weeping (Job 7:11; Mat 26:75).
**T1.5.2** — Variable: sometimes voiced complaint, sometimes silent embittered condition.
**T1.6.1** — Sustained bitterness hardens into a fixed retrospective stance (Linden's embitterment, T7.3) — the NT's reason for forbidding it (Col 3:19).
**T1.7.1–.3** — Bitterness is incurred or administered, not received as a gift. Limited.

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries
**T2.1** — No spirit-level location. Negative.
**T2.2** — Located at the **soul** level in 10 occurrences — the clearest seat-signal of any small characteristic; "bitterness of soul" (1Sa 1:10; Job 7:11) is the idiom. Bitterness is pre-eminently a soul-state.
**T2.3** — Located in the **heart** in 3 occurrences (e.g. Pro 14:10, "the heart knows its own bitterness").
**T2.4 / T2.5** — No mind or other soul-subset location. Negative on mind (though the moral-evaluative faculty, T3.8, gives bitterness a cognitive colouring without a mind-seat).
**T2.6** — Linked to the flesh once; bitterness is otherwise an interior soul-state.
**T2.7** — Where bodily, direction runs soul→body (the bitter soul registering bodily); limited data.
**T2.9.1** — Origin is double and distinctive: bitterness is **received-from-outside** (the loss/injustice that embitters) and, uniquely, **bestowed-by-God** in the sufferer's account (Rut 1:13; Job 9:18) — the only characteristic with a clear God-as-giver origin.
**T2.9.2** — Origin is therefore multiple: circumstance, oppressor, and (as named in lament) God's own hand.
**T2.9.3** — Origin shifts: inflicted by oppressors (Exo 1:14), incurred by loss (2Ki 4:27), attributed to God (Job; Naomi).
**T2.10** — No constitutional movement across levels evidenced beyond soul/heart co-location.

## T3 — The Inner Faculties
Bitterness is the cluster's one characteristic with a **moral-evaluative** core (moral_evaluation 12, affect 5).
**T3.1 Perception / T3.3 Memory / T3.5 Creativity / T3.7 Agency / T3.11 Relational** — Not engaged at faculty level. Negative.
**T3.2 Cognition** — Engaged at the edge: bitterness involves an evaluative appraisal of the past (the soul judging its loss), bordering cognition, though the tagged faculty is moral-evaluation.
**T3.4 Affect** — Engaged: bitterness is felt grief with a bitter quality.
**T3.6 Volition** — Engaged negatively: the NT command not to be embittered (Col 3:19) implies bitterness is, in part, a stance that can be refused — a volitional dimension.
**T3.8 Moral evaluation** — Engaged centrally and uniquely: bitterness carries a sustained evaluative stance (this was unjust / should not have been) — the defining faculty of this characteristic.
**T3.9 Conscience** — Not directly engaged. Negative.
**Pattern** — Bitterness is distinguished from every other M03 characteristic by engaging moral-evaluation, not affect alone; it is grief that has taken up a verdict about its cause, which is why it can be both a legitimate lament and a forbidden hardening.

## T4 — Relational Interfaces
**T4.1 God→human** — God is named (in lament) as the one who has dealt bitterly (Rut 1:13; Job 27:2) — bitterness can be experienced as coming from God's hand in affliction. Basis: providential, within suffering.
**T4.2 Human→God** — Bitterness is voiced *to* and *against* God in lament (Job 7:11; 10:1) — the embittered soul brings its complaint Godward; the posture is raw, accusing honesty.
**T4.3 Giving** — Bitterness is inflicted by oppressors on others (Exo 1:14, the Egyptians made their lives bitter) — a negative "giving".
**T4.4 Receiving** — The oppressed receive embittered lives from their oppressors (Exo 1:14); the bereaved receive bitterness from loss (2Ki 4:27).
**T4.5 Boundaries** — Operates within bonds (a wife embittered, the NT warning to husbands, Col 3:19) and across enmity (oppressor to oppressed).
**T4.6 Spiritual beings** — No occurrence relates bitterness to angelic or adversarial beings. Negative.

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension
**T5.1 Transformation** — Bitterness can deform (a hardened retrospective stance) or, as honest lament, be carried before God toward resolution (Hannah's bitter prayer answered, 1Sa 1:10–20).
**T5.2 Sequence** — In Hannah's narrative: bitter soul → poured-out prayer → no longer sad — bitterness named to God moves toward relief.
**T5.3 Mechanism** — Mechanism is appraisal: bitterness forms when loss is judged unjust or inflicted; it resolves through acknowledgement and reframing (T7.3, the justice dimension).
**T5.4 Suffering** — Bitterness is a **product of** suffering, specifically suffering perceived as unjust or inflicted (Exo 1:14; Job); it is the embittering of the soul under affliction.
**T5.5 Formation/sanctification** — Negatively formative: the NT forbids settled bitterness (Col 3:19), making its refusal part of sanctified relating; Hannah shows the godly path of carrying bitterness to God rather than nursing it.
**T5.6 Eschatological** — No eschatological orientation in the evidence. Negative.

## T6 — Structural Relationships
**T6.1 Co-occurrence** — Same-verse with **D (weeping)** most (×3) — bitter weeping (Mat 26:75); lesser with B, J, C.
**T6.2 Sequential** — Bitterness can follow distress unrelieved (the B→F hardening) and precede bitter weeping or complaint.
**T6.3 Causal/constitutive** — Produced by unjust/inflicted suffering; can itself produce bitter speech and bitter weeping.
**T6.4 Vocabulary/root sharing** — The `mar`/`ma.rar` root spans bitterness and the anger-bleed (`ma.rar` as "provoke/rage"), tying F to anger (M02); `pikrainō`/`pikria` is the NT bitterness family (cf. "root of bitterness", Heb 12:15, outside this lemma set). (Cross-cluster — flagged; the M02 boundary is the key open question.)
**T6.5 Distinctions** — Nearest neighbours are **A (inner pain)** and, by the anger-bleed, **M02 (anger)**. The distinction from A is the evaluative verdict bitterness carries (A is felt ache without the judgement); the distinction from anger is direction (bitterness is retrospective and self-corroding; anger is outward and active).

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation
**T7.1.1** — `mar` (bitter), `ma.rar` (to be/​make bitter), `mar.rah`/`me.mer`/`mam.ror` (bitterness); Greek `pikrainō` (to embitter), `pikrōs` (bitterly); the root is the taste of bitterness transferred to the soul.
**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: adjective (`mar`, bitter), verb (`ma.rar`/`pikrainō`, to embitter), noun (bitterness), adverb (`pikrōs`, bitterly) — a full grammatical spread.
**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: bitter ↔ bitterness ↔ bitterly ↔ embittered — the band of soul-bitterness.
**T7.1.4** — The vocabulary distinguishes the quality (`mar`, bitter) from the act (`ma.rar`, to embitter) from the manner (`pikrōs`, bitterly).
**T7.1.5** — Opposite: sweetness (the taste antonym), present implicitly.
**T7.1.6** — A person-type term is implicit in Naomi's renaming herself **Mara** ("bitter") — the bitter one.
**T7.1.7** — No supplication term. Negative.
**T7.1.8** — OT `mar`/`ma.rar` continue into NT `pikrainō`/`pikria`; the taste-metaphor of the embittered soul is stable, and the NT adds an explicit prohibition (Col 3:19; Eph 4:31 "let all bitterness... be put away", outside this set).
**T7.1.10** — The arc runs from the bitter soul of OT lament (Naomi, Hannah, Job) to the NT's forbidding of settled bitterness — grief's bitterness named honestly in the OT, guarded against in the NT.
**T7.2.1** — In Rut 1:20 the bitterness term carries Naomi's self-renaming — the predicate that reinterprets her identity through loss.
**T7.2.2** — Forms span narrative (Ruth; Exodus), wisdom (Proverbs; Job), gospel (Matthew), and epistle (Colossians).
**T7.2.4** — Settings are domestic-lament (Ruth; Hannah), the legal-dispute lament (Job), and ethical instruction (Colossians).
**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor: **Ruth 1:20** — "Call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me" most fully expresses bitterness as a soul-state named before God, attributed to his hand, in honest grief.
**T7.2.6** — The anchor uniquely reveals bitterness as a name the grieving soul can take upon itself before God — lament that reinterprets identity through loss without yet being condemned.
**T7.3.1** — Framework: clinical stress/embitterment research — Linden's embitterment-disorder concept; the justice-appraisal literature.
**T7.3.2** — Linden's finding that bitterness is chronic, retrospectively oriented, and justice-focused (distinct from acute grief) illuminates the cluster's bitterness vocabulary precisely — bitterness sits at the intersection of emotional suffering and cognitive appraisal, matching its moral-evaluative faculty tag.
**T7.3.3** — Divergence: the science treats bitterness as a disorder to be resolved by addressing the justice dimension; the biblical material both legitimises bitterness as honest lament *before God* (Naomi, Job) and forbids it as a settled stance *toward others* (Col 3:19) — a moral distinction the clinical frame does not draw.
**T7.3.4** — The science's grief-vs-bitterness distinction (loss-focused vs justice-focused) directly supports keeping F distinct from A/C/D, and invites testing the `ma.rar` anger-bleed against M02 in the cross-cluster pass.

## 1. What this characteristic is
F names grief **as embittered condition** — the soul made bitter. It carries a moral colouring the other characteristics lack (`mar` reads as moral-evaluation), and is the one felt-state idiom the corpus seats squarely in the soul.

## 13. Synthesis notes (provisional)

- **Interpretation:** F is distinctively the *bitter soul* idiom, and uniquely it can be **God-given**: Naomi names herself bitter by the LORD's hand (Rut 1:13,20), and God fills Job with bitterness (Job 9:18) — bitterness as a divinely-administered grief.

# M03 · Characteristic G — Torment / acute affliction · Findings by tier question

- **File:** wa-m03-char-g-tier-findings-v1_0-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Related:** evidence base wa-m03-char-g-torment-v1_0-20260619.md; tier framework wa-tier-catalogue-restructured-v2-20260611.md (T-codes are the reference key); science lens wa-m03-grief-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md (Section 2); obslog wa-obslog-m03-ve-char-derive-v2-20260619.md.
- **Scope:** every live tier question answered as a self-contained finding (prose can be written from it without returning to source data); citations inline. Negative findings stated explicitly. Retired constructs (T1.2.3, T1.8, T2.8, T5.7, T6.6, T6.7) omitted. Field-absent questions answered by inference from verse identities and present fields, as agreed.
- **Status:** v1_0.
- **Evidence summary:** 15 verses, **New Testament only**; faculty = affect (4) + cognition (3); seat soul ×1; no divine role recorded; valence neutral 6 / sinful 3; lead terms `basanizō` (12), `basanos` (3) — torture-level affliction; uniquely carries a spiritual-beings interface and a strong eschatological register.

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
**T0.1.1** — Torment images God indirectly as the righteous judge whose final judgement includes the torment of the impenitent and the devil (Rev 14:10; Rev 20:10) and from whom the demons recoil, fearing torment "before the time" (Mat 8:29). God is not the bearer of torment but the one whose judgement defines its ultimate reference.
**T0.1.2** — Torment is **not** related to God as a state he bears; no divine role is recorded on these verses. It is borne by sufferers, the lost (Luk 16:23), and finally the adversary (Rev 20:10).
**T0.1.3** — The absence of any divine bearing frames torment as an extremity of creaturely (and adversarial) suffering, not a divine attribute.
**T0.2.1** — Torment serves, in the evidence, chiefly as the marker of judgement and of acute affliction (the rich man's torment, Luk 16:23–28); it equips nothing positive in the person — it is suffering at the extreme.
**T0.2.2** — Torment belongs wholly to the fallen/judgement order; it has no place in original design and is the very content of final judgement (Rev 20:10).
**T0.2.3** — Strongly future-oriented, but toward judgement rather than fullness: torment is the eschatological end of the impenitent and the devil (Rev 14:10; 20:10).
**T0.3.1–.3** — No verse ties torment to the image of God. Negative on image-bearing.
**T0.4.1–.2** — Torment is eschatological/apocalyptic in reference: Revelation deploys it for final judgement (Rev 14:10; 20:10), a present-foretaste→final-reality direction.

## T1 — Definition
**T1.1.1** — "Torment / acute affliction": suffering at the torture level — imposed, overwhelming, often eschatological. The name signals extremity.
**T1.1.2** — `basanizō` (to torture, torment), `basanos` (torment) — Greek terms from the language of testing/torture, applied to acute affliction.
**T1.1.3** — The terms carry an implication of imposition — torment is inflicted, whether by circumstance, judgement, or adversary.
**T1.2.1** — Predominantly an **action** (12) over status (3) — torment is something done to the sufferer.
**T1.2.2** — Simple — a single extremity of affliction.
**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite: rest / relief from suffering (Rev 14:11 sets "no rest" against it). Cross-cluster, named.
**T1.3.2** — Torment excludes rest and ease utterly.
**T1.3.3** — It is the severe pole of suffering, beyond ordinary pain (A) or pressure (B).
**T1.4.1** — Operates physically (a boat tormented by the waves, Mat 14:24; Mar 6:48), bodily-medically (those severely afflicted/tormented, Mat 4:24; Mat 8:6), psychologically (Lot's righteous soul tormented, 2Pe 2:8), and eschatologically (Luk 16:23; Rev 20:10).
**T1.4.2** — Operates differently by register — physical buffeting, bodily disease, inner moral torment, and final judgement.
**T1.4.3** — Torment can issue in a cry (the demons' "have you come to torment us?", Mat 8:29), but it is not characteristically speech-based.
**T1.5.1** — The immediate response is a cry of protest or dread (Mat 8:29; Mar 5:7; Luk 8:28).
**T1.5.2** — Variable across the registers (physical, moral, eschatological).
**T1.6.1** — Sustained torment is, in its eschatological form, unending ("the smoke of their torment goes up for ever", Rev 14:11).
**T1.7.1–.3** — Torment is inflicted, not received as a gift. Negative on reception-framing.

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries
**T2.1** — No spirit-level location. Negative. **T2.2** — Soul-level once (Lot's righteous soul tormented, 2Pe 2:8). **T2.3 / T2.4 / T2.5** — No heart, mind, or other soul-subset location. Negative.
**T2.6** — Torment is often bodily in reference (disease, buffeting) but rarely tied to a named organ; the body is the site, not a specific part.
**T2.7** — Where bodily, torment is imposed on the body from without (waves, disease) — an outside→body direction rather than soul→body.
**T2.9.1** — Origin is **received-from-outside** — inflicted by circumstance, disease, judgement, or adversary; never generated within.
**T2.9.2–.3** — Origin varies: natural (storm), pathological (disease), moral (Lot's vexed soul), and judicial (final judgement).
**T2.10** — No constitutional movement across levels evidenced. Negative.

## T3 — The Inner Faculties
Torment engages **affect** (4) with a **cognitive** component (3 — the tormenting awareness, e.g. Lot's soul tormented by what he saw, 2Pe 2:8).
**T3.1 Perception** — Engaged at the edge in 2Pe 2:8 (tormented by *seeing and hearing* lawless deeds), but not characteristically. **T3.2 Cognition** — Engaged where torment is the anguish of awareness (2Pe 2:8). **T3.3, T3.5, T3.7, T3.11** — Not engaged. Negative.
**T3.4 Affect** — Engaged: torment is acute affective suffering.
**T3.6 Volition / T3.8 Moral evaluation / T3.9 Conscience** — Not engaged at faculty level (the moral framing of judgement-torment sits in valence/context).
**Pattern** — Torment is affect at its extreme, occasionally joined by the cognition of unbearable awareness; it is distinguished from ordinary pain (A) by intensity and imposition.

## T4 — Relational Interfaces
**T4.1 God→human** — Indirect: God's final judgement is the reference of eschatological torment (Rev 14:10; 20:10), but no verse shows God extending torment as a relational gift. Basis: judicial.
**T4.2 Human→God** — Not present; torment is not directed Godward. Negative.
**T4.3 Giving / T4.4 Receiving** — Torment is inflicted (received from circumstance, disease, or judgement), not given person-to-person as a benefit.
**T4.5 Boundaries** — Operates across the living (disease, distress) and the dead/judged (Luk 16; Rev).
**T4.6 Spiritual beings** — **Yes — uniquely.** Torment is the site of an adversarial interface: demons dread it and protest being tormented "before the time" (Mat 8:29; Mar 5:7; Luk 8:28; cf. the locusts tormenting men, Rev 9:5; the devil's final torment, Rev 20:10). This is the only M03 characteristic with a developed spiritual-beings interface.

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension
**T5.1 Transformation** — Torment is not formative in the persons who bear it; it is endured or judicial. Negative on positive transformation.
**T5.2 Sequence** — In the eschatological texts, impenitence → final torment (Rev 14:9–11).
**T5.3 Mechanism** — Mechanism is infliction — by force (waves), disease, awareness (2Pe 2:8), or judgement.
**T5.4 Suffering** — Torment **is** suffering at its extreme — the torture-level of affliction; it is suffering itself, not a response to it.
**T5.5 Formation/sanctification** — No formative/sanctifying role in the evidence. Negative.
**T5.6 Eschatological** — Strongly oriented: torment is a defining content of final judgement (Rev 14:10; 20:10) — the cluster's most eschatologically loaded characteristic.

## T6 — Structural Relationships
**T6.1 Co-occurrence** — Sparse same-verse co-occurrence (with H once); torment largely stands alone as an extremity.
**T6.2 Sequential** — In judgement texts, follows impenitence; in narrative, follows the encounter with disease or the demonic.
**T6.3 Causal/constitutive** — Produced by storm, disease, awareness, or judgement; constitutes the severe pole of suffering.
**T6.4 Vocabulary/root sharing** — `basanizō`/`basanos` are a distinct NT family (from the testing-stone metaphor); little vocabulary overlap with the OT grief terms. (Cross-cluster — flagged.)
**T6.5 Distinctions** — Nearest neighbour is **A (inner pain)** at the severe end; the distinction is intensity and imposition — torment is acute, inflicted, often eschatological or adversarial, where A is the ordinary felt ache.

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation
**T7.1.1** — `basanizō` (to torment/torture), `basanos` (torment); the root lies in the touchstone/testing metaphor, sharpened to torture-level affliction.
**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: verb (to torment) and noun (torment) — predominantly verbal/inflicted.
**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: torment ↔ torture ↔ severe suffering ↔ being buffeted.
**T7.1.4** — The vocabulary distinguishes the act (`basanizō`) from the state/place (`basanos`, "the place of torment", Luk 16:28).
**T7.1.5** — Opposite: rest (Rev 14:11, "no rest"), present antonymically.
**T7.1.6–.7** — No person-type or supplication term. Negative.
**T7.1.8** — NT-only; there is no OT lexical antecedent in this set — torment's intensification is a NT development (esp. its eschatological use).
**T7.1.9** — The eschatological-torment usage (Revelation) is effectively a NT-period deployment of the term for final judgement.
**T7.1.10** — The arc is NT and bimodal: present acute affliction (storm, disease, vexed soul) and final judgement (Revelation).
**T7.2.1** — In Luk 16:23 the term names the rich man's condition in Hades — "in torment" defines his state.
**T7.2.2** — Forms: gospel narrative (Matthew, Mark, Luke), epistle (2 Peter), and apocalyptic (Revelation) — the apocalyptic carrying the eschatological weight.
**T7.2.4** — Settings: the demonic encounter, the deathbed/afterlife (Luk 16), and final judgement (Revelation).
**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor: **Luke 16:23–28** — the rich man "in torment" in Hades most fully expresses torment as acute, conscious, irremediable affliction with an eschatological frame.
**T7.2.6** — The anchor uniquely reveals torment as a *conscious, communicative* extremity — the tormented man still sees, remembers, and pleads, making torment a state of unrelieved awareness, not oblivion.
**T7.3.1** — Framework: clinical psychology of suffering (Cassell, *The Nature of Suffering*).
**T7.3.2** — Cassell's account of suffering as a threat to the whole person illuminates torment as the extremity where the person is overwhelmed, not merely pained — matching the term's reach beyond physical hurt (2Pe 2:8, the tormented righteous soul).
**T7.3.3** — Divergence: the science has no category for eschatological or adversarial torment; the biblical material's judicial and demonic uses (Rev; Mat 8:29) lie wholly outside the clinical frame.
**T7.3.4** — The science surfaces nothing the evidence misses; rather, the biblical torment vocabulary exceeds the science's scope at the eschatological/adversarial end — a divergence to carry into synthesis.

## 1. What this characteristic is
G names grief **as acute, often imposed, torment** — `basanizō`/`basanos`, torture-level affliction. It is exclusively New Testament here and leans toward the eschatological and the physically overwhelming.
