# M03 · Characteristic H — Travail / labour-pangs (metaphor) · Findings by tier question

- **File:** wa-m03-char-h-tier-findings-v1_0-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Related:** evidence base wa-m03-char-h-travail-v1_0-20260619.md; tier framework wa-tier-catalogue-restructured-v2-20260611.md (T-codes are the reference key); science lens wa-m03-grief-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md (Section 3); obslog wa-obslog-m03-ve-char-derive-v2-20260619.md.
- **Scope:** every live tier question answered as a self-contained finding (prose can be written from it without returning to source data); citations inline. Negative findings stated explicitly. Retired constructs (T1.2.3, T1.8, T2.8, T5.7, T6.6, T6.7) omitted. Field-absent questions answered by inference from verse identities and present fields, as agreed.
- **Status:** v1_0.
- **Evidence summary:** 12 verses (OT 9 / NT 3); no inner faculty tagged (figurative); no constitutional seat recorded; God = giver ×1 (Job 21:17); valence neutral 10; lead terms `che.vel` (pangs, 9), `ōdinō` (be in labour, 3) — the childbirth figure for anguish that comes suddenly and cannot be averted.

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
**T0.1.1** — Travail images God as the one who apportions pangs in judgement (God distributes "pains in his anger", Job 21:17) and, in the prophets, as the one whose acts bring on a nation's birth-pang anguish (Jer 13:21). It pictures God as sovereign over the onset of inescapable anguish.
**T0.1.2** — Travail is related to God as **giver** in one verse (Job 21:17, God distributing pains); otherwise it is borne by persons and nations, not by God.
**T0.1.3** — God's apportioning rather than bearing of pangs frames travail as a creaturely anguish that God can ordain.
**T0.2.1** — Travail serves, figuratively, to mark anguish that is sudden, gripping, and productive of something (a birth) — it equips the language of unavoidable, purposive pain.
**T0.2.2** — As literal childbirth pain it belongs to the fallen order (Gen 3:16, the multiplied pangs — though that verse's `e.tsev` sits in A); as a figure it describes the fallen experience of sudden anguish.
**T0.2.3** — Future-oriented in its NT use: birth-pangs become the figure of the present age's anguish straining toward a new birth (Gal 4:19, until Christ is formed; the woman in birth-pangs, Rev 12:2) — present travail anticipates a coming birth.
**T0.3.1–.3** — No verse ties travail to the image of God. Negative on image-bearing.
**T0.4.1–.2** — Travail is strongly typological/figurative: the birth-pang carries covenantal and apocalyptic meaning (Isa 66:7, Zion's birth; Rev 12:2, the woman in labour) — the human experience of labour established as the pattern for anguish that issues in new birth, a present→consummation direction.

## T1 — Definition
**T1.1.1** — "Travail / labour-pangs": grief and anguish figured as the pains of childbirth — sudden, gripping, inescapable, and productive. The name signals the birth metaphor.
**T1.1.2** — `che.vel` (birth-pang), `ōdinō` (to be in labour); the terms are the literal vocabulary of childbirth applied to anguish.
**T1.1.3** — The terms carry an implication of inevitability and onset — pangs that seize and cannot be deferred (Isa 13:8; Jer 13:21).
**T1.2.1** — Predominantly a **status** (9) — the gripped condition of being in pangs.
**T1.2.2** — Compound by metaphor: travail fuses physical pain, suddenness, and the expectation of a birth.
**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite: the ease of safe deliverance / painless birth (Isa 66:7, Zion delivered "before she was in labour"). Cross-cluster, named.
**T1.3.2** — Travail excludes calm and control; pangs overtake.
**T1.3.3** — It is the figure of sudden seizing anguish, distinct from sustained ache (A) or pressure (B).
**T1.4.1** — Operates as the figure for a nation's terror (pangs seize them, Isa 13:8; Jer 49:24), for personal anguish, and for spiritual labour (Paul "in travail until Christ is formed", Gal 4:19).
**T1.4.2** — Operates literally (childbirth, Job 39:3) and figuratively (national and spiritual anguish).
**T1.4.3** — Travail can issue in a cry (the cry of a woman in labour, Jer 4:31 — though that verse's term sits in I), but it is not characteristically speech-based.
**T1.5.1** — The immediate response is being gripped/seized — pangs taking hold (Isa 13:8).
**T1.5.2** — Consistent: sudden onset and gripping.
**T1.6.1** — Sustained travail strains toward a birth — its over-time orientation is productive (Gal 4:19).
**T1.7.1–.3** — Travail is undergone, not received as a gift. Negative on reception.

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries
**T2.1–T2.5** — No constitutional seat is recorded for travail at any level (spirit, soul, heart, mind, other soul-subset). It is figured bodily, not located in a named inner seat. Negative throughout.
**T2.6** — The body (the womb, the loins) is the implicit site of the metaphor, though a named inner organ is not the locus.
**T2.7** — As a bodily figure, travail runs body→whole-person: the bodily pang stands for total anguish.
**T2.9.1** — Origin is the onset of overwhelming circumstance — received-from-outside (the enemy, the day of calamity) — and once divinely apportioned (Job 21:17).
**T2.9.2–.3** — Origin varies: literal childbirth, national catastrophe (Jer 13:21), divine distribution (Job 21:17), spiritual labour (Gal 4:19).
**T2.10** — No constitutional movement across levels evidenced. Negative.

## T3 — The Inner Faculties
No inner faculty is tagged on the travail terms — they are figurative bodily descriptors rather than direct faculty-engagements.
**T3.1–T3.11** — Not engaged at faculty level in the evidence. This is itself the finding: travail is a **bodily metaphor** for anguish, so it engages the inner faculties only by the felt-states it figures (A, B), not directly.
**Pattern** — Travail's non-engagement of any faculty marks it as a figure rather than a primitive inner-state; it lends the cluster its image of inescapable, productive anguish without being itself a discrete faculty-engaging characteristic.

## T4 — Relational Interfaces
**T4.1 God→human** — God apportions pangs (Job 21:17) and brings on the birth-pang anguish of nations through his acts (Jer 13:21). Basis: judicial/providential.
**T4.2 Human→God** — Not directed Godward in these verses. Negative.
**T4.3 Giving** — Paul's travail is extended *for* others — "I am in travail until Christ is formed in you" (Gal 4:19), a redemptive labour on another's behalf. This is the one clear relational extension.
**T4.4 Receiving** — Not characteristically received person-to-person.
**T4.5 Boundaries** — Operates over individuals (childbirth), nations (prophetic), and the church (Gal 4:19).
**T4.6 Spiritual beings** — The apocalyptic woman in travail (Rev 12:2) sits in a cosmic-conflict scene, but travail itself is not an interface with spiritual beings. Largely negative.

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension
**T5.1 Transformation** — Travail is transformative by figure: it strains toward a birth — Paul's travail aims at Christ being formed (Gal 4:19), a real formation.
**T5.2 Sequence** — The inherent sequence is pangs → birth; the metaphor's whole force is the productive movement from anguish to new life.
**T5.3 Mechanism** — Mechanism is the gripping onset that issues in delivery — anguish as the necessary precursor to birth.
**T5.4 Suffering** — Travail is suffering figured as productive — pangs are the **context** of a coming birth; suffering here is purposive, oriented toward an outcome.
**T5.5 Formation/sanctification** — Gal 4:19 makes travail the figure of formative spiritual labour — the apostolic anguish by which Christ is formed in others.
**T5.6 Eschatological** — Strongly oriented: birth-pangs are a NT figure for the present age's anguish before the new birth (Rev 12:2; cf. the wider birth-pang motif) — travail anticipates consummation.

## T6 — Structural Relationships
**T6.1 Co-occurrence** — Sparse same-verse co-occurrence (with E, B, G once each); travail mostly stands as a figure attaching to a scene.
**T6.2 Sequential** — Inherently sequential (pangs→birth); attaches to scenes of sudden calamity.
**T6.3 Causal/constitutive** — Produced by sudden overwhelming circumstance; constitutes the figure of productive anguish.
**T6.4 Vocabulary/root sharing** — `che.vel` (pang) shares its consonantal form with the out-of-scope homonym for cord/region (set aside); `ōdinō`/`ōdin` is the NT labour family. (Cross-cluster — flagged; note the homonym separation.)
**T6.5 Distinctions** — Nearest neighbours are **A (inner pain)** and **B (distress)**; travail is distinguished as the *figure* of sudden, gripping, productive pain rather than a felt-state in its own right — a distinction of register (metaphor vs primitive).

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation
**T7.1.1** — `che.vel` (birth-pang), `ōdinō`/`ōdin` (to be in labour / labour); roots in the literal vocabulary of childbirth.
**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: noun (pang) and verb (to be in labour) — the figure works as both the pain and the act.
**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: pang ↔ labour ↔ birth-pain ↔ agony — the childbirth band applied to anguish.
**T7.1.4** — The vocabulary distinguishes the pang (`che.vel`) from the act of labouring (`ōdinō`).
**T7.1.5–.7** — No internal opposite, person-type, or supplication term. Negative.
**T7.1.8** — OT `che.vel`-pang continues into NT `ōdinō`; the birth-pang figure is stable and gains an eschatological charge in the NT.
**T7.1.10** — The arc runs from prophetic national birth-pangs (Isaiah, Jeremiah) to apostolic spiritual travail (Gal 4:19) and apocalyptic birth (Rev 12:2) — anguish always oriented toward a coming birth.
**T7.2.1** — In Gal 4:19 the travail term carries Paul's pastoral anguish — the labour by which Christ is to be formed in the Galatians.
**T7.2.2** — Forms: prophecy (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea), wisdom (Job), epistle (Galatians), and apocalyptic (Revelation).
**T7.2.4** — Settings: covenant judgement (the prophetic birth-pangs of the nations), and eschatological birth (Rev 12).
**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor: **Galatians 4:19** — "my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you" most fully expresses travail as productive, redemptive anguish borne for another.
**T7.2.6** — The anchor uniquely reveals travail as *vicarious and formative* — anguish willingly borne so that new life (Christ formed) may come in another.
**T7.3.1** — Framework: physiology of grief and the clinical reality of labour (psychosomatic research; the labour analogy).
**T7.3.2** — The science notes that grief and labour share genuine physiological features (involuntary contractions, waves of pain, exhaustion), making the biblical birth-pang figure "more than literary" — it rests on a real bodily analogue.
**T7.3.3** — Divergence: the science treats labour as a physiological process; the biblical material loads it with covenantal and eschatological meaning (new birth, the age to come) that lies outside the physiological frame.
**T7.3.4** — The shared physiology supports treating travail as the cluster's bodily image of *productive* anguish — distinct from the depleting toil-pain of A — a distinction to test in synthesis.

# M03 · Characteristic I — Debilitating grief (faint / weak / waste) · Findings by tier question

- **File:** wa-m03-char-i-tier-findings-v1_0-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Related:** evidence base wa-m03-char-i-debilitation-v1_0-20260619.md; tier framework wa-tier-catalogue-restructured-v2-20260611.md (T-codes are the reference key); science lens wa-m03-grief-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md (Section 3); obslog wa-obslog-m03-ve-char-derive-v2-20260619.md.
- **Scope:** every live tier question answered as a self-contained finding (prose can be written from it without returning to source data); citations inline. Negative findings stated explicitly. Retired constructs (T1.2.3, T1.8, T2.8, T5.7, T6.6, T6.7) omitted. Field-absent questions answered by inference from verse identities and present fields, as agreed.
- **Status:** v1_0.
- **Evidence summary:** 16 verses (OT only); faculty = affect (12) + perception (3); seat heart 3 / soul 2; God = agent ×1 (Isa 53:10, “put him to grief”); valence neutral 13 / sinful 1; lead terms `cha.lah` (grievous/sick, 12), `dav.va` (faint, 3) — grief that weakens and sickens the body.

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
**T0.1.1** — Debilitating grief images God most pointedly at Isa 53:10, where "it was the will of the LORD to crush him; he has put him to grief" — God is the agent who lays grievous sickness on the Servant. The divine character reflected is sovereign purpose working even through grief that crushes.
**T0.1.2** — Debilitating grief is related to God as **agent** once (Isa 53:10); it is not borne by God himself, except as the Servant (read christologically) bears the grief God lays on him.
**T0.1.3** — That God lays grief but is not (in this vocabulary) himself made sick frames the characteristic as a creaturely weakening that God can ordain to purpose (Isa 53).
**T0.2.1** — Where a purpose appears, it is the Servant's grief working redemption (Isa 53:10, the grief that makes him an offering); otherwise debilitating grief equips nothing — it depletes.
**T0.2.2** — It belongs to the fallen condition — grief that wounds incurably (Jer 30:12, "your hurt is incurable") — except where God ordains it to purpose (Isa 53).
**T0.2.3** — No general orientation to future fullness; its trajectory is toward sickness/wasting, save the Servant's grief which is oriented to a redemptive outcome (Isa 53:10–11). Limited.
**T0.3.1–.3** — No verse ties debilitating grief to the image of God. Negative on image-bearing.
**T0.4.1–.2** — Isa 53:10 is christological/typological: the LORD putting the Servant to grief establishes the divine→human pattern in which grief becomes redemptive offering.

## T1 — Definition
**T1.1.1** — "Debilitating grief": grief that weakens, sickens, and faints the person — where sorrow crosses into bodily failure. The name signals the toll grief takes on strength.
**T1.1.2** — `cha.lah` (to be/​become weak, sick, grieved), `dav.va` (faint), `ne.dud` (tossing); the terms denote grief shading into sickness and exhaustion.
**T1.1.3** — The terms carry a somatic implication — grief registering as the body's weakening.
**T1.2.1** — Predominantly an **action/process** (12) — the becoming-weak of grief — with some quality (faint, 3).
**T1.2.2** — Compound at the edge: it fuses felt grief with bodily debilitation.
**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite: strength / health / a sustained heart. Cross-cluster, named.
**T1.3.2** — It excludes vigour; grief here saps the body's capacity.
**T1.3.3** — It is the point where felt grief (A) or its causes cross into bodily failure — the boundary with A is the somatic collapse.
**T1.4.1** — Operates as grievous wounding (Jer 30:12, an incurable hurt), heart-sickness ("hope deferred makes the heart sick", the `cha.lah` idiom), faintness (`dav.va`), and restless tossing (Job 7:4).
**T1.4.2** — Operates individually (sickened grief) and nationally (Nah 3:19, an incurable wound).
**T1.4.3** — Debilitating grief can issue in a cry of distress (Jer 4:31) but is not characteristically speech-based; it is more often the silent sinking of strength.
**T1.5.1** — The immediate response is faintness/weakening — the body giving way (`dav.va`; Job 7:4, the restless wasting of the night).
**T1.5.2** — Consistent: grief presenting as bodily decline.
**T1.6.1** — Sustained debilitating grief becomes chronic sickness and incurable wounding (Jer 30:12; Nah 3:19).
**T1.7.1–.3** — It is undergone, not received as a gift. Negative.

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries
**T2.1** — No spirit-level location. Negative. **T2.2** — Soul-level in 2 occurrences. **T2.3** — Heart in 3 occurrences — the heart made sick by grief (the `cha.lah` heart-sickness idiom). **T2.4 / T2.5** — No mind or other soul-subset. Negative.
**T2.6** — The body/flesh is the implicit site (faintness, wasting, sickness), though debilitation is described as a whole-body weakening more than a single organ.
**T2.7** — Direction runs soul→body: inner grief saps bodily strength — the clearest cluster case (with E) of grief feeding back into the body.
**T2.9.1** — Origin is the grief or wound received-from-outside (betrayal, threat, loss), and once divinely laid (Isa 53:10).
**T2.9.2–.3** — Origin varies: relational (1Sa 22:8, none grieved for the speaker), threat (Jer 4:31), accumulated groaning (Lam 1:22), divine purpose (Isa 53:10).
**T2.10** — Movement runs soul→body (grief into bodily failure); no spirit-level movement. This is the characteristic that most clearly shows grief crossing the soul-body boundary downward.

## T3 — The Inner Faculties
Debilitating grief is **affect** (12) with a **perceptual** component (3 — the faint/sick perception of one's own weakening).
**T3.1 Perception** — Engaged at the edge: the faintness terms carry a perceptual sense of the body's failing (`dav.va`). **T3.2, T3.3, T3.5, T3.7, T3.11** — Not engaged. Negative.
**T3.4 Affect** — Engaged: it is grief-affect crossing into bodily depletion.
**T3.6 Volition / T3.8 Moral evaluation / T3.9 Conscience** — Not engaged at faculty level (Isa 1:5's "whole heart faint" carries a moral context, but the engaged faculty is affect/perception).
**Pattern** — Debilitating grief engages affect with a perceptual-somatic edge; it is the characteristic where grief most clearly becomes a bodily event, distinguishing it from the purely interior A.

## T4 — Relational Interfaces
**T4.1 God→human** — God lays grief on the Servant to purpose (Isa 53:10); basis: redemptive, sovereign.
**T4.2 Human→God** — Not characteristically directed Godward in these verses. Negative.
**T4.3 Giving / T4.4 Receiving** — Not extended or received as a benefit; debilitating grief is incurred from loss, threat, or (for the Servant) divine appointment.
**T4.5 Boundaries** — Operates over individuals (sick heart) and nations (incurable wound, Nah 3:19; Jer 30:12).
**T4.6 Spiritual beings** — No occurrence relates it to angelic or adversarial beings. Negative.

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension
**T5.1 Transformation** — Debilitating grief mostly depletes rather than transforms; the singular exception is the Servant's grief, ordained to redemptive transformation (Isa 53:10–11).
**T5.2 Sequence** — In Isa 53 the sequence is divine will → the Servant put to grief → offering → fruit ("he shall see his offspring").
**T5.3 Mechanism** — Mechanism is the sapping of bodily strength under grief (the somatic toll, T7.3).
**T5.4 Suffering** — Debilitating grief is the **product of** suffering at the point where it overwhelms the body — incurable wounds, faintness, wasting (Jer 30:12; Job 7:4).
**T5.5 Formation/sanctification** — No general formative role; the Servant's grief (Isa 53) is uniquely redemptive-formative for others.
**T5.6 Eschatological** — Limited; the Servant's grief is oriented to a redemptive outcome (Isa 53:10–11), but the OT wasting-grief verses carry no eschatological orientation. Largely negative.

## T6 — Structural Relationships
**T6.1 Co-occurrence** — Same-verse most with **A (inner pain)** (×2), and with B, D, E — debilitation is where the felt ache (A) and the cry (E) cross into bodily failure.
**T6.2 Sequential** — Tends to follow sustained grief (the chronic, incurable end of A/B); in Isa 53 it follows divine appointment.
**T6.3 Causal/constitutive** — Produced by sustained grief, wounding, and (for the Servant) divine will; constitutes the somatic collapse of grief.
**T6.4 Vocabulary/root sharing** — `cha.lah` ranges across "be weak / be sick / be grieved", bridging grief and illness vocabulary. (Cross-cluster — flagged.)
**T6.5 Distinctions** — Nearest neighbour is **A (inner pain)**. The distinction is the somatic outcome: A is the felt ache; debilitation is that ache (or its cause) crossing into bodily weakening and sickness — a distinction of constitutional consequence (soul→body).

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation
**T7.1.1** — `cha.lah` (to be weak / sick / grieved), `dav.va` (faint), `ne.dud` (tossing); roots in sickness, faintness, and restlessness.
**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: verb (to become weak/grieved), adjective/quality (faint) — debilitation is process-led.
**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: grievous ↔ sick ↔ weak ↔ faint ↔ wasting — the band where grief meets bodily failure.
**T7.1.4** — The vocabulary distinguishes the process (`cha.lah`, becoming weak/sick) from the resulting state (faint).
**T7.1.5–.7** — No internal opposite, person-type, or supplication term. Negative.
**T7.1.8** — OT-only in this set; `cha.lah`'s grief-sense is a Hebrew development of a wider weakness/sickness verb.
**T7.1.10** — The arc runs from the incurable wounds of the prophets (Jer 30:12; Nah 3:19) to the Servant's redemptive grief (Isa 53:10) — grief that wastes, and grief that God ordains to heal.
**T7.2.1** — In Isa 53:10 the grief term carries the clause of divine purpose — the LORD's will to put the Servant to grief.
**T7.2.2** — Forms: narrative (1 Samuel), wisdom (Job; Ecclesiastes), prophecy (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Nahum, Amos), and lament (Lamentations).
**T7.2.4** — Settings: personal lament, prophetic woe (incurable wounds), and the Servant Song (Isa 53).
**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor: **Isaiah 53:10** — "it was the will of the LORD to crush him; he has put him to grief" most fully expresses debilitating grief as divinely ordained and redemptively purposed.
**T7.2.6** — The anchor uniquely reveals that grief which crushes can be the appointed means of redemption — the Servant's debilitating grief made an offering for many.
**T7.3.1** — Framework: physiology/psychosomatics of grief (Engel's biopsychosocial model; the bereavement-physiology research — immune suppression, broken-heart syndrome, fatigue).
**T7.3.2** — The science documents that grief produces measurable bodily debilitation — immune suppression, cardiovascular effects (Takotsubo "broken heart"), fatigue — giving the biblical wasting/sickness vocabulary a literal physiological basis.
**T7.3.3** — Divergence: the science treats grief-debilitation as a health outcome to be mitigated; the biblical material includes grief-debilitation ordained to redemptive purpose (Isa 53), a meaning outside the clinical frame.
**T7.3.4** — The bereavement-physiology research supports treating debilitation as the genuine somatic end of grief (with E) — and the broken-heart finding invites testing the heart-sickness idiom in synthesis.

# M03 · Characteristic J — Voiced complaint / grievance · Findings by tier question

- **File:** wa-m03-char-j-tier-findings-v1_0-20260619.md · **Date:** 2026-06-19
- **Related:** evidence base wa-m03-char-j-complaint-v1_0-20260619.md; tier framework wa-tier-catalogue-restructured-v2-20260611.md (T-codes are the reference key); science lens wa-m03-grief-scienceextract-v1_0-20260513.md (Section 4); obslog wa-obslog-m03-ve-char-derive-v2-20260619.md.
- **Scope:** every live tier question answered as a self-contained finding (prose can be written from it without returning to source data); citations inline. Negative findings stated explicitly. Retired constructs (T1.2.3, T1.8, T2.8, T5.7, T6.6, T6.7) omitted. Field-absent questions answered by inference from verse identities and present fields, as agreed.
- **Status:** v1_0.
- **Evidence summary:** 14 verses (OT only); faculty = affect (14) + cognition (14) — the **only** M03 characteristic with a full cognitive dimension; seat soul ×1; God = object ×1 (complaint poured before him, Psa 64:1); valence neutral 9 / sinful 1; single lead term `si.ach` — the complaint/​musing poured out, characteristically before God.

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design
**T0.1.1** — Voiced complaint images God as the one who receives and attends to the poured-out grievance: the psalmist pours his complaint *before* the LORD (Psa 142:2) and asks God to hear his complaint (Psa 64:1). The divine character reflected is a God who invites and hears the reasoned grievance of the afflicted.
**T0.1.2** — Complaint is related to God as the **object/addressee** who hears it (Psa 64:1); it is not borne by God. Its theological weight is that grievance may be brought to God.
**T0.1.3** — God's hearing rather than complaining frames complaint as the creaturely grievance he legitimately receives.
**T0.2.1** — Complaint serves to give grief a voice and a case — to "give free utterance to" the soul's bitterness (Job 10:1) and to lay the grievance before God (Psa 142:2). It equips the sufferer to bring sorrow into articulate, God-directed speech.
**T0.2.2** — Complaint answers the fallen experience of affliction; yet it is also a sanctioned mode of address to God (the lament psalms), not merely a defect.
**T0.2.3** — No explicit orientation to future fullness; complaint seeks present hearing and relief. The one positive note (Psa 104:34, "may my meditation/`si.ach` be pleasing") points to complaint's kin, godly musing. Largely negative on eschatological orientation.
**T0.3.1–.3** — No verse ties complaint to the image of God. Negative on image-bearing.
**T0.4.1–.2** — Complaint is not deployed typologically; it functions within the lament tradition as the form of God-directed grievance.

## T1 — Definition
**T1.1.1** — "Voiced complaint / grievance": grief made articulate — poured out as a reasoned case, characteristically before God. The name signals speech and grievance, not mute feeling.
**T1.1.2** — `si.ach` — the term ranges across *complaint*, *musing*, *meditation*, *talk* — the inner discourse that can be poured out as grievance.
**T1.1.3** — The term carries a cognitive-communicative implication: complaint reasons and voices, orienting the enquiry toward articulate inner speech directed outward (often Godward).
**T1.2.1** — Wholly a **status** (14/14) — complaint is the condition of the burdened, voicing soul.
**T1.2.2** — Compound: complaint fuses felt grief (affect) with reasoned articulation (cognition) — uniquely in the cluster.
**T1.3.1** — Structural opposite: silent contentment / settled praise (the antithesis of grievance). Cross-cluster, named.
**T1.3.2** — Complaint excludes mute resignation; it insists on voicing the grievance.
**T1.3.3** — It is grief that has become articulate case-making, distinct from the inarticulate groan (E) and the mute ache (A).
**T1.4.1** — Operates as grievance poured out before God (Psa 142:2; Psa 64:1), as the bitter free-utterance of the suffering soul (Job 10:1; Job 23:2), and as anxious musing (1Sa 1:16, Hannah's "great anxiety and vexation"); the same root also covers godly meditation (Psa 104:34) and even derisive musing (1Ki 18:27).
**T1.4.2** — Operates Godward (lament before the LORD) and inwardly (musing/meditation) — the term spans grievance and reflection.
**T1.4.3** — Complaint **is** the speech-based mode of grief — its defining mode is articulate utterance (Job 10:1, "I will give free utterance to my complaint").
**T1.5.1** — The immediate movement is to pour it out — to voice the grievance rather than contain it (Psa 142:2).
**T1.5.2** — Consistent: complaint presses toward utterance.
**T1.6.1** — Sustained complaint, voiced to God, moves toward relief or resolution (Hannah's complaint, once spoken, ends her sadness, 1Sa 1:18); unaddressed, it cycles in the suffering soul (Job).
**T1.7.1–.3** — Complaint is voiced, not received as a gift. Negative on reception.

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries
**T2.1** — No spirit-level location. Negative. **T2.2** — Soul-level once (the soul's complaint, Job 10:1's "bitterness of my soul"). **T2.3 / T2.4 / T2.5** — No heart, mind, or other soul-subset seat recorded. Negative — notably, despite its cognitive dimension, complaint is not seated in a "mind" in the evidence.
**T2.6** — No body-part link. Negative — complaint is articulate, not somatic.
**T2.7** — No body-direction. Negative.
**T2.9.1** — Origin is the affliction or anxiety that presses the soul to speak — received-from-outside (suffering, vexation), then voiced from within.
**T2.9.2–.3** — Origin varies: personal distress (Hannah, 1Sa 1:16), bodily/spiritual suffering (Job), affliction and faintness (Psa 102:1).
**T2.10** — No constitutional movement across levels; complaint moves from inner burden to outward speech (an inward→expressive movement rather than a cross-level one).

## T3 — The Inner Faculties
Complaint uniquely engages **both affect (14) and cognition (14)** — every occurrence carries both.
**T3.1 Perception / T3.3 Memory / T3.5 Creativity / T3.7 Agency / T3.11 Relational** — Not engaged at faculty level. Negative.
**T3.2 Cognition** — Engaged fully and distinctively: complaint reasons, frames a grievance, and argues a case (Job 23:2–4, ordering his case before God) — the only M03 characteristic that engages cognition throughout.
**T3.4 Affect** — Engaged fully: complaint is felt grief and bitterness given articulate form.
**T3.6 Volition** — Engaged at the edge: the choice to "give free utterance" (Job 10:1) is volitional, though the tagged faculties are affect and cognition.
**T3.8 Moral evaluation / T3.9 Conscience** — Not engaged at faculty level (Pro 23:29's "complaining" carries a moral context but engages affect/cognition).
**Pattern** — Complaint is the cluster's one affect-plus-cognition characteristic: grief that thinks and speaks its grievance. This makes it the bridge between the felt-states and the reasoning/speaking faculties — the point at which grief becomes a case brought before God.

## T4 — Relational Interfaces
**T4.1 God→human** — God receives and hears complaint (Psa 64:1); the relationship is one in which grievance is invited.
**T4.2 Human→God** — Centrally present: complaint is the classic God-directed grief-speech — "I pour out my complaint before him" (Psa 142:2); Hannah's bitter complaint to the LORD (1Sa 1:16); Job's case laid before God (Job 23:2). The inner posture is honest, often raw, dependence.
**T4.3 Giving / T4.4 Receiving** — Not extended or received person-to-person as a benefit; complaint is directed to God or vented inwardly.
**T4.5 Boundaries** — Operates within the covenant relationship (the afflicted to their God) and inwardly (musing); scope is the suffering believer before God.
**T4.6 Spiritual beings** — No occurrence relates complaint to angelic or adversarial beings. Negative.

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension
**T5.1 Transformation** — Complaint can be transformative when voiced to God: Hannah's complaint, once poured out and heard, changes her countenance — "her face was no longer sad" (1Sa 1:18). Voicing the grievance Godward reorders the inner state.
**T5.2 Sequence** — Hannah's narrative gives a clear before→after: bitter, complaining soul → poured-out prayer → settled, no longer sad.
**T5.3 Mechanism** — Mechanism is articulation before God — bringing the grievance into ordered, addressed speech, which itself relieves (the lament-psalm pattern).
**T5.4 Suffering** — Complaint is the **response to** sustained suffering — the vocalisation of distress that has not resolved (Job; Psa 102:1, the afflicted who faints and pours out his complaint).
**T5.5 Formation/sanctification** — Complaint participates in formation as the sanctioned lament that keeps the sufferer in honest relationship with God rather than in silence or despair (the lament psalms model this).
**T5.6 Eschatological** — No eschatological orientation in the evidence; complaint seeks present hearing. Negative.

## T6 — Structural Relationships
**T6.1 Co-occurrence** — Sparse same-verse co-occurrence (with F, E, B once each); complaint largely stands as the articulate voicing alongside felt distress.
**T6.2 Sequential** — Complaint follows the pressing of distress (B) and the bitterness of soul (F), giving them voice; in Hannah it precedes relief.
**T6.3 Causal/constitutive** — Produced by affliction and anxiety; constitutes the articulate, God-directed expression of grief.
**T6.4 Vocabulary/root sharing** — `si.ach` spans complaint, musing, and meditation — bridging grief-grievance with reflective/meditative vocabulary (Psa 104:34's godly `si.ach`). (Cross-cluster — flagged; the complaint/meditation range is notable.)
**T6.5 Distinctions** — Nearest neighbours are **E (sighing/groaning)** and **F (bitterness)**. The distinction from E is articulacy (complaint reasons and speaks; groaning is wordless); from F, direction and form (complaint is voiced grievance, often Godward and relievable; bitterness is a settled embittered stance). The distinction is of kind — complaint is the cognitive-articulate member of the cluster.

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation
**T7.1.1** — `si.ach` — to muse, meditate, talk, complain; the root denotes inner discourse that can be poured out, ranging from grievance to godly meditation.
**T7.1.2** — Grammatical range: noun (complaint/​musing) — complaint is a borne, voiced condition.
**T7.1.3** — Semantic range: complaint ↔ grievance ↔ anxiety ↔ musing ↔ meditation — uniquely spanning grief-speech and reflective thought.
**T7.1.4** — The same term distinguishes the bitter grievance (Job 10:1) from the pleasing meditation (Psa 104:34) — a single root holding both the lament and its godly counterpart.
**T7.1.5** — Opposite: silent resignation, or settled praise; present by contrast.
**T7.1.6–.7** — No distinct person-type or supplication term, though complaint itself functions as a seeking-speech toward God. Limited.
**T7.1.8** — OT-only in this set; `si.ach` has no single NT lexical successor in the cluster, though the lament/petition it embodies continues in NT prayer.
**T7.1.10** — The arc presents complaint as the OT lament voice — the afflicted soul's grievance poured out before God, holding together grief and reasoned speech.
**T7.2.1** — In Psa 142:2 the complaint term is the direct object of "I pour out" — the grievance laid before God.
**T7.2.2** — Forms: narrative (1 Samuel; 1–2 Kings), wisdom (Job; Proverbs), and psalm/lament (Psalms).
**T7.2.4** — Settings: individual lament before God (Psalms; Job), and personal distress brought to prayer (Hannah).
**T7.2.5** — Primary anchor: **Psalm 142:2** — "I pour out my complaint before him; I tell my trouble before him" most fully expresses complaint as grief made articulate and brought to God.
**T7.2.6** — The anchor uniquely reveals complaint as a *legitimate, God-directed* pouring-out — grief that is neither suppressed nor merely vented but addressed to God as the one who hears.
**T7.3.1** — Framework: clinical stress research — complaint as the vocalisation of sustained, unresolved distress (Lazarus and Folkman's coping; the lament-as-coping literature).
**T7.3.2** — The science frames complaint as the vocalisation of distress that has not resolved — matching `si.ach` as the cry that the trouble persists; voicing distress to a witness reliably reduces it, illuminating why poured-out complaint relieves (Hannah, 1Sa 1:18).
**T7.3.3** — Divergence: the science treats complaint as venting toward regulation; the biblical material makes it a covenantal address to God who hears — the "witness" is not merely present but is the LORD, which reframes the relief as relational, not merely cathartic.
**T7.3.4** — The witnessed-distress finding supports the lament tradition's value and invites testing complaint's God-directedness (with D's and E's God-directed forms) as a "grief addressed to God" axis in the cross-cluster pass.

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design

### T0.1 · Divine Nature Reflected

- **T0.1.1** — *divine relation in the verse*  
  Yes — God stands in relation to the characteristic as agent: 22 · object: 12 · giver: 12 · possessor: 2 · addressee: 1 (e.g. **Deu 28:63** (*su.s* 'took delight')). Where no divine lemma is present it is not related to God in that verse.
- **T0.1.2** — *borne by God or only the creature*  
  God himself bears/acts the characteristic in 22 occ (divine *agent*) — so it is borne by both God and the creature, not the creature alone. *(Inferential as to 'divine image':)* a state God shares belongs to the image.

### T0.2 · Created Purpose

- **T0.2.1** — *purpose/role/effect in the person*  
  Yes — the immediate-response field shows effects following the characteristic (e.g. blow trumpets; **Num 10:10** (*sim.chah* 'gladness')). Beyond that the lexical states no further purpose.
- **T0.2.2** — *created design, fallen, both, or undeterminable*

- **T0.2.3** — *orientation toward future fullness*

## T1 — Definition

### T1.1 · Name and Naming

- **T1.1.1** — *programme name and essential nature*  
  In the programme it is **Rejoicing and gladness — the affective act of joy**. The name signals an inner-being phenomenon whose dominant faculty is affect: 544 and whose grammatical kind is action: 311 · status: 210.
- **T1.1.2** — *Hebrew/Greek terms at definitional level*  
  Primary terms: sa.mach 'to rejoice', sim.chah 'joy', chairo 'to rejoice', chara 'joy', gil_verb 'to rejoice', su.s 'to rejoice'…. At the definitional level the lemma meanings centre on the affective act of joy.
- **T1.1.3** — *directional/relational/constitutional implication*  
  The name carries: directed at situation: 79 · abstract: 72 · person: 60; seated in heart: 64 · soul: 18; relational force with: 17 · over: 13 · in: 13.

  By grammatical kind it is action: 311 · status: 210 · quality: 23 · UNRESOLVED: 1 — i.e. predominantly an act.
- **T1.2.2** — *simple or compound*  
  **Simple** — a single faculty (affect: 544) is engaged.

### T1.3 · Boundary

- **T1.3.1** — *structural opposite*  
  *(Inferential.)* Grief (M03) — sorrow, the affect that excludes gladness. The lexical carries no dedicated antonym term within M04; the contrast is read from co-occurrence/usage.

  At its edge it excludes its *illicit* form — the 44 sinful/forbidden occurrences mark joy/delight wrongly placed (e.g. **Pro 24:17** (*gil_verb* 'glad')); the right characteristic resists this.
- **T1.3.3** — *where it ends — what it is not*  
  It is not the *quality* that pleases (that is C) nor *directed* delight-in (that is B): A is the affect/act of gladness itself.

### T7.3 · Human Science Frameworks

- **T7.3.1** — *primary framework*  
  Positive psychology / affective neuroscience — Seligman (*Authentic Happiness*, *Flourish*); Fredrickson's broaden-and-build (2001); mesolimbic dopamine/oxytocin; the hedonic–eudaimonic distinction.
- **T7.3.2** — *where it illuminates*  
  Broaden-and-build illuminates the expansive, outward, communal joy the lexical shows — joy that rejoices *with* others (*sunchairo*) and issues in song; the exultation/triumphing band (*renanah, alitsut*) matches a high-arousal victory/deliverance joy.
- **T7.3.3** — *where it diverges*  
  Science treats joy as reactive to circumstance and to be maximised; the lexical shows commanded joy (valence *commanded* 69) and joy sharing verses with grief (Grief co-occurrence 57) — a complexity (joy in suffering, joy enjoined) the immanent model does not accommodate.
- **T7.3.4** — *gaps surfaced*  
  Hedonic adaptation predicts joy fades to baseline; the lexical's renewed, God-anchored causes and its praise/song output (savoring, Bryant & Veroff) read as anti-adaptation mechanisms worth a verse check.

### T7.3 · Human Science Frameworks

- **T7.3.1** — *primary framework*  
  Hedonic psychology / reward neuroscience — Berridge's wanting–liking dissociation; Kahneman's experiencing vs remembering self; nucleus accumbens/opioid 'liking'.

  The wanting–liking distinction illuminates the lexical's delight as *liking* — resting in and returning to a valued good (the savouring band *shaashuim, oneg*) rather than craving; the volition tag matches eudokeo's appreciative 'well-pleased'.
- **T7.3.3** — *where it diverges*

- **T7.3.2** — *where it illuminates*

- **T7.3.3** — *where it diverges*

- **T7.3.4** — *gaps surfaced*

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design

### T0.1 · Divine Nature Reflected

- **T0.1.1** — *divine relation in the verse*  
  Yes — God stands in relation to the characteristic as agent: 25 · object: 5 · addressee: 1 · possessor: 1 (e.g. **Gen 18:14** (*pa.la* 'hard')). Where no divine lemma is present it is not related to God in that verse.
- **T0.1.2** — *borne by God or only the creature*  
  God himself bears/acts the characteristic in 25 occ (divine *agent*) — so it is borne by both God and the creature, not the creature alone. *(Inferential as to 'divine image':)* a state God shares belongs to the image.

### T0.2 · Created Purpose

- **T0.2.1** — *purpose/role/effect in the person*  
  Yes — the immediate-response field shows effects following the characteristic (e.g. lasting sicknesses; **Deu 28:59** (*pa.la* 'extraordinary')). Beyond that the lexical states no further purpose.
- **T0.2.2** — *created design, fallen, both, or undeterminable*  
  **Both.** Valence shows the characteristic as righteous/commanded (23) — created design — and as sinful/forbidden (4) — a fallen distortion. *(Inferential from valence.)*
- **T0.2.3** — *orientation toward future fullness*  
  **Silence.** The lexical carries no eschatological marker; future-fullness is not evidenced.

### T0.3 · Image-Bearer Expression

- **T0.3.1** — *aspect of divine likeness instantiated*  
  *(Inferential.)* Since God himself wonder, marvel and amazement (divine *agent* 25), the human capacity instantiates that divine likeness.
- **T0.3.2** — *shared with God or creaturely analogue*  
  **Shared** between God and the person — God is recorded as bearer/agent as well as the creature.
- **T0.3.3** — *condition of the divine image indicated*  
  **Silence.** The lexical does not measure the condition of the divine image from the characteristic's presence or absence.

### T0.4 · Typological Significance

  **Silence.** No typological use is encoded in the lexical fields.

## T1 — Definition

### T1.1 · Name and Naming

- **T1.1.1** — *programme name and essential nature*  
  In the programme it is **Wonder, marvel and amazement**. The name signals an inner-being phenomenon whose dominant faculty is affect: 97 · cognition: 82 and whose grammatical kind is action: 78 · status: 18.
- **T1.1.2** — *Hebrew/Greek terms at definitional level*  
  Primary terms: pa.la 'to wonder', pe.le 'wonder', thaumazō 'to marvel', te.mah 'wonder', thambeō 'to astonish', thauma 'marvel'…. At the definitional level the lemma meanings centre on wonder, marvel and amazement.
- **T1.1.3** — *directional/relational/constitutional implication*  
  The name carries: directed at abstract: 31 · person: 8 · God: 7; seated in soul: 3 · heart: 2; relational force for: 4 · to: 2 · in: 2.

### T1.2 · Kind

- **T1.2.1** — *act / disposition / condition / quality*  
  By grammatical kind it is action: 78 · status: 18 · quality: 1 — i.e. predominantly an act.
- **T1.2.2** — *simple or compound*  
  **Compound** — the faculty profile combines affect: 97 · cognition: 82 · moral_evaluation: 13, so the characteristic is not a single bare faculty.

### T1.3 · Boundary

- **T1.3.1** — *structural opposite*  
  *(Inferential.)* the mundane/expected — what does not exceed the frame; no antonym term in M04. The lexical carries no dedicated antonym term within M04; the contrast is read from co-occurrence/usage.
- **T1.3.2** — *what it excludes at its edge*  
  At its edge it excludes its *illicit* form — the 4 sinful/forbidden occurrences mark joy/delight wrongly placed (e.g. **Psa 131:1** (*pa.la* 'marvelous')); the right characteristic resists this.
- **T1.3.3** — *where it ends — what it is not*  
  It is not joy (A): wonder is a cognitive affect of being exceeded, not gladness.

### T1.4 · Modes of Operation

- **T1.4.1** — *mode(s) incl. grammatical form*  
  It operates as action: 78 · status: 18 · quality: 1 across Hebrew, Greek, Aramaic terms — i.e. as action verbs, status nouns, and/or quality adjectives in the proportions shown.
- **T1.4.2** — *mode varies by context/level*  
  Yes — its realisation varies: action vs status vs quality (action: 78 · status: 18 · quality: 1), and its seat varies (soul: 3 · heart: 2) by context.
- **T1.4.3** — *communicative/speech mode*  
  Yes — a communicative mode is present: *commanded* in 2 occ and *addressed to another* in 5 occ (e.g. **Num 15:3** (*pa.la* 'fulfill')). It also co-occurs with Speech (M42)/Praise (M22) — outward voicing.

### T7.3 · Human Science Frameworks

- **T7.3.1** — *primary framework*  
  Psychology of awe / elevation — Keltner & Haidt (2003); Stellar et al.; Haidt's elevation (warm, expansive response to moral excellence).
- **T7.3.2** — *where it illuminates*  
  Awe research illuminates the lexical's positive-direction wonder (response to God's 'wondrous works'); elevation matches wonder at unexpected goodness — both produce accommodation (the catch of breath, stillness) the lexical's cognition+affect profile reflects.
- **T7.3.3** — *where it diverges*  
  Science locates awe in vastness/novelty generally; the lexical's wonder is overwhelmingly God-directed (divine agent 25) and shades into 'too hard/surpassing' — the limit of understanding, a theological specificity science does not adjudicate.
- **T7.3.4** — *gaps surfaced*  
  Familiarity reduces wonder (science); the lexical's tie to *remembering* God's wonders (Remembrance co-occurrence) reads as a deliberate anti-familiarity practice worth verse investigation.

### T7.3 · Human Science Frameworks

- **T7.3.1** — *primary framework*  
  Positive psychology — gratitude research — Emmons & McCullough (2003); Emmons (*Thanks!*). Gratitude as cognitive (recognising a benefit) + affective (appreciation), inherently relational (requires a benefactor).
- **T7.3.2** — *where it illuminates*  
  Gratitude's relational constitution illuminates the lexical exactly: faculty *perception/memory* (recognition, not elation), God as addressee — thanksgiving directed to a specific benefactor (God).
- **T7.3.3** — *where it diverges*  
  McCullough's conditions (benefit good, intentional, non-obligatory) are interpersonal; the lexical's covenantal benefactor (God) amplifies gratitude beyond that register; commanded gratitude (valence *commanded* 6) also diverges from spontaneous-emotion models.
- **T7.3.4** — *gaps surfaced*  
  Entitlement and hedonic adaptation erode gratitude (science); whether the lexical encodes anti-adaptation recollection (gratitude tied to remembered benefit) is a verse question.

# M05 Characteristic A — Love: Tier-Catalogue Application (T0–T7)

- **Filename:** wa-m05-a-tier-answers-v1_0-20260620.md · **Version:** v1_0 · **Date:** 2026-06-20
- **Cluster:** M05 — "Love, Compassion and Kindness" · **Characteristic:** A — Love / Affectionate Attachment
- **What this is:** every active question in the tier catalogue (126 questions, T0–T7) applied to characteristic A, each answer evidenced and quoted from the verse corpus so prose can be developed directly from it without reference to source.
- **Evidence basis:** the 300 distinct love occurrences (18 terms: agapaō / agapē, ahav-family, fileō and the phil-compounds, the embodied tokens cheq / filēma / katafileō, and the beloved/lovely terms), quoted verbatim from wa-ve-lexical-extract-M05-20260620.
- **Companion:** wa-m05-a-love-v1_0-20260620.md (exhaustive evidence-and-analysis file).
- **Method note:** per-verse "in this verse" questions are answered across the corpus with quoted exemplars; **"Silent"** = the evidence does not speak (with a one-line reason).
- **Change note (v1_0):** first issue.

---

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design

**T0.1.1** — Yes, in every relation the catalogue names. **God as agent:** "if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another" (1Jn 4:11). **God as giver/source:** "love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God" (1Jn 4:7). **God as object:** "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart" (Mat 22:37). **God as possessor:** "the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all" (2Cor 13:14).

**T0.1.2** — Borne by God himself, pre-eminently and originally: "In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son" (1Jn 4:10). The pattern — God loves first, the creature loves in response and derivation — establishes love as the deepest point of the divine likeness: the human capacity to love is a created participation in what God himself is ("God is love", the corpus's theological centre).

**T0.2.1** — Yes. Love is the sum and aim of the commandments — "You shall love the Lord your God … and your neighbor as yourself" (Luk 10:27) — and the criterion of true life: "If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed" (1Cor 16:22). Without it all else is void: "but have not love, I am a noisy gong" (1Cor 13:1).

**T0.2.2** — Both. As created design it is the orientation toward God and neighbour the person is *made* for (Great Commandment); within the fallen condition it appears disordered (love of the world, 1Jn 2:15; love of self/gain, 2Ti 4:10; 2Pe 2:15). The same capacity serves design when rightly aimed and sin when misaimed.

**T0.2.3** — Yes — love is what abides into the fullness: "So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love" (1Cor 13:13), and "Love never ends" (1Cor 13:8). It orients the person toward an enduring future state.

**T0.3.1** — The likeness of **self-giving toward another** — God who "so loved us … and sent his Son" (1Jn 4:10) reproduced in the person who lays down life "for his friends" (Joh 15:13) and loves "one another" (1Jn 4:11).

**T0.3.2** — **Shared.** The same term names God's love and the person's: "he loved us" / "we also ought to love" (1Jn 4:11) — a genuine common reality, the creature's love derived from and modelled on God's.

**T0.3.3** — Presence indicates the renewed image and knowledge of God — "whoever loves has been born of God and knows God" (1Jn 4:7); absence indicates its lack — "Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love" (the corpus's logic; cf. 1Jn 4:7–8). Love is presented as the diagnostic of the image's condition.

**T0.4.1** — Yes — **christologically and covenantally, divine-instance-establishing-the-pattern**: God's love in sending the Son (1Jn 4:10) is the archetype the human love points back to and imitates ("as I have loved you"; cf. Joh 15:13). Direction: the divine instance grounds the human.

---

## T1 — Definition

**T1.1.1** — Love. The name signals the **core bonding affection** — the inward movement that attaches the self to another and commits it toward the good (or possession) of what is loved; the cluster's headline and moral pivot.

**T1.1.2** — Greek **agapaō / agapē** name volitional, covenantal love ("God so loved", 1Jn 4:11); **fileō / philia** affectionate love ("love one another with brotherly affection"); the phil-compounds name kinship love (filadelfia, filostorgos). Hebrew **ahav / ahavah** name love broadly, from covenant ("Abraham your friend", 2Ch 20:7) to disordered desire (1Ki 11:2). Definitionally the field runs from chosen commitment to felt affection to embodied attachment.

**T1.1.3** — The name carries a **directional** implication: love is always *of* something — it must have an object, and that object determines its worth (T1.3.2). Relationally it is other-binding; constitutionally it engages the whole inner person (T2.1).

**T1.2.1** — Both an **act and a disposition/condition**: the corpus tags love almost evenly as *action* (149 — "love one another", 1Jn 4:11) and *status/quality* (151 — "Love is patient and kind", 1Cor 13:4). It is a thing done and a thing borne.

**T1.2.2** — **Compound.** Love combines affection (the felt warmth, "brotherly affection", 2Pe 1:7), volition/commitment ("love your enemies"; the commanded register, 70 occurrences), valuation/moral-evaluation (the choosing of an object), and embodied expression (kiss, embrace). 1Cor 13:4–7 unfolds it into patience, kindness, humility, endurance — a compound of constituent qualities.

**T1.3.1** — Its structural opposite is **hatred**. The corpus pairs them directly: love co-occurs with sin.ah ("hating") as its contrary — "Amnon hated her with very great hatred … greater than the love" (2Sa 13:15); "whoever hates his life in this world will keep it" set against "whoever loves his life loses it" (Joh 12:25).

**T1.3.2** — At its edge love **excludes and resists rival attachment** — it cannot be given to God and the world at once: "Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him" (1Jn 2:15); "you cannot serve God and money" (the same logic, 2Ti 4:10 "in love with this present world").

**T1.3.3** — Love is **not mere feeling and not self-seeking**: "Love … does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant … it does not insist on its own way" (1Cor 13:4–5). It ends where affection turns acquisitive (the disordered loves of gain, glory, self) — there it has become its own counterfeit.

**T1.4.1** — It operates as **both verb and state**: as enacted love ("love one another earnestly from a pure heart", 1Pe 1:22) and as predicated quality ("Love is patient", 1Cor 13:4). Its manner is self-giving ("gave himself"; "lay down his life", Joh 15:13).

**T1.4.2** — Yes — mode varies by **object and direction**: toward God it is whole-person devotion (Mat 22:37); toward neighbour, active good-doing (Luk 10:27); toward the brethren, affectionate loyalty (1Pe 1:22); toward the wrong object, disordered craving (1Jn 2:15). It also varies by constitutional depth (heart/soul/mind together, Mat 22:37).

**T1.4.3** — Yes — love operates in a **commanded and addressed** mode pervasively: "A new commandment … that you love one another"; "You shall love" (Mat 22:37; Luk 10:27); and it is expressed in speech-acts of greeting and blessing ("Greet one another with a holy kiss", 1Cor 16:20).

**T1.5.1** — The immediate response love shows is **action toward the beloved** — sending, giving, laying down life ("he loved us and sent his Son", 1Jn 4:10; "lay down his life for his friends", Joh 15:13) — and bodily expression (embrace, kiss: "they embraced Paul and kissed him", Act 20:37).

**T1.5.2** — Consistent in direction (toward the object) but **varied in expression** — from sacrificial self-giving to affectionate greeting to, in the disordered cases, grasping after the object (best seats, gain, world).

**T1.6.1** — Over time love **establishes knowledge of God and belonging** — "whoever loves has been born of God and knows God" (1Jn 4:7) — and binds persons together: "knit together in love" (Col 2:2). It produces the enduring inner reality that "abides" (1Cor 13:13).

**T1.6.3** — The immediate response is an act of self-giving; the sustained effect is a **settled bond and knowledge** — love that "abides" and "never ends" (1Cor 13:8, 13), a formed orientation rather than a single act.

**T1.7.1** — Love takes hold rightly from **a pure heart, good conscience, and sincere faith** — "the aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith" (1Ti 1:5) — and as response to being first loved (1Jn 4:11; 4:19 "we love because he first loved us").

**T1.7.2** — It is blocked or distorted by **rival attachment and hypocrisy** — love of the world drives out love of the Father (1Jn 2:15); love must be "genuine"/unhypocritical (anupokritos co-occurs, Rom 12:9 "Let love be genuine"). **No adversarial spirit** is shown distorting it directly — that branch is **Silent**.

**T1.7.3** — The person in whom love is present but does not take hold is the one who professes it falsely or partially — whose love is "in word" only, or misdirected; the corpus shows misdirected love (toward world/self) rather than a developed portrait of failed uptake. **Largely Silent.**

---

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries

**T2.1.1** — **Heart** (24 — "love … from a pure heart", 1Pe 1:22; "rooted and grounded in love", Eph 3:17), **soul** (15 — "loved him as his own soul", 1Sa 18:3), **mind** (3), and uniquely **all three together**: "love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind" (Mat 22:37; Mar 12:30; Luk 10:27). Also **conscience** ("a good conscience", 1Ti 1:5) and **flesh** (Gal 5:13).

**T2.1.2** — The pattern shows love is the affection that **engages the whole inner being** — no other M05 characteristic is shown engaging heart, soul, and mind at once. Its seat is the deepest and broadest in the cluster; the body link (embrace, kiss) is **expressive**, not constitutive.

**T2.10.1** — Yes — love moves **onto the person from God as external source**: "love is from God" (1Jn 4:7); "we love because he first loved us" (the received→given movement, 1Jn 4:19); *origin* = received-from-outside (8 occurrences). It then moves outward to neighbour ("love one another", 1Jn 4:11).

**T2.7.1** — The body link runs **soul→body (expressive)**: the inner bond is expressed in embrace and kiss — "they embraced Paul and kissed him" (Act 20:37); "Greet one another with a holy kiss" (1Cor 16:20). Direction: the inner affection manifests bodily.

**T2.9.1** — **Bestowed by God** ("love is from God", 1Jn 4:7) and **received from another** in being first loved ("he first loved us", 1Jn 4:19); also generated within in the disordered cases (love of self/world). Multiple origins.

**T2.9.2** — **Multiple and context-dependent**: divine in its right form (1Jn 4:7), self-generated in its disordered form (love of the world); the origin shifts with the object.

---

## T3 — The Inner Faculties

**T3.1.1 · Perception (engage?)** — Yes, partially (11 occurrences tagged perception). Love is bound to perceiving and knowing the beloved: "if anyone loves God, he is known by God" (1Cor 8:3); "what no eye has seen … God has prepared for those who love him" (1Cor 2:9).

**T3.1.2 · Perception (effect)** — It directs attentive regard toward its object — love "knows" and is "known" (1Cor 8:3). 

**T3.1.3 · Perception (pattern)** — Perception is engaged but secondary to affect; love perceives in order to attach, indicating its perceptive dimension serves the bond rather than standing alone.

**T3.2.1 · Cognition (engage?)** — Yes (13 occurrences): love is commanded as a knowing devotion — "with all your mind" (Mat 22:37) — and is "genuine" by discernment (Rom 12:9). 

**T3.2.2 · Cognition (effect)** — It engages the mind in devotion and in discerning the true object; love and knowledge of God are joined ("whoever loves … knows God", 1Jn 4:7).

**T3.2.3 · Cognition (pattern)** — Cognition is a real but minor strand (13 of 300) — love is chiefly affective, with the mind enlisted, not the seat.

**T3.3.1 / T3.3.2 / T3.3.3 · Memory** — **Silent.** No occurrence engages love as a memorial faculty.

**T3.4.1 · Affect (engage?)** — Yes, dominantly — affect is the band's primary faculty (263 of 300). Love is the felt bond: warmth, longing, and attachment ("loved him as his own soul", 1Sa 18:3).

**T3.4.2 · Affect (effect)** — It produces the whole register of bonded feeling — devotion, tenderness ("a tender heart", 1Pe 3:8), and, disordered, craving (love of gain/glory).

**T3.4.3 · Affect (pattern)** — The overwhelming affect dominance marks love as **the cluster's defining affection** — the felt bond from which the other characteristics' affections can be seen as specifications.

**T3.5.1 / T3.5.2 / T3.5.3 · Creativity** — **Silent.** No engagement with imagination or origination.

**T3.6.1 · Volition (engage?)** — Yes — love is **commanded** (70 occurrences), which presupposes the will: "You shall love" (Mat 22:37); "love one another" (1Jn 4:11). Commanded love is chosen, not merely felt.

**T3.6.2 · Volition (effect)** — It directs the will toward the good of another, even sacrificially ("lay down his life for his friends", Joh 15:13) and toward the right object against rival pulls (1Jn 2:15).

**T3.6.3 · Volition (pattern)** — That love can be *commanded* shows it is not purely affective but **volitional at its core** — a directing of the self that the person is answerable for.

**T3.7.1 · Agency (engage?)** — Yes — love acts: it "is patient and kind", "bears all things … endures all things" (1Cor 13:4–7); it gives and lays down life (Joh 15:13).

**T3.7.2 · Agency (effect)** — It moves the person to self-giving action and service ("through love serve one another", Gal 5:13).

**T3.7.3 · Agency (pattern)** — The near-even action typing (149) shows love is as much **enacted** as felt — its agency is integral, not incidental.

**T3.8.1 · Moral evaluation (engage?)** — Yes (13 occurrences tagged moral_evaluation): love is the standard by which conduct is measured — "the fulfilling of the law" — and its objects are morally weighed (love of God good, love of world evil, 1Jn 2:15).

**T3.8.2 · Moral evaluation (effect)** — It is itself the criterion: without love, gifts are worthless (1Cor 13:1–3); with the wrong object, love is sin (1Jn 2:15).

**T3.8.3 · Moral evaluation (pattern)** — Uniquely in the cluster, love's moral value **flips on its object** (24 sinful + 1 forbidden) — the moral-evaluation faculty is decisively engaged because love must be rightly aimed to be good.

**T3.9.1 · Conscience (engage?)** — Yes, lightly (2 occurrences): love issues "from a pure heart and a good conscience" (1Ti 1:5).

**T3.9.2 · Conscience (effect)** — Genuine love is bound to a clear conscience; the two are named together as its source (1Ti 1:5).

**T3.9.3 · Conscience (pattern)** — Conscience is a minor but real seat — love rightly held is conscience-clean, indicating moral integrity as a condition of true love.

**T3.10.1 · Conscientiousness (engage?)** — Yes — love integrates feeling, will, and action: it is felt, commanded, and enacted in one ("love one another earnestly from a pure heart", 1Pe 1:22).

**T3.10.2 · Conscientiousness (effect)** — It yields steady other-directed conduct — patience, kindness, endurance (1Cor 13:4–7).

**T3.10.3 · Conscientiousness (pattern)** — Love reads as a **whole-person integration** — the most comprehensive of the cluster's characteristics, engaging affect, will, mind, and conscience together.

**T3.11.1 · Relational capacity (engage?)** — Yes, constitutively — love *is* the equipment for connection: "love one another" (1Jn 4:11); "knit together in love" (Col 2:2).

**T3.11.2 · Relational capacity (effect)** — It binds persons — to God (Mat 22:37), to one another (1Pe 1:22), to the brethren (filadelfia) — and is the bond's very substance.

**T3.11.3 · Relational capacity (pattern)** — The dominant other-experiencer pattern confirms love as **fundamentally relational**: its whole being is in the binding of persons.

---

## T4 — Relational Interfaces

**T4.1.1 · God→human** — Yes, foundationally: "he loved us and sent his Son" (1Jn 4:10); "God so loved us" (1Jn 4:11). God's love moves first toward the person.

**T4.1.2 · basis** — **Unconditional and prior** — "not that we have loved God but that he loved us" (1Jn 4:10); love precedes the creature's response ("he first loved us", 1Jn 4:19). Covenantal in form (Abraham "your friend", 2Ch 20:7).

**T4.1.3 · what it shows of God** — That God's disposition is **self-giving toward the person** to the point of sending the Son — love is God's defining orientation toward humanity.

**T4.2.1 · human→God** — Yes — the first commandment: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind" (Mat 22:37); "if anyone loves God, he is known by God" (1Cor 8:3).

**T4.2.2 · inner posture required** — **Whole-person devotion** — heart, soul, mind, strength together (Mar 12:30) — undivided from rival loves (1Jn 2:15).

**T4.2.3 · what it shows** — That the person's relationship with God is **total self-orientation toward him** — love is the right name for the creature's whole movement toward the Creator.

**T4.3.1 · human→human giving** — Yes, dominantly — "love one another" (1Jn 4:11); "lay down his life for his friends" (Joh 15:13); affectionate greeting (1Cor 16:20).

**T4.3.2 · giver's inner conditions** — A **pure heart, good conscience, sincere faith** (1Ti 1:5), and love that is "genuine"/unhypocritical (Rom 12:9; 1Pe 1:22 "sincere brotherly love").

**T4.3.3 · what the giver must have received/become** — They must first have **been loved by God** — "we love because he first loved us" (1Jn 4:19); "if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another" (1Jn 4:11). Received love is the precondition of given love.

**T4.4.1 · human→human receiving** — Yes — love is taken up in being loved and in the command's reception ("beloved by the Lord", 2Th 2:13; "brothers beloved", the addressed register).

**T4.4.2 · conditions accompanying / blocking uptake** — Uptake accompanies a pure heart and faith (1Ti 1:5); it is blocked by rival love (1Jn 2:15) and hypocrisy.

**T4.4.3 · state of one who meets it but does not take it up** — **Silent / partial:** the corpus shows the one who loves the world rather than the Father (1Jn 2:15) but does not develop a portrait of love offered and refused.

**T4.5.1 · within bonds vs across distance** — Both, and the command stretches it **across distance**: beyond the brethren to the neighbour (Luk 10:27) and, in the cluster's wider teaching, the enemy — love that does not depend on existing bond.

**T4.5.2 · within covenant only, or crossing** — It **crosses covenantal boundaries** — neighbour-love (Luk 10:27) reaches beyond the covenant community; love is owed where no reciprocity is expected.

**T4.5.3 · relational scope** — Widest in the cluster: God, neighbour, brethren, the stranger — explicitly inclusive. The only ones "excluded" are the wrong *objects* (world, money, self), not persons.

**T4.6.1 / T4.6.2 / T4.6.3 · Spiritual beings** — **Silent.** No occurrence shows love operating toward, attacked by, or mediated through angelic or adversarial beings (the disordered-love material concerns objects, not spirits).

---

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension

**T5.1.1 · Transformation** — Yes — love changes both **condition** ("born of God", 1Jn 4:7) and **orientation** (reorienting the self from world to God, 1Jn 2:15; from self to neighbour, Gal 5:13).

**T5.1.2 · reversible / irreversible** — **Silent** on reversibility directly, though "love never ends" (1Cor 13:8) implies permanence of the formed reality.

**T5.2.1 · Sequence of inner states** — Yes — the received→given sequence: **being first loved → loving in return → loving one another** ("we love because he first loved us", 1Jn 4:19; "if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another", 1Jn 4:11).

**T5.3.1 · Mechanism of change** — By **encounter with prior love** ("he first loved us", 1Jn 4:19) and by **command/cultivation** ("love one another earnestly", 1Pe 1:22) — both sudden grounding and sustained practice.

**T5.3.2 · mechanism differ across contexts** — Yes: divine love grounds by gift (1Jn 4:10); human love grows by command and practice (1Pe 1:22); disordered love forms by misdirected craving (1Jn 2:15).

**T5.4.1 · Suffering / affliction** — Yes — love operates as **costly self-giving under affliction**: "lay down his life for his friends" (Joh 15:13); Paul writes "out of much affliction and anguish of heart … to let you know the abundant love that I have for you" (2Cor 2:4).

**T5.4.2 · what suffering does to it** — Suffering **proves and deepens** love — it is shown bearing affliction for the beloved's sake (2Cor 2:4; the cross as love's measure, 1Jn 4:10).

**T5.5.1 · Formation and sanctification** — Yes, centrally — love is the goal of the sanctified life ("the aim of our charge is love", 1Ti 1:5), grows "earnestly" (1Pe 1:22), and is the crown of the virtue-chain (2Pe 1:7 "brotherly affection with love"). It shapes the person over the whole arc.

**T5.6.1 · Eschatological trajectory** — Yes — love is what **endures into the consummation**: "Love never ends" (1Cor 13:8); "now faith, hope, and love abide … but the greatest of these is love" (1Cor 13:13). Present love anticipates the abiding state.

---

## T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics

**T6.1.1 · Co-occurrence** — Love co-occurs most with **the heart and soul** (co-seated, kardia / psuchē / nephesh), **holiness** (hagios), **truth** (alētheia), **faith** (pistis), **hope** (elpis), **grace** (charis), **peace** (eirēnē), **patience** (makrothumia), **goodness** (agathos), and **genuineness/unhypocrisy** (anupokritos) — and with its antonym **hate** (sin.ah).

**T6.1.2 · what co-occurrence shows** — Love sits at the **centre of the inner-being landscape**, bound to the constitutional seats (heart/soul) and to the theological virtues (faith, hope), and defined against hatred. Its company is the widest of any cluster characteristic.

**T6.2.1 · Sequential relationship** — Yes — love **follows being loved** ("we love because he first loved us", 1Jn 4:19) and **heads the virtue-chain** ("supplement … brotherly affection with love", 2Pe 1:7). It is consistently the culminating term.

**T6.2.2 · what the sequence shows** — The relationship is **causal and developmental**: divine love causes human love; love completes the chain of virtues ("the greatest of these", 1Cor 13:13).

**T6.3.1 · does it produce another?** — Yes — love produces the cluster's other characteristics: "Love is patient and kind" (1Cor 13:4) names kindness (C) and patience as love's own operations; it issues in service (Gal 5:13).

**T6.3.2 · is it produced by another?** — Produced by **faith** ("faith working through love") and grounded in **God's prior love** (1Jn 4:19); the corpus presents love as both root and fruit.

**T6.3.3 · constituent of / constituted by another?** — Love is **constituted by** patience, kindness, humility, endurance (1Cor 13:4–7 unfolds it into these) and is itself a **constituent of** the Spirit's fruit (Gal 5:22, heading the list). It is the comprehensive characteristic of which others are facets.

**T6.4.1 · shared vocabulary** — Love shares vocabulary across the cluster: **fileō/philia** with friendship (F); **filadelfia/storgos** with kinship; and its operations (patient, **kind** — chrēstos) reach into kindness (C) and gentleness (E).

**T6.4.2 · shared root architecture** — The **phil-** root generates terms across love (fileō), friendship (filos, filia), kinship (filadelfia), and benevolence (filanthrōpia) — a single root spanning several characteristics.

**T6.4.3 · what the sharing shows** — The phil-root sharing shows love is the **generative centre** of the affectional field — friendship, kinship, and benevolence are species of love's bonding.

**T6.5.1 · nearest neighbour and distinction** — The nearest neighbour is **friendship (F)** (the phil-bond). The distinction: love is the **affection itself**, given to any object (God, neighbour, even wrongly the world); friendship is the **standing peer-bond** within which mutual love lives. Love is the movement; friendship is the relationship.

**T6.5.2 · precise boundary at overlap** — Where they overlap (Joh 15:13, love laid down "for his friends"), the boundary is: friendship names *who* (the bonded peers); love names *what is given* (the self-giving). 

**T6.5.3 · distinction of degree, kind, direction, or level?** — One of **kind**: love is an affection/act; friendship is a relational status. Against kindness (C) the distinction is **direction-of-aim** (love fastens on an object; kindness is borne loyalty).

---

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation

**T7.1.1 · primary terms and root meanings** — Greek **agapaō/agapē** (volitional, esteeming love), **fileō/philia** (affectionate love, phil-root), the phil-compounds (kinship); Hebrew **ahav/ahavah** (love, broad). Roots converge on **attachment/bonding** — chosen and felt.

**T7.1.2 · grammatical range** — Verb (agapaō, fileō, ahav), noun (agapē, philia, ahavah), adjective/participle (beloved — agapētos; lovely — prosfilēs). The full range (act, state, quality) shows love operates **as deed, condition, and attribute** alike.

**T7.1.3 · semantic range** — From covenant devotion (Mat 22:37) through sacrificial self-giving (Joh 15:13), affectionate kinship (2Pe 1:7), and embodied tenderness (embrace, kiss) to disordered craving (1Jn 2:15). One of the widest semantic ranges in the programme.

**T7.1.4 · terms distinguishing aspects** — Yes — **agapē** (volitional/given) is partly distinguished from **philia** (affectionate/felt), and the **beloved** terms (agapētos, yedidut) name the *received/object* aspect against the active verbs. The disposition-vs-act distinction is carried by the noun/verb pair.

**T7.1.5 · term for the opposite/absence** — Not within band A, but the opposite **hatred** (sin.ah / miseō) is its lexical contrary and co-occurs (2Sa 13:15; Joh 12:25). 

**T7.1.6 · person-type term** — Yes — **the beloved** (agapētoi — "Beloved, let us love one another", 1Jn 4:7) and **friend/lover** (ahev — "Abraham your friend", 2Ch 20:7) name the one characterised by love.

**T7.1.7 · supplication / seeking term** — **None** specific to love (one does not "seek love from" another by a dedicated term). **Silent.**

**T7.1.8 · OT↔NT continuity / development** — Hebrew **ahavah** (broad love, covenantal and affectional) develops into the NT's differentiated **agapē** (elevated to name God's self-giving love and the Christian command) alongside **philia**. Continuity of the bonding field; development toward agapē as the theologically loaded term.

**T7.1.9 · NT-coined / newly elevated term** — **agapē**: though attested earlier, the NT decisively **elevates** it to name God's love and the supreme command (1Cor 13; 1Jn 4) — a near-coinage in significance. The elevation shows love re-centred on God's self-giving as the pattern.

**T7.1.10 · full vocabulary arc** — The arc spans **covenant devotion → self-giving agapē → affectionate philia → kinship phil-compounds → embodied tokens (kiss, embrace) → disordered craving** — the complete range of bonding from the divine pattern to its human counterfeits.

**T7.2.1 · function of the primary term in its primary verse** — In **Mat 22:37** agapaō is the **governing imperative** ("You shall love the Lord your God …") on which "all the Law and the Prophets depend" — the term carries the whole weight of the commandment.

**T7.2.2 · literary forms** — **Law/gospel command** (Mat 22:37), **epistolary exposition** (1Cor 13; 1Jn 4), **narrative** (1Sa 18 Jonathan–David; the kiss texts), **wisdom** (Pro), **prophecy** (Hos). Responsible reading honours each — the hymn of 1Cor 13 as praise-definition, the command as covenant obligation.

**T7.2.3 · logical structure** — 1Jn 4:10–11: premise — God loved us first and sent his Son; conclusion — "we also ought to love one another." 1Cor 13:1–3: premise — without love all gifts are nothing; conclusion — love is supreme. Love is consistently the **ground and the goal** of the argument.

**T7.2.4 · contextual setting** — **Covenantal** (Great Commandment), **liturgical/communal** (holy kiss, brotherly love), **eschatological** (love abides, 1Cor 13:13). The settings show love as the substance of covenant life oriented to the end.

**T7.2.5 · primary anchor verse** — **1Jn 4:10** — "In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" — most fully expresses love's essential character: divine, prior, self-giving, defining. **1Cor 13** is the descriptive anchor; **Mat 22:37** the imperative anchor.

**T7.2.6 · what the anchor shows that no other shows** — 1Jn 4:10 alone **defines love by God's initiating self-gift** rather than by human emotion — locating love's origin and pattern in God's sending of the Son, against which all human love is response.

**T7.3.1 · most useful human-science framework** — **Developmental psychology / attachment theory** (Bowlby, Ainsworth; Sternberg's triangular theory; Hatfield's passionate vs companionate love).

**T7.3.2 · where the framework illuminates** — Attachment science illuminates love as a **bonding system** with an embodied basis (oxytocin released through touch, eye-contact) — matching the cluster's embodied vocabulary (embrace, kiss); and Hatfield's passionate/companionate distinction maps onto the **agapē/philia** registers. Secure attachment as ground for outward love illuminates why the corpus grounds neighbour-love in being first loved by God (1Jn 4:19).

**T7.3.3 · where evidence and framework diverge** — Science explains love by evolved bonding, reciprocity, and in-group preference; the corpus **commands love to enemies, strangers, and those from whom no reciprocal benefit is expected** (neighbour-love, Luk 10:27), and grounds it in God's self-giving (1Jn 4:10) — a scope and ground the science framework cannot generate.

**T7.3.4 · aspect surfaced by the framework** — The passionate/companionate and agapē/philia distinction invites a **closer verse test of whether the corpus's agapaō and fileō are functionally distinguished** — the band's data shows overlap rather than a clean split (both affect-tagged), **flagging further verse investigation** of the two registers.

---

## Coverage summary

- **Answered substantively:** T0 (all), T1 (all, T1.7.3 partial), T2 (all), T3 perception/cognition/affect/volition/agency/moral-evaluation/conscience/conscientiousness/relational (substantive), T4.1–T4.5 (substantive), T5 (all), T6 (all), T7 (all bar T7.1.7 silent).
- **Silent:** T1.7.2 (adversarial branch), T1.7.3 (partial), T3.3 memory, T3.5 creativity, T4.4.3 (partial), T4.6 spiritual beings, T5.1.2, T7.1.7.
- **Defining signal across the grid:** love's moral value **flips on its object** (T3.8.3) and it **engages the whole inner being** (T2.1.2) — the broadest and most morally pivotal characteristic in the cluster.

---

## §1 — Definition & scope of the characteristic

Love is the cluster's **core bonding affection** — the inward movement that attaches a person to another, commits the self toward the good (or the possession) of what is loved, and, when disordered, fastens on the wrong object. It is the headline characteristic of M05 and its moral pivot.

The band gathers: Greek **agapaō / agapē** (G0025 / G0026), the volitional, covenantal love-word; **fileō / filos / filia** (G5368 / G5384 / G5373), affectionate and friendship love; and the kinship compounds — **filadelfia / filadelfos** (brotherly), **filostorgos** (familial-tender), **filandros / filoteknos** (husband- / child-loving). Hebrew **ahav / ahavah / ahev / ahav** (H0157 / H0160 / H0158) "to love / love / lover", with the beloved-and-lovely terms **yedidut, naeh, prosfilēs**. Embodied tokens of affection complete it: **cheq** (H2436, bosom / embrace / arms), **filēma / katafileō** (G5370 / G2705, kiss). **isopsuchos** (like-minded) marks affectional unity.
