## §5 — Observation (grounded in the 300 distinct occurrences above)

- **Dominantly affective, with a will/value strand.** Faculty is *affect* in 263 occurrences, with smaller *moral_evaluation* (13), *cognition* (13) and *perception* (11) strands: to love is partly to value and choose, not only to feel.
- **As much done as borne.** Type is *action* (149) ≈ *status* (135), with little *quality* (16) — love is more enacted than the borne dispositions (contrast gentleness, almost all status).
- **Valence flips on the OBJECT — the highest disordered load in the cluster.** 138 *righteous* + 70 *commanded*, but **24 *sinful* + 1 *forbidden*** — more negative-valence occurrences than any other M05 band. Every disordered case is love aimed at the wrong object: the world (1Jn 2:15, the lone *forbidden*; 2Ti 4:10; Joh 3:19 "loved the darkness"), money / gain (2Pe 2:15), human glory (Joh 12:43), status and best seats (Luk 11:43; Mat 23:6), one's own life (Joh 12:25), falsehood (Rev 22:15), and the disordered attachments of 1Ki 11:2 and 2Sa 13:15. Same faculty, opposite moral worth — set entirely by what is loved.
- **Other-directed.** *Other* (95) + *other-addressed* (65) outweigh *self* (38).
- **It engages the whole inner being.** When a seat is named it is *heart* (24) + *soul* (15) + *mind* (3); the Great Commandment names them together — "love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind" (Mat 22:37; Mar 12:30; Luk 10:27). Jonathan "loved him as his own soul" (1Sa 18:3; 20:17). No other M05 affection is shown engaging heart, soul, and mind at once.
- **A divine act and a divine gift.** Divine involvement: God as *object* (22, the one to be loved), *agent* (20, God loves), *possessor* (7), *giver* (2). 1 John anchors the circuit — love is "from God" (1Jn 4:7; *origin* = received-from-outside), "if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another" (1Jn 4:11).
- **Embodied tokens.** *cheq* carries the loved one in the bosom / arms (Isa 40:11 the shepherd; Num 11:12), and the kiss expresses affection — including its perversion in Judas's betraying kiss (Luk 22:48; Mat 26:48–49, tagged *sinful*).

## §6 — Interpretation (labelled; inferential where marked)

- **Love is the cluster's defining affection and its moral hinge.** Alone among the bands it carries a large disordered register, *because* love is constitutively directional — it must have an object, and the object sets its worth. Love is therefore not a flat good but an orientation requiring right ordering. The connection to a doctrine of rightly-ordered love (*ordo amoris*) is **INFERENTIAL (GR-PROG-009)** and labelled as such.
- **The agapaō / fileō distinction is present but not lexically sharp.** Both tag *affect*; *agapaō* carries *moral_evaluation* somewhat more often. Whether the fields bear out the traditional volitional-vs-affectionate split is **additional discovery flagged** — the current data does not cleanly separate them.
- **Whole-inner-being engagement.** The Great-Commandment seat-cluster (heart + soul + mind + strength) is the strongest evidence in M05 that one of its affections engages the *entire* inner being rather than a single faculty — directly relevant to the programme's spirit–soul–body question.

## §7 — Reflection (cultural reach and tentative application — not prescriptive)

- **The most overloaded word in the field.** "Love" carries at least four registers here — covenant/volitional (*agapē*), affectionate (*philia*), embodied (kiss / embrace), and disordered (love of world / self) — collapsed into one English word. Reader-facing output should resist flattening them.
- **The disordered-love evidence speaks to contemporary application,** but the verses locate the danger in the *object*, not the faculty; I record this without moralising.
- **Love is bodily-expressed** (kiss, embrace, bosom), a datum for the body / expression dimension of the spirit–soul–body interface — flagged, not developed.

## §8 — Boundary & data-quality notes

- **Counts are distinct verse-term occurrences** (300), de-duplicated from 307 raw tagged occurrences per **Flag 7** (intra-verse duplicate tagging; minor in this band — *a.hev* +6, *agapē* +1). Raw vs distinct is stated in §2.
- **Thin terms retained on label:** *isopsuchos* (like-minded; *perception*, n=1) and the familial compounds *filostorgos / filandros / filoteknos* (n=1 each) are thin; kept in A on their gloss, flagged.
- **filadelfia** (brotherly love) borders F (fellowship) but is *affect*-tagged and kept in A.
- **Betraying-kiss occurrences** (*sinful*) are genuine A-band evidence — the affection-token weaponised — retained with their tags.
- **agapaō / fileō** senses overlap in the extract; no field cleanly separates them (see §6) — additional discovery flagged.

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design

**T0.1.1** — Yes, predominantly **God as agent**: "for his mercy is very great" (1Ch 21:13); "grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive" (1Ki 8:50); "the Father of mercies and God of all comfort" (2Cor 1:3). Also **possessor** ("his great mercy", 1Pe 1:3) and **giver** ("mercy … from God the Father", 1Ti 1:2).

**T0.1.2** — Borne by God far more than by the creature in this band (agent-dominant, 60 of the divine-tagged occurrences). The pattern marks compassion as **primarily a revealed divine attribute** that the human bears derivatively — "the Lord your God is gracious and merciful" (2Ch 30:9) is the ground from which human mercy is called.

**T0.2.1** — Yes — compassion moves God to forgive and restore ("forgive your people … and grant them compassion", 1Ki 8:50) and moves the person to spare, relieve, and give alms ("gave alms generously to the people", Act 10:2). Its effect is the preservation of the vulnerable.

**T0.2.2** — **Both**, with a bounded edge: as design, compassion mirrors God's own mercy toward the needy; within the fallen condition it is both rightly exercised (toward the weak) and rightly *withheld* (in judicial/herem contexts — "do not spare them", 1Sa 15:3). The bounding belongs to the order of justice within the fallen world.

**T0.2.3** — Yes — God's mercy is the ground of future hope: "his mercy … has caused us to be born again to a living hope" (1Pe 1:3); future restoration turns on finding compassion (2Ch 30:9). It orients toward a mercy yet to be fully received.

**T0.3.1** — The likeness of **mercy toward the weak and guilty** — God who pities the needy reproduced in the person of "compassionate hearts" (Col 3:12) and the "tender heart" (1Pe 3:8).

**T0.3.2** — **Shared**, but asymmetrically — compassion is chiefly God's (agent-dominant) and derivatively the person's; the human instance images the divine ("the Father of mercies … who comforts us … so that we may be able to comfort", 2Cor 1:3–4).

**T0.3.3** — Presence images God's mercy (Col 3:12 "God's chosen ones … compassionate hearts"); its hardening is the mark of the unmerciful — "because he had no pity" (2Sa 12:6); "the mercy of the wicked is cruel" (Pro 12:10). **Partly inferential** as an image-doctrine.

**T0.4.1** — Yes — **covenantal/christological, divine establishing the pattern**: God's mercy in the womb-yearning over Ephraim ("my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy on him", Jer 31:20) and "the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us" (Luk 1:78) point typologically to the mercy realised in Christ's visitation.

---

## T1 — Definition

**T1.1.1** — Compassion (with mercy, pity). The name signals the **visceral, other-regarding stirring** toward another's plight that moves to spare and relieve — felt, in the Hebrew, in the womb (*rachamim*).

**T1.1.2** — Hebrew **racham / rachamim** (compassion, from *rechem*, the womb), **chus** (to pity), **chamal** (to spare); Greek **eleos / eleeō** (mercy), **oiktirmos** (compassion), the **splanchna** family (moved in the bowels). Definitionally the terms locate compassion in the **viscera** and direct it toward the suffering or guilty.

**T1.1.3** — The name carries a **downward, other-directed** implication — mercy moves from the stronger toward the weaker, the able toward the needy, the wronged toward the guilty ("have mercy on me", Mat 15:22).

**T1.2.1** — Chiefly an **act** (action 143), with a substantial **disposition/quality** register (status 89, quality 23): mercy is shown and pity is enacted ("spared", "had mercy"), yet also borne as a "compassionate heart" (Col 3:12).

**T1.2.2** — **Compound**: it combines a felt stirring (affect — the yearning heart, 1Ki 3:26), a perceiving of the plight (perception — "the eye … pities"), and an enacted relief (sparing, almsgiving). The Hebrew womb-image fuses feeling and origin.

**T1.3.1** — Its structural opposite is **cruelty / mercilessness** — "the mercy of the wicked is cruel" (Pro 12:10); "because he had no pity" (2Sa 12:6) — the hardened refusal to be moved.

**T1.3.2** — It excludes **indifference and hardness** toward suffering; at its edge it resists the calculating self-interest that "was unwilling to take one of his own flock" (2Sa 12:4).

**T1.3.3** — Compassion is **not the suspension of justice**: it is rightly *bounded* — "your eye shall not pity" in lex talionis (Deu 19:21) and "do not spare" Amalek (1Sa 15:3); misplaced sparing is sin (Saul/Agag, 1Sa 15:9). It ends where pity would overthrow justice or covenant fidelity.

**T1.4.1** — It operates as a **felt-then-enacted movement**: the heart "yearns" (1Ki 3:26) and the hand spares/gives. Grammatically the band is action-heavy (verbs of having mercy, sparing) with a noun register (mercies, compassion).

**T1.4.2** — Yes — mode varies by **object**: toward the needy it is relief and almsgiving (Act 10:2); toward the guilty it is forgiveness ("grant them compassion", 1Ki 8:50); toward the condemned in judicial/herem settings it is *withheld* (1Sa 15:3). It varies by context more than any other band's characteristic.

**T1.4.3** — Yes — compassion is **invoked and commanded in speech**: the cry "Have mercy on me, O Lord" (Mat 15:22), the petition "grant them compassion" (1Ki 8:50), and the command to "put on … compassionate hearts" (Col 3:12).

**T1.5.1** — The immediate response is **relief, sparing, or forgiveness**: "out of pity for him, the master … released him and forgave him the debt" (Mat 18:27); the yearning heart that gives up the child to save it (1Ki 3:26).

**T1.5.2** — Consistent in direction (toward relieving the plight) but **varied in act** — sparing, forgiving, giving alms, yielding the contested good.

**T1.6.1** — Over time compassion **establishes a merciful disposition** — the "compassionate heart" and "tender heart" (Col 3:12; 1Pe 3:8) — and, received from God, a "living hope" (1Pe 1:3).

**T1.6.3** — The immediate response is a single act of relief; the sustained effect is a **formed tenderness** of heart (Col 3:12) and a settled hope grounded in God's mercy (1Pe 1:3).

**T1.7.1** — It takes hold under a **perceived, undeserved plight and felt connection** — the yearning over one's own (1Ki 3:26 "her heart yearned for her son"), the seeing of need (Psa 72:13 "he has pity on the weak and the needy").

**T1.7.2** — It is blocked by **hardness, self-interest, and (rightly) by the demands of justice**: "no pity" (2Sa 12:6); unwillingness to give from one's own (2Sa 12:4); and the judicial bar on pity (Deu 19:21). **No adversarial spirit** is shown distorting it — that branch is **Silent**.

**T1.7.3** — The person in whom compassion is present but unrealised is shown in **misplaced sparing** — Saul spares Agag and the best of the flock against the command (1Sa 15:9, 15:15): compassion present but disordered into disobedience.

---

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries

**T2.1.1** — **Inward-parts / bowels** (the seat of the Hebrew *rachamim* and Greek *splanchna*): "my heart yearns for him; I will surely have mercy" (Jer 31:20); "the tender mercy [splanchna] of our God" (Luk 1:78); "her heart yearned for her son" (1Ki 3:26). **Soul** (9 — Psa 72:13), **heart** (1), and **conscience** (1). The eye is engaged as the organ of pity ("your eye shall not pity", Deu 19:21).

**T2.1.2** — Compassion is the **most somatically-seated affection in the cluster** — felt in the womb/bowels before it is deliberated. The pattern (visceral seat + perceiving eye + enacted relief) shows a movement from body to act, indicating a pre-cognitive, embodied origin.

**T2.10.1** — Yes — it moves **from God onto the person** (mercy "from God the Father", 1Ti 1:2; received-from-outside, 3 occurrences) and **from within the viscera outward** to the act of relief (the yearning heart → giving up the child, 1Ki 3:26).

**T2.7.1** — The body link runs **body→soul and soul→act (emphatic)**: the womb/bowels are the *seat* from which mercy arises (Jer 31:20), making the link emphatic and originating, not merely expressive.

**T2.9.1** — **Bestowed by God** ("his great mercy", 1Pe 1:3) and **generated within** in the visceral stirring (1Ki 3:26). No generational or adversarial origin appears.

**T2.9.2** — **Multiple** — divine source (God the Father of mercies, 2Cor 1:3) and the inward stirring (the yearning heart) — and context-dependent (relief vs withholding).

---

## T3 — The Inner Faculties

**T3.1.1 · Perception (engage?)** — Yes (30 occurrences tagged perception): compassion is bound to **seeing** — "your eye shall not pity" (Deu 19:21); pity follows the registering of the plight ("he has pity on the weak and the needy", Psa 72:13).

**T3.1.2 · Perception (effect)** — Seeing the sufferer moves the viscera; the eye is the gateway to mercy, and closing it ("your eye shall not pity") is how mercy is barred.

**T3.1.3 · Perception (pattern)** — The recurrent eye-idiom marks compassion as **perceptually triggered** — it begins in the sight of need, distinguishing it from the other affections.

**T3.2.1 / T3.2.2 / T3.2.3 · Cognition** — **Silent / minimal.** No occurrence is tagged to the cognitive faculty; compassion in this band is visceral and perceptual, not a knowing or reasoning — its non-engagement with cognition marks it as pre-deliberative.

**T3.3.1 · Memory (engage?)** — Yes, lightly: compassion is bound to *remembering* — God "remembers" his mercy (the zakhar co-occurrence, 7×), and almsgiving is "remembered before God" (Act 10:31). 

**T3.3.2 · Memory (effect)** — God's recollection of mercy moves him to relent; the person's mercy is held in divine memory.

**T3.3.3 · Memory (pattern)** — Memory engagement is minor but real — mercy is tied to covenant remembrance, indicating its rootedness in remembered relationship.

**T3.4.1 · Affect (engage?)** — Yes, dominantly (affect 255): compassion is the felt stirring — "her heart yearned" (1Ki 3:26); "my heart yearns for him" (Jer 31:20).

**T3.4.2 · Affect (effect)** — It produces the yearning, the being-moved ("out of pity … released him", Mat 18:27) that issues in relief.

**T3.4.3 · Affect (pattern)** — Affect dominance with a visceral seat marks compassion as **feeling localised in the body** — the most embodied of the cluster's affections.

**T3.5.1 / T3.5.2 / T3.5.3 · Creativity** — **Silent.** No engagement with imagination or origination.

**T3.6.1 · Volition (engage?)** — Yes — compassion is **commanded** ("put on … compassionate hearts", Col 3:12) and is exercised as a choice to spare or relieve (or, wrongly, to withhold against command, 1Sa 15:9).

**T3.6.2 · Volition (effect)** — It directs the will toward relief; its disorder is a will that spares what should not be spared (Saul, 1Sa 15:9) or withholds what should be given.

**T3.6.3 · Volition (pattern)** — The bounded valence (forbidden/sinful sparing) shows the will must govern compassion's exercise — mercy is right or wrong by whether the will keeps it within justice.

**T3.7.1 · Agency (engage?)** — Yes — compassion acts: it spares, releases, forgives, gives alms ("gave alms generously", Act 10:2; "released him and forgave him the debt", Mat 18:27).

**T3.7.2 · Agency (effect)** — It moves the powerful to relieve the powerless — the master forgiving the servant (Mat 18:27); the king pitying the needy (Psa 72:13).

**T3.7.3 · Agency (pattern)** — Action-heavy typing confirms compassion is **enacted mercy** — its agency (relief, sparing, almsgiving) is integral.

**T3.8.1 · Moral evaluation (engage?)** — Yes — compassion is morally weighed: right toward the needy, wrong when it spares the condemned ("the mercy of the wicked is cruel", Pro 12:10; misplaced sparing, 1Sa 15:9).

**T3.8.2 · Moral evaluation (effect)** — It is assessed against justice — mercy that obstructs justice is condemned (Deu 19:21; 1Sa 15), mercy toward the needy is righteousness.

**T3.8.3 · Moral evaluation (pattern)** — The forbidden/sinful register (7 + 7) is unique in marking compassion as **bounded by justice** — it is the one affection the corpus shows being rightly withheld.

**T3.9.1 · Conscience (engage?)** — Lightly (1 occurrence): the merciless act troubles the moral witness — "because he had no pity" pronounces guilt (2Sa 12:6, in Nathan's conviction of David).

**T3.9.2 · Conscience (effect)** — The absence of pity is convicted as sin; mercy clears, mercilessness condemns.

**T3.9.3 · Conscience (pattern)** — Conscience engagement is minimal; compassion touches moral evaluation more than the convicting conscience.

**T3.10.1 · Conscientiousness (engage?)** — Yes — compassion integrates perceiving the need, being moved, and acting (Psa 72:13; Mat 18:27) — awareness, affect, and deed together.

**T3.10.2 · Conscientiousness (effect)** — It yields consistent relief of the vulnerable; its failure yields hardness.

**T3.10.3 · Conscientiousness (pattern)** — Compassion reads as an **integrated response** moving from sight to feeling to action.

**T3.11.1 · Relational capacity (engage?)** — Yes — compassion is the equipment for connection with the suffering other (the yearning over one's own, 1Ki 3:26; mercy toward captives, 2Ch 30:9).

**T3.11.2 · Relational capacity (effect)** — It binds the merciful to the pitied — forgiving the debtor, relieving the needy — repairing or preserving relationship.

**T3.11.3 · Relational capacity (pattern)** — Strongly other-directed (other 105 + addressed 48 vs self 40), compassion is **fundamentally relational and asymmetric** — directed from the able toward the needy.

---

## T4 — Relational Interfaces

**T4.1.1 · God→human** — Yes, dominantly: "his mercy is very great" (1Ch 21:13); "grant them compassion" (1Ki 8:50); "the Father of mercies" (2Cor 1:3). God's compassion moves toward the person.

**T4.1.2 · basis** — **Covenantal and responsive** — "if you return to the Lord … find compassion" (2Ch 30:9); grounded in God's character, "gracious and merciful, slow to anger" (the channun/rachum formula). Extended to the guilty who return.

**T4.1.3 · what it shows of God** — That God is **disposed to relent and relieve** — his greatness expressed as mercy toward the distressed and forgiveness toward the penitent (1Ki 8:50).

**T4.2.1 · human→God** — Yes — the cry for mercy is the person's movement toward God: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David" (Mat 15:22); "let me fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercy is very great" (1Ch 21:13).

**T4.2.2 · inner posture required** — **Distress and dependence** — the appeal of the helpless casting themselves on God's mercy (1Ch 21:13; Mat 15:22).

**T4.2.3 · what it shows** — That the person relates to God **as the needy to the merciful** — the posture of the supplicant who has only God's compassion to appeal to.

**T4.3.1 · human→human giving** — Yes — mercy extended person to person: sparing, forgiving the debt (Mat 18:27), giving alms (Act 10:2), the king's pity on the needy (Psa 72:13).

**T4.3.2 · giver's inner conditions** — A **compassionate, tender heart** (Col 3:12; 1Pe 3:8) and freedom from the hardness that "had no pity" (2Sa 12:6).

**T4.3.3 · what the giver must have received/become** — They must have **received God's mercy** — "the Father of mercies … who comforts us … so that we may be able to comfort" (2Cor 1:3–4): received mercy is the spring of given mercy.

**T4.4.1 · human→human receiving** — Yes — the pitied receive relief (the forgiven debtor, Mat 18:27; the captives who "find compassion", 2Ch 30:9).

**T4.4.2 · conditions accompanying / blocking uptake** — Uptake accompanies the plight acknowledged; it is blocked where the merciful is hardened (2Sa 12:6) or where justice forbids (Deu 19:21).

**T4.4.3 · state of one who meets it but does not take it up** — **Silent / partial:** the forgiven-but-unmerciful servant (Mat 18, who received mercy yet showed none) is the nearest case — mercy received but not passed on.

**T4.5.1 · within bonds vs across distance** — Both: most natural within bonds (the yearning over one's own son, 1Ki 3:26) yet extended across distance to captives (2Ch 30:9) and the needy stranger (Psa 72:13).

**T4.5.2 · within covenant only, or crossing** — It **crosses covenantal boundaries** in relief of the needy (Psa 72:13) and is **bounded by covenant** in the herem/judicial cases (1Sa 15:3) — compassion both reaches beyond and is checked by covenant.

**T4.5.3 · relational scope** — Broad (the weak, needy, guilty, captive) but **uniquely bounded** — the condemned in judicial/herem contexts are explicitly excluded from pity (Deu 19:21; 1Sa 15:3).

**T4.6.1 / T4.6.2 / T4.6.3 · Spiritual beings** — **Silent.** No occurrence shows compassion operating toward, attacked by, or mediated through angelic or adversarial beings.

---

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension

**T5.1.1 · Transformation** — Yes — compassion changes the sufferer's **condition** (the debtor released, Mat 18:27; the captives restored, 2Ch 30:9) and, received from God, the person's standing ("born again to a living hope", 1Pe 1:3).

**T5.1.2 · reversible / irreversible** — **Silent** on reversibility, though the unmerciful servant's later judgment (Mat 18) implies received mercy can be forfeited.

**T5.2.1 · Sequence of inner states** — Yes — **plight perceived → heart moved/yearns → relief enacted**: "her heart yearned for her son" → she yields him to save him (1Ki 3:26); "out of pity … released him" (Mat 18:27).

**T5.3.1 · Mechanism of change** — By **encounter with mercy** (received relief, forgiveness) and by **the visceral movement** that perception of suffering triggers (1Ki 3:26).

**T5.3.2 · mechanism differ across contexts** — Yes: divine mercy works by sovereign relenting (1Ki 8:50); human mercy by the moved heart acting (Mat 18:27); its withholding by the demand of justice (1Sa 15:3).

**T5.4.1 · Suffering / affliction** — Yes, constitutively — compassion is the **response to suffering**: it arises at the sight of the afflicted (Psa 72:13) and meets distress with relief (1Ch 21:13 "I am in great distress … his mercy is very great").

**T5.4.2 · what suffering does to it** — Suffering is the **occasion that evokes** compassion — the plight of the weak draws it out; in the merciful, the experience of having been pitied deepens the capacity to pity (2Cor 1:3–4).

**T5.5.1 · Formation and sanctification** — Yes — compassion is "put on" as a garment of the chosen (Col 3:12) and listed among the marks of the sanctified ("a tender heart", 1Pe 3:8) — it forms the merciful character over time.

**T5.6.1 · Eschatological trajectory** — Yes — God's mercy grounds the future: "according to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again to a living hope" (1Pe 1:3); "the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high" (Luk 1:78). Present mercy anticipates final visitation.

---

## T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics

**T6.1.1 · Co-occurrence** — Compassion co-occurs most with **kindness/steadfast love** (chesed, 19×), **graciousness** (channun/chanan — the "gracious and merciful" formula, 21×), the within-band **pity/sparing** terms (chus, chamal), **remembrance** (zakhar), **the soul/life** (nephesh, co-seated), **peace** (eirēnē), and, by contrast, with **transgression/abomination** (pesha, toevah — the wrong that mercy meets).

**T6.1.2 · what co-occurrence shows** — Compassion stands in a **covenant-mercy complex** — fused with grace and steadfast love (the classic "gracious and merciful, abounding in steadfast love" triad) — and is characteristically directed at sin and need (transgression, the soul in distress).

**T6.2.1 · Sequential relationship** — Yes — compassion **follows the perceiving of need/transgression** and **precedes forgiveness/relief**: "forgive your people … and grant them compassion" (1Ki 8:50) — mercy as the hinge between sin seen and relief given.

**T6.2.2 · what the sequence shows** — The relationship is **causal**: perceived plight causes the yearning; the yearning causes the act of relief.

**T6.3.1 · does it produce another?** — Yes — compassion produces **comfort** (D): "the Father of mercies and God of all comfort" (2Cor 1:3) — mercy issuing in consolation; and **forgiveness** (1Ki 8:50).

**T6.3.2 · is it produced by another?** — It is bound up with **grace** and **steadfast love** as their near-equivalent (the channun/chesed pairing); it flows from God's covenant character.

**T6.3.3 · constituent of / constituted by another?** — Compassion is a **constituent of God's covenant goodness** (gracious, merciful, steadfast-loving) and, with kindness and humility, a constituent of the "compassionate heart" put on by the chosen (Col 3:12).

**T6.4.1 · shared vocabulary** — It shares the **chesed** field with kindness (C) at the lexical edge (the "gracious and merciful, abounding in steadfast love" formula joins them), and the **splanchna** (bowels) imagery overlaps with love's embodied register.

**T6.4.2 · shared root architecture** — The **racham** root (rachamim, rachum, racham) generates the band internally; *rechem* (womb) is its root-image, shared with no other characteristic — a distinct visceral architecture.

**T6.4.3 · what the sharing shows** — The chesed-overlap shows compassion and kindness as **adjacent faces of covenant mercy** — compassion the felt stirring, chesed the kept commitment.

**T6.5.1 · nearest neighbour and distinction** — The nearest neighbour is **kindness/chesed (C)**. The distinction: compassion is the **affective, often momentary stirring toward a plight** (felt in the viscera, action-led); chesed is the **borne, durable loyalty** (status/quality, possessor-dominant). Compassion responds; chesed keeps.

**T6.5.2 · precise boundary at overlap** — Where they overlap (the mercy formulae), the boundary is **duration and typing**: compassion is enacted relief at a moment of need; chesed is steadfast love that endures "forever".

**T6.5.3 · distinction of degree, kind, direction, or level?** — One of **kind and duration** (momentary affective relief vs durable borne loyalty); against comfort (D) the distinction is **stage** (compassion feels the plight; comfort comes alongside to console).

---

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation

**T7.1.1 · primary terms and root meanings** — Hebrew **racham/rachamim** (compassion, from *rechem* the womb), **chus** (pity), **chamal** (spare); Greek **eleos/eleeō** (mercy), **oiktirmos** (compassion), **splanchnizō** (be moved in the bowels). Roots converge on a **visceral movement** (womb, bowels) toward the needy.

**T7.1.2 · grammatical range** — Verbs (racham, chus, chamal, eleeō, splanchnizō), nouns (rachamim, eleos, oiktirmos), adjectives (rachum, eleēmōn, eusplanchnos — "good-gutted"). The range shows compassion as **act, attribute, and disposition**.

**T7.1.3 · semantic range** — From visceral yearning (Jer 31:20) through pity, sparing, and forgiveness (1Ki 8:50) to enacted almsgiving (Act 10:2) and bounded withholding (Deu 19:21). A range from felt stirring to material relief to its just limitation.

**T7.1.4 · terms distinguishing aspects** — Yes — the **act** terms (eleeō, splanchnizō — to have mercy/be moved) are distinguished from the **disposition** adjectives (rachum, eusplanchnos — merciful, tender-hearted), and **eleēmosunē** (alms) names the *enacted/given* form distinct from the felt stirring.

**T7.1.5 · term for the opposite/absence** — Yes — the antonym terms **aneleēmōn / anileōs** ("merciless") name the absence; "the mercy of the wicked is cruel" (Pro 12:10) names it in context.

**T7.1.6 · person-type term** — Yes — **rachum / eleēmōn** (merciful one): "Blessed are the merciful" (the Beatitude register); "the Lord your God is gracious and merciful" (2Ch 30:9).

**T7.1.7 · supplication / seeking term** — Yes — the **cry for mercy** is a recurrent speech form: "Have mercy on me, O Lord" (Mat 15:22) — *eleeō* in the imperative as the supplication for compassion.

**T7.1.8 · OT↔NT continuity / development** — The OT **racham/chesed** mercy (covenant, visceral, "gracious and merciful") continues into the NT **eleos/oiktirmos/splanchna**, with the womb/bowels imagery preserved (splanchna). Continuity of the visceral covenant-mercy field; development toward mercy realised in Christ's "tender mercy" (Luk 1:78).

**T7.1.9 · NT-coined term** — **None** clearly coined; the splanchna-verbs intensify existing imagery rather than coin a new concept. **Silent.**

**T7.1.10 · full vocabulary arc** — The arc spans **womb-yearning (rachamim) → pity/sparing (chus, chamal) → mercy/forgiveness (eleos) → tender-heartedness (eusplanchnos) → almsgiving (eleēmosunē) → its merciless opposite (aneleēmōn)** — the complete range of being-moved toward the needy and its failure.

**T7.2.1 · function of the primary term in its primary verse** — In **Luk 1:78** ("because of the tender mercy of our God") oiktirmos/splanchna is the **cause** of God's visitation — the term grounds the whole salvation-clause. In **2Cor 1:3** oiktirmos names God by his mercies.

**T7.2.2 · literary forms** — **Narrative** (1Ki 3; 1Sa 15; Mat 18 parable), **law** (Deu pity-prohibitions), **psalm** (Psa 72), **prophecy** (Jer 31), **epistle/canticle** (2Cor 1; Luk 1). Responsible reading honours the judicial law's bounding of pity distinctly from the psalm's praise of it.

**T7.2.3 · logical structure** — 2Cor 1:3–4: premise — God is the Father of mercies who comforts us; conclusion — therefore we can comfort others "with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted." 1Ki 8:50: petition — forgive and grant compassion — grounded in God's merciful character.

**T7.2.4 · contextual setting** — **Covenantal** (2Ch 30:9 return-and-find-compassion), **judicial** (Deu pity-prohibitions; 1Sa 15 herem), **liturgical/petitionary** (1Ch 21:13; Mat 15:22), and **eschatological** (Luk 1:78). The judicial setting shows compassion's unique bounding.

**T7.2.5 · primary anchor verse** — **Luk 1:78** — "because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high" — most fully expresses compassion's essential character: visceral (splanchna), divine, and salvific. **Jer 31:20** is the OT anchor (the womb-yearning).

**T7.2.6 · what the anchor shows that no other shows** — Luk 1:78 alone **joins the visceral seat (splanchna) to the dawn of salvation** — compassion as the very motive of God's redemptive visitation, the bowels-mercy made the engine of redemption.

**T7.3.1 · most useful human-science framework** — **Social neuroscience / clinical psychology** — empathy and compassion research (Batson's empathy-altruism; Singer's shared-pain neuroimaging; Neff's self-compassion).

**T7.3.2 · where the framework illuminates** — The shared-pain research (witnessing another's pain activates one's own pain circuits) is the **literal basis of compassion as co-suffering** — illuminating the splanchna/rachamim somatic vocabulary; and Batson's empathy-altruism (empathic concern reliably motivates other-directed action) illuminates compassion's action-heavy typing. The womb-etymology aligns with a "primal, pre-cognitive" movement of the viscera — matching the corpus's pre-deliberative (no cognition tag) profile.

**T7.3.3 · where evidence and framework diverge** — Science explains compassion by in-group similarity and is undercut by dehumanisation and out-group distance; the corpus extends mercy to the **guilty, the captive, and the enemy who returns** (2Ch 30:9; 1Ki 8:50) and grounds it in God's character — and, conversely, the corpus *bounds* pity by justice (Deu 19:21; 1Sa 15) in a way the empathy account does not address.

**T7.3.4 · aspect surfaced by the framework** — **Compassion fatigue** (empathic arousal overwhelming rather than motivating) surfaces a question the corpus's bounded-pity material may answer differently — whether the *withholding* of pity in judicial contexts is a moral boundary rather than a depletion; and whether the cluster includes resources for sustaining compassion (cross-link to comfort, D). **Flagged for further verse work.**

## §1 — Definition & scope of the characteristic

Compassion is the cluster's **visceral, other-regarding response to another's plight** — the inward stirring, often seated in the womb or bowels, that moves a person to spare, pity, show mercy, or give relief to the vulnerable or the one liable to judgment.

The band gathers: Hebrew **racham / rachamim / rachum / rachamani** (H7355 / H7356 / H7349 / H7362) "to have compassion / compassion / compassionate", cognate with *rechem*, the womb; **chus** (H2347, to pity); **chamal / chemlah / machmal** (H2550 / H2551 / H4263, to spare / sparing); the Aramaic **rachamin** (H7359). Greek **eleeō / eleos / eleēmōn / eleēmosunē** (G1653 / G1656 / G1655 / G1654) "to have mercy / mercy / merciful / alms"; **oiktirmos / oiktirmōn / oikteirō** (G3628 / G3629 / G3627, compassion); the *splanchna* family — **splanchnizō / eusplanchnos / polusplanchnos** (G4697 / G2155 / G4184), moved in the bowels; **sumpatheō / sumpathēs** (G4834 / G4835, sympathy); **eleeinos** (G1652, pitiable).

---

## §5 — Observation (grounded in the 257 distinct occurrences above)

- **Affective, with a strand of seeing.** Faculty is *affect* in 255 occurrences plus a marked *perception* strand (30): compassion is tied to sight — the recurring idiom "your eye shall (not) pity" makes the eye the organ through which the plight is registered.
- **Enacted.** Type is *action*-heavy (143 vs *status* 89, *quality* 23): mercy is *shown*, the needy *spared*, alms *given*.
- **Mostly positive, but uniquely BOUNDED.** Valence is *righteous* (145) / *neutral* (62) / *commanded* (14), yet carries a distinctive **forbidden (7) + sinful (7)** register found in almost no other band: pity is *forbidden* in specific judicial and holy-war contexts — "your eye shall not pity" in lex talionis (Deu 19:13, 19:21; 25:12) and apostasy / idolatry cases (Deu 7:16; 13:8), and "do not spare" Amalek (1Sa 15:3). Saul's misplaced sparing of Agag is the *sinful* counter-case (1Sa 15:9, 15:15). Compassion is thus right toward the needy yet wrong where it obstructs justice or covenant fidelity.
- **The most somatically-seated affection in the cluster.** Where a seat is named: *soul* (9), *inward-parts / bowels* (4 — Isa 63:15; Jer 31:20 "my heart yearns"; Luk 1:78 "the tender mercy [*splanchna*] of our God"), *heart* (1), *conscience* (1). Hebrew *rachamim* (womb) and Greek *splanchna* (bowels) locate compassion in the viscera.
- **Primarily a divine attribute.** Divine involvement is *agent*-dominant (60) — God has compassion far more often than humans in this band — with *possessor* (22) and *giver* (13): "his mercy is very great" (1Ch 21:13); "gracious and merciful, slow to anger" (Joe 2:13); "the tender mercy of our God" (Luk 1:78).
- **Other-directed.** *Other* (105) + *other-addressed* (48) outweigh *self* (40); object is characteristically a *person* (69), often the weak, needy, or guilty.

## §6 — Interpretation (labelled; inferential where marked)

- **Compassion is the affection of the stronger toward the weaker.** Its object is the vulnerable or the one liable to judgment, and its dominant divine-agency profile reads as a revealed attribute of God that humans are called to mirror — the mirroring logic is **INFERENTIAL (GR-PROG-009)** and labelled.
- **The forbidden-pity material is a genuine boundary on the characteristic, not an anomaly.** The corpus does not treat compassion as a flat universal: it is bounded by justice and covenant fidelity. This is recorded as data, not editorial judgment.
- **A strong body→inner-being datum.** The womb / bowels seat (*rachamim* / *splanchna*) is among the clearest evidence in M05 that an inner affection is felt in the body — material for the spirit–soul–body interface.

## §7 — Reflection (cultural reach and tentative application — not prescriptive)

- **Ethically charged material requiring careful framing.** The "eye shall not pity" and "do not spare Amalek" texts are liable to misreading and are sensitive across cultures and interest groups; any reader-facing treatment must hold them in their judicial / covenantal frame and must not generalise them. I flag this as a place needing careful framing — not a conclusion.
- **The somatic seat travels poorly between cultures.** Bowels / womb as the seat of mercy is vivid in Hebrew and Greek and opaque in modern English "compassion" — relevant for translation-aware audiences.
- **Mercy is enacted** (alms, sparing, relief), tying the inner affection to concrete action; application noted, not concluded.

## §8 — Boundary & data-quality notes

- **Counts are distinct verse-term occurrences** (257), de-duplicated from 262 raw per **Flag 7** (minor in this band — *eleeō* +2, *chamal* +2, *eleos* +1). Raw vs distinct is stated in §2.
- **eleēmosunē** ("alms / charity") is the enacted form of mercy — kept in B though it shades toward almsgiving as an act.
- **Forbidden / sinful occurrences are retained as in-band evidence** — they define the characteristic's bounds.
- **chamal** "spare" includes mundane / negative senses (Job 20:13 "loath to let it go"); retained with their tags.
- **Aramaic rachamin** (1 occ) is thin; retained.

# M05 Characteristic C — Kindness / Steadfast Love (chesed) / Goodness: Tier-Catalogue Application (T0–T7)

- **Filename:** wa-m05-c-tier-answers-v1_0-20260620.md · **Version:** v1_0 · **Date:** 2026-06-20
- **Cluster:** M05 — "Love, Compassion and Kindness" · **Characteristic:** C — Kindness / Steadfast Love / Goodness
- **What this is:** every active tier-catalogue question (126, T0–T7) applied to characteristic C, evidenced and quoted from the verse corpus, self-contained for prose development without reference to source.
- **Evidence basis:** the 323 distinct occurrences (chesed/chasad/chasid; the chrēstos and agathos families; filanthrōpia, filagathos), quoted verbatim from wa-ve-lexical-extract-M05-20260620. **Two corrections applied:** chesed H2617B/H2616B (extract gloss "shame") are CC-confirmed chesed-I, merged with H2617A/H2616A; intra-verse duplication de-duplicated (615 raw → 323 distinct; chesed = 169 distinct verses).
- **Companion:** wa-m05-c-kindness-v1_0-20260620.md.
- **Method note:** per-verse questions answered across the corpus with quoted exemplars; **"Silent"** = evidence does not speak (with reason).
- **Change note (v1_0):** first issue.

---

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design

**T0.1.1** — Yes, pre-eminently **God as possessor**: "Oh give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!" (1Ch 16:34); the great self-revelation "The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love" (Exo 34:6). Also **object** ("show me the steadfast love of the Lord", 1Sa 20:14) and **giver** ("God gave Daniel favor", Dan 1:9).

**T0.1.2** — Borne by God as a defining, enduring attribute — his steadfast love "endures forever" (1Ch 16:34) and is proclaimed as his name (Exo 34:6). Possessor-dominant: chesed is presented first as something that *is God's*, which the person then keeps derivatively — marking it the most God-anchored characteristic of the cluster.

**T0.2.1** — Yes — kindness keeps covenant and does good: "deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai" (1Ki 2:7); the agathos stream is "doing honest work … so that he may have something to share" (Eph 4:28). It leads the person to faithful, beneficent action.

**T0.2.2** — **Created design**, restored and commanded: it images God's own covenant character (Exo 34:6) and is "put on" by the renewed (Col 3:12), fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:22 kindness/goodness). Its failures (cruelty, withholding) belong to the fallen condition.

**T0.2.3** — Yes — chesed's "forever" (1Ch 16:34) orients toward an enduring future; the agathos stream toward "every good work" prepared for the person (the good-works trajectory). It moves toward a fullness of covenant faithfulness.

**T0.3.1** — The likeness of **faithful, loyal goodness** — God who keeps "covenant and steadfast love" (1Ki 8:23) reproduced in the person who deals loyally (1Ki 2:7) and does good (Eph 4:28).

**T0.3.2** — **Shared**, and most directly of the cluster — chesed is God's name (Exo 34:6) and the human's covenant duty ("your loyalty to your friend", 2Sa 16:17); the human keeps the same loyalty God keeps.

**T0.3.3** — Presence images God's faithfulness (the chasid, "your godly one", Deu 33:8); absence is faithlessness or cruelty — "a cruel man hurts himself" (Pro 11:17), "many a man proclaims his own steadfast love, but a faithful man who can find?" (Pro 20:6). **Partly inferential** as image-doctrine.

**T0.4.1** — Yes — **covenantal, divine establishing the pattern**: Exo 34:6's self-revelation of "abounding in steadfast love" is the covenant name that all later chesed (divine and human) reflects; chesed "endures forever" (1Ch 16:34) points to the everlasting covenant fidelity realised in Christ.

---

## T1 — Definition

**T1.1.1** — Kindness / steadfast love. The name signals **settled, loyal benevolence** — the kept commitment that does good and keeps faith; love made durable.

**T1.1.2** — Hebrew **chesed** (covenant steadfast-love, loyalty, kindness), **chasad** (be kind), **chasid** (the godly/loyal one); Greek **chrēstos/chrēstotēs** (kind/kindness), the **agathos** family (good/goodness). Definitionally chesed binds *kindness* to *covenant loyalty* — a faithfulness that the Greek "kindness/goodness" terms render in the NT.

**T1.1.3** — The name carries a **covenantal-relational** implication: chesed is loyalty *within a bond* — "your loyalty to your friend" (2Sa 16:17), "keeping covenant and steadfast love" (1Ki 8:23). It is benevolence that is also fidelity.

**T1.2.1** — A **disposition / borne quality** — the most disposition-like in the cluster: *status* (180) + *quality* (127), only 13 *action*. Kindness is something one *is* and *keeps* ("are merciful kings", 1Ki 20:31), not chiefly a discrete act.

**T1.2.2** — **Compound**: chesed fuses kindness (benevolence) with loyalty/faithfulness (covenant fidelity) — hence its constant pairing with *emet/emunah* ("steadfast love and faithfulness") and *berit* (covenant). The agathos stream adds moral goodness and good works.

**T1.3.1** — Its structural opposite is **cruelty and faithlessness** — "a cruel man hurts himself" (Pro 11:17); the unfaithful who cannot keep chesed (Pro 20:6 "a faithful man who can find?").

**T1.3.2** — At its edge it excludes **withholding and pretence**: "He who withholds kindness from a friend forsakes the fear of the Almighty" (Job 6:14); self-display — "many a man proclaims his own steadfast love" (Pro 20:6) — and fickleness, "your love is like a morning cloud" (Hos 6:4).

**T1.3.3** — Kindness is **not mere feeling and not a moment's favour**: it is *kept* love. It ends where benevolence is unfaithful or boasted — the fickle and the self-proclaiming chesed are its counterfeits (Hos 6:4; Pro 20:6).

**T1.4.1** — It operates as a **borne, kept quality** expressed in faithful dealing — "deal loyally" (1Ki 2:7), "showed kindness" (1Sa 15:6). Grammatically the band is noun/adjective-heavy (a standing property), rarely a finite act-verb.

**T1.4.2** — Yes — mode varies by **direction**: God's chesed kept toward his people (1Ki 8:23); the person's chesed kept toward friend (2Sa 16:17), kin (1Ki 2:7), and the vulnerable (1Sa 15:6 kindness shown to the Kenites). The agathos stream operates as active good-doing (Eph 4:28).

**T1.4.3** — Yes — chesed is **invoked and commanded in speech**: the request "show me the steadfast love of the Lord" (1Sa 20:14), the charge "deal loyally" (1Ki 2:7), and its praise "his steadfast love endures forever" (1Ch 16:34).

**T1.5.1** — The immediate response kindness shows is **faithful beneficence** — dealing loyally, showing kindness, doing good ("I will deal kindly with Hanun … for his father dealt kindly with me", 1Ch 19:2).

**T1.5.2** — Consistent — kindness characteristically answers prior kindness in kept faithfulness (1Ch 19:2), and where it fails it does so by withholding (Job 6:14), not by a varied response.

**T1.6.1** — Over time chesed **establishes covenant trust and a faithful character** — the chasid ("godly one", Deu 33:8; "saints/faithful ones", 1Sa 2:9) — and, in the agathos stream, a "good conscience" (1Ti 1:5).

**T1.6.3** — The immediate response is an act of loyal kindness; the sustained effect is the **formed faithfulness** of the chasid — a standing identity of covenant loyalty (1Sa 2:9; 2Ch 6:41).

**T1.7.1** — It takes hold rightly under **the fear of the Lord and covenant fidelity** — withholding it "forsakes the fear of the Almighty" (Job 6:14); it is kept by those who "keep covenant" (1Ki 8:23).

**T1.7.2** — It is blocked by **cruelty, self-interest, boasting, and fickleness** (Pro 11:17; Pro 20:6; Hos 6:4) and by forsaking the fear of God (Job 6:14). **No adversarial spirit** is shown distorting it — **Silent**.

**T1.7.3** — The person in whom chesed is present but does not take hold is the **boaster of his own steadfast love** (Pro 20:6) and the one whose love is "like a morning cloud … that goes early away" (Hos 6:4) — chesed professed but not kept.

---

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries

**T2.1.1** — **Heart** (15 — "with all their heart", 1Ki 8:23 context of keeping covenant), **soul** (14), **conscience** (5 — the agathos "good conscience", 1Ti 1:5; Act 23:1), **flesh** (5 — the appeal of "a good conscience", 1Pe 3:21). Distinctively, chesed engages the **conscience** through the goodness stream more than any other M05 characteristic.

**T2.1.2** — The pattern shows chesed seated in the **heart/soul** (the covenant-keeping centre) and uniquely touching the **conscience** (good conscience). It is **less faculty-saturated** than the affections (affect tagged on only ~half), indicating a relational/moral *property* as much as a felt state.

**T2.10.1** — Yes — chesed moves **from God onto the person** (Dan 1:9 "God gave Daniel favor"; received-from-outside, 8 occurrences) and is kept *within* the heart toward others; God's chesed reaches the person and is mirrored outward.

**T2.7.1** — The body link is faint and **expressive/indicative** (the "good conscience" appealed to in baptism, 1Pe 3:21); chesed is not a somatic characteristic. Largely **Silent** on an emphatic body link.

**T2.9.1** — **Bestowed by God** (Dan 1:9; God's own chesed as source, Exo 34:6) and **kept by the person** as covenant duty (1Ki 2:7). Origin is divine gift mirrored in human fidelity.

**T2.9.2** — **Multiple** — God as the original possessor and giver (Exo 34:6; Dan 1:9), the person as keeper — and stable across contexts (chesed is, by definition, the *enduring* form).

---

## T3 — The Inner Faculties

**T3.1.1 / T3.1.2 / T3.1.3 · Perception** — **Silent.** No occurrence engages the perceptive faculty; chesed is a kept disposition, not a perceiving.

**T3.2.1 · Cognition (engage?)** — Lightly. Goodness engages knowing in the "good conscience" and discernment of good from evil ("Bad company ruins good morals", 1Cor 15:33; "doing honest work", Eph 4:28) — but chesed itself is not a knowing.

**T3.2.2 · Cognition (effect)** — Where engaged, it disposes the mind toward the good and faithful course; mostly minimal.

**T3.2.3 · Cognition (pattern)** — Cognition is marginal — chesed is borne and kept, not reasoned; its near-silence here marks it a property of fidelity rather than thought.

**T3.3.1 · Memory (engage?)** — Yes, lightly — chesed is bound to **remembrance**: God "remembers" his steadfast love and covenant (the zakhar co-occurrence, 10×; "remember … your steadfast love", Psa 25:6 register).

**T3.3.2 · Memory (effect)** — God's remembering of his chesed secures the covenant; the person's chesed is "good deeds … remembered" (the agathos register, 2Ch 32:32).

**T3.3.3 · Memory (pattern)** — Memory engagement is real but secondary — chesed is rooted in *remembered covenant*, consistent with its loyalty-character.

**T3.4.1 · Affect (engage?)** — Partially (affect 172 of 323): chesed has a warm, loving register ("love", "lovingkindness"), but it is **less affect-saturated** than love or compassion — much of it is borne covenant property without a felt-state tag.

**T3.4.2 · Affect (effect)** — Where affective, it is the warmth of loyal love (chesed as "lovingkindness"); but its defining note is fidelity more than feeling.

**T3.4.3 · Affect (pattern)** — The partial affect-tagging marks chesed as **a quality of will-and-relationship more than of feeling** — distinguishing it from the affect-saturated love and compassion.

**T3.5.1 / T3.5.2 / T3.5.3 · Creativity** — **Silent.** No engagement with imagination or origination.

**T3.6.1 · Volition (engage?)** — Yes — chesed is **kept by the will**: "deal loyally" (1Ki 2:7), "show kindness" (1Sa 15:6); its failure is the will that withholds (Job 6:14). Kindness/goodness is also commanded (Gal 5:22 fruit; Col 3:12 put on).

**T3.6.2 · Volition (effect)** — It directs the will to faithful benevolence and good works (Eph 4:28); its disorder is a will that boasts its own chesed or lets it lapse (Pro 20:6; Hos 6:4).

**T3.6.3 · Volition (pattern)** — Chesed's "kept" character makes it a **virtue of the faithful will** — loyalty sustained by choice over time, not a passing affect.

**T3.7.1 · Agency (engage?)** — Yes — kindness/goodness acts: dealing loyally (1Ki 2:7), doing good and sharing (Eph 4:28; Gal 6:6), "good deeds" (2Ch 32:32).

**T3.7.2 · Agency (effect)** — It moves the person to faithful beneficence — covenant kindness shown, good works done.

**T3.7.3 · Agency (pattern)** — Though status-dominant, where agency appears it is **faithful action flowing from the borne disposition** — the good person does good because they *are* good (the agathos logic).

**T3.8.1 · Moral evaluation (engage?)** — Yes, strongly — the agathos stream *is* moral evaluation: assessing and doing the *good* — "doing honest work" (Eph 4:28), "good morals" (1Cor 15:33), and chesed weighed against faithlessness (Pro 20:6).

**T3.8.2 · Moral evaluation (effect)** — It establishes the standard of the good and faithful; its failure (cruelty, boasting) is judged against it.

**T3.8.3 · Moral evaluation (pattern)** — Overwhelmingly righteous (172) with the few sinful cases being **deficient or counterfeit** kindness (withholding, boasting, fickleness) — chesed "sins" by *absence/pretence*, not by misdirection (unlike love).

**T3.9.1 · Conscience (engage?)** — Yes — distinctively, through the goodness stream: "the aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience" (1Ti 1:5); "having a good conscience" (1Pe 3:16); "I have lived my life before God in all good conscience" (Act 23:1).

**T3.9.2 · Conscience (effect)** — Goodness yields and rests on a clear conscience; rejecting it makes "shipwreck of their faith" (1Ti 1:19).

**T3.9.3 · Conscience (pattern)** — C is the **one M05 characteristic that substantially engages the conscience** (5 occurrences via "good conscience") — goodness and moral self-witness are joined.

**T3.10.1 · Conscientiousness (engage?)** — Yes — chesed integrates faithful awareness, will, and action: keeping covenant "with all their heart" (1Ki 8:23) and doing good works as a settled pattern (2Ch 32:32).

**T3.10.2 · Conscientiousness (effect)** — It yields a dependable, faithful character — the chasid whose loyalty can be relied upon (2Sa 16:17).

**T3.10.3 · Conscientiousness (pattern)** — Chesed is the cluster's clearest case of **character-level conscientiousness** — a stable, conscience-bearing fidelity expressed in consistent good.

**T3.11.1 · Relational capacity (engage?)** — Yes, constitutively — chesed *is* covenant-relational equipment: "your loyalty to your friend" (2Sa 16:17), kindness shown across relationships (1Ch 19:2; 1Sa 15:6).

**T3.11.2 · Relational capacity (effect)** — It binds persons in durable loyalty — the kept faithfulness that sustains covenant bonds (1Ki 8:23) and friendship (2Sa 16:17).

**T3.11.3 · Relational capacity (pattern)** — Strongly other-directed (other 97 + addressed 69 vs self 28), chesed is **relational fidelity** — its whole nature is keeping faith with another.

---

## T4 — Relational Interfaces

**T4.1.1 · God→human** — Yes, dominantly: God's steadfast love kept toward his people — "keeping covenant and steadfast love" (1Ki 8:23); "abounding in steadfast love" (Exo 34:6); "God gave Daniel favor" (Dan 1:9).

**T4.1.2 · basis** — **Covenantal** — chesed is kept "with your servants who walk before you with all their heart" (1Ki 8:23); grounded in God's character and oath, enduring "forever" (1Ch 16:34). Faithful, not merely responsive.

**T4.1.3 · what it shows of God** — That God is **faithful** — his goodness is not fickle but kept; "the Lord is good; for his steadfast love endures forever" (1Ch 16:34) shows a disposition of unwavering loyal love.

**T4.2.1 · human→God** — Yes — the chasid's devotion and the appeal for God's chesed: "let your priests … be clothed with salvation, and let your saints rejoice in your goodness" (2Ch 6:41); "show me the steadfast love of the Lord" (1Sa 20:14).

**T4.2.2 · inner posture required** — **Covenant fidelity and the fear of the Lord** — walking "before you with all their heart" (1Ki 8:23); withholding kindness "forsakes the fear of the Almighty" (Job 6:14).

**T4.2.3 · what it shows** — That the person relates to God as **covenant partner** — the chasid is the one loyal to the covenant, mirroring God's loyalty (Deu 33:8; 2Ch 6:41).

**T4.3.1 · human→human giving** — Yes — chesed extended person to person: "deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai" (1Ki 2:7); "you showed kindness to all the people of Israel" (1Sa 15:6); honest sharing (Eph 4:28).

**T4.3.2 · giver's inner conditions** — **Faithfulness and the fear of God** (Job 6:14), a "good conscience" (1Ti 1:5), and freedom from self-display (Pro 20:6).

**T4.3.3 · what the giver must have received/become** — They must have **received God's chesed** and become faithful — chesed answers prior chesed ("for his father dealt kindly with me", 1Ch 19:2), and the renewed "put on … kindness" (Col 3:12).

**T4.4.1 · human→human receiving** — Yes — kindness is received in kept loyalty ("with such loyalty they met me", 1Ki 2:7) and as favour ("God gave Daniel favor … in the sight of the chief", Dan 1:9).

**T4.4.2 · conditions accompanying / blocking uptake** — Uptake accompanies covenant trust; it is blocked by the cruelty or fickleness of the giver (Pro 11:17; Hos 6:4).

**T4.4.3 · state of one who meets it but does not take it up** — **Silent / partial** (cf. T1.7.3 — the unfaithful who do not keep chesed).

**T4.5.1 · within bonds vs across distance** — Primarily **within covenant bonds** (friend, kin, people — 2Sa 16:17; 1Ki 2:7) but extended across to others (the Kenites, 1Sa 15:6; Daniel among foreigners, Dan 1:9).

**T4.5.2 · within covenant only, or crossing** — Chesed is **covenant-defined** at its core (kept within the bond) yet **crosses** in acts of kindness to outsiders (1Sa 15:6) — covenant-shaped but not covenant-confined.

**T4.5.3 · relational scope** — Friends, kin, the people of God, and outsiders shown kindness; its scope is the network of covenant and the vulnerable within reach. No class is excluded by the characteristic itself.

**T4.6.1 / T4.6.2 / T4.6.3 · Spiritual beings** — **Silent.** No occurrence shows chesed operating toward, attacked by, or mediated through angelic or adversarial beings.

---

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension

**T5.1.1 · Transformation** — Yes — chesed forms the **faithful character** (the chasid) over time and, as goodness, transforms conduct ("Let the thief no longer steal, but rather … do honest work", Eph 4:28 — a reorientation of the person's whole pattern).

**T5.1.2 · reversible / irreversible** — **Silent** on reversibility, though the fickle chesed "like a morning cloud" (Hos 6:4) and the "shipwreck" of a rejected good conscience (1Ti 1:19) show kindness/goodness can lapse.

**T5.2.1 · Sequence of inner states** — Yes, in the reform pattern: from stealing to honest work to sharing (Eph 4:28) — a sequence from old conduct to good. Chesed otherwise is shown as a kept constant rather than a staged movement.

**T5.3.1 · Mechanism of change** — By **covenant fidelity sustained** and by **received goodness reproduced** (1Ch 19:2 — kindness answering prior kindness); the agathos stream by reform of conduct (Eph 4:28).

**T5.3.2 · mechanism differ across contexts** — Yes: God's chesed by sovereign faithfulness (Exo 34:6); the chasid's by covenant loyalty kept; the agathos reform by deliberate change of conduct (Eph 4:28).

**T5.4.1 · Suffering / affliction** — Yes — chesed is the refuge in distress: "I am in great distress. Let me fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercy/steadfast love is very great" (1Ch 21:13 register; cf. chesed's "endures forever" as ground of hope in affliction). 

**T5.4.2 · what suffering does to it** — Affliction **drives the person to rely on God's chesed** — the enduring steadfast love is the thing appealed to when all else fails (1Ch 16:34; the lament-to-praise pattern).

**T5.5.1 · Formation and sanctification** — Yes, centrally — kindness/goodness is **fruit of the Spirit** (Gal 5:22), "put on" by the chosen (Col 3:12), and the chasid is the sanctified, covenant-loyal person (1Sa 2:9; 2Ch 6:41). It forms the faithful character over the whole arc.

**T5.6.1 · Eschatological trajectory** — Yes — chesed "endures forever" (1Ch 16:34) and the chasid is preserved ("He will guard the feet of his faithful ones", 1Sa 2:9). Present faithfulness anticipates the everlasting covenant love.

---

## T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics

**T6.1.1 · Co-occurrence** — Chesed co-occurs above all with **faithfulness/truth** (emet/emunah — "steadfast love and faithfulness", 36×), **covenant** (berit, 12×), **covenant-keeping** (shamar, 17×), **remembrance** (zakhar, 10×), **compassion** (rachamim, 10×), **justice and righteousness** (mishpat/tsedaqah, 16×), and **love** (agapē/agapaō). The agathos stream co-occurs with truth and the good conscience.

**T6.1.2 · what co-occurrence shows** — Chesed sits at the **heart of the covenant-faithfulness complex** — fused with faithfulness, covenant, justice, and compassion (the "steadfast love and faithfulness / justice and righteousness" formulae). It is the relational glue of God's covenant character.

**T6.2.1 · Sequential relationship** — Yes — chesed **accompanies covenant-keeping** ("keeping covenant and steadfast love", 1Ki 8:23) and **grounds** compassion and forgiveness; it is consistently *paired* rather than sequenced — chesed-and-emet move together.

**T6.2.2 · what the sequence shows** — The relationship is **constitutive/correlational** — chesed and faithfulness are two faces of one covenant fidelity; chesed and compassion are companion mercies (Exo 34:6).

**T6.3.1 · does it produce another?** — Yes — chesed produces **trust and the chasid's loyalty**, and the agathos goodness produces **good works** and a clear conscience (1Ti 1:5; Eph 4:28).

**T6.3.2 · is it produced by another?** — It flows from **God's covenant character** and is reproduced by **received kindness** (1Ch 19:2); the chasid's chesed is produced by God's prior chesed.

**T6.3.3 · constituent of / constituted by another?** — Chesed is a **constituent of God's covenant goodness** (paired with faithfulness, compassion, justice in Exo 34:6) and, with compassion and humility, a constituent of the "compassionate heart … kindness" put on by the chosen (Col 3:12).

**T6.4.1 · shared vocabulary** — Chesed shares the **mercy field** with compassion (B — the "merciful and gracious … steadfast love" formula joins them) and the **agathos/chrēstos** "good/kind" terms reach into the moral-goodness field; "love" (agapē) co-occurs (chesed as covenant-love).

**T6.4.2 · shared root architecture** — The **chesed/chasad/chasid** root generates the band's Hebrew core (kindness, to-be-kind, the godly one); the **agath-** and **chrēst-** roots generate the Greek goodness/kindness stream — distinct roots converging on one characteristic.

**T6.4.3 · what the sharing shows** — The chesed↔compassion overlap shows them as **adjacent covenant mercies** (kept loyalty vs felt stirring); the agathos overlap shows kindness and moral goodness as one field in the NT.

**T6.5.1 · nearest neighbour and distinction** — The nearest neighbour is **compassion (B)**. The distinction: chesed is the **borne, durable, kept loyalty** (status/quality, possessor-dominant, "endures forever"); compassion is the **felt, often momentary visceral stirring** toward a plight (affect/action, agent-dominant). Chesed keeps; compassion is moved.

**T6.5.2 · precise boundary at overlap** — Where they overlap (Exo 34:6 "merciful and gracious … abounding in steadfast love"), the boundary is **duration and typing** — compassion the immediate mercy, chesed the steadfast love that endures.

**T6.5.3 · distinction of degree, kind, direction, or level?** — One of **kind and duration** (kept disposition vs felt movement); against love (A) the distinction is **fidelity vs affection** — chesed is love made loyal and durable.

---

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation

**T7.1.1 · primary terms and root meanings** — Hebrew **chesed** (covenant steadfast-love/loyalty/kindness), **chasid** (the loyal/godly one); Greek **chrēstos/chrēstotēs** (kind/kindness), **agathos** (good). Roots converge on **benevolence bound to fidelity**.

**T7.1.2 · grammatical range** — Noun (chesed, chrēstotēs, agathos as substantive "good"), verb (chasad, chrēsteuomai "be kind", agathopoieō "do good"), adjective (chasid "godly", chrēstos "kind", agathos "good"). The range shows kindness as **disposition, act, and quality**, weighted to the borne forms.

**T7.1.3 · semantic range** — From covenant loyalty (1Ki 8:23) through kindness/favour (Dan 1:9), goodness and good works (Eph 4:28), to the personified "godly one/saints" (Deu 33:8; 2Ch 6:41). A range from steadfast love to moral goodness to covenant-faithful identity.

**T7.1.4 · terms distinguishing aspects** — Yes — **chesed** (borne loyal disposition) is distinguished from the act of *doing* good (agathopoieō, agathoergeō), and **chasid** names the *person-type* distinct from the quality. The disposition/act/person distinction is fully lexicalised.

**T7.1.5 · term for the opposite/absence** — No single antonym in band, but the opposite is named — **cruelty** ("a cruel man", Pro 11:17) and faithlessness ("a faithful man who can find?", Pro 20:6); the agathos opposite is **ponēros** ("evil", co-occurring).

**T7.1.6 · person-type term** — Yes, strongly — **chasid** (the godly/loyal one, "your saints/faithful ones", 1Sa 2:9; 2Ch 6:41; Deu 33:8) is the dedicated person-type for the one who embodies chesed.

**T7.1.7 · supplication / seeking term** — Yes — the request **"show me the steadfast love"** (*asah chesed* — "show me the steadfast love of the Lord", 1Sa 20:14) is the seeking form for chesed from another.

**T7.1.8 · OT↔NT continuity / development** — OT **chesed** (covenant steadfast-love/loyalty) develops into NT **chrēstotēs / agathōsynē** (kindness/goodness as fruit of the Spirit, Gal 5:22) and **filanthrōpia** (benevolence). Continuity of loyal benevolence; the covenant-loyalty dimension is carried implicitly into the NT kindness terms.

**T7.1.9 · NT-coined term** — **None** clearly coined; the NT renders chesed through existing Greek goodness/kindness vocabulary rather than a coinage. **Silent.**

**T7.1.10 · full vocabulary arc** — The arc spans **covenant steadfast-love (chesed) → the godly/loyal one (chasid) → kindness (chrēstotēs) → goodness/good works (agathos) → benevolence (filanthrōpia)** — the complete range of loyal benevolence from God's covenant name to the faithful person to the kind deed.

**T7.2.1 · function of the primary term in its primary verse** — In **Exo 34:6** chesed is the **climactic predicate of God's self-revealed name** ("abounding in steadfast love") — the term carries the covenant character God proclaims of himself. In **1Ch 16:34** it is the ground of thanksgiving ("his steadfast love endures forever").

**T7.2.2 · literary forms** — **Theophany/self-revelation** (Exo 34:6), **narrative** (1Ki 2; 1Sa 15; Dan 1), **psalm/thanksgiving** (1Ch 16:34), **wisdom** (Pro 11; 20), **prophecy** (Hos 6), **epistle** (1Cor 13; Eph 4; the good-conscience texts). Responsible reading honours the theophany's weight and the proverb's general pattern distinctly.

**T7.2.3 · logical structure** — Job 6:14: premise — to withhold kindness from a friend; conclusion — "forsakes the fear of the Almighty" (kindness as the test of true piety). 1Ch 16:34: premise — the Lord is good; conclusion — give thanks, for his steadfast love endures forever. Chesed is consistently the **bond between God's goodness and the covenant response**.

**T7.2.4 · contextual setting** — **Covenantal** (Exo 34:6; 1Ki 8:23), **liturgical** (1Ch 16:34 thanksgiving; 2Ch 6:41), **wisdom-ethical** (Pro), and **communal** (the good-conscience texts). The covenantal setting is decisive — chesed is covenant fidelity.

**T7.2.5 · primary anchor verse** — **Exo 34:6** — "The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love" — most fully and directly expresses chesed's essential character as God's self-named covenant loyalty. **1Ch 16:34** is the doxological anchor ("endures forever").

**T7.2.6 · what the anchor shows that no other shows** — Exo 34:6 alone **places chesed within God's self-revealed name** — making steadfast love not merely something God does but part of who God declares himself to be, the covenant character all human chesed reflects.

**T7.3.1 · most useful human-science framework** — **Behavioural science / positive psychology** — prosocial-behaviour and kindness research (Batson; Curry's finding that acts of kindness raise the doer's wellbeing; agreeableness as the prosocial trait).

**T7.3.2 · where the framework illuminates** — Prosocial-behaviour research illuminates the band's data that kindness is a **stable disposition expressed in beneficent action** (the agathos good-works stream), and the kindness-wellbeing link illuminates "a man who is kind benefits himself" (Pro 11:17). Internalised prosocial *values/identity* match the chasid as a kindness-identity.

**T7.3.3 · where evidence and framework diverge** — The science treats kindness as prosocial behaviour shaped by norms, reciprocity, and mood; the corpus's **chesed carries covenant loyalty** — "a theologically structured relational category (loyal to a specific covenant with a specific God)" — which the prosocial account does not capture, and grounds kindness in God's covenant name (Exo 34:6) and the fear of the Lord (Job 6:14).

**T7.3.4 · aspect surfaced by the framework** — The reciprocity-vs-genuine-concern distinction surfaces a question for the corpus: chesed answering prior chesed (1Ch 19:2) looks reciprocal, yet God's chesed is unilateral and enduring — inviting a verse test of whether covenant chesed transcends the reciprocity the science describes. **Flagged for further verse work.**

## §1 — Definition & scope of the characteristic

Kindness is the cluster's disposition of **settled, loyal benevolence** — the standing goodness that keeps faith and acts for another's good. Its Old-Testament core is **chesed** (H2617), covenant "steadfast love" / loyal-kindness, predominantly God's; its New-Testament stream is **chrēstos / chrēstotēs / chrēsteuomai** (kindness) and the **agathos** family (goodness, good works, the good conscience); **chasid** (H2623) names the person who embodies it — the godly / loyal one, the "saint". The band also gathers **filanthrōpia** (benevolence) and **filagathos** (lover of good). Where love (A) is an affection that fastens on an object and compassion (B) a stirring toward the weak, kindness is the *kept commitment* — love made loyal and durable.

## §5 — Observation (grounded in the 323 distinct occurrences above)

- **A borne quality, not an act — the most disposition-like band.** Type is *status* (180) + *quality* (127) with only 13 *action*: kindness / goodness is a standing attribute one *has* and *keeps*. The contrast with comfort (almost all action) and the near-absence of action verbs is the band's clearest structural mark.
- **Less faculty-saturated than the affections.** *affect* is tagged on 172 of 323 — chesed-as-covenant-quality often carries no faculty tag, being a relational and moral *property* as much as a felt affection.
- **Overwhelmingly righteous; it "sins" by absence, not misdirection.** Valence is *righteous* (172) + *neutral* (43) + *commanded* (16), with only **7 *sinful***. Those are deficient or counterfeit kindness — withholding it (Job 6:14), the cruel man (Pro 11:17), self-proclaimed chesed (Pro 20:6; 19:22), fickle love "like a morning cloud" (Hos 6:4). Where love sins by wrong *object*, kindness fails by *absence* or *pretence*.
- **Strongly God-associated, as a kept property.** Object type is *abstract* (32) ≈ *God* (31) > *person* (19); divine involvement is **possessor-dominant (35)** — chesed *belongs* to God: "his steadfast love endures forever" (1Ch 16:34); "show me the steadfast love of the Lord" (1Sa 20:14). Where compassion was *agent*-dominant (God *does* it), chesed is *possessor*-dominant (it *is* God's, a covenant property He keeps) — with *object* (15), *agent* (9), *giver* (4) following.
- **Sense centred on covenant loyalty.** "steadfast love" dominates, with a goodness sub-stream (*good*, *good deeds*, *good conscience*), *kindness / kindly*, *loyalty / loyally*, and *godly* (the chasid).
- **Seat includes the conscience.** Where a seat is named: *heart* (15), *soul* (14), *conscience* (5), *flesh* (5) — the *conscience* via the "good conscience" (agathos: 1Ti 1:5; 1:19; 1Pe 3:16; Act 23:1). Goodness uniquely touches the conscience.

## §6 — Interpretation (labelled; inferential where marked)

- **C is the cluster's covenant-fidelity characteristic.** Not a momentary affection but a *kept commitment* — steadfast love that endures, loyalty that does not fail. Its possessor-dominant divine profile frames chesed first as a property of God's character; the call for humans to keep the same is **INFERENTIAL (GR-PROG-009)** and labelled.
- **A possible OT→NT continuity — INFERENTIAL.** The Hebrew chesed (covenant steadfast-love) and the Greek chrēstotēs / agathōsynē (kindness / goodness as fruit of the Spirit, Gal 5:22) occupy one field; whether they form a single developing line is flagged inferential pending the cross-testament read.
- **The characteristic personified.** The chasid is the one who *embodies* chesed — an inner-being characteristic becoming an identity ("the godly", "the saints"). Relevant to how the programme handles characteristic-to-identity.

## §7 — Reflection (cultural reach and tentative application — not prescriptive)

- **chesed is the single most translation-contested term in the cluster** (mercy / lovingkindness / loyalty / steadfast love). Reader-facing output must hold its covenant-loyalty core rather than reduce it to sentiment.
- **The good-conscience seat** ties goodness to moral self-awareness — material for the conscience dimension of the programme.
- **The "deficient kindness" cases** (withholding, boasting, fickleness) frame kindness as *faithfulness*, not display — application noted, not concluded.

## §8 — Boundary & data-quality notes

- **Flag 5 (gloss) applied:** H2617B / H2616B relabelled and **merged** into H2617A / H2616A per CC — all occurrences are chesed-I; the genuine chesed-II ("reproach", ~2 occ) is *not* present in this band.
- **Flag 7 (dedup + A/B collapse) applied:** 615 raw → 323 distinct (chesed = 169 distinct verses). The earlier per-Strong's de-duplication (491) still double-counted the 166 verses carrying *both* H2617A and H2617B for the same token; merging the split removes that. Counts here are distinct (raw stated in §2).
- **chasid** ("godly / saint") straddles characteristic-vs-identity — kept in C as the personification of chesed; flagged.
- **agathos** "good" is broad; included where it engages moral goodness / benevolence (good works, good conscience), which the faculty and valence tags support.
