# M05 Characteristic D — Comfort / Consolation / Encouragement: Tier-Catalogue Application (T0–T7)

- **Filename:** wa-m05-d-tier-answers-v1_0-20260620.md · **Version:** v1_0 · **Date:** 2026-06-20
- **Cluster:** M05 — "Love, Compassion and Kindness" · **Characteristic:** D — Comfort / Consolation / Encouragement
- **What this is:** every active tier-catalogue question (126, T0–T7) applied to characteristic D, evidenced and quoted from the verse corpus, self-contained for prose development without reference to source.
- **Evidence basis:** the 237 distinct occurrences (Hebrew nacham, tanchum, lavav; Greek parakaleō / paraklēsis, oikodomeō / oikodomē), quoted verbatim from wa-ve-lexical-extract-M05-20260620. Counts de-duplicated (252 raw → 237 distinct, Flag 7).
- **Companion:** wa-m05-d-comfort-v1_0-20260620.md.
- **Method note:** per-verse questions answered across the corpus with quoted exemplars; **"Silent"** = evidence does not speak (with reason).
- **Change note (v1_0):** first issue.

---

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design

**T0.1.1** — Yes, **God as agent**: "the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction" (2Cor 1:3–4). Also **giver** (the comfort God supplies, 2Cor 1:4) and **object** (the appeal made *to* the Lord, "Three times I pleaded with the Lord", 2Cor 12:8).

**T0.1.2** — Borne by God as "the God of all comfort" (2Cor 1:3) — comfort is named a divine title. God comforts and the person, having been comforted, comforts others (2Cor 1:4) — establishing comfort as a divine attribute the person relays rather than originates.

**T0.2.1** — Yes — comfort relieves the afflicted and builds up the community: "the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation" (1Cor 14:3); David sends "to console" the grieving (1Ch 19:2); brothers come "to comfort" the mourner (1Ch 7:22).

**T0.2.2** — **Both**, weighted to the fallen condition: comfort answers a world of affliction, grief, and weakness ("comforts us in all our affliction", 2Cor 1:4) — its very operation presupposes distress to be relieved; yet the upbuilding of persons toward maturity belongs to created/redeemed design (1Cor 14:3).

**T0.2.3** — Yes — comfort is bound to **hope and salvation**: it co-occurs with hope (elpis), perseverance (hupomonē), and salvation (sōtēria); the consolation of the Scriptures sustains the person toward future hope. It orients beyond present affliction.

**T0.3.1** — The likeness of **coming alongside the afflicted** — God who comforts "in all our affliction" reproduced in the person who consoles the grieving (1Ch 7:22) and builds up the weak (1Cor 14:3).

**T0.3.2** — **Shared**: God comforts, and the comforted "comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God" (2Cor 1:4) — the same comfort, passed on.

**T0.3.3** — Presence images God's consoling care; its corruption is the false comfort — building "the tombs of the prophets" (Luk 11:47) or emboldening a weak conscience to sin (1Cor 8:10). **Partly inferential** as image-doctrine.

**T0.4.1** — Yes — the comfort relayed from God to others (2Cor 1:4) is **typological of divine consolation**, the divine instance grounding the human ministry of comfort. Direction: divine establishing the pattern.

---

## T1 — Definition

**T1.1.1** — Comfort (consolation, encouragement). The name signals **coming alongside another in distress** — to console the grieving and to strengthen, urge, and build up.

**T1.1.2** — Hebrew **nacham** (to comfort, lit. "be sorry"), **tanchum** (consolation), **lavav** (encourage); Greek **parakaleō / paraklēsis** (the *para-kaleō* "call alongside" — comfort *and* exhort/appeal), **oikodomeō / oikodomē** (build up, edify). The Greek hinge term shows comfort and summons are one movement.

**T1.1.3** — The name carries a **come-alongside** directional implication — *para-* "beside": the comforter draws near the afflicted to relieve and strengthen (1Ch 7:22; 2Cor 1:4).

**T1.2.1** — Chiefly an **act** — the most enacted characteristic in the cluster: *action* (188) far above *status* (48). Comfort is something *done* to another — comforting, urging, building up — not borne as a state.

**T1.2.2** — **Compound**, spanning two registers under one hinge: **consolation** (soothing the grieving — nacham, tanchum) and **exhortation/edification** (urging, appealing, building up — parakaleō, oikodomeō). The compound holds soothing and summoning together.

**T1.3.1** — Its structural opposite is **affliction left unrelieved / discouragement** — the state comfort answers ("a comforter is far from me, one to revive my spirit", Lam 1:16 register; "Reproaches have broken my heart … I looked … for comforters, but I found none", Psa 69:20).

**T1.3.2** — At its edge it excludes **false or harmful upbuilding** — building that does not help ("'All things are lawful,' but not all things build up", 1Cor 10:23) and emboldening into sin ("will he not be encouraged … to eat?", 1Cor 8:10).

**T1.3.3** — Comfort is **not flattery and not mere relief of feeling**: it includes summons and correction (parakaleō "I appeal to you … that all of you agree", 1Cor 1:10; "I exhort the elders", 1Pe 5:1). It ends where soothing becomes the false comfort that builds tombs (Luk 11:47).

**T1.4.1** — It operates as an **enacted coming-alongside** — comforting, consoling, urging, building up — and as **speech**: "I appeal to you, brothers" (1Cor 1:10); "I urge you" (1Cor 16:15). Grammatically the band is verb-heavy (the action register).

**T1.4.2** — Yes — mode varies sharply by context: toward the grieving it is **consolation** (1Ch 7:22); toward the wayward or weak it is **exhortation/appeal** (1Cor 1:10; 1Pe 5:1); toward the church it is **edification** ("build up the church", 1Cor 14:12).

**T1.4.3** — Yes, pervasively — comfort is **fundamentally communicative**: it operates through appeal, exhortation, encouragement, and prophecy "for … upbuilding and encouragement and consolation" (1Cor 14:3). It is a speech-borne characteristic more than any other in the cluster.

**T1.5.1** — The immediate response comfort produces is **relief and renewed courage** — the afflicted strengthened, the discouraged "encouraged" (1Cor 14:31), the grieving consoled (1Ch 7:22).

**T1.5.2** — Varied by need — consolation for the griever, courage for the fearful, upbuilding for the weak — but consistent in its direction toward relief and strengthening.

**T1.6.1** — Over time comfort **builds up and establishes** — "build up the church" (1Cor 14:12), "comfort your hearts and establish them in every good work" (2Th 2:17) — producing settled strength and maturity.

**T1.6.3** — The immediate response is momentary relief/courage; the sustained effect is **establishment** — hearts comforted *and established* (2Th 2:17), the church built up over time (1Cor 14).

**T1.7.1** — It takes hold rightly in the context of **affliction met by love** — comfort "in all our affliction" (2Cor 1:4), upbuilding done "in love" (the 1Cor edification ethic) and "for upbuilding" rather than self-display (1Cor 14).

**T1.7.2** — It is blocked or distorted by **self-serving or harmful building** (1Cor 8:10; 1Cor 10:23) and by the absence of any comforter ("I found none", Psa 69:20). **No adversarial spirit** is shown distorting it — **Silent**.

**T1.7.3** — The person who is offered comfort but does not take it up is the **inconsolable** — "my soul refuses to be comforted" (Psa 77:2); "she refused to be comforted" (the Rachel/Jacob register) — comfort met but not received.

---

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries

**T2.1.1** — **Heart** (8 — "comfort your hearts and establish them", 2Th 2:17; "encourage your hearts", Col 4:8), **soul** (4 — "strengthening the souls of the disciples", Act 14:22), **mind** (1 — "I appeal to you … that you agree", 1Cor 1:10), **conscience** (1 — the weak conscience "encouraged"/built up, 1Cor 8:10), **inward-parts** (1 — "the hearts of the saints have been refreshed", Phm 7).

**T2.1.2** — Comfort engages the **heart and soul** (the seat of courage and grief) and, through its exhortation register, the **mind**. Its seat is the affective-volitional centre; the body link is faint (refreshed "hearts", Phm 7) — **functional/expressive**.

**T2.10.1** — Yes — comfort moves **from God onto the person and then through the person to others**: "comforts us … so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God" (2Cor 1:4) — a clear received→relayed movement (received-from-outside, 5 occurrences).

**T2.7.1** — The body link runs **inward (refreshment) and is expressive** — "the hearts of the saints have been refreshed" (Phm 7); largely interior, not an emphatic somatic seat.

**T2.9.1** — **Bestowed by God** ("the God of all comfort", 2Cor 1:3) and **mediated by persons** (David's messengers "to console", 1Ch 19:2; prophecy that consoles, 1Cor 14:3). Origin is God, channelled through the comforter.

**T2.9.2** — **Multiple and relayed** — God the source, the comforted person the channel (2Cor 1:4); the origin is consistently external-to-the-afflicted (received from God or another).

---

## T3 — The Inner Faculties

**T3.1.1 / T3.1.2 / T3.1.3 · Perception** — **Largely Silent** (2 minor occurrences). Comfort is not primarily a perceptive faculty; the comforter perceives the affliction, but the characteristic itself operates as relief and exhortation, not perception.

**T3.2.1 · Cognition (engage?)** — Yes (16 occurrences): the exhortation/appeal register engages the mind — "I appeal to you … that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions … in the same mind" (1Cor 1:10); prophecy that instructs "so that all may learn" (1Cor 14:31).

**T3.2.2 · Cognition (effect)** — It persuades and instructs — comfort-as-exhortation moves the mind toward agreement, learning, and resolve (1Cor 1:10; 1Cor 14:31).

**T3.2.3 · Cognition (pattern)** — Cognition is a real strand (the exhortation pole), distinguishing comfort's *parakaleō*-as-appeal from the purely affective consolation pole.

**T3.3.1 / T3.3.2 / T3.3.3 · Memory** — **Silent.** No occurrence engages comfort as a memorial faculty.

**T3.4.1 · Affect (engage?)** — Yes, dominantly (affect 230): comfort meets grief and fear with relief — "came to comfort him" the mourner (1Ch 7:22); "comfort your hearts" (2Th 2:17).

**T3.4.2 · Affect (effect)** — It relieves grief and fear and restores courage — the discouraged "encouraged" (1Cor 14:31), the grieving consoled, the refused comfort leaving the soul in distress (Psa 77:2).

**T3.4.3 · Affect (pattern)** — Affect dominance with a high *self*-experiencer share marks comfort as the **most received affection** — it is felt as relief *in* the afflicted, not only extended.

**T3.5.1 / T3.5.2 / T3.5.3 · Creativity** — **Silent.** No engagement with imagination or origination.

**T3.6.1 · Volition (engage?)** — Yes — comfort-as-exhortation appeals to the will: "I urge you, brothers" (1Cor 16:15); "I exhort the elders" (1Pe 5:1); "encouraging them to continue in the faith" (Act 14:22).

**T3.6.2 · Volition (effect)** — It moves the will to persevere, agree, and remain faithful (Act 14:22 "continue in the faith"; 1Cor 1:10 "agree").

**T3.6.3 · Volition (pattern)** — The commanded/exhortation register (35 commanded) shows comfort engages the will as much as the feeling — it summons as well as soothes.

**T3.7.1 · Agency (engage?)** — Yes, strongly — comfort acts: consoling, building up, exhorting are deeds done to another ("build up the church", 1Cor 14:12; "sent comforters", 1Ch 19:3).

**T3.7.2 · Agency (effect)** — It strengthens and establishes the other — "strengthening the souls of the disciples" (Act 14:22), "the other person is … built up" (1Cor 14:17).

**T3.7.3 · Agency (pattern)** — The action-dominant typing (188) confirms comfort is **the cluster's most agentive characteristic** — its very being is enacted toward another.

**T3.8.1 · Moral evaluation (engage?)** — Partially — comfort/edification is weighed by whether it truly *helps* and *builds up*: "not all things are helpful … not all things build up" (1Cor 10:23); the false comfort of building tombs is condemned (Luk 11:47).

**T3.8.2 · Moral evaluation (effect)** — Right comfort builds up; wrong "comfort" emboldens to sin (1Cor 8:10) or honours the killers of the prophets (Luk 11:47) — comfort is morally assessed by its effect.

**T3.8.3 · Moral evaluation (pattern)** — Mostly neutral-valenced (87) because the appeal/urge speech-acts are morally neutral in themselves; the few sinful cases mark the boundary where "building up" turns harmful.

**T3.9.1 · Conscience (engage?)** — Yes, in one decisive negative case: a weak conscience wrongly "encouraged"/built up to act against itself — "will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat?" (1Cor 8:10).

**T3.9.2 · Conscience (effect)** — Misapplied edification can **wound** the conscience (1Cor 8:10–12); rightly applied, comfort establishes the heart "in every good work" (2Th 2:17).

**T3.9.3 · Conscience (pattern)** — Conscience engagement is minor but pointed — comfort must not embolden against conscience, marking an ethical limit on edification.

**T3.10.1 · Conscientiousness (engage?)** — Yes — comfort integrates perceiving the need, willing the other's good, and acting (sending comforters, 1Ch 19:2; exhorting to continue, Act 14:22).

**T3.10.2 · Conscientiousness (effect)** — It yields steady ministry to the afflicted and the building up of the community over time (1Cor 14).

**T3.10.3 · Conscientiousness (pattern)** — Comfort reads as an **integrated, other-directed ministry** — awareness, will, and action converging on the strengthening of another.

**T3.11.1 · Relational capacity (engage?)** — Yes, constitutively — comfort *is* relational ministry: coming alongside (para-), consoling, building up "one another" (the mutual-edification ethic).

**T3.11.2 · Relational capacity (effect)** — It repairs and strengthens bonds — refreshing "the hearts of the saints" (Phm 7), knitting the church together (1Cor 14), restoring the grieving.

**T3.11.3 · Relational capacity (pattern)** — Strongly relational, with the highest *self*-experiencer share — comfort both **binds the comforter to the afflicted** and is **received within** the afflicted, a two-way ministry.

---

## T4 — Relational Interfaces

**T4.1.1 · God→human** — Yes — "the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction" (2Cor 1:3–4). God comforts the person directly.

**T4.1.2 · basis** — **Responsive to affliction and grounded in mercy** — comfort flows from "the Father of mercies" to those "in all our affliction" (2Cor 1:3–4). Given to the distressed.

**T4.1.3 · what it shows of God** — That God is **the consoler of the afflicted** — his mercy expressed as comfort that meets every affliction (2Cor 1:4).

**T4.2.1 · human→God** — Yes — the appeal/plea to God: "Three times I pleaded [parakaleō] with the Lord about this, that it should leave me" (2Cor 12:8) — the person's entreaty toward God.

**T4.2.2 · inner posture required** — **Dependence in affliction** — the plea of the afflicted casting the need on the Lord (2Cor 12:8).

**T4.2.3 · what it shows** — That the person turns to God **as the source of comfort and relief** — the one entreated in distress.

**T4.3.1 · human→human giving** — Yes, dominantly — comfort extended person to person: "sent messengers to console" (1Ch 19:2); "I appeal to you, brothers" (1Cor 1:10); "build up the church" (1Cor 14:12); "exhort the elders" (1Pe 5:1).

**T4.3.2 · giver's inner conditions** — Love and the desire for the other's upbuilding (the 1Cor 14 ethic of edification in love), and having oneself been comforted by God (2Cor 1:4).

**T4.3.3 · what the giver must have received/become** — They must have **received God's comfort** — "the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God" (2Cor 1:4): received comfort is the source of given comfort.

**T4.4.1 · human→human receiving** — Yes, prominently — comfort is **received**: the comforted, the built-up, the encouraged ("the other person is … built up", 1Cor 14:17; "the hearts of the saints have been refreshed", Phm 7). Comfort has the cluster's highest *self*-experiencer share.

**T4.4.2 · conditions accompanying / blocking uptake** — Uptake accompanies a heart open to consolation; it is blocked by a soul that "refuses to be comforted" (Psa 77:2) or grief too deep for present comfort (Psa 69:20).

**T4.4.3 · state of one who meets it but does not take it up** — The **inconsolable**: "my soul refuses to be comforted" (Psa 77:2) — comfort offered and refused, the soul remaining in distress.

**T4.5.1 · within bonds vs across distance** — Operates **within bonds** (brothers comforting the mourner, 1Ch 7:22; the church's mutual upbuilding) and across distance (messengers sent to console, 1Ch 19:2).

**T4.5.2 · within covenant only, or crossing** — Primarily **within the community** (the upbuilding of the church, 1Cor 14) but extended in acts of consolation to others (1Ch 19:2 to Hanun).

**T4.5.3 · relational scope** — The afflicted, the grieving, the weak, the church — comfort's scope is wherever there is distress to relieve; no class is excluded.

**T4.6.1 / T4.6.2 / T4.6.3 · Spiritual beings** — **Silent.** No occurrence shows comfort operating toward, attacked by, or mediated through angelic or adversarial beings (the co-occurring "enemy" is human).

---

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension

**T5.1.1 · Transformation** — Yes — comfort changes the afflicted's **condition** (the grieving consoled, the weak built up) and **orientation** (the discouraged "encouraged … to continue in the faith", Act 14:22) — both state and stance toward the affliction.

**T5.1.2 · reversible / irreversible** — **Silent** on reversibility; the refused comfort (Psa 77:2) shows the change is not automatic.

**T5.2.1 · Sequence of inner states** — Yes — **affliction → comfort received → comfort relayed**: "who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction" (2Cor 1:4) — a clear before/after with onward movement.

**T5.3.1 · Mechanism of change** — By **coming-alongside and speech** — consolation, exhortation, and edification delivered to the afflicted (1Cor 14:3); and by **received divine comfort** (2Cor 1:4).

**T5.3.2 · mechanism differ across contexts** — Yes: grief is met by consolation (1Ch 7:22); weakness by upbuilding (1Cor 14); waywardness by exhortation/appeal (1Cor 1:10); the church by mutual edification.

**T5.4.1 · Suffering / affliction** — Yes, constitutively — comfort is **the response to affliction**: "comforts us in all our affliction" (2Cor 1:4); it co-occurs with affliction/pressure (thlipsis) and perseverance (hupomonē). Affliction is its native context.

**T5.4.2 · what suffering does to it** — Suffering is the **occasion that calls comfort forth**, and the comfort received in suffering **equips the sufferer to comfort others** (2Cor 1:4) — suffering becomes a school of consolation.

**T5.5.1 · Formation and sanctification** — Yes — comfort builds up the person and the church toward maturity ("build up the church", 1Cor 14:12; "establish them in every good work", 2Th 2:17) — edification is formative over the whole arc.

**T5.6.1 · Eschatological trajectory** — Yes — comfort is bound to **hope and perseverance**: it co-occurs with hope (elpis), perseverance (hupomonē), and salvation (sōtēria); the consolation that sustains the afflicted points them toward the hope held out. Present comfort anticipates final relief.

---

## T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics

**T6.1.1 · Co-occurrence** — Comfort co-occurs most with **affliction/pressure** (thlipsis), **hope** (elpis), **perseverance** (hupomonē), **love** (agapē), **joy/rejoicing** (chairō), **the assembly** (ekklēsia — the object of edification), **prophecy** (profēteuō — the means of upbuilding), **salvation** (sōtēria), **peace, grace**, and **faithfulness** (pistos).

**T6.1.2 · what co-occurrence shows** — Comfort sits in an **affliction-and-hope complex** — it is the ministry that meets affliction (thlipsis) with consolation and turns the afflicted toward hope (elpis) and perseverance (hupomonē), within the upbuilding of the assembly.

**T6.2.1 · Sequential relationship** — Yes — comfort **follows affliction** and **precedes hope/perseverance**: the consolation of the Scriptures yields hope; comfort received yields comfort given (2Cor 1:4). It is the hinge between distress and renewed endurance.

**T6.2.2 · what the sequence shows** — The relationship is **causal/developmental**: affliction occasions comfort; comfort produces hope, perseverance, and the capacity to comfort others.

**T6.3.1 · does it produce another?** — Yes — comfort produces **hope and perseverance** (the elpis/hupomonē it sustains) and the **mutual love** of the built-up community.

**T6.3.2 · is it produced by another?** — Produced by **compassion/mercy** ("the Father of mercies and God of all comfort", 2Cor 1:3 — mercy issuing in comfort) and by **love** (the edifying love of 1Cor).

**T6.3.3 · constituent of / constituted by another?** — Comfort is the **enacted face of mercy** (B issuing in D, 2Cor 1:3) and a **constituent of the church's upbuilding** (edification as the corporate good).

**T6.4.1 · shared vocabulary** — The hinge **parakaleō** ("appeal/exhort/comfort") shares the speech-appeal register with the cluster's commands; **oikodomeō** ("build up") is shared with the corporate edification field; comfort co-occurs lexically with love (agapē).

**T6.4.2 · shared root architecture** — The **para-kaleō / paraklēsis** root generates the band's exhortation-consolation core; **oikodom-** generates the edification terms — two roots, one come-alongside characteristic.

**T6.4.3 · what the sharing shows** — The parakaleō sharing shows comfort, exhortation, and appeal are **one act in the NT** — to come alongside is at once to console and to summon.

**T6.5.1 · nearest neighbour and distinction** — The nearest neighbour is **compassion (B)**. The distinction: compassion is the **felt stirring** toward the afflicted (affect, viscerally seated); comfort is the **enacted coming-alongside** that relieves and strengthens (action-dominant, speech-borne). Compassion feels; comfort acts and speaks.

**T6.5.2 · precise boundary at overlap** — Where they overlap (2Cor 1:3 "Father of mercies and God of all comfort"), the boundary is **stage**: compassion is the mercy felt; comfort is the consolation delivered.

**T6.5.3 · distinction of degree, kind, direction, or level?** — One of **stage and mode** (felt mercy vs enacted/spoken relief); against love (A) the distinction is **function** — comfort is love deployed toward the afflicted.

---

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation

**T7.1.1 · primary terms and root meanings** — Hebrew **nacham** (comfort, "be sorry/relent"), **tanchum** (consolation), **lavav** (encourage); Greek **parakaleō / paraklēsis** (*para-kaleō*, "call alongside" — comfort/exhort/appeal), **oikodomeō / oikodomē** (build up). Roots converge on **coming alongside to relieve and strengthen**.

**T7.1.2 · grammatical range** — Verb (nacham, parakaleō, oikodomeō), noun (tanchum, paraklēsis, oikodomē). The strongly verbal weighting confirms comfort operates as **enacted ministry** more than borne quality.

**T7.1.3 · semantic range** — From consoling the grieving (1Ch 7:22) through encouraging the fearful (Act 14:22), appealing/urging (1Cor 1:10; 1Cor 16:15), to building up the church (1Cor 14:12) and pleading with God (2Cor 12:8). One of the widest action-ranges in the cluster — soothing to summoning.

**T7.1.4 · terms distinguishing aspects** — Yes — **nacham/tanchum** (console — the soothing pole) are distinguished from **parakaleō-as-exhort** (urge/appeal — the summoning pole) and **oikodomeō** (build up — the strengthening pole). The disposition-vs-act distinction is carried by the noun (paraklēsis) vs verb (parakaleō).

**T7.1.5 · term for the opposite/absence** — No single antonym, but the opposite is named contextually — the **comfortless** state ("a comforter is far from me", Lam 1:16; "comforters, but I found none", Psa 69:20).

**T7.1.6 · person-type term** — Yes — the **comforter** ("comforters", 1Ch 19:3; the *paraklētos* register beyond this band) names the one who comforts.

**T7.1.7 · supplication / seeking term** — Yes — **parakaleō** itself functions as the plea ("I pleaded with the Lord", 2Cor 12:8; "I appeal to you", 1Cor 1:10) — the same term seeks comfort and gives exhortation.

**T7.1.8 · OT↔NT continuity / development** — OT **nacham** (console, with the "be sorry/relent" sense) continues into NT **parakaleō**, which **develops** the field to fuse consolation with exhortation and edification (and stands behind the Spirit as *paraklētos*). Continuity of consolation; development into a fuller come-alongside ministry.

**T7.1.9 · NT-coined / developed term** — **parakaleō / paraklēsis** is decisively **developed** in the NT to carry comfort, exhortation, and appeal together (and grounds the title *Paraclete*) — a development whose breadth has no single OT equivalent.

**T7.1.10 · full vocabulary arc** — The arc spans **consoling the grieving (nacham) → encouraging (lavav) → appealing/exhorting (parakaleō) → building up (oikodomeō) → consolation as a divine title (the God of all comfort)** — the full range of coming alongside to relieve and strengthen.

**T7.2.1 · function of the primary term in its primary verse** — In **2Cor 1:3–4** paraklēsis/parakaleō is the **defining divine title and the engine of the relay** — God is "the God of all comfort, who comforts us … so that we may be able to comfort" — the term governs the whole received→given argument.

**T7.2.2 · literary forms** — **Narrative** (1Ch 7; 19), **psalm/lament** (Psa 69; 77), **prophecy** (Isaiah's consolation register), **epistle** (2Cor 1; 1Cor 14; 1Pe 5). Responsible reading honours the lament's unrelieved grief distinctly from the epistle's confident consolation.

**T7.2.3 · logical structure** — 2Cor 1:3–4: premise — God comforts us in all affliction; conclusion — therefore we can comfort others with the comfort we received. 1Cor 14: premise — prophecy builds up; conclusion — strive to excel in building up the church. Comfort is consistently the **means by which affliction is turned toward strength**.

**T7.2.4 · contextual setting** — **Communal and pastoral** (the upbuilding of the church, 1Cor 14; exhortation of elders, 1Pe 5), **consolatory** (grief and lament, 1Ch 7; Psa 77), and **eschatological-hopeful** (comfort tied to hope and salvation). The communal-pastoral setting is decisive.

**T7.2.5 · primary anchor verse** — **2Cor 1:3–4** — "the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God" — most fully expresses comfort's essential character: divine source, affliction-meeting, and relayed to others.

**T7.2.6 · what the anchor shows that no other shows** — 2Cor 1:3–4 alone displays the **received→given relay** in full — comfort is not retained but passed on, the comforted becoming comforters — the defining circuit of the characteristic.

**T7.3.1 · most useful human-science framework** — **Clinical psychology** — compassion-focused therapy and consolation psychology (Gilbert), and **positive psychology** of encouragement (self-efficacy through social support).

**T7.3.2 · where the framework illuminates** — Compassion-focused therapy's attention to the **capacity to receive as well as offer comfort** illuminates the band's high *self*-experiencer share (comfort is received — Psa 77:2; 1Cor 14:17); encouragement psychology illuminates the upbuilding/edification stream (strengthening through supportive speech, Act 14:22; 1Cor 14:3).

**T7.3.3 · where evidence and framework diverge** — Science frames comfort as interpersonal support and therapeutic technique; the corpus grounds comfort in **God as "the God of all comfort"** (2Cor 1:3) and makes it a relayed divine gift, and fuses it with **exhortation** (parakaleō) in a way that exceeds therapeutic consolation — comfort that also summons and builds toward maturity.

**T7.3.4 · aspect surfaced by the framework** — The receiving-comfort literature surfaces the **inconsolable** as a clinical reality ("my soul refuses to be comforted", Psa 77:2) and invites a verse test of what the corpus shows about comfort *refused* or *delayed* — a dimension the band touches but does not fully develop. **Flagged for further verse work.**

---

## Coverage summary

- **Answered substantively:** T0 (all), T1 (all), T2 (all), T3 cognition/affect/volition/agency/moral-evaluation/conscience/conscientiousness/relational (substantive), T4.1–T4.5 (substantive), T5 (all), T6 (all), T7 (all).
- **Silent:** T1.7.2 (adversarial branch), T3.1 perception (largely), T3.3 memory, T3.5 creativity, T4.6 spiritual beings, T5.1.2.
- **Defining signals across the grid:** comfort is the **most enacted** characteristic (action-dominant — T1.2.1), the **most received** (highest self-experiencer — T3.4.3, T4.4), and works through a **received→given relay** from God (T2.10, T5.2, T7.2.6), with parakaleō fusing **consolation and exhortation** (T1.2.2).

## §1 — Definition & scope of the characteristic

Comfort is the cluster's characteristic of **coming alongside another in distress** — to console the grieving and to strengthen, urge, and encourage them onward. Its hinge term **parakaleō / paraklēsis** (G3870 / G3874) spans both registers at once: *to comfort* and *to exhort / appeal*. The band gathers Hebrew **nacham** (H5162, to comfort, lit. "be sorry"), **tanchum** (H8575, consolation), **lavav** (H3823, to encourage); and Greek **parakaleō / paraklēsis** with **oikodomeō / oikodomē** (G3618 / G3619, to build up / edify — the metaphorical strengthening sense, kept in scope per CC verification). Where compassion (B) *feels* toward the afflicted, comfort *acts* toward them.

---

## §5 — Observation (grounded in the 237 distinct occurrences above)

- **The most enacted band in the cluster.** Type is *action* (188) far above *status* (48): comfort is *done* to another — comforted, urged, encouraged, built up — not borne as a state.
- **Two registers under one hinge term.** Sense splits between **consolation** (comfort the grieving — Gen 50:21 "comforted them"; Rut 2:13; nacham / tanchum / paraklēsis) and **exhortation / appeal** (urge, beg, exhort — parakaleō "I appeal to you", "they begged him"). *parakaleō* carries both — to encourage is at once to soothe and to summon.
- **The band most about RECEIVING ministry.** Experiencer shows an unusually high *self* share — *other* (86) but *self* (52) and *other-addressed* (33): comfort is frequently *received* ("my soul refuses to be comforted", Psa 77:2), unlike love, compassion, and kindness, which are predominantly *given*.
- **More neutral-valenced.** Valence is *neutral* (87) ≈ *righteous* (77) + *commanded* (35), *sinful* (3) — because "appeal / urge / beg" is often a neutral speech-act rather than a moral state.
- **God as the comforter, comfort passed on.** Divine involvement is *agent*-led (29): "the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction" (2Cor 1:3–4); *origin* = received-from-outside (5). Comfort received from God is relayed to others.
- **Faculty affect with a cognition strand.** *affect* (230) + *cognition* (16): the exhortation / appeal sense engages the mind (persuasion), not only feeling.
- **Edification seat.** "comfort your hearts" (2Th 2:17), "strengthening the souls of the disciples" (Act 14:22), "encourage your hearts" (Col 4:8; Eph 6:22) — *heart* (8), *soul* (4).

## §6 — Interpretation (labelled; inferential where marked)

- **D is the cluster's come-alongside characteristic** — its defining motion is *toward* another's distress to relieve and strengthen. The double sense of *parakaleō* (console + exhort) shows comfort and summons as one act: to encourage is both to soothe and to urge onward.
- **A received→given circuit.** Comfort received from God is passed to others (2Cor 1:4), paralleling love's "from God" circuit (1Jn 4). The link between the two circuits is **INFERENTIAL (GR-PROG-009)** and labelled.
- **oikodomeō sits here as metaphorical strengthening.** Its literal "build" sense (tombs, houses) is non-inner-being and is tagged *sinful / neutral* in the data; the band holds only the *edify / build up* sense, which CC's faculty evidence confirmed as genuinely inner-being.

## §7 — Reflection (cultural reach and tentative application — not prescriptive)

- **The double register fragments in translation.** English "encourage" blurs *console* and *urge*; reader-facing output should distinguish them.
- **The high self-experiencer share makes D the band most about receiving ministry** — the comforted become comforters — relevant to application but noted, not concluded.
- **"Building up" as a metaphor for inner strengthening** is culturally vivid; flagged for the edification / expression dimension.

## §8 — Boundary & data-quality notes

- **Flag 7 (dedup) applied:** 252 raw → 237 distinct (parakaleō +14). Counts distinct (raw in §2).
- **oikodomeō / oikodomē kept per CC** (faculty-bearing edify sense); literal-build occurrences (Luk 11:47–48 "build the tombs") are tagged *sinful / neutral* and retained with their tags — they mark the boundary between literal building and inner edification.
- **parakaleō's appeal / urge sense** produces many neutral speech-act occurrences; retained as in-band (the term's genuine range), flagged.

# M05 Characteristic E — Gentleness: Tier-Catalogue Application (T0–T7)

- **Filename:** wa-m05-e-tier-answers-v1_0-20260620.md · **Version:** v1_0 · **Date:** 2026-06-20
- **Cluster:** M05 — "Love, Compassion and Kindness" · **Characteristic:** E — Gentleness / Meekness / Forbearance
- **What this is:** every active question in the tier catalogue (WA-tier-catalogue-current-state-v2-20260619, 126 questions, T0–T7) applied to characteristic E. Each answer is evidenced and quoted from the verse corpus so that prose can be developed directly from it; no reference back to the source extract or the companion analysis file is needed.
- **Evidence basis:** the 30 distinct gentleness occurrences (8 terms: praus / prautēs / praotēs, epieikēs / epieikeia, anavah / anvah, anexikakos), quoted verbatim from wa-ve-lexical-extract-M05-20260620.
- **Companion:** wa-m05-e-gentleness-v1_0-20260620.md (the exhaustive evidence-and-analysis file); this document re-expresses all of its analytics through the question grid.
- **Method note — per-verse questions at characteristic level.** Catalogue questions phrased "in this verse" are answered across the corpus with quoted exemplar verses, since this file treats the characteristic as a whole. **"Silent"** means the verse evidence does not speak to the question (recorded per the catalogue's "record none" instruction), with a one-line reason.
- **Change note (v1_0):** first issue — template for the M05 tier-answer series.

---

## T0 — Divine Image and Created Design

**T0.1.1** — *Is the characteristic predicated of God / related to God, and in what relation?*
Yes, in two relations. **God as the one who bears it (possessor):** "You have given me the shield of your salvation … and your gentleness made me great" (2Sa 22:36; identically Psa 18:35). **Christ as the one whose gentleness is the named standard (object/pattern):** "I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ" (2Cor 10:1). Elsewhere gentleness is human and not predicated of God (e.g. Gal 5:23; Tit 3:2).

**T0.1.2** — *Is it ever borne by God himself or only by the creature, and what does the pattern indicate?*
It is borne by God: his "gentleness made me great" (Psa 18:35) attributes gentleness to God as the source of the petitioner's exaltation, and Christ's "meekness and gentleness" (2Cor 10:1) is the explicit pattern. It is overwhelmingly creaturely in the corpus (commanded, pursued, put on), but the divine instances establish it as a genuine point of the divine likeness, not an exclusively human trait.

**T0.2.1** — *Does the evidence state a purpose, role, or effect the characteristic serves in the person?*
Yes. It leads to exaltation and inheritance — "the meek … shall inherit the earth" (Mat 5:5); "humility comes before honor" (Pro 18:12; 22:4 "the reward for humility and fear of the Lord is riches and honor and life"); and it is salvific in its reception — "receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls" (Jam 1:21).

**T0.2.2** — *Does its role belong to created design, the fallen condition, both, or not determinable?*
The evidence presents it as a **restored and commanded good** — fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:23), a garment to "put on" (Col 3:12) — operating within the fallen condition (restoring the "caught in transgression", Gal 6:1; enduring "the unjust", 1Pe 2:18). Whether it belongs to unfallen created design is not directly stated; **labelled inferential** that a virtue this consistently enjoined and Spirit-given reflects created design marred and restored.

**T0.2.3** — *Is there orientation toward a future fullness?*
Yes — "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth" (Mat 5:5) orients present gentleness toward a future possession; "The Lord is at hand" frames present reasonableness (Php 4:5); and humility is the refuge sought against "the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:3).

**T0.3.1** — *What aspect of the divine likeness does it instantiate?*
The likeness of **strength exercised in restraint** — God's gentleness that makes the lowly great (Psa 18:35) and Christ's meekness that corrects without crushing (2Cor 10:1; 2Ti 2:25), reproduced in the person who restores gently (Gal 6:1) and corrects opponents with gentleness (2Ti 2:25).

**T0.3.2** — *Shared between God and the person, or an exclusively creaturely analogue?*
**Shared.** The same quality is named of God (Psa 18:35), of Christ (2Cor 10:1), and commanded of the person (Col 3:12; 1Ti 6:11) — a genuine common term, not merely an analogue.

**T0.3.3** — *What does its presence or absence indicate about the divine image in the person?*
The evidence pairs gentleness with the renewed self ("God's chosen ones, holy and beloved", Col 3:12; the Spirit's fruit, Gal 5:23) and its opposite with the unrenewed ("a man's heart is haughty", Pro 18:12; "violent … quarrelsome", 1Ti 3:3). **Labelled inferential**: presence tracks the renewed image, absence the haughty/contentious condition; the corpus shows the correlation without stating an image-doctrine.

**T0.4.1** — *Is the characteristic used typologically; if so which reality and in which direction?*
Yes, **christologically, divine-instance-establishing-the-pattern**. "Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey" (Mat 21:5) reads the meek king typologically; "the meekness and gentleness of Christ" (2Cor 10:1) makes Christ's gentleness the pattern the human instance points back to.

---

## T1 — Definition

**T1.1.1** — *What is it called, and what does the name signal?*
Gentleness (also meekness, humility, forbearance). The name signals a **settled mildness of temper — strength held in restraint** — governing how a person bears wrong and meets others, as the verses consistently show (gentle "to everyone", Php 4:5; "not violent but gentle", 1Ti 3:3).

**T1.1.2** — *What do the primary Hebrew and Greek terms show definitionally?*
The lexical glosses: praus / prautēs / praotēs — "gentle, meek, the positive moral quality of dealing with people in a kind way"; epieikēs / epieikeia — "gentle, considerate … with an implication of tolerance and graciousness"; anavah / anvah — "humility, gentleness, meekness"; anexikakos — "enduring, or patient under evils and injuries, not resentful". Together they show a quality defined by **its manner toward others and its bearing under injury**.

**T1.1.3** — *What directional / relational / constitutional implication does the name carry?*
Relational and **other-directed**: it is gentleness *toward* people ("toward all people", Tit 3:2; "to everyone", Php 4:5; "correcting his opponents", 2Ti 2:25). Constitutionally it is a borne quality, not an act (see T1.2.1).

**T1.2.1** — *What kind of inner-being phenomenon is it?*
A **disposition / borne quality**. Across the corpus the term is overwhelmingly a *status* or *quality* (29 of 30 occurrences) and only once an *action* — it is something one *is* and *has* ("a gentle and quiet spirit", 1Pe 3:4; "put on … meekness", Col 3:12), not chiefly something one does.

**T1.2.2** — *Is it simple or compound; if compound, which elements?*
**Compound at its edges.** Its core is restraint-toward-others, but the vocabulary folds in humility (anavah, "humility comes before honor", Pro 18:12), forbearance/non-resentment (anexikakos, "patiently enduring evil", 2Ti 2:24), and reasonableness/tolerance (epieikēs, "Let your reasonableness be known", Php 4:5). It combines mildness, lowliness, and forbearance.

**T1.3.1** — *What is its structural opposite?*
**Harshness / violence / contentiousness.** The verses name the opposite directly: "not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome" (1Ti 3:3); "not be quarrelsome but kind … patiently enduring evil" (2Ti 2:24); "avoid quarreling … be gentle" (Tit 3:2). Pride is its opposite on the humility axis — "a man's heart is haughty" set against "humility" (Pro 18:12).

**T1.3.2** — *What does it exclude or resist at its edge?*
It excludes quarrelsomeness, violence, evil-speaking, and self-assertion: "speak evil of no one, … avoid quarreling" (Tit 3:2); and it resists resentment under injury — "patiently enduring evil" (2Ti 2:24).

**T1.3.3** — *Where does it end and another thing begin — what is it not?*
It is **not weakness or timidity**: the gentle Paul is "bold toward you when I am away" (2Cor 10:1); the meek king is still the conquering king who rides "in your majesty … victoriously" (Psa 45:4). It ends where mildness becomes mere passivity; gentleness retains strength and acts (restores, corrects, defends).

**T1.4.1** — *In what mode(s) does it operate, including grammatical/stem form and manner?*
It operates as a **manner qualifying an action** — most often adverbially, "with/in gentleness": coming "in a spirit of gentleness" (1Cor 4:21), restoring "in a spirit of gentleness" (Gal 6:1), correcting "with gentleness" (2Ti 2:25), making a defense "with gentleness and respect" (1Pe 3:15). Grammatically the band is dominated by nouns and adjectives (a borne quality) rather than finite verbs.

**T1.4.2** — *Does the mode vary by context, direction, or level?*
Yes. Toward inferiors/the fallen it is restorative (Gal 6:1); toward opponents it is corrective (2Ti 2:25); toward all it is courteous (Tit 3:2; Php 4:5); under unjust masters it is submissive endurance (1Pe 2:18); before God it is humble seeking (Zep 2:3).

**T1.4.3** — *Does it operate through a communicative or speech-based mode?*
Yes, markedly. Gentleness governs **how one speaks**: the defense "with gentleness and respect" (1Pe 3:15), correcting opponents "with gentleness" (2Ti 2:25), "speak evil of no one … show perfect courtesy" (Tit 3:2), and the entreaty made "by the meekness … of Christ" (2Cor 10:1) and "in your kindness to hear us" (Act 24:4).

**T1.5.1** — *What first / most immediate inner-being response follows the characteristic?*
The corpus tags few immediate responses; where present they are paradoxical — **boldness** ("humble when face to face … but bold toward you when I am away", 2Cor 10:1) and the **lowly royal entry** ("humble, and mounted on a donkey", Mat 21:5). Gentleness does not produce timidity but a composed boldness.

**T1.5.2** — *Is that immediate response consistent or varied?*
Sparse and varied; the evidence is thin on an immediate response, since gentleness is presented as a standing quality rather than a triggering event. **Largely silent** beyond the two instances above.

**T1.6.1** — *What does it produce in the inner being over time?*
**Honour, inheritance, and preservation.** "Humility comes before honor" (Pro 18:12; Pro 22:4 honour, riches, and life); "the meek … shall inherit the earth" (Mat 5:5); and received with meekness, the word "is able to save your souls" (Jam 1:21).

**T1.6.3** — *How does the sustained effect differ from the immediate response?*
The immediate register (composed boldness, lowly bearing) is a present manner; the sustained effect is a standing reversal — the lowly are made great (Psa 18:35), the meek inherit (Mat 5:5), the humble are honoured (Pro 18:12). The manner is momentary; the outcome is exaltation over time.

**T1.7.1** — *Under what inner conditions does it take hold or operate rightly?*
Under **wisdom and the fear of the Lord**: "By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom" (Jam 3:13); "the wisdom from above is … gentle" (Jam 3:17); "the fear of the Lord is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honor" (Pro 15:33); and in the "spiritual" person (Gal 6:1).

**T1.7.2** — *Under what conditions is it blocked, distorted, or resisted (incl. another spirit)?*
By **haughtiness, quarrelsomeness, and violence**: "a man's heart is haughty" (Pro 18:12) blocks humility; the "drunkard … violent … quarrelsome" (1Ti 3:3) is its negation. **No adversarial or angelic spirit** is shown distorting it in the corpus — that branch is **Silent**.

**T1.7.3** — *What is the inner state of one in whom it is present but does not take hold?*
**Silent.** The corpus contrasts the gentle with the haughty/violent person but does not depict a person in whom gentleness is offered yet fails to take hold.

---

## T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries

**T2.1.1** — *At which constitutional level(s) is it located, and how is each engaged?*
**Heart:** "the hidden person of the heart … a gentle and quiet spirit" (1Pe 3:4); "a man's heart is haughty, but humility …" (Pro 18:12). **Soul:** received with meekness, the word is "able to save your souls" (Jam 1:21). **Inward person / the renewed self:** "Put on … meekness" (Col 3:12). It also engages the **mind** functionally (see T3.2).

**T2.1.2** — *What does the pattern of engaged and absent levels indicate?*
Gentleness seats in the **heart and soul** (the hidden, governing centre — 1Pe 3:4 "the hidden person of the heart") and is mind-governed (T3.2), but it **never engages perception, memory, or creativity** (T3.1/3.3/3.5 silent). The seat is deep (heart/soul) yet the faculty engaged is cognitive rather than affective — a settled, governed quality rather than a felt surge.

**T2.10.1** — *Does it move across levels, or onto the person from an external source?*
Yes — **from the Spirit onto the person**: gentleness is "fruit of the Spirit" (Gal 5:23), and God's gentleness is what "made me great" (Psa 18:35), implying a movement from God/Spirit to the inner person. No spirit→soul→body sequence is otherwise detailed.

**T2.7.1** — *Where a body link exists, in which direction does it run?*
The one clear body link runs **soul→body (expressive)**: the inner "gentle and quiet spirit" is set against outward "adorning" (1Pe 3:4), the hidden disposition expressed in conduct rather than ornament. Otherwise the body link is faint; largely **functional/expressive**, not emphatic.

**T2.9.1** — *Where does the evidence say it originates?*
**Bestowed by God / the Spirit:** "fruit of the Spirit … gentleness" (Gal 5:23); "your gentleness made me great" (Psa 18:35). Also **cultivated by the person** as something pursued and put on: "Pursue … gentleness" (1Ti 6:11); "Put on … meekness" (Col 3:12). Origin is thus both divine gift and human cultivation.

**T2.9.2** — *Is the origin single or multiple, and does it change with context?*
**Multiple** — divine bestowal (Gal 5:23) and human pursuit/donning (1Ti 6:11; Col 3:12) co-exist; the gift is received and then actively put on. No generational or adversarial origin appears.

---

## T3 — The Inner Faculties

**T3.1.1 / T3.1.2 / T3.1.3 · Perception** — **Silent.** No occurrence engages the inner senses or discernment as perception; gentleness is not presented as a mode of perceiving. The consistent non-engagement marks it as a temper, not a sense.

**T3.2.1 · Cognition (engage?)** — Yes. Gentleness is the only faculty-tagged dimension in this band, and it is tagged **cognition**, never affect. It is bound to wisdom and understanding: "Who is wise and understanding among you? … the meekness of wisdom" (Jam 3:13); "the wisdom from above is … gentle, open to reason" (Jam 3:17); "reasonableness" (epieikēs, Php 4:5).

**T3.2.2 · Cognition (effect)** — It renders thought **reasonable and teachable**: "open to reason" (Jam 3:17), "able to teach" (2Ti 2:24), and reasonableness "known to everyone" (Php 4:5). Gentleness disposes the mind to receive ("receive with meekness the implanted word", Jam 1:21).

**T3.2.3 · Cognition (pattern)** — The exclusive cognition-tagging across the band indicates gentleness is a **mind-governed restraint** — a deliberate, considered temper rather than a spontaneous feeling. This is its defining faculty signature.

**T3.3.1 / T3.3.2 / T3.3.3 · Memory** — **Silent.** No occurrence engages the holding or retrieving of inner-being reality across time; gentleness is not presented as a memorial faculty.

**T3.4.1 · Affect (engage?)** — **No / Silent.** Strikingly, **no** gentleness occurrence is tagged to the affective faculty. Unlike love, compassion, kindness, and comfort (all affect-led), gentleness does not present as a felt emotion.

**T3.4.2 · Affect (effect)** — **Silent** (no affective engagement to report).

**T3.4.3 · Affect (pattern)** — The complete absence of affect tagging across all 30 occurrences is itself a finding: gentleness is constitutionally a **governed quality of the will-and-mind**, distinguished from the cluster's affections precisely by not being a feeling.

**T3.5.1 / T3.5.2 / T3.5.3 · Creativity** — **Silent.** No engagement with imagination or the capacity to originate.

**T3.6.1 · Volition (engage?)** — Yes. Gentleness is **commanded and pursued**, which engages the will: "Pursue … gentleness" (1Ti 6:11); "Put on … meekness" (Col 3:12); "restore him in a spirit of gentleness" (Gal 6:1, a chosen manner).

**T3.6.2 · Volition (effect)** — It directs the will toward **restraint and restoration** rather than retaliation — choosing to correct gently (2Ti 2:25), to bear with others (Eph 4:2 "bearing with one another"), and to endure evil without resentment (2Ti 2:24).

**T3.6.3 · Volition (pattern)** — The heavy *commanded* load (the imperatives to pursue, put on, receive) shows gentleness as a **virtue of the will that is cultivated**, not a temperament merely possessed.

**T3.7.1 · Agency (engage?)** — Partially. Gentleness qualifies acts of agency — restoring (Gal 6:1), correcting (2Ti 2:25), making a defense (1Pe 3:15), showing courtesy (Tit 3:2) — it governs *how* the person acts.

**T3.7.2 · Agency (effect)** — It moderates the exercise of power: the one with authority comes "with love in a spirit of gentleness" rather than "with a rod" (1Cor 4:21); the strong "restore" the fallen gently (Gal 6:1).

**T3.7.3 · Agency (pattern)** — Where agency appears, gentleness is its **governor**, not its engine — it shapes the manner of action across contexts (correction, defense, rule).

**T3.8.1 · Moral evaluation (engage?)** — Yes. Gentleness is assessed against the standard of right: it is "the positive moral quality of dealing with people" (lexical), wholly righteous or commanded across the corpus, and "against such things there is no law" (Gal 5:23).

**T3.8.2 · Moral evaluation (effect)** — It is itself a measure of righteous conduct, paired with righteousness and goodness: "the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness" (Psa 45:4); "full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere" (Jam 3:17).

**T3.8.3 · Moral evaluation (pattern)** — The uniformly positive valence (zero sinful/forbidden across 30 occurrences) marks gentleness as a **stable moral good** in the corpus, never disordered — unlike love, whose valence flips on its object.

**T3.9.1 / T3.9.2 / T3.9.3 · Conscience** — **Silent.** No occurrence engages the conscience (the acute witness of sin, guilt, conviction); gentleness touches moral evaluation (T3.8) but not the convicting conscience in this corpus.

**T3.10.1 · Conscientiousness (engage?)** — Yes — gentleness integrates moral awareness, will, and action: the "spiritual" person *chooses* to *restore* the fallen *gently* (Gal 6:1), and the servant is "kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil" (2Ti 2:24) — awareness, volition, and conduct together.

**T3.10.2 · Conscientiousness (effect)** — It yields conduct that is consistent and dependable in manner — "show perfect courtesy toward all people" (Tit 3:2), "let your reasonableness be known to everyone" (Php 4:5).

**T3.10.3 · Conscientiousness (pattern)** — Gentleness reads as a **character-level integration** (a settled disposition expressed in steady conduct), consistent with its status/quality typing.

**T3.11.1 · Relational capacity (engage?)** — Strongly. Gentleness is constitutionally other-directed equipment for connection: restoring (Gal 6:1), bearing with one another (Eph 4:2), correcting opponents toward repentance (2Ti 2:25), courtesy "toward all people" (Tit 3:2).

**T3.11.2 · Relational capacity (effect)** — It **preserves and repairs** relationship — turning correction into a path to "repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth" (2Ti 2:25) and bearing "with one another in love" (Eph 4:2).

**T3.11.3 · Relational capacity (pattern)** — The dominant other-experiencer pattern (gentleness shown toward others, rarely toward self) indicates it is **fundamentally relational** — its whole operation is in the meeting of persons.

---

## T4 — Relational Interfaces

**T4.1.1 · God→human (engage?)** — Yes: "your gentleness made me great" (2Sa 22:36; Psa 18:35) — God's gentleness operates toward the person, exalting the lowly.

**T4.1.2 · God→human (basis)** — Presented as **responsive grace within covenant relationship** — bound to "the shield of your salvation" (Psa 18:35) and to the fear of the Lord that precedes honour (Pro 15:33). Not stated as strictly conditional or unconditional; **partly inferential**.

**T4.1.3 · God→human (what it shows of God)** — That God's disposition toward the person is **condescending and exalting** — his greatness expressed as gentleness that lifts the small (Psa 18:35), the pattern Christ embodies (2Cor 10:1).

**T4.2.1 · human→God (engage?)** — Yes: "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land … seek humility" (Zep 2:3); the humility joined to "the fear of the Lord" (Pro 15:33; 22:4) is the person's posture toward God.

**T4.2.2 · human→God (inner posture required)** — **Lowliness and submission** — seeking the Lord and doing "his just commands" in humility (Zep 2:3); a non-haughty heart (Pro 18:12).

**T4.2.3 · human→God (what it shows)** — That right relationship with God is entered **from below** — the humble are those hidden "on the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:3) and rewarded with "riches and honor and life" (Pro 22:4).

**T4.3.1 · human→human giving (engage?)** — Yes, dominantly: gentleness is extended person-to-person — restoring (Gal 6:1), correcting (2Ti 2:25), serving even harsh masters (1Pe 2:18), courtesy to all (Tit 3:2), defense to enquirers (1Pe 3:15).

**T4.3.2 · giver's inner conditions** — The giver is **"spiritual"** (Gal 6:1), **wise** ("the meekness of wisdom", Jam 3:13), and **self-watchful** ("Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted", Gal 6:1).

**T4.3.3 · what the giver must have received/become** — They must have **received the word with meekness** (Jam 1:21) and **put on** the renewed self ("as God's chosen ones … put on … meekness", Col 3:12) and the Spirit's fruit (Gal 5:23) before extending it.

**T4.4.1 · human→human receiving (engage?)** — Yes: "receive with meekness the implanted word" (Jam 1:21) shows gentleness as the posture of *uptake*; and being corrected "with gentleness" aims at the recipient's "repentance" (2Ti 2:25).

**T4.4.2 · conditions accompanying / blocking uptake** — Uptake is accompanied by meekness and aims at repentance (Jam 1:21; 2Ti 2:25); it is blocked by the haughty heart (Pro 18:12) and the quarrelsome temper (1Ti 3:3). 

**T4.4.3 · state of one who meets it but does not take it up** — **Silent** (not depicted; cf. T1.7.3).

**T4.5.1 · within bonds vs across distance** — It operates **across distance and difference**, not only within bonds: "gentle … toward all people" (Tit 3:2), reasonableness "known to everyone" (Php 4:5), and even toward "the unjust" master (1Pe 2:18) and "opponents" (2Ti 2:25).

**T4.5.2 · within covenant only, or crossing covenantal boundaries** — It **crosses boundaries** — extended "to everyone" / "all people" (Php 4:5; Tit 3:2) and to opponents (2Ti 2:25), not confined to the covenant community.

**T4.5.3 · relational scope (who included / excluded)** — **Universal in scope:** everyone, all people, the unjust, opponents. No class is excluded; gentleness is owed even where it is not reciprocated (1Pe 2:18).

**T4.6.1 / T4.6.2 / T4.6.3 · Spiritual beings interface** — **Silent.** No occurrence shows gentleness operating toward, attacked by, or mediated through angelic or adversarial beings.

---

## T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension

**T5.1.1 · Transformation (engage / which)** — Yes — it changes both **condition and orientation**: received with meekness, the word "is able to save your souls" (Jam 1:21, condition); restoring the transgressor "in a spirit of gentleness" reorients the fallen toward repentance (Gal 6:1; 2Ti 2:25, orientation).

**T5.1.2 · reversible or irreversible** — **Silent** on reversibility as such; the salvific reception (Jam 1:21) implies a decisive change but the corpus does not address reversibility directly.

**T5.2.1 · Sequence of inner states** — A sequence appears in correction: gentle correction → "God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth" (2Ti 2:25) — gentleness (before) producing repentance and knowledge (after). Otherwise sequences are sparse.

**T5.3.1 · Mechanism of change** — By **gradual formation and reception** rather than sudden event: "Pursue … gentleness" (1Ti 6:11), "Put on … meekness" (Col 3:12), "receive with meekness the implanted word" (Jam 1:21) — cultivation and uptake.

**T5.3.2 · mechanism differ across contexts** — Yes: in the person it forms by pursuit/donning (1Ti 6:11; Col 3:12); toward others it works by gentle correction that may yield repentance (2Ti 2:25); under injustice it works by patient endurance (1Pe 2:18; 2Ti 2:24).

**T5.4.1 · Suffering / affliction (relation)** — Yes, as a **response to and context for** affliction: servants "subject to … masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust" (1Pe 2:18); the Lord's servant "patiently enduring evil" (anexikakos, 2Ti 2:24).

**T5.4.2 · what suffering does to the characteristic** — Suffering is the **arena that proves** gentleness — it is borne under the unjust master and under evil without resentment (1Pe 2:18; 2Ti 2:24); the evidence shows it *enduring* rather than being diminished.

**T5.5.1 · Formation and sanctification** — Yes, centrally: gentleness is **fruit of the Spirit** (Gal 5:23), a garment of "God's chosen ones" to "put on" (Col 3:12), and an object of pursuit alongside the virtues of the sanctified life (1Ti 6:11) — it participates in the long arc of character formation.

**T5.6.1 · Eschatological trajectory** — Yes: "the meek … shall inherit the earth" (Mat 5:5) anticipates a future possession; "The Lord is at hand" frames present reasonableness (Php 4:5); and humility is the present refuge against "the day of the anger of the Lord" (Zep 2:3). Present gentleness anticipates future inheritance and vindication.

---

## T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics

**T6.1.1 · Co-occurrence (which / how often)** — In the verse evidence gentleness co-occurs most with **humility** (tapeinos / tapeinofrosunē — Col 3:12; Eph 4:2), **patience** (makrothumia — Col 3:12; Eph 4:2; with anexikakos 2Ti 2:24), **wisdom** (sofia — Jam 3:13, 3:17), **righteousness** (Psa 45:4; 1Ti 6:11), **the fear of the Lord** (Pro 15:33; 22:4), **love** (Eph 4:2; 1Cor 4:21), and **comfort/encouragement** (parakaleō — entreaty, 2Cor 10:1; Act 24:4), with **glory/honour** and **goodness** also adjacent.

**T6.1.2 · what co-occurrence shows** — Gentleness sits in a **cluster of restraint-and-relationship virtues** (humility, patience, forbearance) and is **generated by wisdom and the fear of the Lord** — its company places it among the dispositions that govern conduct toward others under God.

**T6.2.1 · Sequential relationship** — Yes: **the fear of the Lord / wisdom precedes gentleness-humility** — "the fear of the Lord is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honor" (Pro 15:33); "the wisdom from above is … gentle" (Jam 3:17). Gentleness in turn precedes honour and inheritance (Pro 18:12; Mat 5:5).

**T6.2.2 · what the sequence shows** — The relationship reads as **causal/constitutive in two directions**: wisdom and the fear of the Lord *produce* gentleness; gentleness *leads to* honour and inheritance — a developmental chain.

**T6.3.1 · does it produce another?** — Yes — gentleness in correction *produces* repentance and knowledge in another: "correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth" (2Ti 2:25).

**T6.3.2 · is it produced by another?** — Yes — by **wisdom** ("the meekness of wisdom", Jam 3:13; wisdom "is … gentle", Jam 3:17) and by the **Spirit** (Gal 5:23).

**T6.3.3 · constituent of / constituted by another?** — Gentleness is a **constituent of wisdom-from-above** ("the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle …", Jam 3:17) and a **constituent of the Spirit's single fruit** (Gal 5:22–23); humility (anavah) is in turn a near-constituent of gentleness in the Hebrew terms.

**T6.4.1 · shared vocabulary** — The Hebrew **anavah / anvah** is glossed both "humility" and "gentleness", sharing vocabulary with the **humility** characteristic (M09 territory). The Greek gentleness terms are distinct to this band.

**T6.4.2 · shared root architecture** — Within the band three roots generate the field: praus/prautēs/praotēs (one root), epieikēs/epieikeia (one root), anavah/anvah (one root). The anavah root reaches **across into humility**; the praus root does not.

**T6.4.3 · what the sharing shows** — The anavah overlap shows gentleness and **humility** are conceptually fused in Hebrew (one term, two glosses) and only differentiated in the Greek, where praotēs (manner toward others) separates from tapeinofrosunē (lowliness of self). **Labelled inferential** as a development across the Testaments.

**T6.5.1 · nearest neighbour and the distinction** — The nearest neighbour is **humility**. The distinction: humility is the person's posture **before God and concerning self** (lowliness — "humility comes before honor", Pro 18:12), whereas gentleness is the manner **toward others** (restraint in dealing — "gentle … toward all people", Tit 3:2). Patience/forbearance is the second neighbour (endurance over time).

**T6.5.2 · precise boundary at apparent overlap** — Where they overlap (anavah carries both), the boundary is **direction**: the same disposition seen *toward God / self* is humility; seen *toward others* is gentleness. Eph 4:2 and Col 3:12 list them together precisely because they are adjacent but distinct.

**T6.5.3 · distinction of degree, kind, direction, or level?** — Primarily **of direction** (toward self/God vs toward others), secondarily of **kind** vis-à-vis patience (manner vs endurance).

---

## T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation

**T7.1.1 · primary terms and root meanings** — Greek **praus / prautēs / praotēs** (the moral quality of dealing kindly with people), **epieikēs / epieikeia** (gentle, considerate, tolerant, gracious), **anexikakos** (patient under evil, not resentful); Hebrew **anavah / anvah** (humility, gentleness, meekness). The roots converge on **mildness-with-strength and lowliness**.

**T7.1.2 · grammatical range** — Nouns (prautēs, epieikeia, anavah), adjectives (praus, epieikēs, anexikakos), with adverbial use ("in/with gentleness"). The dominance of **nouns and adjectives** over finite verbs shows the characteristic operates as a **borne quality**, not chiefly an act.

**T7.1.3 · semantic range** — From "meek / humble" (Mat 5:5; Mat 21:5) through "gentle / considerate" (1Ti 3:3; Tit 3:2) to "reasonable / tolerant" (Php 4:5; Jam 3:17 "open to reason") and "courteous" (Tit 3:2) and "patient under evil / not resentful" (2Ti 2:24). A breadth running lowliness → mildness → reasonableness → forbearance.

**T7.1.4 · terms distinguishing aspects (disposition vs act, etc.)** — Yes: the band is almost entirely **disposition/quality** terms (praus, prautēs, epieikēs as borne traits) with the lone forbearance term anexikakos naming endurance *under* injury. It does **not** carry a distinct "received vs given" pair.

**T7.1.5 · term for the structural opposite / absence** — Not a single antonym term, but the opposite is named lexically in context — "violent … quarrelsome" (1Ti 3:3), "quarrelsome" (2Ti 2:24) — and on the humility axis, "haughty" (Pro 18:12). **No dedicated antonym lexeme** in the band.

**T7.1.6 · person-type term** — Yes — **praus** functions substantivally for the person who has it: "Blessed are the **meek**" (Mat 5:5); "the **humble** of the land" (anavah, Zep 2:3).

**T7.1.7 · supplication / seeking term** — **None** specific to gentleness; though humility is the posture of seeking the Lord ("seek … humility", Zep 2:3), there is no term for *seeking gentleness from another*. **Silent.**

**T7.1.8 · OT↔NT continuity / development** — The OT term **anavah** centres on **humility (lowliness before God)** in wisdom and psalm contexts (Pro 15:33; Zep 2:3; Psa 45:4), while the NT **praotēs / epieikēs** centre on **gentleness toward people** in epistolary ethics (Gal 5:23; Tit 3:2). One field; the centre of gravity moves from posture-before-God to manner-toward-others. **Labelled inferential.**

**T7.1.9 · NT-coined term** — **None evidenced** in the band; no coinage is signalled. **Silent.**

**T7.1.10 · full vocabulary arc** — The complete arc spans **lowliness (anavah/humility) → meekness (praus) → gentleness/consideration (epieikēs) → reasonableness/tolerance (Php 4:5; Jam 3:17) → forbearance under injury (anexikakos)** — a single disposition of strength-in-restraint viewed from self-before-God to manner-toward-others to bearing-under-wrong.

**T7.2.1 · function of the primary term in its primary verse** — In **Mat 5:5** ("Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth") praus is the **subject-class** of a beatitude — the meek are the ones pronounced blessed and promised inheritance; the term carries the whole weight of the blessing.

**T7.2.2 · literary forms and what they require** — The evidence spans **beatitude** (Mat 5:5), **wisdom proverb** (Pro 15:33; 18:12; 22:4), **psalm** (Psa 18:35; 45:4), **prophetic summons** (Zep 2:3), and **epistolary paraenesis** (Gal 5:23; Col 3:12; Tit 3:2; 1Pe). Responsible reading requires honouring each form — proverb as general pattern, beatitude as eschatological pronouncement, paraenesis as community command.

**T7.2.3 · logical structure of key arguments** — E.g. Jam 3:13–17: premise — true wisdom shows itself in conduct; conclusion — therefore "show his works in the meekness of wisdom", because "the wisdom from above is … gentle". And Pro 18:12: premise — pride precedes destruction; conclusion — humility precedes honour. Gentleness is consistently the **middle term between a right inner condition and an outcome of honour/inheritance**.

**T7.2.4 · contextual setting** — **Covenantal-ethical and communal** — virtue lists for the renewed community (Col 3:12; Eph 4:2; Gal 5:23), conduct toward outsiders (Tit 3:2; 1Pe 3:15), and **eschatological** framing (Mat 5:5; Zep 2:3). The setting shows gentleness as ordered community life under God and toward the world.

**T7.2.5 · primary anchor verse** — **2Cor 10:1** — "by the meekness and gentleness of Christ" — most fully and directly expresses the characteristic's essential character, grounding it in Christ and holding together its paradox (humble yet bold). **Mat 5:5** is the eschatological anchor.

**T7.2.6 · what the anchor shows that no other verse shows** — 2Cor 10:1 alone **grounds gentleness in Christ as its source-pattern** and displays its paradox in one breath — "the meekness and gentleness of Christ — I who am humble when face to face … but bold toward you when I am away" — showing gentleness is not weakness but governed strength.

**T7.3.1 · most useful human-science framework** — **Behavioural science / positive psychology and trait theory**: gentleness maps onto the Big Five **agreeableness** dimension (low aggressiveness combined with warmth and consideration) and is treated as a settled, self-regulated character trait.

**T7.3.2 · where the framework illuminates** — Trait psychology illuminates the band's data that gentleness is a **stable disposition rather than a situational response** — "a settled, self-regulated quality … not merely the absence of aggression but the presence of controlled, other-directed care" — matching the corpus's status/quality typing and its mind-governed (cognition) signature.

**T7.3.3 · where evidence and framework diverge** — The science treats gentleness as a temperament/trait shaped by heredity and parenting; the corpus presents it as **fruit of the Spirit** (Gal 5:23) and **patterned on Christ** (2Cor 10:1), commanded and "put on" — a grounding (divine gift, christological pattern, eschatological reward in Mat 5:5) the trait account cannot generate.

**T7.3.4 · aspect surfaced by the framework calling for further verse work** — The agreeableness/self-regulation literature frames gentleness as **emotion regulation**; yet the corpus tags gentleness to **cognition, never affect**, raising the question whether biblical gentleness is better read as a *governed-mind* virtue than an *emotion-regulation* one. **Flagged for further verse investigation**, especially a faculty read on the Hebrew anavah terms (untagged here).

---

## Coverage summary

- **Answered substantively:** T0 (all), T1 (all bar T1.7.3 silent), T2 (all), T3 cognition/affect/volition/agency/moral-evaluation/conscientiousness/relational (substantive), T4.1–T4.5 (substantive), T5 (all), T6 (all), T7 (all bar T7.1.7, T7.1.9 silent).
- **Silent (evidence does not speak):** T1.5.2 (partial), T1.7.2 (adversarial branch), T1.7.3, T3.1 perception, T3.3 memory, T3.4 affect (a *significant* silence — see T3.4.3), T3.5 creativity, T3.9 conscience, T4.4.3, T4.6 spiritual beings, T5.1.2, T7.1.7, T7.1.9.
- **Most significant silence:** the total absence of **affect** tagging (T3.4) — gentleness is the cluster's one characteristic that is *not* a feeling but a mind-governed, borne quality.

## §1 — Definition & scope of the characteristic

Gentleness is the cluster's **restraint** disposition: a settled mildness of temper — strength held deliberately in check — that governs *how* a person bears wrong, exercises authority, and meets others. Where bands A–D are affections that reach *toward* another (love, pity, kindness, comfort), E governs the **manner and limits** of that reach: power withheld, provocation absorbed, correction softened.

The band gathers two language streams. Hebrew **anavah / anvah** (H6038 / H6037) — rendered "gentleness, meekness, humility" — carries the posture of lowliness, frequently paired with the fear of the Lord and set before honour. Greek **praus / prautēs / praotēs** (G4239 / G4240 / G4236) — "meek, gentleness" — and **epieikēs / epieikeia** (G1933 / G1932) — "gentle, reasonable, forbearing, yielding" — carry the relational manner enjoined in New-Testament instruction. **anexikakos** (G0420, "enduring evil, not resentful") sits at the forbearance edge of the band.

## §5 — Observation (grounded in the 30 occurrences above)

- **Faculty is mind-governed, never affective.** Where a faculty is tagged (11/30, all on the Greek *praus* / *epieikēs* terms) it is uniformly **cognition** — no occurrence in the band is tagged *affect*. This sets E apart from the affect-dominated A–D bands: gentleness reads as a measured, deliberate restraint, not a felt affection.
- **It is a borne quality, not an act.** Type is *status* (20) and *quality* (9), with only one *action*. The characteristic is a disposition one *has*, not a thing one *does*.
- **Wholly positive, and heavily enjoined.** Valence is *righteous* (18) + *commanded* (11) + one *neutral*, with **zero** sinful or forbidden. Eleven of thirty are *commanded* — the New-Testament paraenesis enjoins it directly (Gal 6:1; Eph 4:2; Col 3:12; 1Ti 6:11; Tit 3:2; Jam 1:21; 1Pe 3:15).
- **It is shown toward others.** Where experiencer is tagged, *other* (8) + *other-addressed* (3) outweigh *self* (2). The evidence ties it to specific relational functions: restoring the fallen "in a spirit of gentleness" (Gal 6:1), correcting opponents "with gentleness" toward "repentance" (2Ti 2:25), the "gentle and quiet spirit" of 1Pe 3:4.
- **When seated, it sits in heart/soul.** Location is rare (4/30) but consistent with the inner being: heart (Pro 18:12; 1Pe 3:4 "the hidden person of the heart"), inward-parts (Col 3:12 "put on"), soul (Jam 1:21 "save your souls").
- **It is a divine attribute and a Christ-pattern.** Divine involvement appears as *possessor* — "your gentleness made me great" (2Sa 22:36 / Psa 18:35) — and as *object* — "the meekness and gentleness of Christ" (2Cor 10:1); the Lord's servant correcting "with gentleness" (2Ti 2:25).
- **Distribution.** The Hebrew *anavah* stream concentrates in OT wisdom and Psalms, where its sense leans **humility** (Pro 15:33; 18:12; 22:4 "humility comes before honour"; Zep 2:3 "seek humility"). The Greek stream concentrates in NT epistles as a **commanded virtue**, including the fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:23) and the Beatitude "the meek shall inherit" (Mat 5:5). Contextual sense spreads across gentleness / meekness / gentle / humility, with *epieikēs* also surfacing as "reasonableness" (Php 4:5) and "courtesy" (Tit 3:2), and *anexikakos* as "enduring evil" (2Ti 2:24).

## §6 — Interpretation (labelled; inferential where marked)

- **E is the governor of the cluster's affections.** A–D supply the outward movement of love; E supplies its temper — the withheld rod (1Cor 4:21), the borne wrong (2Ti 2:24), the softened correction (Gal 6:1; 2Ti 2:25). Read with the cognition-faculty tag, this is a deliberate, mind-governed control of strength rather than a spontaneous feeling.
- **A possible OT→NT centre-of-gravity shift — INFERENTIAL (GR-PROG-009).** The Hebrew *anavah* leans *humility* (lowliness before God and before honour); the Greek *praotēs / epieikēs* leans *gentleness toward people* (manner in relationship and correction). The field is one; its gravitational centre appears to move from posture-before-God to manner-toward-others. Labelled inferential pending a dedicated cross-testament read; not upgraded here.
- **An enjoined, imitable virtue.** The heavy *commanded* load plus the explicit Christ-pattern (2Cor 10:1) frames gentleness as something put on and learned, not a temperament one is simply born with.

## §7 — Reflection (cultural reach and tentative application — not prescriptive)

- **"Meekness" is culturally mis-heard as weakness.** The evidence reads against that: gentleness is God's own attribute that "made me great" (Psa 18:35), the manner in which authority is exercised (1Cor 4:21; 1Ti 3:3), and a strength under restraint. Any reader-facing output should expect and address this misreading.
- **Translation fragments the field.** The same *praus* is "meek" (Mat 5:5) and "gentle" (1Pe 3:4); *epieikēs* is "reasonable" (Php 4:5) and "courteous" (Tit 3:2). A reader who meets only one English word sees only part of the characteristic — relevant for cross-cultural and multi-translation audiences.
- **Situated, not generalised, application.** The verses attach gentleness to concrete functions — restoring the fallen, correcting opponents, marital conduct (1Pe 3:4), eldership qualification (1Ti 3:3). I record these situated uses without generalising them into a universal prescription; application is noted, not concluded.

## §8 — Boundary & data-quality notes

- **anexikakos** ("not resentful / enduring evil", 2Ti 2:24) is kept *inside* E as positive forbearance, not placed in the antonym/boundary set — it names a virtue, not its negation.
- **Faculty evidence is Greek-side only.** All 11 faculty tags fall on the Greek terms (all *cognition*); the Hebrew *anavah / anvah* carry no faculty in the extract. The "mind-governed" reading therefore rests on Greek-side evidence — **additional discovery flagged:** a faculty read on the Hebrew terms would confirm or qualify it.
- **Reference variant.** "Phili 4:5" (epieikēs, "reasonableness") = **Philippians 4:5**; the extract uses a "Phili" book-code variant against the Session-A spec's "Php". Noted, not corrected (outside this task).
- **Band membership** for E is a working judgement (fresh distillation, not yet researcher-locked); no term in E was a genuine close call except *anexikakos* (resolved above).
